1007265304937350|d4c3.headline: Develop with 5...Nf6; grabbing 5...dxc3 opens lines to your king
1007265304937350|d4c3.why: 5...dxc3 grabs a second pawn but opens lines for White's queen: 6.Bxf7+ Kxf7 7.Qd5+ forks the king and the bishop on c5, and after 7...Kf8 8.Qxc5+ Black's king has lost the right to castle. 5...Nf6 develops and counterattacks the pawn on e4 instead. After 6.e5 d5 Black hits the bishop on c4, and the knight lands on e4 after 7.Bb5 Ne4.
1007265304937350|d4c3.principle: Take gambit pawns only if you can consolidate: with f7 exposed and the bishop on c5 loose, develop with a counter-threat instead.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. d4

1012847495954800|d7d6.headline: Hit the queen with 3...Nf6 and develop with tempo.
1012847495954800|d7d6.why: 3...d6 is too slow: White plays 4.Bc4, threatening mate on f7, and Black has to spend the next moves defending. 3.Nf3 did nothing for the queen on h5, so 3...Nf6 develops while attacking both the queen and the pawn on e4, and White must move the queen again with 4.Qh4.
1012847495954800|d7d6.principle: When the opponent's queen comes out early, develop the piece that attacks it, so each of your developing moves costs them a queen move.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qh5/2...Nc6

1012847495954800|g7g6.headline: Kick the queen with a developing move: 3...Nf6
1012847495954800|g7g6.why: 3...g6 chases the queen with a pawn move that develops nothing and weakens the kingside, and after 4.Qg5 White simply offers a queen trade, so the error 3.Nf3 goes unpunished. 3...Nf6 develops a knight while attacking both the queen on h5 and the pawn on e4, so White must move the queen again. After 4.Qh4 Black is ahead in development and free to play in the centre.
1012847495954800|g7g6.principle: Against an early queen, attack it with a piece that develops, not with a pawn move that only weakens your position.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qh5/2...Nc6

1017365272404305|b1c3.headline: Take the free pawn with 3.Nxe5: e5 has no defender
1017365272404305|b1c3.why: 2...Bc5 left e5 attacked once and not defended at all, and 3.Nc3 gives Black time to fix that: in the engine line 3...d6 holds the pawn and the game is level. 3.Nxe5 just takes it. The theory calls this Busch-Gass gambit unsound; Black can transpose to a Stafford gambit with 3...Nc6 4.Nxc6 dxc6, but stays a pawn down.
1017365272404305|b1c3.principle: Check what is loose after every opponent move: an undefended centre pawn is worth taking when the replies are under control.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Bc5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Bc5/3. Nxe5

1017365272404305|d2d3.headline: Take the free e5 pawn
1017365272404305|d2d3.why: 2...Bc5 left e5 attacked once and not defended at all, and 3.d3 fails to capitalise: Black gets time to defend it with 3...d6. 3.Nxe5 simply takes the pawn; the gambit is considered unsound, and if Black hits back with 3...Qh4, either 4.Qe2 or the sharper 4.d4 deals with the threat to f2.
1017365272404305|d2d3.principle: Before a quiet move, check what the opponent left undefended: a central pawn is worth taking when the piece that takes it is safe.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Bc5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Bc5/3. Nxe5

1017365272404305|d2d4.headline: Take the free pawn with 3.Nxe5; 3.d4 lets Black swap it
1017365272404305|d2d4.why: 2...Bc5 leaves the e5 pawn with no defender. 3.d4 lets Black trade it off with 3...exd4, and after 4.Bc4 d6 5.Nxd4 material is level and so is the game. 3.Nxe5 takes it: the theory calls this gambit unsound, because if 3...Qh4, threatening mate on f2 and hitting the knight, 4.Qe2 meets both threats. In the engine line 3...Nc6 4.Nxc6 dxc6 turns it into a Stafford gambit and you stay a pawn up with a clear advantage.
1017365272404305|d2d4.principle: Start with captures, then check your opponent's forcing replies: here the e5 pawn is free, and the only scary answer, ...Qh4, is met by Qe2.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Bc5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Bc5/3. Nxe5

1017365272404305|f1c4.headline: Take the free e5 pawn: the Busch-Gass gambit is unsound
1017365272404305|f1c4.why: 2...Bc5 leaves the e5 pawn with no defender, which hands White a clear advantage. 3.Bc4 throws that away by giving Black time for 3...Nc6 or 3...d6, and the game is level again. Take it with 3.Nxe5: Black's idea is 3...Qh4, hitting f2 and the knight, but 4.Qe2 meets both threats, and theory rates the gambit unsound as long as you stay calm.
1017365272404305|f1c4.principle: Accept a gambit pawn when you can meet the threats behind it; declining for safety gives back the advantage the gambit handed you.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Bc5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Bc5/3. Nxe5

105834763665320|d4d3.headline: Develop and guard the pawn instead of pushing it
105834763665320|d4d3.why: 3...d3 gives the pawn back for nothing: after 4.Qxd3 White's queen is developed and Black has spent another move on a pawn. 3...Bc5 develops the bishop to a square where it guards d4, and if White recaptures with 4.Nxd4, Black gets normal Scotch play, here hitting e4 with 4...Nf6.
105834763665320|d4d3.principle: When you can keep material by developing, develop; a pawn push that hands the pawn back develops your opponent's queen instead.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. Nf3

105834763665320|f7f5.headline: Develop with 3...Bc5; 3...f5 drops d4 and weakens your king
105834763665320|f7f5.why: 3...f5 does nothing for the pawn on d4: 4.Nxd4 wins it back with the knight centralised, and the pawn move has weakened Black's king while developing nothing. 3...Bc5 develops the bishop toward the centre with an eye on d4. After 4.Nxd4 Nf6 Black attacks e4 and is ahead in development, and 4...Nc6 would transpose to the Classical Scotch.
105834763665320|f7f5.principle: When pawns are traded in the centre, develop a piece toward the contested square instead of making a pawn move away from it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. Nf3

1062777786489002|c1b2.headline: Kick the f6 queen with 8.e5, then take back on d4
1062777786489002|c1b2.why: 8.Bb2 lets Black push 8...d3, so you can no longer take on d4 and your own c3 pawn blocks the bishop. After 9.e5 Qh6 10.Nbd2 Nge7 11.Ne4 d5 Black has developed and is still two pawns up. 8.e5 hits the queen, and taking the pawn fails because Re1 would pin the queen on the e-file. After 8...Qd8 9.Re1 Be7 10.cxd4 you have won a pawn back and have a big centre while Black's pieces sit at home.
1062777786489002|c1b2.principle: Gain time by attacking a queen that came out early: 8.e5 drives it back, and 10.cxd4 then rebuilds your centre safely.
sources: Mihail Marin, Beating the Open Games, ch. 7 (Quality Chess preview) | https://www.sjakkbutikken.no/media/productimages/preview-beating-the-open-games.pdf
Evans Gambit (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evans_Gambit

ideas.title: Moves that gain time
ideas.text: 8.e5 kicks the f6 queen with a pawn. Taking on e5 fails: once Black's knight and queen capture there, Re1 pins the queen to the king.

ideas.title: Watch the long diagonal
ideas.text: The f6 queen eyes your a1 rook through d4. Opening that diagonal now lets 8...Nxd4 and 10...Qxa1 win the rook.

ideas.title: Rebuild the centre with cxd4
ideas.text: Your pawns paid for c3 and d4. Here drive the queen off f6 first, then take back with 10.cxd4 to rebuild the centre.

ideas.title: Quiet moves cost the centre
ideas.text: Quiet bishop moves let Black keep the d4 pawn: after 8...d3 you can't take on d4, and your c3 pawn blocks the b2 bishop.

habit.why: 8.Bb2 lets Black push 8...d3, so you can no longer take on d4 and your own c3 pawn blocks the bishop. After 9.e5 Qh6 10.Nbd2 Nge7 11.Ne4 d5 Black has developed and is still two pawns up.

strays.text: Black pushes past with 8...d3 and keeps the extra pawns.

taught.why: 8.e5 hits the queen, and taking the pawn fails because Re1 would pin the queen on the e-file. After 8...Qd8 9.Re1 Be7 10.cxd4 you have won a pawn back and have a big centre while Black's pieces sit at home.

enforces.text: The pawn kicks the queen; your rook and 10.cxd4 follow with tempo.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 8.Bg5 hits the queen, but 8...Qg6 steps away and eyes your e4 pawn. Black develops with 9...Nge7, castles, and is still a pawn up after 11.cxd4.
alternatives.after: 8.e5 kicks the queen with a pawn and keeps your bishop. After 8...Qd8 the queen is back home, and 10.cxd4 builds a big centre.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 8.cxd4 opens the long diagonal for the f6 queen: after 8...Nxd4 9.Nbd2 Nxf3+ 10.Nxf3 Qxa1 Black wins your a1 rook.
alternatives.after: 8.e5 first chases the queen off the long diagonal. Only then is 10.cxd4 safe, and your pawns stand on d4 and e5.

1086376395792345|d8f6.headline: Don't copy 2.Qf3; develop the knight with 2...Nf6
1086376395792345|d8f6.why: 2...Qf6 copies White's mistake: it brings the queen out with four minor pieces at home and takes f6 from Black's own knight, which is exactly what is wrong with 2.Qf3. White just develops with 3.Nc3 and 4.Bc4 and gains time. 2...Nf6 puts the knight on its best square and blocks the queen on f3 from f7.
1086376395792345|d8f6.principle: Answer an early queen by developing, not by bringing out your own; a knight on f6 shuts the queen out of f7.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qf3

1086376395792345|f7f6.headline: Against 2.Qf3, develop 2...Nf6 instead of pushing the f-pawn
1086376395792345|f7f6.why: 2...f6 develops nothing, takes the best square from Black's king's knight and weakens the diagonal toward Black's king that White's bishop uses after 3.Bc4. 2...Nf6 develops the knight to its natural square and blocks the queen on f3 from f7, so Black can develop freely while White's queen sits in the knight's way.
1086376395792345|f7f6.principle: Answer an early queen with a developing move; a pawn move that weakens your king gives the queen and bishop the target they want.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qf3

1086376395792345|g8h6.headline: Answer the early queen with normal development
1086376395792345|g8h6.why: 2...Nh6 puts the knight on the rim, where it plays no part in the centre, and White develops calmly with 3.Bc4 and 4.Ne2. 2...Nf6 develops toward the centre and blocks the queen's line to f7; after 3.Bc4 Black can gain space with 3...c6 and ...d5, and the early queen becomes a target.
1086376395792345|g8h6.principle: An early queen on f3 blocks White's own knight and can be attacked; develop normally and gain time against it with pawn moves.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qf3

1095756382312296|d1e2.headline: 8.Nb5: the knight and f4 bishop hit d6 and c7
1095756382312296|d1e2.why: 8.Qe2 develops but threatens nothing, so 8...a6 takes b5 from your knight at once. After 9.a4 d6 10.Rd1 e5 Black has covered d6 and keeps the extra pawn. 8.Nb5 threatens a knight check on d6 and a fork on c7, both backed by the bishop on f4. After 8...Qa5+ 9.Kf1 Kf8 10.Bc7 b6 11.Bd6+ Nge7 Black has lost the right to castle and your bishop owns d6.
1095756382312296|d1e2.principle: When your opponent leaves a hole, hit it at once: ...e6 without ...d6 left d6 open to your knight and f4 bishop, so 8.Nb5 strikes before ...a6.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3/4...Nc6/5. Nf3/5...g6

ideas.title: Knight jump to d6
ideas.text: Black played ...e6 without ...d6, so no pawn guards d6. Your f4 bishop backs up a knight check on d6 and a fork on c7.

ideas.title: ...a6 shuts the door
ideas.text: Black's answer is ...a6, taking b5 from your knight. Give Black one quiet move, and 8...a6 makes d6 safe.

ideas.title: Morra setup on autopilot
ideas.text: Queen to e2 and rook to d1 is the standard Morra setup, but against ...g6 with ...e6 a concrete hit beats finishing it.

ideas.title: Gambit pawn buys time
ideas.text: You are a pawn down for quick development and open lines. Spend that time on threats, or Black catches up and keeps the pawn.

habit.why: 8.Qe2 develops but threatens nothing, so 8...a6 takes b5 from your knight at once. After 9.a4 d6 10.Rd1 e5 Black has covered d6 and keeps the extra pawn.

strays.text: It gives Black time for 8...a6 and 9...d6, closing the hole.

taught.why: 8.Nb5 threatens a knight check on d6 and a fork on c7, both backed by the bishop on f4. After 8...Qa5+ 9.Kf1 Kf8 10.Bc7 b6 11.Bd6+ Nge7 Black has lost the right to castle and your bishop owns d6.

enforces.text: With the f4 bishop behind it, the knight hits d6 and c7 at once.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: Castling is natural, but 8...a6 takes b5 from your knight. After 9.Bb3 Nge7 10.e5 b5 Black castles next and stays a pawn up.
alternatives.after: 8.Nb5 strikes before ...a6. Your king can wait in the centre, since Black's only check, 8...Qa5+ 9.Kf1, doesn't help Black.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 8.Bd6 puts the bishop in the hole, but it threatens nothing. After 8...a6 9.a4 b6 10.O-O Nge7 Black castles and keeps the pawn.
alternatives.after: 8.Nb5 sends the knight, which checks on d6 and forks on c7, and keeps the f4 bishop behind it. Black's king gets stuck in the centre.

1095756382312296|e1h1.headline: Don't castle yet: 8.Nb5 hits d6 and c7 first
1095756382312296|e1h1.why: Castling is natural, but it gives Black the move 8...a6, which takes b5 from your knight. After 9.Bb3 Nge7 10.e5 b5 11.Ne4 O-O Black has castled and stays a pawn up. 8.Nb5 threatens a knight check on d6 and a fork on c7, both backed by the bishop on f4. After 8...Qa5+ 9.Kf1 Kf8 10.Bc7 b6 11.Bd6+ Nge7 Black has lost the right to castle and your bishop owns d6.
1095756382312296|e1h1.principle: When your opponent leaves a hole, hit it at once: ...e6 without ...d6 left d6 open to your knight and f4 bishop, so 8.Nb5 strikes before ...a6.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3/4...Nc6/5. Nf3/5...g6

1102494195291015|f3g5.headline: Recapture on c3 with a knight, not a lone f7 raid
1102494195291015|f3g5.why: 8.Ng5 moves the knight a second time with two minor pieces still at home, and 8...Ne5 covers f7 while hitting your bishop. After 9.Nxf7 Nxf7 10.Bxf7+ Kxf7 you have given a knight for a pawn on top of the gambit pawns. 8.Nxc3 wins a pawn back and develops a piece, with the knight heading for b5 against the d6 bishop and c7. After 8...Kf8 9.Nb5 Bc5 10.Qd5 Qe7 11.Nxc7 you win material and Black's king can no longer castle.
1102494195291015|f3g5.principle: In a gambit, win material back with developing moves; a lone raid lets the defender cover and hit back.

ideas.title: Development is your compensation
ideas.text: You are three pawns down for time and open lines. 8.Nxc3 wins one back while bringing out a sleeping piece.

ideas.title: Ng5 needs a real target
ideas.text: 8.Ng5 moves the same knight again, and 8...Ne5 covers f7 while hitting your bishop, so the f7 raid only loses a piece.

ideas.title: The d6 bishop blocks Black's d-pawn
ideas.text: 5...Bd6 blocks the d7 pawn, so Black's c8 bishop and queenside are slow, and the d6 bishop and c7 are targets.

ideas.title: Kick the d6 bishop with e5
ideas.text: 8.e5 hits the d6 bishop with tempo, and after 8...Bb4 9.Qb3 your queen and bishop aim at f7.

habit.why: 8.Ng5 moves the knight a second time with two minor pieces still at home, and 8...Ne5 covers f7 while hitting your bishop. After 9.Nxf7 Nxf7 10.Bxf7+ Kxf7 you have given a knight for a pawn on top of the gambit pawns.

strays.text: 8...Ne5 covers f7, so the knight trip only loses material.

taught.why: 8.Nxc3 wins a pawn back and develops a piece, with the knight heading for b5 against the d6 bishop and c7. After 8...Kf8 9.Nb5 Bc5 10.Qd5 Qe7 11.Nxc7 you win material and Black's king can no longer castle.

enforces.text: The pawn comes back with a developing move, and the knight joins the attack.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 8.Qb3 aims at f7, but with the bishop on d6 Black answers 8...Qe7, and after 9.Re1 Nf6 and 10...O-O Black is safe and two pawns up.
alternatives.after: 8.Nxc3 develops a piece with gain of time; the queen sortie lets Black cover f7 with 8...Qe7 and castle.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 8.e5 is a good move: it kicks the d6 bishop with tempo, and after 8...Bb4 9.Qb3 your queen and bishop hit f7. Another move is a little stronger.
alternatives.after: Both work: 8.Nxc3 develops first and keeps it simple, while 8.e5 kicks the bishop and takes back on c3 two moves later.
alternatives.idea: Kick the d6 bishop with e5

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 8.Qd5 threatens f7, but 8...Qe7 defends and 9...Nf6 drives your queen back with 10.Qd3. Black then castles two pawns up.
alternatives.after: 8.Nxc3 develops a piece instead; the early queen move just gets chased while your queenside stays at home.

1110098787406126|c1e3.headline: Chase the g4 bishop with 6.f3 so it can't trade itself off
1110098787406126|c1e3.why: 6.Be3 blocks the pin but lets Black trade bishops with 6...Bxe2 7.Qxe2. After 7...Nf6 8.Nf3 c6 9.O-O-O Nd5 Black's queen is no longer a target and much of your lead is gone. 6.f3 attacks the bishop and also blocks its path to e2, so Black can't trade. After 6...Bf5 7.g4 Bg6 8.f4 you threaten to push to f5, hitting queen and bishop at once, and Black must spend 8...f5 to stop it.
1110098787406126|c1e3.principle: A piece that pawns can chase and cut off from its exchange is a target: each pawn move gains space with tempo.

ideas.title: Mind the pin on e2
ideas.text: Black's queen on e6 pins your e2 bishop to your king, and the g4 bishop is ready to trade it off.

ideas.title: Black's bishop trade on e2
ideas.text: Black wants 6...Bxe2 to swap off your bishop and settle the queen. Quiet moves like 6.Be3 allow it.

ideas.title: Chase the bishop with pawns
ideas.text: 6.f3 hits the bishop and blocks its way to e2. After 6...Bf5 7.g4 Bg6 8.f4 a pawn on f5 would hit queen and bishop.

ideas.title: Push d5 while you lead
ideas.text: Black's king is still on e8 and only queen and bishop are out. Later 10.d5 hits the queen again.

habit.why: 6.Be3 blocks the pin but lets Black trade bishops with 6...Bxe2 7.Qxe2. After 7...Nf6 8.Nf3 c6 9.O-O-O Nd5 Black's queen is no longer a target and much of your lead is gone.

strays.text: It lets Black swap off the bishop and settle the queen.

taught.why: 6.f3 attacks the bishop and also blocks its path to e2, so Black can't trade. After 6...Bf5 7.g4 Bg6 8.f4 you threaten to push to f5, hitting queen and bishop at once, and Black must spend 8...f5 to stop it.

enforces.text: Each pawn move hits the bishop and gains space toward Black's queen.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.d5 hits the queen, but Black first trades with 6...Bxe2 and after 7.Ngxe2 Qd7 the queen is safe. The bishop that was Black's problem piece is gone.
alternatives.after: 6.f3 keeps the bishop on the board as a target: it can no longer reach e2, and 7.g4 and 8.f4 chase it while you gain space.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 6.h3 attacks the bishop, but Black just trades with 6...Bxe2 7.Ngxe2 Qd7, and your pawn move did nothing to the queen.
alternatives.after: 6.f3 also attacks the bishop but stands between g4 and e2, so Black can't trade and has to run with 6...Bf5.

1132065952318888|g5f3.headline: Punish 6...f6 with 7.Qh5+ instead of retreating
1132065952318888|g5f3.why: 7.Nf3 saves the knight but admits the trip to g5 cost two moves, and 7...Nf7 8.b4 Bb6 9.a4 a5 10.b5 Ne7 11.O-O O-O lets Black castle safely. The diagonal that 6...f6 opened toward Black's king goes unused. 7.Qh5+ uses the diagonal 6...f6 opened: blocking with the knight on f7 allows mate, and after 7...Ke7 Black can never castle. Then 8.Nf7 forks queen and rook, and 8...Qe8 9.Bxh6 gxh6 10.Qf3 Rf8 11.Nxh6 wins a pawn with Black's king stuck in the centre.
1132065952318888|g5f3.principle: Checks, captures and threats first: 7.Qh5+ uses the diagonal 6...f6 opened before Black can castle, while 7.Nf3 just retreats.

ideas.title: Punish ...f6 with a check
ideas.text: 6...f6 kicked your knight but opened the e8-h5 diagonal. 7.Qh5+ uses it before Black can castle.

ideas.title: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
ideas.text: The check is the follow-up: after 7...Ke7 8.Nf7 your knight forks the queen and the h8 rook.

ideas.title: Use the e6 hole
ideas.text: 6...f6 also left e6 without pawn cover, so 7.Ne6 forces 7...Bxe6 8.Bxe6 and your bishop gets a strong post.

ideas.title: Ng5 needs a real target
ideas.text: Retreating with 7.Nf3 means the trip to g5 cost two moves and Black castles in peace. Look for a target before going back.

habit.why: 7.Nf3 saves the knight but admits the trip to g5 cost two moves, and 7...Nf7 8.b4 Bb6 9.a4 a5 10.b5 Ne7 11.O-O O-O lets Black castle safely. The diagonal that 6...f6 opened toward Black's king goes unused.

strays.text: Retreating lets Black castle and never uses the opened e8-h5 diagonal.

taught.why: 7.Qh5+ uses the diagonal 6...f6 opened: blocking with the knight on f7 allows mate, and after 7...Ke7 Black can never castle. Then 8.Nf7 forks queen and rook, and 8...Qe8 9.Bxh6 gxh6 10.Qf3 Rf8 11.Nxh6 wins a pawn with Black's king stuck in the centre.

enforces.text: The check drags Black's king to e7, where it can never castle.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7.Ne6 uses the hole 6...f6 left: after 7...Bxe6 8.Bxe6 you have the bishop pair and a bishop deep in Black's camp, a safe edge. There is an even stronger move.
alternatives.after: 7.Qh5+ is stronger: it drags Black's king to e7 for good and sets up the 8.Nf7 fork. 7.Ne6 gives a small, safe edge instead.

1189776554630624|c6d4.headline: Against the Scotch, take with the pawn: 3...exd4.
1189776554630624|c6d4.why: 3...Nxd4 trades Black's only developed piece. After 4.Nxd4 exd4 5.Qxd4 White's queen sits in the centre and Black has nothing out. 3...exd4 is played almost every time: it releases the tension and keeps the knight. After 4.Nxd4 Black develops with tempo against White's centre, as with 4...Nf6.
1189776554630624|c6d4.principle: When the centre opens, capture with a pawn and keep your developed pieces rather than trading them off for nothing.

Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...exd4

1189776554630624|d7d5.headline: Take back on d4; don't open a second front with ...d5
1189776554630624|d7d5.why: 3...d5 leaves e5 to White's knight: 4.Nxe5 dxe4 5.Bb5 pins the knight on c6, and White is well ahead in development while Black has only one piece out. 3...exd4 is played in 99.6% of master games: it releases the central tension and removes White's d-pawn. After 4.Nxd4 Black can develop with tempo by hitting the centre with 4...Bc5 or 4...Nf6.
1189776554630624|d7d5.principle: When White's d-pawn attacks your e5 pawn, trade it off so White is left with one centre pawn, instead of leaving your own pawn hanging.

1189776554630624|d7d6.headline: In the Scotch, take with 3...exd4 and free your game
1189776554630624|d7d6.why: 3...d6 keeps the tension but lets White gain space with tempo: 4.d5 kicks the knight to e7, and after 5.c4 g6 6.Nc3 Bg7 7.c5 White is attacking on the queenside while Black is cramped. 3...exd4 is played in 99.6% of master games: it releases the tension and opens the game. After 4.Nxd4 Nf6 Black develops with an attack on e4.
1189776554630624|d7d6.principle: A knight on c6 standing in front of White's d-pawn is a target; trade the pawn off before it can kick the knight and gain space.

1189776554630624|f7f5.headline: Take on d4; don't open your king with f5
1189776554630624|f7f5.why: 3...f5 ignores the attack on e5 and opens the diagonal to your king: after 4.Nxe5 fxe4 5.Nxc6 bxc6 6.Qh5+ Black has to walk the king out with 6...Ke7. 3...exd4 releases the tension, removes White's threat of 4.d5 and leads to an open, balanced game; after 4.Nxd4 Black can develop with tempo by 4...Nf6 or 4...Bc5 against the centralised knight.
1189776554630624|f7f5.principle: With the king still in the centre, resolve the central tension first and keep the f-pawn home, since moving it opens lines toward your own king.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4

1189776554630624|f7f6.headline: Don't prop up e5 with the f-pawn; take on d4
1189776554630624|f7f6.why: 3...f6 holds e5 but takes f6 from Black's knight and opens the diagonal from c4 to Black's king: in the line 4.Bc4 d6 5.O-O Nge7 6.c3 Bd7 7.Qb3 the bishop and queen line up on f7, and 8.Bf7+ lands. 3...exd4 releases the tension and opens the game with plenty of space for both sides, and after 4.Nxd4 Nf6 Black develops normally. Masters choose it in 99.6% of games.
1189776554630624|f7f6.principle: Defend a centre pawn with pieces or trade it, not with the f-pawn, which blocks your knight and weakens the squares around your king.

1189776554630624|f8d6.headline: Take 3...exd4; 3...Bd6 blocks your own d-pawn for nothing.
1189776554630624|f8d6.why: White threatens 4.d5, kicking the knight and winning e5, and 3...Bd6 shuts in Black's d-pawn and queen's bishop. After 4.c3 exd4 5.cxd4 White has a full pawn centre and the bishop has to move again with 5...Bb4+. 3...exd4 releases the tension and is played in 99.6% of master games: after 4.Nxd4 Nf6 Black develops with tempo against the e4 pawn.
1189776554630624|f8d6.principle: When White strikes at e5 with a pawn, capture to release the tension; a bishop standing in front of your d-pawn can't help hold the centre.

1189776554630624|g7g6.headline: Release the tension with 3...exd4; 3...g6 drops e5
1189776554630624|g7g6.why: 3...g6 ignores the attack on e5: 4.dxe5 wins the pawn, and after 4...d6 5.exd6 Qxd6 6.Qxd6 Bxd6 the queens are off with Black simply a pawn down. 3...exd4 is played in 99.6% of master games: it releases the tension, and after 4.Nxd4 Black develops with tempo, 4...Nf6 against e4 or 4...Bc5 against the knight.
1189776554630624|g7g6.principle: When a pawn attacks your centre pawn, capture so the trade happens on your terms and your pieces get open lines.

1189776554630624|g8f6.headline: In the Scotch, take on d4 before d5 kicks your knight
1189776554630624|g8f6.why: 3...Nf6 ignores the threat to e5: 4.d5 drives the knight on c6 back with 4...Nb8, and 5.Nxe5 wins the pawn. 3...exd4 is played almost every time: it removes the pawn that was attacking, and after 4.Nxd4 Nf6 Black develops with tempo against e4. Masters choose it in 99.6% of games.
1189776554630624|g8f6.principle: e5 is attacked twice and only the knight on c6 defends it, so trade on d4 before that defender can be driven away.

1206106476480095|d5e6.headline: Take on c6, not e6: the c6 pawn falls next
1206106476480095|d5e6.why: 9.Bxe6+ Kxe6 trades off your active bishop and lets the queens come off: 10.Qh3+ Qf5 11.Qxf5+ Kxf5 is an endgame where Black's king is safe and active. You keep one extra pawn, much less than you could have. 9.Bxc6 takes the knight, and after 9...bxc6 10.Qxc6 your queen wins a second pawn and hits the e6 bishop and the a8 rook. Queens stay on, so Black's king on f7 stays exposed.
1206106476480095|d5e6.principle: Take the piece whose capture leaves something loose: removing the c6 knight wins c6 too, while the trade on e6 only frees Black's king.

ideas.title: Take off the defenders
ideas.text: 9.Bxc6 removes the knight. The e6 bishop blocks Black's queen from c6, so 10.Qxc6 wins a pawn.

ideas.title: Keep the queens on
ideas.text: Black's king on f7 can't castle; that is your attack. Trading queens lets it walk to safety.

ideas.title: Black wants trades
ideas.text: The e6 bishop hits your d5 bishop and Black's queen offers a trade; each trade makes the king safer.

habit.why: 9.Bxe6+ Kxe6 trades off your active bishop and lets the queens come off: 10.Qh3+ Qf5 11.Qxf5+ Kxf5 is an endgame where Black's king is safe and active. You keep one extra pawn, much less than you could have.

strays.text: The trade on e6 leads straight to a queen trade on f5.

taught.why: 9.Bxc6 takes the knight, and after 9...bxc6 10.Qxc6 your queen wins a second pawn and hits the e6 bishop and the a8 rook. Queens stay on, so Black's king on f7 stays exposed.

enforces.text: The c6 knight goes, and the e6 bishop blocks Black's queen from guarding c6.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 9.Qxf6+ gxf6 10.Bxe6+ Kxe6 trades queens and bishops; Black's king becomes an active endgame piece and most of your edge is gone.
alternatives.after: 9.Bxc6 keeps the queens on, and 10.Qxc6 wins a second pawn while Black's king stays exposed.

1206106476480095|f3f6.headline: Keep queens on: take the c6 knight with 9.Bxc6
1206106476480095|f3f6.why: 9.Qxf6+ gxf6 trades off the queen that pressures Black's king. After 10.Bxe6+ Kxe6 Black's king is active in the endgame, and most of your advantage is gone. 9.Bxc6 takes the knight, and after 9...bxc6 10.Qxc6 your queen wins a second pawn and hits the e6 bishop and the a8 rook. Queens stay on, so Black's king on f7 stays exposed.
1206106476480095|f3f6.principle: Play to your trump: Black's king can't castle, so keep the queens on and win material with your minor pieces.

1251051945717105|a5c7.headline: Develop with 7...Nf6; your queen has moved enough
1251051945717105|a5c7.why: 7...Qc7 moves the queen a third time and puts it on the c-file, where White's rook will come. After 8.d5 Bd7 9.Rc1 Nf6 10.Nf3 Qd8 11.dxe6 Bxe6 12.Ng5 your queen is back home, your king is still in the centre and White's pieces hit e6. 7...Nf6 develops a new piece and leaves the queen where it is. After 8.Bc4 Nc6 9.Nf3 Be7 10.O-O O-O you have castled, and only then does the queen move again, with 11...Qc7.
1251051945717105|a5c7.principle: Don't keep moving the queen early: 6.Nc3 already gained time on it, so 7...Nf6 develops while 7...Qc7 hands White another tempo.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. c3/2...d5/3. exd5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. d4/2...d5/3. Nd2/3...c5/4. exd5

ideas.title: Develop, don't move the queen again
ideas.text: Your queen has moved twice already. Each extra queen move is a free tempo for White; bring out the knights and bishops instead.

ideas.title: Nc3 hits the queen
ideas.text: Once ...cxd4 freed c3, White's knight came out with tempo on your queen, and the d2-bishop now lines up on a5 behind it.

ideas.title: White's isolated d-pawn
ideas.text: White's d4 pawn is isolated. White's reward is quick development, and the pawn can push while you're behind, as in 8.d5.

habit.why: 7...Qc7 moves the queen a third time and puts it on the c-file, where White's rook will come. After 8.d5 Bd7 9.Rc1 Nf6 10.Nf3 Qd8 11.dxe6 Bxe6 12.Ng5 your queen is back home, your king is still in the centre and White's pieces hit e6.

strays.idea: Develop, don't move the queen again
strays.text: A third queen move hands White another free tempo.

taught.why: 7...Nf6 develops a new piece and leaves the queen where it is. After 8.Bc4 Nc6 9.Nf3 Be7 10.O-O O-O you have castled, and only then does the queen move again, with 11...Qc7.

enforces.idea: Develop, don't move the queen again
enforces.text: Knights and bishop come out first; the queen moves only after castling.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 7...Bb4 pins the knight, but 8.a3 Bxc3 9.Bxc3 hits your queen and sends it back with 9...Qd8. After 10.Qg4 Kf8 you can't castle and White has both bishops.
alternatives.after: 7...Nf6 keeps your dark-squared bishop at home to guard g7, and White gets no extra tempo on your queen.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7...Qb6 eyes b2 and d4, but it's a third queen move. After 8.Nf3, 9.Bc4 and 10.Qe2 White develops quickly, and 12.Be3 hits your queen again.
alternatives.after: 7...Nf6 develops instead, and the queen waits until you've castled, as with 11...Qc7 in the main line.
alternatives.idea: Develop, don't move the queen again

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7...Nc6 develops, but 8.Bb5 pins the knight. After 9.Nf3 Qb6 10.Ne5 Be7 11.Bxc6+ bxc6 your pawns are split and the queen has moved again.
alternatives.after: 7...Nf6 develops the kingside first, so you castle sooner (10...O-O), and ...Nc6 follows once White's bishop has gone to c4, as in 8.Bc4 Nc6.
alternatives.idea: Develop, don't move the queen again

1261108510304489|e1h1.headline: Hit f7 with 7.Qb3 before Black's knight comes out
1261108510304489|e1h1.why: 7.O-O gives Black a free move: 7...Nf6 hits e4, and after 8.e5 Ne4 9.cxd4 d5 10.exd6 Nxd6 your centre is gone and you are still a pawn down. Castling is the usual gambit move in other Evans lines, but here it wastes the moment. 7.Qb3 aims queen and bishop at f7, so Black has to deal with it. After 7...Na5 8.Bxf7+ Kf8 9.Qa4 Kxf7 10.Qxa5 you have won back a pawn, and Black's king has lost the right to castle.
1261108510304489|e1h1.principle: Look at forcing moves first: 7.Qb3 threatens f7 at once, while 7.O-O gives Black time for ...Nf6 and ...d5.
sources: Renette & Zavatarelli, Neumann, Hirschfeld and Suhle | https://books.google.com/books?id=iKk4EQAAQBAJ

ideas.title: The centre is the payment
ideas.text: 4.b4 gave a pawn for a big centre. Rebuild e4 and d4 with cxd4, and pick moves that gain time.

ideas.title: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
ideas.text: A queen on b3 lines up with the c4-bishop on f7. Taking there pays only if a queen move then wins a loose piece.

ideas.title: Black hits back with ...d5
ideas.text: Given a free move, Black plays ...Nf6 and ...d5, attacking e4 and opening the centre while you are still pawns down.

habit.why: 7.O-O gives Black a free move: 7...Nf6 hits e4, and after 8.e5 Ne4 9.cxd4 d5 10.exd6 Nxd6 your centre is gone and you are still a pawn down. Castling is the usual gambit move in other Evans lines, but here it wastes the moment.

strays.text: Black gets ...Nf6 and ...d5 in before your centre is rebuilt.

taught.why: 7.Qb3 aims queen and bishop at f7, so Black has to deal with it. After 7...Na5 8.Bxf7+ Kf8 9.Qa4 Kxf7 10.Qxa5 you have won back a pawn, and Black's king has lost the right to castle.

enforces.idea: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
enforces.text: 8.Bxf7+ works because 9.Qa4 then hits the loose a5-knight.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7.cxd4 rebuilds your pawn centre at once, the main idea of the Evans, and keeps a fair game. There is a slightly more forcing move.
alternatives.after: 7.Qb3 first forces Black to deal with f7; a 19th-century annotation rated it above 7.cxd4. The engine rates the two close.

1273971384127904|g8h6.headline: Block f7 with 3...Nf6, not with a knight on the rim
1273971384127904|g8h6.why: 3...Nh6 stops the mate but puts the knight on the edge, where 4.d4 opens the bishop on c1 onto it; after 4...Qe7 the queen blocks the bishop on f8, and White builds a big centre with 5.Nc3 and 6.d5. 3...Nf6 blocks the queen's line to f7, develops toward the centre and attacks e4. White's queen on f3 has also taken the knight's best square, so after 4.Ne2 Be7 Black castles in comfort.
1273971384127904|g8h6.principle: Parry the threat with a developing move that fights for the centre: from f6 the knight blocks the queen and also attacks e4.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qf3

1314504257002276|f1d3.headline: Close the centre with 3.e5 instead of defending with Bd3
1314504257002276|f1d3.why: The theory notes call 3.Bd3 irregular: after 3...dxe4 4.Bxe4 Nf6 Black develops with tempo on the bishop, which must move again, or be swapped for a knight with 5.Nc3 Nxe4 6.Nxe4, giving up the bishop pair. In the line 5.Bf3 Bf5 Black has easy development and is slightly better. 3.e5, the advance variation and the masters' top choice (39.9%), closes the centre and gains space; after 3...Bf5 4.Nf3 e6 5.Be2 White keeps a small edge. 3.Nc3, 3.Nd2 and 3.exd5 are also good.
1314504257002276|f1d3.principle: Don't put a piece where the opponent can make it move again with tempo; every extra move of the same piece is development your opponent gets for free.

1317312578379376|f3c6.headline: The f6 queen guards c6: check on h5 instead
1317312578379376|f3c6.why: 10.Qxc6+ grabs a pawn that Black's queen on f6 guards along the sixth rank: 10...Qxc6 wins your queen for a pawn. After 11.O-O Qg6 12.Kh1 Bb7 Black's queen and bishop already aim at g2. 10.Qh5+ checks first, and 10...g6 pushes a pawn that weakens Black's kingside. Then 11.Qe2 keeps your queen safe and on the board against a king that can't castle, and you stay a pawn up.
1317312578379376|f3c6.principle: Before a capture, especially one with check, count the defenders, including a queen guarding along a rank.

ideas.title: Keep the queens on
ideas.text: Black's king can't castle and stands in the centre; that is your attack. Trading queens lets it walk to safety.

ideas.title: Count the defenders of c6
ideas.text: The c6 pawn looks free, but Black's queen on f6 guards it along the sixth rank.

ideas.title: Check, then keep the queen safe
ideas.text: 10.Qh5+ g6 11.Qe2 forces a pawn forward and keeps your queen safe and on the board.

ideas.title: Black wants trades and tempo
ideas.text: Black's queen on f6 offers a trade, and moves like 10...e4 and 11...Bf5 gain time on your queen.

habit.why: 10.Qxc6+ grabs a pawn that Black's queen on f6 guards along the sixth rank: 10...Qxc6 wins your queen for a pawn. After 11.O-O Qg6 12.Kh1 Bb7 Black's queen and bishop already aim at g2.

strays.text: The queen on f6 guards c6, so the capture loses your queen.

taught.why: 10.Qh5+ checks first, and 10...g6 pushes a pawn that weakens Black's kingside. Then 11.Qe2 keeps your queen safe and on the board against a king that can't castle, and you stay a pawn up.

enforces.idea: Check, then keep the queen safe
enforces.text: Forces 10...g6 with check, then the queen steps back to e2.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 10.Qxf6 gxf6 trades off your attacker. Black's king is safe, and the open files make up for the pawn, as in 11.d3 Rg8 12.Rg1 Rb8.
alternatives.after: 10.Qh5+ g6 11.Qe2 keeps the queens on, so Black's king stays in the centre and the split pawns stay weak.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 10.Qc3 hits e5, but 10...e4 and 11...Bf5 gain time on your queen, and 13...Qxc3 trades queens anyway. Black's king is safe and most of your edge is gone.
alternatives.after: 10.Qh5+ also moves the queen, but with check, and after 11.Qe2 it stays on the board instead of being traded.

132233271809428|a7a6.headline: Break the pin with 5...Bd7 so a piece retakes on c6
132233271809428|a7a6.why: 5...a6 doesn't prepare a recapture with a piece, so 6.Bxc6+ bxc6 leaves you with doubled c-pawns. After 7.d3 c4 8.dxc4 you even drop a pawn trying to free them. 5...Bd7 breaks the pin, and after 6.Bxc6 Bxc6 your pawns stay healthy and you keep the bishop pair. Then 7.d4 Nh6 8.O-O Nf5 puts pressure on d4, the usual French plan.
132233271809428|a7a6.principle: Your c6 knight is pinned to your king, so neutralise the pin: 5...Bd7 means a trade on c6 is met by the bishop, while 5...a6 leaves you with doubled c-pawns.

ideas.title: Retake on c6 with a piece
ideas.text: Against the bishop on b5, have a piece ready to take back on c6, so a trade there doesn't leave you with doubled c-pawns.

ideas.title: Pressure on d4
ideas.text: With White's pawns on e5 and f4, aim at d4: ...Qb6, the knight via h6 to f5, and ...cxd4 hit the base of the chain.

ideas.title: French pawn chain
ideas.text: This is a French structure: White's e5 and f4 gain space, but the f4 pawn hems in White's c1 bishop.

habit.why: 5...a6 doesn't prepare a recapture with a piece, so 6.Bxc6+ bxc6 leaves you with doubled c-pawns. After 7.d3 c4 8.dxc4 you even drop a pawn trying to free them.

strays.idea: Retake on c6 with a piece
strays.text: After 6.Bxc6+ only a pawn can take back.

taught.why: 5...Bd7 breaks the pin, and after 6.Bxc6 Bxc6 your pawns stay healthy and you keep the bishop pair. Then 7.d4 Nh6 8.O-O Nf5 puts pressure on d4, the usual French plan.

enforces.idea: Retake on c6 with a piece
enforces.text: The bishop is ready to take back on c6.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...Qb6 is ready to take back with the queen: 6.Bxc6+ Qxc6 keeps your pawns intact, and 8...Nh6 and 9...Nf5 follow. A good move.
alternatives.after: Both are fine. 5...Bd7 develops a piece and keeps the bishop pair after 6.Bxc6 Bxc6; with 5...Qb6 the queen does the recapturing.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.idea: Retake on c6 with a piece
alternatives.before: 5...Ne7 adds a second guard to c6, so a trade there is met by a knight, and the knight can go on to f5. A good move.
alternatives.after: Equally good: its line 6.c3 Bd7 7.Bxc6 Bxc6 8.d4 Nf5 reaches the same plan of taking back with the bishop.

1336500176424022|e7e5.headline: Castle before you open the centre in the Modern
1336500176424022|e7e5.why: 4...e5 lets White open the centre with 5.dxe5 dxe5 6.Qxd8+ Kxd8: the queens come off, Black loses the right to castle, and White develops with gain of time through 7.Be3 and 8.O-O-O+ along the open d-file. 4...Nf6 develops the last kingside piece and prepares to castle with 5.Be3 O-O, and only then does Black strike at the centre with 6...c5.
1336500176424022|e7e5.principle: Before you open the centre with a pawn break, castle; a queen trade with your king still on e8 can leave it stranded in the middle.

1364829931449246|c1e3.headline: Keep the queens on with 7.Qd3; Black is the cramped side
1364829931449246|c1e3.why: 7.Be3 develops but lets Black trade queens: 7...Qxd4 8.Bxd4 Ne7 9.Be3 Be6 10.Bxe6 fxe6, and Black is comfortable. Without queens your extra space counts for much less. 7.Qd3 sidesteps the trade and still guards e4 and your c4 bishop. After 7...Be7 8.O-O c6 9.Re1 you have more space and a lead in development, with the queens still on.
1364829931449246|c1e3.principle: Play to your imbalances: your edge is space and development, which count most with queens on, so dodge the trade 6...Qf6 offers.
sources: Semi-Italian Opening (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-Italian_Opening

ideas.title: Keep the queens on
ideas.text: Your extra space and lead in development count most with queens on. 6...Qf6 offers a trade, so step aside rather than allow it.

ideas.title: Black wants a queen trade
ideas.text: 6...Qf6 hits your queen on d4. A trade would ease Black's cramped position, as after 7.Be3 Qxd4 8.Bxd4.

ideas.title: Guard e4 and c4
ideas.text: From d3 your queen still guards the e4 pawn and the c4 bishop, so you can castle without leaving anything loose.

ideas.title: Castle and use the e-file
ideas.text: Then castle and put a rook on e1, as in 8.O-O c6 9.Re1, while you keep more space.

habit.why: 7.Be3 develops but lets Black trade queens: 7...Qxd4 8.Bxd4 Ne7 9.Be3 Be6 10.Bxe6 fxe6, and Black is comfortable. Without queens your extra space counts for much less.

strays.text: 7...Qxd4 takes the queens off, and Black is no longer cramped.

taught.why: 7.Qd3 sidesteps the trade and still guards e4 and your c4 bishop. After 7...Be7 8.O-O c6 9.Re1 you have more space and a lead in development, with the queens still on.

enforces.text: The queen steps aside, so Black stays cramped.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.Qxf6 trades queens yourself and develops Black's knight: after 7...Nxf6 8.Nc3 Be6 9.Bb3 O-O-O Black is fully developed and castled.
alternatives.after: 7.Qd3 keeps the queens on, so Black stays cramped and your lead in development still matters. 7.Qxf6 hands over most of your edge.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7.Qe3 is sound: it avoids the queen trade and guards e4. It blocks your c1 bishop, though, and 7...Be6 8.Bd3 Qh4 gives Black active play.
alternatives.after: 7.Qd3 does the same job, also guards the c4 bishop and leaves the c1 bishop free. The engine rates the two moves equally.

1436063243700465|f6d5.headline: Recapture with the pawn, 4...cxd5, so e4 can't chase your knight
1436063243700465|f6d5.why: 4...Nxd5 puts the knight where a pawn can hit it: 5.e4 Nb6 builds White a full pawn centre with tempo, and after 6.h3 g6 7.Nc3 Bg7 White is clearly better. The pawn on d5 is attacked three times and not defended at all, so you can choose how to take it back. 4...cxd5, played in 99.7% of master games, recaptures toward the centre and keeps a pawn on d5, so White has no e4 with tempo; after 5.Bf4 Nc6 6.Nc3 a6 the game is level.
1436063243700465|f6d5.principle: A knight in the centre that an enemy pawn can attack loses time when it is chased; recapture with a pawn when you can.

1436639890177008|e4e5.headline: Your bishop is attacked: save it with 4.Bb5+
1436639890177008|e4e5.why: 4.e5 ignores the pawn on d5 that attacks your bishop, and 4...dxc4 simply wins it. After 5.Na3 Nh6 6.O-O Nc6 7.Nxc4 b5 you get a pawn back, but Black stays a piece for a pawn ahead. 4.Bb5+ moves the bishop out of attack with check, using the diagonal that ...d5 before ...Nc6 leaves open. After 4...Bd7 5.Bxd7+ Qxd7 6.exd5 Qxd5 7.Nc3 you develop with a hit on the queen and the game is level.
1436639890177008|e4e5.principle: Checks, captures and threats first: when ...d5 attacks your bishop, answer with a forcing move like 4.Bb5+ or 4.exd5, not a push that ignores it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Bc4

ideas.title: Black's ...d5 hits your bishop
ideas.text: 3...d5 attacks the c4-bishop. You must deal with it now: check, capture or retreat.

ideas.title: Check on the a4-e8 diagonal
ideas.text: Black played ...d5 before ...Nc6, so your bishop can jump to b5 with check, as Wikibooks warns.

ideas.title: Castle, then prepare d4
ideas.text: Once the bishop is safe, develop, castle and play d4, as with 7.Nc3 and 8.d4.

habit.why: 4.e5 ignores the pawn on d5 that attacks your bishop, and 4...dxc4 simply wins it. After 5.Na3 Nh6 6.O-O Nc6 7.Nxc4 b5 you get a pawn back, but Black stays a piece for a pawn ahead.

strays.text: The push leaves the attacked bishop on c4 to be taken.

taught.why: 4.Bb5+ moves the bishop out of attack with check, using the diagonal that ...d5 before ...Nc6 leaves open. After 4...Bd7 5.Bxd7+ Qxd7 6.exd5 Qxd5 7.Nc3 you develop with a hit on the queen and the game is level.

enforces.text: The check saves the bishop with tempo and trades it off.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.exd5 removes the attacking pawn, the choice of 93% of club players. After 4...exd5 your bishop is safe and you can develop and castle; it's fully sound.
alternatives.after: 4.Bb5+ is just as good: it saves the bishop with check first, and after 4.exd5 exd5 5.Bb5+ Nc6 the same check comes a move later. Both keep the game level.

144526251450061|g1f3.headline: After 2...Bf5, take on d5 before Black can support it
144526251450061|g1f3.why: 3.Nf3 gives Black time to support d5 with 3...e6, reaching a solid Queen's Gambit Declined with the bishop already outside the pawn chain. 2...Bf5 left d5 without pawn support, and 3.cxd5 punishes that: Black has no pawn ready to recapture. To win the pawn back Black plays 3...Bxb1 4.Rxb1 Qxd5, giving White the bishop pair and an easy game.
144526251450061|g1f3.principle: Strike at a centre pawn as soon as it has lost its pawn support, before your opponent can add ...e6.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...Bf5

1453935289757629|c1f4.headline: Against the Marshall Defence, take on d5 and gain time
1453935289757629|c1f4.why: 3.Bf4 leaves c4 hanging: 3...dxc4 takes the pawn and 4...b5 holds on to it. 3.cxd5 takes a pawn Black can only win back with a piece, and that piece becomes a target. If 3...Nxd5, then 4.e4 gains a tempo and the centre; if 3...Qxd5, then 4.Nc3 hits the queen.
1453935289757629|c1f4.principle: Trade on d5 when Black can only recapture with a piece, then gain time by attacking that piece with pawns and knights.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...Nf6
Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...Nf6/3. cxd5

1454642951891787|f6d7.headline: Trade queens first, then put the knight on d5
1454642951891787|f6d7.why: Both queens face each other on the open d-file and the pawn on e5 attacks the knight on f6. 5...Nfd7 saves the knight by moving it a second time and keeps the queens on, and after 6.f4 White builds a big centre with quick development and a clear edge. 5...Qxd1+ trades queens first, 6.Nxd1 recaptures, and only then 6...Nd5 puts the knight on a strong central square; without queens, White's extra space matters much less.
1454642951891787|f6d7.principle: When your knight is attacked and the queens face each other, look at the forcing trade first: it settles the position before you spend a tempo retreating.

1454642951891787|f6g4.headline: Make the queen trade yourself so your king keeps castling
1454642951891787|f6g4.why: 5...Ng4 leaves the queens on, so 6.Qxd8+ Kxd8 strands Black's king in the centre without castling rights. After 7.Nf3 Bg7 8.Bf4 the e5 pawn is firmly defended, the knight on g4 has moved twice for nothing, and 9.Rd1+ and 10.Bb5 keep harassing the king. 5...Qxd1+ makes the trade on Black's terms: White recaptures with 6.Nxd1, Black's king keeps its castling rights, and the knight escapes the e5 pawn's attack with 6...Nd5.
1454642951891787|f6g4.principle: With the queens facing each other down an open file, make the capture yourself, so your opponent's piece recaptures and your king stays home.

1455931362502230|c8f5.headline: After 4.Bf4, c4 is undefended: take it with 4...dxc4
1455931362502230|c8f5.why: 4.Bf4 develops a bishop but leaves c4 attacked once and defended not at all. 4...Bf5 lets that go, and 5.Qb3 attacks b7, which the bishop stopped guarding when it left c8, so White takes over the initiative. Take the pawn with 4...dxc4: the theory says that after 4.Bf4 Black keeps it without White getting compensation, which is why 4.e3, ruling out 4...dxc4, is the normal move.
1455931362502230|c8f5.principle: After each opponent move, check what has become loose: a developing move that leaves the c4 pawn unguarded is a free pawn.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6

1479849493158304|d2d3.headline: Against 3...Qa5, take the centre with 4.d4.
1479849493158304|d2d3.why: 4.d3 is too modest: it shuts in the bishop on f1 and gives up the centre, so Black develops comfortably with ...g6, ...Bg7 and ...c5. 4.d4 is the main line, played 78% of the time. It pins White's own knight for now, but it claims the centre and frees d2 for the bishop. The knight can then move with tempo against the black queen.
1479849493158304|d2d3.principle: When the opponent spends time on queen moves, use it to build a full pawn centre with both centre pawns.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qa5

1479849493158304|f1b5.headline: Against 3...Qa5, build the centre with 4.d4
1479849493158304|f1b5.why: 4.Bb5+ achieves nothing: 4...Bd7 blocks with a developing move, and White soon retreats with 5.Be2, having spent two moves on the bishop. 4.d4 is the main line, chosen in 77.6% of master games: it takes the centre and frees d2 for the bishop, so White can later move the knight with tempo on the queen.
1479849493158304|f1b5.principle: With the opponent's queen out early, take the centre and develop; the queen becomes a target later, a pointless check only wastes time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qa5

1483132126480579|c1d2.headline: Push 7.e5 instead of the passive 7.Bd2
1483132126480579|c1d2.why: 7.Bd2 makes no threat and does nothing for e5 or f7, so Black develops in peace. After 7...d6 8.h3 Nf6 9.O-O O-O Black has castled and keeps the extra pawn. 7.e5 takes f6 from the g8 knight and blocks the g7 bishop, and 7...Nxe5 fails to 8.Nxe5 Bxe5 9.Bxf7+ Kxf7 10.Qd5+. After 7...Nh6 8.O-O O-O 9.Bf4 d6 10.exd6 exd6 your pieces are active for the pawn; masters choose 7.e5 in 48.5% of games.
1483132126480579|c1d2.principle: A pawn down, you must keep Black busy: 7.e5 cramps Black's kingside, while a passive bishop move gives Black time to castle and keep the pawn.

ideas.title: The e4-e5 break
ideas.text: Against ...Nc6 and ...Bg7, e5 blocks the g7 bishop and takes f6 from the g8 knight, so it usually goes to h6 instead.

ideas.title: e5 is guarded by tactics
ideas.text: Taking 7...Nxe5 runs into 8.Nxe5 Bxe5 9.Bxf7+ Kxf7 10.Qd5+ and 11.Qxe5+: your bishop and queen win the piece back.

ideas.title: Pressure on f7
ideas.text: Your c4 bishop aims at f7, and a knight on g5 adds a second attacker. Black covers with ...Nh6 or trades the bishop via ...Ne5.

ideas.title: Gambit pawn buys time
ideas.text: You are a pawn down for quick development. Quiet bishop moves let Black castle and keep the pawn.

habit.why: 7.Bd2 makes no threat and does nothing for e5 or f7, so Black develops in peace. After 7...d6 8.h3 Nf6 9.O-O O-O Black has castled and keeps the extra pawn.

strays.text: A quiet bishop move gives Black the time to consolidate the pawn.

taught.why: 7.e5 takes f6 from the g8 knight and blocks the g7 bishop, and 7...Nxe5 fails to 8.Nxe5 Bxe5 9.Bxf7+ Kxf7 10.Qd5+. After 7...Nh6 8.O-O O-O 9.Bf4 d6 10.exd6 exd6 your pieces are active for the pawn; masters choose 7.e5 in 48.5% of games.

enforces.text: The pawn on e5 keeps the g8 knight off f6 and blunts the g7 bishop.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: Castling is a good move, played in 39% of master games. After 7...d6 8.Ng5 Ne5 9.Qb3 Nxc4 10.Qxc4 Black trades off your c4 bishop, and there is a more forcing move.
alternatives.after: 7.e5 is the masters' first choice (48.5%): it keeps the g8 knight off f6, while after castling 7...d6 lets Black meet the f7 pressure with ...Ne5.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7.Ng5 adds a second attacker on f7, but 7...Nh6 covers it and Black castles next. Playable, though the knight has moved twice and there is a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 7.e5 gains space and keeps the g8 knight off f6; after 7.Ng5 Nh6 8.O-O O-O Black is safe and your knight has to find a new job.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7.Bf4 develops, but 7...Nf6 hits e4 at once, and after 8...Nh5 Black's knight gains time on your bishop. Playable, but there is a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 7.e5 takes f6 before the knight gets there, so Black has to make do with ...Nh6; after 7.Bf4 Nf6 the knight arrives first.

1483132126480579|c1g5.why: 7.Bg5 pins nothing, because the e7 pawn still shields the queen, and it lets Black develop 7...Nf6 with an attack on e4. After 8.h3 d6 9.O-O O-O Black is castled and still a pawn up. 7.e5 takes f6 from the g8 knight and blocks the g7 bishop, and 7...Nxe5 fails to 8.Nxe5 Bxe5 9.Bxf7+ Kxf7 10.Qd5+. After 7...Nh6 8.O-O O-O 9.Bf4 d6 10.exd6 exd6 your pieces are active for the pawn; masters choose 7.e5 in 48.5% of games.
1483132126480579|c1g5.principle: A pawn down, you must keep Black busy: 7.e5 cramps Black's kingside, while a bishop move with no target gives Black time to castle and keep the pawn.

1513949415486855|e4d5.headline: Gain space with 4.e5 instead of releasing the tension
1513949415486855|e4d5.why: 4.exd5 exd5 releases the tension and gives Black an open, symmetrical position with free development, so most of your edge disappears. Black's threat was 4...dxe4, and 4.e5, the main move in 84.2% of master games, meets it by taking space with tempo on the knight on f6, which the theory describes as the main answer to ...Nf6. After 4...Nfd7 Black has to attack your centre with ...c5 and ...Nc6, and you support it with 6.c3 and castle, keeping the extra space.
1513949415486855|e4d5.principle: When you can choose between a space advantage and a symmetrical exchange, keep the imbalance that favours you: the e5 pawn cramps Black, while exd5 leaves nothing to play for.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. d4/2...Nf6

1557996217562153|c2c3.headline: Answer 2...Nc6 with 3.d5, kicking the knight
1557996217562153|c2c3.why: 3.c3 defends d4 passively, and Black hits the centre at once with 3...d5. After 4.exd5 Qxd5 5.Nf3 Nf6 6.Be2 cxd4 7.cxd4 e6 Black develops easily and your chance to gain space is gone. 3.d5 steps out of the c5 pawn's reach, gains space and attacks the knight on c6. After 3...Na5 4.Nf3 g6 5.h4 the knight is stuck on the rim and you start gaining space on the kingside too.
1557996217562153|c2c3.principle: A knight that your pawn can attack is a target: 3.d5 gains space and drives it away instead of defending d4.

ideas.title: Chase the knight with pawns
ideas.text: 2...Nc6 puts the knight where your d-pawn can hit it. 3.d5 gains space and drives it from c6 with tempo.

ideas.title: Black's threat: ...cxd4
ideas.text: 2...Nc6 adds a second attacker on d4, so 3...cxd4 wins a pawn unless you act.

ideas.title: Knight on the rim
ideas.text: After 3.d5 Na5 the knight is offside on a5, and your d5 pawn takes c6 and e6 away from Black's pieces.

ideas.title: The c-for-d trade
ideas.text: Trading Black's c-pawn for your d-pawn is the point of 1...c5. 3.Nf3 cxd4 4.Nxd4 allows it: an ordinary Open Sicilian.

habit.why: 3.c3 defends d4 passively, and Black hits the centre at once with 3...d5. After 4.exd5 Qxd5 5.Nf3 Nf6 6.Be2 cxd4 7.cxd4 e6 Black develops easily and your chance to gain space is gone.

strays.text: You defend d4 instead of using it to hit the knight.

taught.why: 3.d5 steps out of the c5 pawn's reach, gains space and attacks the knight on c6. After 3...Na5 4.Nf3 g6 5.h4 the knight is stuck on the rim and you start gaining space on the kingside too.

enforces.text: The pawn gains space and drives the knight away with tempo.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 3.dxc5 gives up your centre pawn, and Black wins the pawn back with tempo: 3...Nf6 4.Bd3 Qa5+ 5.Nc3 e6 and 6...Bxc5.
alternatives.after: 3.d5 keeps your pawn in the centre and gains space, while 3.dxc5 hands Black easy development.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 3.Nf3 lets Black make the trade 1...c5 aims for: 3...cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 e5 is an ordinary Open Sicilian with nothing extra for you.
alternatives.after: 3.d5 avoids the trade and punishes 2...Nc6 by chasing the knight, which keeps a clear space edge.

1557996217562153|g1f3.headline: Punish 2...Nc6 with 3.d5 before Black takes on d4
1557996217562153|g1f3.why: 3.Nf3 doesn't stop 3...cxd4, and after 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 e5 6.Ndb5 d6 it is a normal Sveshnikov-type Open Sicilian. Black got the trade 1...c5 aims for, and 2...Nc6 goes unpunished. 3.d5 steps out of the c5 pawn's reach, gains space and attacks the knight on c6. After 3...Na5 4.Nf3 g6 5.h4 the knight is stuck on the rim and you start gaining space on the kingside too.
1557996217562153|g1f3.principle: A knight that your pawn can attack is a target: 3.d5 gains space and drives it away before Black can take on d4.
sources: Geza Maroczy, Paul Morphy | https://books.google.com/books?id=rWHKEQAAQBAJ

ideas.title: Chase the knight with pawns
ideas.text: 2...Nc6 puts the knight where your d-pawn can hit it. 3.d5 gains space and drives it from c6 with tempo.

ideas.title: Black's threat: ...cxd4
ideas.text: 2...Nc6 adds a second attacker on d4, so 3...cxd4 wins a pawn unless you act.

ideas.title: Knight on the rim
ideas.text: After 3.d5 Na5 the knight is offside on a5, and your d5 pawn takes c6 and e6 away from Black's pieces.

ideas.title: The c-for-d trade
ideas.text: Trading Black's c-pawn for your d-pawn is the point of 1...c5. 3.Nf3 cxd4 4.Nxd4 allows it: an ordinary Open Sicilian.

habit.why: 3.Nf3 doesn't stop 3...cxd4, and after 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 e5 6.Ndb5 d6 it is a normal Sveshnikov-type Open Sicilian. Black got the trade 1...c5 aims for, and 2...Nc6 goes unpunished.

strays.text: Black trades c-pawn for d-pawn and reaches a normal Open Sicilian.

taught.why: 3.d5 steps out of the c5 pawn's reach, gains space and attacks the knight on c6. After 3...Na5 4.Nf3 g6 5.h4 the knight is stuck on the rim and you start gaining space on the kingside too.

enforces.text: The pawn gains space and drives the knight away with tempo.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 3.dxc5 gives up your centre pawn, and Black wins the pawn back with tempo: 3...Nf6 4.Bd3 Qa5+ 5.Nc3 e6 and 6...Bxc5.
alternatives.after: 3.d5 keeps your pawn in the centre and gains space, while 3.dxc5 hands Black easy development.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 3.c3 defends d4, but Black hits the centre straight away, and after 4.exd5 Qxd5 5.Nf3 Nf6 Black develops easily.
alternatives.after: 3.d5 uses the d-pawn to attack the knight and gain space instead of defending it.

15856967415293|c1g5.headline: Castle with 7.O-O; 7.Bg5 is chased off by 7...Nge7 and 8...h6
15856967415293|c1g5.why: 7.Bg5 hits the queen, but 7...Nge7 blocks with a developing move, and with c3 still pinned you have to retake with 8.Nxd4. Then 8...h6, 9...Ne5 and 10...N5g6 chase your bishops while Black castles a pawn up. Castling ends the pin, so 8.cxd4 is threatened at once. After 7...Nf6 8.cxd4 Nxe4 9.d5 hits the c6 knight, 10.Qd4 hits e4 and g7, and 11.Bg5 brings the bishop in with an attack on the f6 knight.
15856967415293|c1g5.principle: Your c3 pawn is pinned to your king, so castle first: 7.O-O makes 8.cxd4 possible, while 7.Bg5 gets chased and you must retake with the knight.
sources: GM John Nunn, Learn to play the Evans Gambit (ChessBase) | https://en.chessbase.com/post/john-nunn-learn-to-play-the-evans-gambit
Evans Gambit (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evans_Gambit
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3

ideas.title: Unpin, then rebuild the centre
ideas.text: The a5 bishop pins your c3 pawn; once your king leaves e1, 8.cxd4 restores your pawns on e4 and d4.

ideas.title: Development is your compensation
ideas.text: You're two pawns down for time and open lines; moving pieces that are already out wastes that pay.

ideas.title: Hit f7 with tempo
ideas.text: Queen on b3 and bishop on c4 aim at f7. A knight jump to g5 only works once Black can no longer cover f7 from h6.

ideas.title: Greed needs a spare tempo
ideas.text: Taking a third pawn on c3 right after you castle is dangerous for Black; after a wasted move it is safe.

habit.why: 7.Bg5 hits the queen, but 7...Nge7 blocks with a developing move, and with c3 still pinned you have to retake with 8.Nxd4. Then 8...h6, 9...Ne5 and 10...N5g6 chase your bishops while Black castles a pawn up.

strays.text: The c3 pawn stays pinned, so you have to retake on d4 with the knight.

taught.why: Castling ends the pin, so 8.cxd4 is threatened at once. After 7...Nf6 8.cxd4 Nxe4 9.d5 hits the c6 knight, 10.Qd4 hits e4 and g7, and 11.Bg5 brings the bishop in with an attack on the f6 knight.

enforces.text: With your king off e1, 8.cxd4 puts a pawn back beside e4.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: Your queen joins the c4 bishop against f7, so Black must spend the reply defending it, as with 7...Qf6. Masters play it in 41% of games, and the engine likes it as much as anything here.
alternatives.after: 7.O-O is the more popular choice (59%) and breaks the pin at once; the engine rates 7.Qb3 just as highly, so both are fine.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 7.Nxd4 wins one pawn back and nothing more: after 7...Nge7 Black develops calmly, castles soon and stays a pawn up, and your e4 pawn stands alone.
alternatives.after: 7.O-O keeps the recapture for the c-pawn: after 7...Nf6 8.cxd4 you have pawns on e4 and d4 again.

15856967415293|f3g5.headline: Castle to break the pin on c3, then retake with 8.cxd4

ideas.title: Unpin, then rebuild the centre
ideas.text: The a5-bishop pins your c3 pawn; once your king leaves e1, 8.cxd4 restores your pawns on e4 and d4.

ideas.title: Development is your compensation
ideas.text: You're two pawns down for time and open lines; moving pieces that are already out wastes that pay.

ideas.title: Hit f7 with tempo
ideas.text: Queen on b3 and bishop on c4 aim at f7. A knight jump to g5 only works once Black can no longer cover f7 from h6.

ideas.title: Greed needs a spare tempo
ideas.text: Taking a third pawn on c3 right after you castle is dangerous for Black; after a wasted move it is safe.

habit.why: 7.Ng5 moves the same knight again while your queenside pieces sleep, and 7...Nh6 covers f7 with a developing move. You castle a move late and Black safely takes a third pawn: 8.O-O dxc3 9.Qb3 O-O 10.Nxc3 d6 leaves you two pawns down with no centre.

strays.text: The pin on c3 stays, giving Black time to guard f7 and grab c3.

taught.why: Castling ends the pin, so 8.cxd4 is threatened at once. After 7...Nf6 8.cxd4 Nxe4 you gain time with every move, 9.d5 hitting the c6-knight and 10.Qd4 forking the loose e4-knight and g7, and the game stays roughly level despite the pawns.

enforces.text: With your king off e1, 8.cxd4 puts a pawn back beside e4.

15856967415293|f3g5.principle: Your c3 pawn is pinned to your king, so deal with the pin first: 7.O-O makes 8.cxd4 possible at once, while 7.Ng5 gives Black time for 7...Nh6 and 8...dxc3.

alternatives.after: 7.O-O is just as good and more popular (59%): it breaks the pin first and keeps your queen free for 10.Qd4, while 7.Qb3 makes Black defend f7 first and castles a move later.

alternatives.after: 7.O-O keeps the recapture for the c-pawn: after 7...Nf6 8.cxd4 you have pawns on e4 and d4 again. GM Mihail Marin calls 7.Nxd4 illogical for giving that up.

1607436244732164|c6d4.headline: 4...Nd4 leaves e5 hanging; develop with 4...Nf6.
1607436244732164|c6d4.why: Moving the knight a second time removes e5's only defender, so 5.Nxe5 wins a pawn and then strikes at f7 with 6.Nxf7. 4...Nf6 develops the knight toward the centre and attacks the pawn on e4, leading to the quiet Giuoco Pianissimo after 5.d3; it is the choice in 89.6% of master games.
1607436244732164|c6d4.principle: A second knight move before the kingside knight is out must win something concrete; here it only abandons the e5 pawn.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. O-O

1642112043242450|f6d5.headline: After 5.exd5, play 5...Na5 and take the bishop off f7
1642112043242450|f6d5.why: 5...Nxd5 opens the door to the Fried Liver: 6.Nxf7 Kxf7 7.Qf3+ drags the black king into the centre, and White brings more pieces with 8.Nc3 while it is stuck there. 5...Na5, the Polerio variation, moves the attacked knight out of the pawn's reach and hits the bishop on c4, ending its pressure on f7. After 6.Bb5+ c6 7.dxc6 bxc6 Black is a pawn down but has the more active pieces, and is considered equal.
1642112043242450|f6d5.principle: With White's knight on g5 and bishop on c4 both aimed at f7, drive the bishop off that diagonal before you open lines near your king.

1642112043242450|f6e4.headline: Save the c6 knight with 5...Na5, hitting the bishop
1642112043242450|f6e4.why: White threatens 6.dxc6, and 5...Ne4 doesn't address it: it moves the f6 knight onto a square where the g5 knight takes it with 6.Nxe4, and the c6 knight is still attacked. 5...Na5, the Polerio variation, is the theory's best move: it gets the knight out of the pawn's way and attacks the c4 bishop. After 6.Bb5+ c6 7.dxc6 bxc6 White is a pawn up, but Black has more active pieces and is considered equal.
1642112043242450|f6e4.principle: First check which of your pieces are attacked; when a pawn hits a knight, move that knight, ideally to a square where it attacks something.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...d5/5. exd5

1652894211754070|g1f3.headline: 4...Bg6 is unusual: strike with 5.e6 before Black plays ...e6
1652894211754070|g1f3.why: Theory calls 4...Bg6 a highly unusual reply to 4.Bd3: Black avoids the bishop trade but hasn't played ...e6, so the e6 square is still open to your pawn. 5.Nf3 lets Black fix that with 5...e6 and reach a normal Advance structure. 5.e6 strikes first: after 5...Qc8 6.exf7+ Bxf7 Black's king is loosened, and 7.Nf3 Nf6 8.Ne5 hits the bishop on f7, with a clear advantage.
1652894211754070|g1f3.principle: When your opponent spends moves shuffling a bishop, open lines with a pawn break before they finish developing.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. e5/3...Bf5/4. Bd3/4...Bg6

1652894211754070|h2h4.headline: Break with 5.e6 while Black's kingside is undeveloped
1652894211754070|h2h4.why: 5.h4, the usual pawn chase against the g6 bishop, gives Black time to trade it with 5...Bxd3 6.cxd3, leaving you with doubled d-pawns and much of your edge gone. 5.e6 strikes before Black has developed a kingside piece: the pawn hits f7, and after 5...Qc8 6.exf7+ Bxf7 7.Nf3 Nf6 8.Ne5 e6 9.Nxf7 Kxf7 you have the bishop pair, Black's king has lost the right to castle, and you keep a clear advantage.
1652894211754070|h2h4.principle: 4...Bg6 handed you a real advantage, and an advantage has to be used at once: open lines against the uncastled king before Black untangles, instead of a slow wing plan.

1657768441002862|g7g6.headline: 3...Nf6 first: an early ...g6 lets the queen recapture on d4
1657768441002862|g7g6.why: 3...g6 lets White take back on d4 with the queen: after 4.d4 cxd4 5.Qxd4 the queen eyes your h8 rook down the long diagonal. Following 5...Nf6 6.Bb5+ Nc6 7.e5 dxe5 8.Qxd8+ the queens come off, and your king has to take back and loses the right to castle. 3...Nf6 attacks e4 first, so after 4.d4 cxd4 White takes back with 5.Nxd4 and you reach the main Open Sicilian. You keep the choice of system, such as the Najdorf with 5...a6.
1657768441002862|g7g6.principle: Knights before bishops: develop the g8 knight first, and decide later whether your bishop goes to g7.
sources: Move Order Tricks in the 2.Nc3 Sicilian! (GM Max Illingworth) | https://www.chess.com/blog/Illingworth/move-order-tricks-in-the-2-nc3-sicilian-1
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Nc3

ideas.title: Hit e4 with ...Nf6 early
ideas.text: 3...Nf6 attacks e4 at once; after 4.d4 cxd4 White takes back with 5.Nxd4 instead of the queen.

ideas.title: Queen on d4 eyes h8
ideas.text: Once your g-pawn has moved, 5.Qxd4 hits h8 down the long diagonal, and you must block before developing freely.

ideas.title: Keep the Open Sicilian choices
ideas.text: After 3...Nf6 4.d4 cxd4 5.Nxd4 you choose your system, such as the Najdorf with 5...a6.

ideas.title: The pin on b5
ideas.text: In the 3...g6 line 6.Bb5+ pins the c6 knight, and 7.e5 opens the centre while your king is uncastled.

habit.why: 3...g6 lets White take back on d4 with the queen: after 4.d4 cxd4 5.Qxd4 the queen eyes your h8 rook down the long diagonal. Following 5...Nf6 6.Bb5+ Nc6 7.e5 dxe5 8.Qxd8+ the queens come off, and your king has to take back and loses the right to castle.

strays.text: Nothing hits e4, so White can take back on d4 with the queen.

taught.why: 3...Nf6 attacks e4 first, so after 4.d4 cxd4 White takes back with 5.Nxd4 and you reach the main Open Sicilian. You keep the choice of system, such as the Najdorf with 5...a6.

enforces.text: The knight hits e4 before the d-pawns are traded.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3...Nc6 develops, and after 4.d4 cxd4 5.Nxd4 it becomes a Classical Sicilian, where 6.Bg5, 7.Qd2 and 8.O-O-O are White's main line. Masters play it 13% of the time, though the engine rates it a bit lower.
alternatives.after: 3...Nf6 usually transposes after 4.d4 cxd4 5.Nxd4, but it keeps c6 free for other setups, so the Najdorf with 5...a6 stays available.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3...a6 aims for a Najdorf, but White isn't committed to 4.d4 yet and can choose a closed setup with g3, where ...a6 is less useful. Masters play it 18% of the time; the engine rates it slightly lower.
alternatives.after: 3...Nf6 makes White deal with e4 first, and after 4.d4 cxd4 5.Nxd4 a6 you get the Najdorf anyway.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3...e6 heads for a Scheveningen, but after 4.d4 cxd4 5.Nxd4 a6 6.Be3 White sets up 7.Qd2 and 8.f3 with a quick attacking plan. Masters rarely play it (2%).
alternatives.after: 3...Nf6 hits e4 at once and keeps both ...e6 and ...e5 setups open.

1694081511794223|g5e6.headline: Win the e6 pawn with 7.Qg4, not with the knight
1694081511794223|g5e6.why: 7.Nxe6 takes the pawn with the knight and leaves f2 guarded only by your king: 7...Bxf2+ 8.Kf1 Qd7 9.Nxc7+ Qxc7 10.Kxf2. You end up a pawn ahead, but your king can't castle and Black's pieces are active. 7.Qg4 hits e6 a second time, and now the 7...Bxf2+ trick just loses the bishop. After 7...Qf6 8.Qxe6+ Nge7 9.Qxf6 gxf6 you're a clean pawn up in an endgame with Black's pawns broken.
1694081511794223|g5e6.principle: Check what's loose on both sides: e6 is loose for Black and f2 for you, so win e6 with 7.Qg4, where the 7...Bxf2+ trick fails.

ideas.title: Pick off the loose e6 pawn
ideas.text: After 6...fxe6 nothing defends the e6 pawn. 7.Qg4 hits it a second time and wins it cleanly.

ideas.title: Watch the f2 trick
ideas.text: Only your king guards f2. With your knight on e6, 7...Bxf2+ pulls the king out; taking the bishop lets a queen check win the knight.

ideas.title: Keep your king able to castle
ideas.text: After 7.Qg4 your king can still castle; after 7.Nxe6 Bxf2+ 8.Kf1 it never can.

habit.why: 7.Nxe6 takes the pawn with the knight and leaves f2 guarded only by your king: 7...Bxf2+ 8.Kf1 Qd7 9.Nxc7+ Qxc7 10.Kxf2. You end up a pawn ahead, but your king can't castle and Black's pieces are active.

strays.text: The knight capture lets 7...Bxf2+ pull your king out and costs you castling.

taught.why: 7.Qg4 hits e6 a second time, and now the 7...Bxf2+ trick just loses the bishop. After 7...Qf6 8.Qxe6+ Nge7 9.Qxf6 gxf6 you're a clean pawn up in an endgame with Black's pawns broken.

enforces.idea: Pick off the loose e6 pawn
enforces.text: The queen wins e6 and your king keeps the right to castle.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.Qf3 eyes the open f-file but doesn't attack e6 at all. After 7...Qe7 8.Qh3 Kd7 Black's king steps up to guard e6.
alternatives.after: 7.Qg4 attacks e6 twice and wins it, while 7.Qf3 lets Black cover it with 7...Qe7 and 8...Kd7.
alternatives.idea: Pick off the loose e6 pawn

17066305934542|f3e5.headline: Save the bishop by taking on f7 with check
17066305934542|f3e5.why: 7.Nxe5 grabs a pawn but leaves your bishop hanging: 7...Nxc4 8.Nxc4 d5 hits the knight and opens the centre. After 9.Nxb6 axb6 10.d3 dxe4 11.dxe4 Qxd1+ the queens are off, your king has lost castling and your edge is gone. 7.Bxf7+ saves the bishop with check and wins a pawn; if the king takes, 8.Nxe5+ exposes it even more. After 7...Kf8 8.Nxe5 Qf6 9.d4 d6 10.Ng6+ Kxf7 11.Nxh8+ you pick up the h8 rook as well.
17066305934542|f3e5.principle: When a piece is attacked, see if it can move with check and win something: 7.Bxf7+ saves the bishop and takes a pawn.
sources: Georgios Souleidis and Karsten Müller, Winning with the Slow (but Venomous!) Italian (New in Chess preview) | https://www.sjakkbutikken.no/media/productimages/preview-winning-with-the-slow-but-venomous-italian.pdf

Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bb6

ideas.title: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
ideas.text: 7.Bxf7+ moves the attacked bishop with check. If the king takes, 8.Nxe5+ checks again; after 7...Kf8 your knight takes e5 next.

ideas.title: Answer a threat with a bigger threat
ideas.text: Black threatens 7...Nxc4. Grabbing e5 ignores the threat; a check makes Black answer you first.

ideas.title: ...Na5 chases the bishop
ideas.text: After 6.b5 the knight jumps to a5 to hit your c4 bishop. Pushing b5 too early invites exactly this.

ideas.title: A king that can't castle
ideas.text: After 7...Kf8 Black's king can never castle, and in the engine line 10.Ng6+ forks king and h8 rook.

habit.why: 7.Nxe5 grabs a pawn but leaves your bishop hanging: 7...Nxc4 8.Nxc4 d5 hits the knight and opens the centre. After 9.Nxb6 axb6 10.d3 dxe4 11.dxe4 Qxd1+ the queens are off, your king has lost castling and your edge is gone.

strays.idea: Answer a threat with a bigger threat
strays.text: You take a pawn while Black takes your bishop.

taught.why: 7.Bxf7+ saves the bishop with check and wins a pawn; if the king takes, 8.Nxe5+ exposes it even more. After 7...Kf8 8.Nxe5 Qf6 9.d4 d6 10.Ng6+ Kxf7 11.Nxh8+ you pick up the h8 rook as well.

enforces.idea: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
enforces.text: The bishop leaves with check and takes f7, so you win material.

1706874451895020|c8g4.headline: A pawn up in the Roscher Gambit, consolidate with 4...g6.
1706874451895020|c8g4.why: 4...Bg4 leaves the knight on e4 and the pawn on b7 both loose, and 5.Bd5 attacks them at once; after 5...Nf6 6.Bxb7 White regains the pawn and then takes the rook in the corner with 7.Bxa8. Black has already won the e4 pawn, and the theory calls the gambit unsound as long as Black keeps it. 4...g6 prepares ...Bg7 and castling, and the knight drops back with 6...Nf6 once White plays 6.Re1.
1706874451895020|c8g4.principle: After accepting a gambit pawn, spend your next moves on development and king safety and keep your pieces defended, rather than starting adventures.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6/2. d4/2...Nf6/3. Nf3

1711540021875497|b8c6.headline: Stop e4 with 3...Nf6; the knight on c6 lets White expand
1711540021875497|b8c6.why: 3...Nc6 doesn't control e4, so White plays 4.e4 and gains space with 5.e5, kicking your knight; after 5...Ne4 6.Ne2 f6 Black has to push pawns to free the position. 3...Nf6 develops and guards e4, so White's knight on c3 is left blocking its own c-pawn with no central break. After 4.Qd3 Bb4 Black pins that knight and jumps in with 5...Ne4.
1711540021875497|b8c6.principle: In closed 1.d4 openings, keep control of e4 so White can't add a second centre pawn; the knight on f6 does that while developing.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. Nc3

1743288401012634|e1h1.headline: Cash in on f7 with 5.Nxf7; 5.O-O lets Black castle
1743288401012634|e1h1.why: 5.O-O ignores the attack on f7 you set up with 4.Ng5, and 5...O-O covers it for good. After 6.d3 d5 7.exd5 Bg4 8.Nf3 Nxd5 the knight is back on f3 and Black has developed freely. 5.Nxf7 forks the d8 queen and h8 rook: after 5...Bxf2+ 6.Kf1 Qe7 7.Nxh8 you win the rook. Black fights back with 7...d5 8.exd5 Nd4, and Quintiliano gives 9.d6 as the right answer, but warns that after 9...Qxd6 Black has real complications and you must play very precisely.
1743288401012634|e1h1.principle: When your attack has created a real target, cash it in at once instead of making a quiet move that lets the opponent cover it.
sources: IM Renato Quintiliano, Is the Traxler Variation still viable? (ChessBase) | https://en.chessbase.com/newsroom/post/is-the-traxler-variation-still-viable-2?page=0
