ideas.title: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
ideas.text: f7 is attacked twice and guarded only by the king. 5.Nxf7 forks queen and rook; 5.Bxf7+ drags the king up.

ideas.title: Ng5 needs a real target
ideas.text: Here f7 is a real target, which is why 4.Ng5 was played. A quiet move lets Black castle and cover it.

ideas.title: Kf1: out of reach of checks
ideas.text: After 5.Nxf7 Bxf2+, step to f1: taking the bishop with the king allows a knight check on e4.

ideas.title: Black's counter on f2
ideas.text: 4...Bc5 ignores f7 and aims at f2, hoping for wild play if you grab on f7 carelessly.

habit.why: 5.O-O ignores the attack on f7 you set up with 4.Ng5, and 5...O-O covers it for good. After 6.d3 d5 7.exd5 Bg4 8.Nf3 Nxd5 the knight is back on f3 and Black has developed freely.

strays.text: f7 was a real target; castling lets Black cover it.

taught.why: 5.Nxf7 forks the d8 queen and h8 rook: after 5...Bxf2+ 6.Kf1 Qe7 7.Nxh8 you win the rook. Black fights back with 7...d5 8.exd5 Nd4, and Quintiliano gives 9.d6 as the right answer, but warns that after 9...Qxd6 Black has real complications and you must play very precisely.

enforces.idea: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
enforces.text: The knight takes on f7 with a fork, and the rook falls.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.Bxf7+ is the masters' main choice (68%) and a safe way to win a pawn: after 5...Ke7 6.Bc4 Black's king can never castle. Black gets the f-file and quick development for it, and the engine rates one other move a little higher.
alternatives.after: Masters prefer 5.Bxf7+ (68%) because it is safe; 5.Nxf7 (21%) wins more material, but only if you know 6.Kf1 after 5...Bxf2+.
alternatives.idea: Hit f7 only with a follow-up

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.d4 opens the centre; after 5...d5 6.Bxd5 Nxd4 7.Bxf7+ Ke7 8.Bc4 you are a pawn up, but Black's active pieces give practical chances.
alternatives.after: 5.Nxf7 cashes in the attack on f7 at once and wins more material, as long as you meet 5...Bxf2+ with 6.Kf1.
alternatives.idea: Hit f7 only with a follow-up

1783814385093536|d7d5.headline: Don't open the centre yet: 5...a6 takes b5 first
1783814385093536|d7d5.why: 5...d5 opens the centre while you have no pieces out: 6.Bb5+ Nc6 7.exd5 exd5 8.Ne5 hits your pinned knight and the isolated d5 pawn. After 8...Bd7 9.Qxd5 Nxe5 10.Qxe5+ White has the pawn back and your king is in check in the middle. 5...a6 keeps White's bishop and knight off b5, so the check and pin from the habit line are gone. After 6.Bf4 Nc6 7.Be2 d6 8.O-O Be7 you develop behind a solid pawn front and keep the extra pawn; masters choose it most often (42%).
1783814385093536|d7d5.principle: White is ahead in development, so keep the centre closed for now: 5...a6 takes b5 away, while 5...d5 opens lines before your pieces are out.
sources: IM Hannes Langrock, The Modern Morra Gambit (excerpt) | https://www.newinchess.com/media/wysiwyg/product_pdf/2702.pdf
Albert Hoogendoorn, The Smith-Morra Gambit, Part I | http://www.chessvictory.com/SmithMorra.pdf
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smith%E2%80%93Morra_Gambit

ideas.title: Take b5 away with ...a6
ideas.text: 5...a6 keeps White's knight and bishop off b5, the entry square Morra players use for checks, pins and jumps to d6 and c7.

ideas.title: The d6 hole
ideas.text: With your e-pawn on e6 and the d-pawn at home, d6 has no pawn guard. A white knight reaching b5 eyes d6 and c7.

ideas.title: Don't open the centre undeveloped
ideas.text: Opening lines helps the side ahead in development. 5...d5 opens the centre while none of your pieces are out.

ideas.title: The e4-e5 break
ideas.text: White's main pawn break: e4-e5 grabs space and cramps you, as in 6.e5 after 5...d6, or 10.e5 in the main line.

habit.why: 5...d5 opens the centre while you have no pieces out: 6.Bb5+ Nc6 7.exd5 exd5 8.Ne5 hits your pinned knight and the isolated d5 pawn. After 8...Bd7 9.Qxd5 Nxe5 10.Qxe5+ White has the pawn back and your king is in check in the middle.

strays.text: The centre opens while your pieces are at home, and the d5 pawn falls.

taught.why: 5...a6 keeps White's bishop and knight off b5, so the check and pin from the habit line are gone. After 6.Bf4 Nc6 7.Be2 d6 8.O-O Be7 you develop behind a solid pawn front and keep the extra pawn; masters choose it most often (42%).

enforces.text: The pawn covers b5 before White's pieces can use it.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...Nc6 develops and reaches the main Morra position; it's played in 38.5% of master games and is fully sound. One other move is slightly more popular.
alternatives.after: Both are main lines. 5...a6 (42%) takes b5 first; 5...Nc6 (38.5%) develops first and transposes to the main Morra tabiya.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...Bb4 pins the c3-knight, but IM Langrock calls it dubious: 6.Qd4 hits the bishop and g7 at once, and after 6...Bf8 the bishop is back home.
alternatives.after: Langrock rates 5...Bb4 dubious, but the engine finds it level, because after 6.Qd4 Bf8 7.Qe5 d6 8.Qg3 White's queen has moved a lot too. 5...a6 is the calmer, more common choice.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...d6 is the Scheveningen setup and holds, but White strikes at once with 6.e5, gaining space after 6...Nc6 7.Bf4 d5.
alternatives.after: Masters prefer 5...a6 (42% to 9%), which keeps b5 covered and your d-pawn flexible; after 5...d6 you must be ready for e4-e5 every move.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...Bc5 develops the bishop outside the pawn chain, but White can still cramp you with 6.Bf4 and later 9.e5, even with your d-pawn at home.
alternatives.after: 5...a6 is the most common master move (42%, against 9% for 5...Bc5). Both are sound; 5...Bc5 invites White's e4-e5 push.

1783814385093536|f8b4.headline: Morra: play 5...a6; 5...Bb4 runs into 6.Qd4
1783814385093536|f8b4.why: 5...Bb4 leaves the bishop loose, and 6.Qd4 hits it and g7 at once. You must retreat with 6...Bf8 or give up the bishop for the knight, and after 7.Qe5 Nc6 8.Qg3 the queen keeps eyeing g7 while you untangle. 5...a6 keeps White's knight off b5, so d6 can't be hit with a knight jump. After 6.Bf4 Nc6 7.Be2 d6 8.O-O Be7 you have a solid setup and the extra pawn, with White's e4-e5 break the thing to watch.
1783814385093536|f8b4.principle: Accept a gambit only if you can consolidate: make the safe move 5...a6 rather than a bishop sortie that White can hit.
sources: Hannes Langrock, The Modern Morra Gambit (excerpt) | https://www.scacco.it/data/attachments/7011/morra.pdf
Hannes Langrock, The Modern Morra Gambit, 2nd ed. (New in Chess excerpt) | https://www.newinchess.com/media/wysiwyg/product_pdf/2702.pdf

ideas.title: The Qd4 double attack
ideas.text: After 5...Bb4, 6.Qd4 hits the loose bishop and g7 at once: the bishop must retreat or take on c3.

ideas.title: Knight jumps to b5, d5, d6
ideas.text: With ...e6 played, d6 has no pawn guard and a knight jumping to b5 aims at it. 5...a6 takes b5 away first.

ideas.title: Morra setup: fast development, open files
ideas.text: For the pawn White gets quick development and the open c-file: 6.Bf4 aims at d6, then castling and 9.Rc1.

ideas.title: The e4-e5 break
ideas.text: White's main pawn lever: e4-e5 gains space and kicks a knight from f6, as in 9...Nf6 10.e5.

habit.why: 5...Bb4 leaves the bishop loose, and 6.Qd4 hits it and g7 at once. You must retreat with 6...Bf8 or give up the bishop for the knight, and after 7.Qe5 Nc6 8.Qg3 the queen keeps eyeing g7 while you untangle.

strays.text: The bishop lands on a loose square where 6.Qd4 hits it and g7.

taught.why: 5...a6 keeps White's knight off b5, so d6 can't be hit with a knight jump. After 6.Bf4 Nc6 7.Be2 d6 8.O-O Be7 you have a solid setup and the extra pawn, with White's e4-e5 break the thing to watch.

enforces.idea: Knight jumps to b5, d5, d6
enforces.text: ...a6 takes b5 from the knight before d6 can be hit.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...Nc6 is sound and popular with masters: it develops and covers d4, which rules out the queen jump there. After 6.Be2 d6 7.O-O Be7 8.Qb3 you have a standard Morra setup.
alternatives.after: 5...a6 first keeps b5 covered against knight jumps, and 5...Nc6 is just as good. Masters split almost evenly (42% to 39%).

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...d6 is sound and leads to the usual ...e6/...d6 Morra setups, though 6.e5 Nc6 7.Bf4 shows White can gain space at once. There is a slightly more flexible move.
alternatives.after: 5...a6 covers b5 first and leaves the d-pawn's decision for later. Both are sound; masters prefer 5...a6 (42% to 9%).

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...Bc5 develops and is playable, but White often answers it with the space-gaining e4-e5, as in 6.Bf4 Nc6 7.a3 and later 9.e5.
alternatives.after: 5...a6 keeps your bishop home until you know where it is safe, and stops the knight jump to b5. Masters prefer it (42% to 9%), though both are sound.

1790000171764366|f3g5.headline: Ng5 hangs the knight to the queen; strike with 5.d4
1790000171764366|f3g5.why: 5.Ng5 drops the knight: with Black's e-pawn on e5 and the f-pawn gone to e6, the diagonal from d8 to g5 is open and 5...Qxg5 just takes it. Black has spent the opening on pawn moves and the trade on e6, so 5.d4, played in 71% of master games, opens the centre while Black's kingside pieces are still at home. After 5...exd4 6.Nxd4 the knight is centralised and eyes the weak e6 pawn.
1790000171764366|f3g5.principle: Before a knight jump, check every enemy piece that can reach the landing square: the queen on d8 covered g5 along the open diagonal.

1890995340270663|d1d5.headline: The queen fork needs check: retreat with 9.Bb3 instead
1890995340270663|d1d5.why: 9.Qd5 is not check, so Black calmly guards the c5 bishop with 9...d6. After 10.Bxg8 Rxg8 11.Ng5 Qe8 you have traded your best attacking bishop and the c3 pawn is still Black's. 9.Bb3 saves the bishop from the king and keeps it on the diagonal toward g8. After 9...d6 10.Nxc3 you win back the c3 pawn with development, and Black's king can never castle.
1890995340270663|d1d5.principle: When the opponent's king has lost castling, keep your attacking pieces and develop: 9.Bb3 saves the bishop and 10.Nxc3 wins back a pawn.
sources: John Nunn, GM tutorial: Learn to play the Evans Gambit (ChessBase) | https://en.chessbase.com/post/john-nunn-learn-to-play-the-evans-gambit
Evans Gambit (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evans_Gambit

ideas.title: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
ideas.text: The queen fork on d5 works only with check. With the king on f8, 9.Qd5 is not check, and 9...d6 guards c5.

ideas.title: Save the bishop, keep the aim
ideas.text: Black's king attacks your f7 bishop. 9.Bb3 saves it and keeps it on the diagonal toward g8.

ideas.title: King in the centre: keep queens
ideas.text: Black's king has lost castling and stands on f8. Keep the queens on and bring pieces out, starting with 10.Nxc3.

habit.why: 9.Qd5 is not check, so Black calmly guards the c5 bishop with 9...d6. After 10.Bxg8 Rxg8 11.Ng5 Qe8 you have traded your best attacking bishop and the c3 pawn is still Black's.

strays.idea: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
strays.text: Without check, the queen on d5 gives Black time for 9...d6.

taught.why: 9.Bb3 saves the bishop from the king and keeps it on the diagonal toward g8. After 9...d6 10.Nxc3 you win back the c3 pawn with development, and Black's king can never castle.

enforces.idea: Save the bishop, keep the aim
enforces.text: The bishop stays aimed at g8, and 10.Nxc3 follows.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 9.Bxg8 Rxg8 is a good choice: the bishop takes a knight before the king can take it, and 10.Ng5 with 11.e5 aims at the boxed-in king.
alternatives.after: The engine rates 9.Bxg8 at least as highly as 9.Bb3. The difference is the plan: 9.Bb3 keeps your bishop aimed at the king, 9.Bxg8 trades it and attacks with knight and pawns.
alternatives.idea: Save the bishop, keep the aim

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 9.Nxc3 is natural and sound: it wins back the c3 pawn and develops. Your f7 bishop is safe for now, since taking it walks into a queen check on d5 that hits c5.
alternatives.after: 9.Nxc3 is accepted too: it just changes the order. 9.Bb3 moves the attacked bishop first and 10.Nxc3 follows; either way Black's king can't castle.
alternatives.idea: King in the centre: keep queens

1891225405277048|f1c4.headline: After 2...b6, take the centre with 3.d4
1891225405277048|f1c4.why: 3.Bc4 points the bishop at a pawn wall on e6, and 3...d5 hits it: after 4.exd5 exd5 it has to retreat with 5.Be2 and White has lost time. 2...b6 did nothing for the centre, so 3.d4 builds a two-pawn centre for free; the masters play it 92.9% of the time. The bishop then develops with 4.Bd3, where it guards e4 against the bishop on b7.
1891225405277048|f1c4.principle: When your opponent spends a move on the wing, occupy the centre with pawns before developing a bishop into a pawn's reach.

1895778820316678|d1b3.headline: Stop Black castling with 8.Ba3, not 8.Qb3
1895778820316678|d1b3.why: 8.Qb3 aims at f7, but 8...O-O covers it, and the queen trip does nothing for your loose e4 pawn. After 9.cxd4 Nxe4 Black is two pawns up and your centre is half gone. 8.Ba3 uses the diagonal the b-pawn opened to stop Black castling, so Black spends 8...d6 to block it. Then 9.e5 Ne4 10.exd6 cxd6 11.Qe2 hits the e4 knight and you develop with tempo; Marin calls 8.Ba3 typical of the Evans, and masters choose it 60% of the time.
1895778820316678|d1b3.principle: In a gambit every move must gain time: 8.Ba3 stops Black castling, while 8.Qb3 lets Black castle and take e4.
sources: GM Mihail Marin, Beating the Open Games, ch. 7 (preview) | https://www.sjakkbutikken.no/media/productimages/preview-beating-the-open-games.pdf
GM John Nunn, Learn to play the Evans Gambit (ChessBase) | https://en.chessbase.com/post/john-nunn-learn-to-play-the-evans-gambit

ideas.title: Evans tempo moves: e5, Ba3, Qb3
ideas.text: 8.Ba3 uses the diagonal your b-pawn opened to stop Black castling; 8.e5 kicks the f6 knight. Each must leave nothing loose.

ideas.title: Evans: the centre is the payment
ideas.text: cxd4 rebuilds pawns on e4 and d4, but e4 must not be left hanging: 8.cxd4 Nxe4 grabs it.

ideas.title: Black wants to castle
ideas.text: 7...Nf6 develops and prepares ...O-O. Once Black's king is on g8, your pressure on f7 is gone.

ideas.title: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
ideas.text: Queen on b3 and bishop on c4 aim at f7, but that only works while Black's king is still on e8.

habit.why: 8.Qb3 aims at f7, but 8...O-O covers it, and the queen trip does nothing for your loose e4 pawn. After 9.cxd4 Nxe4 Black is two pawns up and your centre is half gone.

strays.text: Black castles at once, and f7 is safe.

taught.why: 8.Ba3 uses the diagonal the b-pawn opened to stop Black castling, so Black spends 8...d6 to block it. Then 9.e5 Ne4 10.exd6 cxd6 11.Qe2 hits the e4 knight and you develop with tempo; Marin calls 8.Ba3 typical of the Evans, and masters choose it 60% of the time.

enforces.idea: Evans tempo moves: e5, Ba3, Qb3
enforces.text: The bishop takes f8 from Black's king and forces a reply.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 8.e5 kicks the f6 knight at once and is a good, popular move (31% of masters). After 8...d5 9.exf6 dxc4 10.fxg7 Rg8 the game gets very sharp.
alternatives.after: Masters prefer 8.Ba3 (60%), and Marin shows that the 8.Ba3 d6 9.e5 Ne4 order can gain a tempo over similar 8.e5 lines.
alternatives.idea: Evans tempo moves: e5, Ba3, Qb3

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 8.cxd4 rebuilds your centre, but leaves e4 loose: after 8...Nxe4 9.d5 Ne7 10.Qd4 Nf6 11.Bg5 you have to work to win back the pawn.
alternatives.after: 8.Ba3 first stops Black castling and keeps e4 from dropping at once; masters play it 60% of the time, 8.cxd4 only 9%.
alternatives.idea: Evans: the centre is the payment

1905410911939124|e1h1.headline: Push 6.f4 so Black's f-pawn can never reach f4
1905410911939124|e1h1.why: 6.O-O lets Black play 6...f4, which shuts in your c1 bishop and starts a pawn storm toward the king you just castled. After 7.h4 Be7 8.Qh5+ Kf8 9.Nc3 Nd4 10.Be3 Bg4 Black's pieces come out with threats against your queen. 6.f4 meets the f-pawn with your own, so 6...f4 never comes, your c1 bishop stays free and the f-file opens toward Black's uncastled king. In 6...fxe4 7.Nc3 Bg4 8.Qd2 Nb4 9.Bb3 exd3 Black grabs pawns, but you develop fast while Black's king is still in the centre.
1905410911939124|e1h1.principle: Ask what Black wants first: 6.f4 stops the ...f4 bind before it starts, while 6.O-O lets it happen.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4

ideas.title: Support the g5 knight
ideas.text: Your g5 knight hits f7 and e6, but no pawn supports it. 6.f4 gives it a pawn guard and stops Black's pawn advancing.

ideas.title: Black's ...f4 bind
ideas.text: If Black's pawn reaches f4 it shuts in your c1 bishop and starts a kingside pawn storm, as after 6.O-O f4.

ideas.title: Hit back in the centre
ideas.text: Black has spent moves on pawns. Open lines and develop fast, as in 6.f4 fxe4 7.Nc3, while Black's king is still on e8.

ideas.title: Don't take on f5
ideas.text: 6.exf5 gives up your central e4 pawn, and 6...Bxf5 develops Black's bishop with nothing lost.

habit.why: 6.O-O lets Black play 6...f4, which shuts in your c1 bishop and starts a pawn storm toward the king you just castled. After 7.h4 Be7 8.Qh5+ Kf8 9.Nc3 Nd4 10.Be3 Bg4 Black's pieces come out with threats against your queen.

strays.text: Castling ignores the threat, and 6...f4 locks in your bishop and storms your king.

taught.why: 6.f4 meets the f-pawn with your own, so 6...f4 never comes, your c1 bishop stays free and the f-file opens toward Black's uncastled king. In 6...fxe4 7.Nc3 Bg4 8.Qd2 Nb4 9.Bb3 exd3 Black grabs pawns, but you develop fast while Black's king is still in the centre.

enforces.text: The f4 pawn guards your g5 knight and opens the f-file.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.exf5 gives up your central e4 pawn, and 6...Bxf5 develops Black's bishop for free. After 7.Nc3 Qd7 Black castles long with easy play.
alternatives.after: 6.f4 meets the f-pawn with a pawn of your own and opens the f-file, instead of helping Black develop.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 6.Qh5+ looks scary, but 6...g6 hits the queen and it has to retreat with 7.Qe2. Black then advances the f-pawn anyway and keeps the bind, as in 8.Nf3 Bg7.
alternatives.after: 6.f4 stops Black's f-pawn for good without moving your queen; 6.Qh5+ just loses time to 6...g6.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 6.Ne6 jumps into e6, but 6...Bxe6 7.Bxe6 trades it off. You get the bishop pair, but Black gains time with 7...Qf6, hitting your bishop, and then pushes the f-pawn.
alternatives.after: 6.f4 keeps your knight and stops Black's pawn for good; after 6.Ne6 the knight is swapped off and Black still gets in 8...f4.

1922438896562435|f1c4.headline: After 2...Nc6, take the whole centre with 3.d4
1922438896562435|f1c4.why: 3.Bc4 runs into 3...d5, which attacks the bishop and frees Black's game; after 4.exd5 exd5 the bishop has to move again with 5.Bb5, and Black's centre is fine. 2...Nc6 put the knight in front of Black's c-pawn, so Black has no quick pawn strike against d4: 3.d4 sets up two central pawns, and after 3...d5 4.e5 White has a clear space advantage. Masters choose it 91% of the time.
1922438896562435|f1c4.principle: When the opponent's piece blocks the pawn that would challenge your centre, put a second pawn in the middle at once.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. Nf3

1931050112551786|e6e5.headline: Recapture 4...exd5: keep a pawn in the centre
1931050112551786|e6e5.why: 4...e5 leaves the d5 pawn hanging and lets White open the f-file: after 5.fxe5 Qxd5 6.Nc3 Qe6 you are simply a pawn down. Your queen keeps getting chased too, as in 7.b3 Nc6 8.Bc4 Qe7. 4...exd5 wins the pawn back at once and opens your c8 bishop's diagonal. After 5.Bb5+ Nc6 6.Nc3 Nf6 you have a free centre and equal chances; all 22 master games went 4...exd5.
1931050112551786|e6e5.principle: Hold the centre with a pawn: after 4.exd5, 4...exd5 takes back with a pawn and frees your c8 bishop, while 4...e5 just leaves a pawn hanging.
sources: Shaun Sedice, Playing the Grand Prix Attack (Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/grand-prix-attack/
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. f4

ideas.title: Strike with ...d5
ideas.text: Against an early f4, ...e6 and ...d5 is the standard reply. After the trade on d5 you have a free centre.

ideas.title: Keep a pawn in the centre
ideas.text: After 4.exd5, take back with the e-pawn: a pawn on d5 holds the centre and opens the diagonal for your c8 bishop.

ideas.title: Bb5 against d5
ideas.text: White's plan against a d5 pawn is a bishop check from b5 and piece pressure. Develop fast with ...Nc6 and ...Nf6.

habit.why: 4...e5 leaves the d5 pawn hanging and lets White open the f-file: after 5.fxe5 Qxd5 6.Nc3 Qe6 you are simply a pawn down. Your queen keeps getting chased too, as in 7.b3 Nc6 8.Bc4 Qe7.

strays.idea: Keep a pawn in the centre
strays.text: It gives up the d5 pawn instead of retaking it.

taught.why: 4...exd5 wins the pawn back at once and opens your c8 bishop's diagonal. After 5.Bb5+ Nc6 6.Nc3 Nf6 you have a free centre and equal chances; all 22 master games went 4...exd5.

enforces.idea: Keep a pawn in the centre
enforces.text: The e-pawn takes back, and a pawn holds d5.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.idea: Keep a pawn in the centre
alternatives.before: 4...Qxd5 wins the pawn back and avoids an isolated d-pawn, but your queen gets chased: 5.Nc3 Qd8 sends it home. Sound, but there is a stronger move.
alternatives.after: 4...exd5 takes back with a pawn, so no knight gains time on your queen, and your c8 bishop's diagonal opens. Every master game chose it.

1957522496653461|f8c5.headline: After 3.d3, develop 3...Nf6 first; 3...Bc5 allows the fork trick.
1957522496653461|f8c5.why: 3...Bc5 lets White play 4.Nxe5, because after 4...Nxe5 5.d4 the pawn forks bishop and knight and White wins the piece back. 3...Nf6 develops the knight toward the centre and adds pressure on e4, and the bishop can still come to c5 later, as in 3...Nf6 4.g3 Bc5.
1957522496653461|f8c5.principle: Bring the king's knight out before the bishop: f6 is clearly its best square, while a bishop on c5 can be hit by a d4 fork.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6

1976310622037328|c7c5.headline: Prepare ...e5 with 5...c6; don't open lines with the king uncastled
1976310622037328|c7c5.why: 5...c5 gives White 6.dxc5, and after 6...Qa5 7.Bb5+ Bd7 Black's king is checked and Black only wins the pawn back with 9...dxc5 once White has developed and castled. 5...c6 is the calm, flexible move: after 6.h3 O-O 7.Bd3 Nbd7 8.a4 e5 Black gets the classic central strike with the king already safe. It is the masters' top choice here.
1976310622037328|c7c5.principle: With the king still on e8, avoid pawn breaks that open lines toward it; castle and prepare the central break with ...c6 and ...Nbd7 instead.

1976310622037328|e7e5.headline: Against 5.Bg5, prepare ...e5 with 5...c6 and castling first.
1976310622037328|e7e5.why: 5...e5 opens the centre too soon: after 6.dxe5 dxe5 7.Qxd8+ Kxd8 the king has lost castling, and 8.Nd5 adds a second attacker to the knight on f6, already hit by the bishop on g5, so after 9.Bxf6+ Bxf6 10.Nxf6 White wins a piece. 5...c6 keeps the centre closed and makes useful moves: Black castles and brings the knight to d7, and only then plays 8...e5, when 9.dxe5 Nxe5 recaptures with a piece instead of trading queens.
1976310622037328|e7e5.principle: Delay ...e5 until you have castled and can recapture with a piece, so a queen trade on d8 doesn't strand your king in the centre.

2036399053007590|b8c6.headline: In the French, follow 1...e6 with ...d5 straight away
2036399053007590|b8c6.why: 2...Nc6 lets White build the full centre with 3.d4, and after 3...d5 4.e5 the knight on c6 blocks Black's c-pawn, the usual lever against White's pawn chain. 2...d5 is played in 92.3% of master games: it claims the centre and attacks the pawn on e4 at once, in the spirit of the French defence.
2036399053007590|b8c6.principle: The e6 pawn is there to support the d-pawn, so push it to d5 and challenge e4 before White can add a second centre pawn.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. Nf3
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. Nf3/2...d5

2067858163173673|d4c6.headline: Save the knight with a threat: 6.Nb5 hits c7
2067858163173673|d4c6.why: 6.Nxc6 saves the knight from 6...Qxd4 but helps Black: 6...dxc6 opens the d-file and frees the c8 bishop. After 7.O-O Be6 8.Bb3 Bc5 Black develops easily and the queen on f6 is well placed. 6.Nb5 saves the knight and threatens to take on c7 with check, forking king and rook. After 6...Bb4+ 7.Bd2 Bxd2+ 8.Nxd2 Kd8 Black must guard c7 with the king and can never castle.
2067858163173673|d4c6.principle: When a piece is attacked, look for a square where it saves itself and makes a threat: 6.Nb5 hits c7.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...exd4/4. Nxd4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...h6

ideas.title: Answer a threat with a bigger threat
ideas.text: Black threatens 6...Qxd4. 6.Nb5 saves the knight and threatens to take on c7 with check, forking king and a8 rook.

ideas.title: Punish the early queen
ideas.text: 5...Qf6 brings the queen out before the minor pieces. Keep your knight active so the queen looks misplaced, rather than trading it off.

ideas.title: King stuck in the centre
ideas.text: In the engine line 6...Bb4+ 7.Bd2 Bxd2+ 8.Nxd2 Kd8 Black guards c7 with the king and gives up castling.

ideas.title: Recapturing towards the centre
ideas.text: After 6.Nxc6 dxc6 Black opens the d-file and frees the c8 bishop, as in 7.O-O Be6.

habit.why: 6.Nxc6 saves the knight from 6...Qxd4 but helps Black: 6...dxc6 opens the d-file and frees the c8 bishop. After 7.O-O Be6 8.Bb3 Bc5 Black develops easily and the queen on f6 is well placed.

strays.idea: Answer a threat with a bigger threat
strays.text: You trade your active knight, and the threat on c7 never comes.

taught.why: 6.Nb5 saves the knight and threatens to take on c7 with check, forking king and rook. After 6...Bb4+ 7.Bd2 Bxd2+ 8.Nxd2 Kd8 Black must guard c7 with the king and can never castle.

enforces.idea: Answer a threat with a bigger threat
enforces.text: The knight escapes and hits c7, so Black must defend.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.Be3 guards the knight and is solid: after 6...Bc5 7.c3 Nge7 8.O-O O-O you reach a classical Scotch set-up. But Black's early queen move goes unpunished.
alternatives.after: 6.Nb5 is sharper: it makes a threat at once and costs Black castling, where 6.Be3 lets Black develop normally.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.c3 props up the knight and steers into a classical Scotch set-up: 6...Bc5 7.Be3 Nge7 8.O-O O-O. It is playable, but Black develops without trouble.
alternatives.after: Against an early ...Qf6 in the plain Scotch, Wikibooks calls the knight jump sharper than propping it up with the c-pawn, and here 6.Nb5 also costs Black castling, which 6.c3 does not.

2067858163173673|d4f3.headline: Save the knight with a threat: 6.Nb5 hits c7
2067858163173673|d4f3.why: 6.Nf3 saves the knight, but it is its third move while your b1 knight and c1 bishop are still at home. After 6...Bb4+ 7.Nbd2 Nge7 8.O-O O-O Black is fully developed and level. 6.Nb5 saves the knight and threatens to take on c7 with check, forking king and rook. After 6...Bb4+ 7.Bd2 Bxd2+ 8.Nxd2 Kd8 Black must guard c7 with the king and can never castle.
2067858163173673|d4f3.principle: When a piece is attacked, look for a square where it saves itself and makes a threat: 6.Nb5 hits c7.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...exd4/4. Nxd4

ideas.title: Don't hand back the tempo
ideas.text: 3...h6 cost Black a tempo. A third knight move, with your b1 knight and c1 bishop still at home, gives it back.

strays.text: A third knight move gives back the tempo Black lost with 3...h6.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy

alternatives.after: 6.Nb5 keeps the knight and makes a threat, so Black's queen on f6 looks misplaced instead of well placed.

2094672111620588|d4e5.headline: Answer 3...f6 with 4.Bc4, aiming at the weakened light squares
2094672111620588|d4e5.why: 3...f6 holds e5 but costs a developing move and opens the a2-g8 diagonal toward Black's king. 4.dxe5 releases the tension: after 4...dxe5 the e5 pawn is firmly protected by the f6 pawn, and White's edge is small. 4.Bc4 develops onto that open diagonal, aiming through f7 at g8, where Black's king wants to castle; after 4...Nc6 5.h3 Nge7 6.O-O exd4 7.Nxd4 you have the extra development the theory says 3...f6 hands White, and a clear advantage.
2094672111620588|d4e5.principle: Black's ...f6 cost them development and weakened their king, so keep building your lead with developing moves and castling, and open the centre once your pieces are ready.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4

2107090482514507|c1e3.headline: Castle to break the pin on your c3-knight
2107090482514507|c1e3.why: 7.Be3 leaves the c3-knight pinned with your king still on e1. After 7...O-O 8.Qe2 Bxc3+ 9.bxc3 Black takes it with check, doubles your c-pawns, and most of your edge is gone. 7.O-O takes your king off the b4-e1 diagonal, so the c3-knight is no longer pinned to it. If Black still trades after 7...O-O 8.Qe2 b6 9.Bg5 Bxc3 10.bxc3, it comes without check and your g5-bishop already pins the f6-knight.
2107090482514507|c1e3.principle: Break a pin before the pinned piece is attacked again: castling takes your king off the b4-e1 diagonal and frees the c3-knight.
sources: IM Alberto Chueca, Scandinavian Defense | https://www.albertochueca.com/blog/scandinavian-defense/
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qd8

ideas.title: Break the pin by castling
ideas.text: The b4-bishop pins your c3-knight to the king. 7.O-O takes the king off that diagonal, so a later ...Bxc3 comes without check.

ideas.title: Pin against pin
ideas.text: Once you've castled, 9.Bg5 pins the f6-knight to Black's queen, so Black's pieces are tied up too.

ideas.title: Bishop shut in by ...e6
ideas.text: 4...e6 came before Black's c8-bishop got out, so it needs ...b6 and ...Bb7 to find a diagonal, as in the 7.O-O line.

ideas.title: Bishop pair vs doubled pawns
ideas.text: Black can take on c3 to double your c-pawns; you get the bishop pair in return, which is fine once your king is safe.

habit.why: 7.Be3 leaves the c3-knight pinned with your king still on e1. After 7...O-O 8.Qe2 Bxc3+ 9.bxc3 Black takes it with check, doubles your c-pawns, and most of your edge is gone.

strays.text: The king stays on e1, so 8...Bxc3+ comes with check.

taught.why: 7.O-O takes your king off the b4-e1 diagonal, so the c3-knight is no longer pinned to it. If Black still trades after 7...O-O 8.Qe2 b6 9.Bg5 Bxc3 10.bxc3, it comes without check and your g5-bishop already pins the f6-knight.

enforces.text: With your king castled, the c3-knight is a normal piece again.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7.Bd2 breaks the pin with a developing move, and after 7...a6 8.a3 Bd6 9.Qe2 b5 10.Ba2 Bb7 11.O-O-O you castle long. It's sound, but another move keeps more of your edge.
alternatives.after: 7.O-O breaks the pin and makes your king safe in one move. After 7.Bd2 you castle long on the side where Black has already pushed ...a6 and ...b5.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7.Bg5 answers the pin with a pin of its own, and after 7...h6 8.Bh4 c5 Black hits your centre. It's sound, but another move keeps more of your edge.
alternatives.after: 7.O-O makes your king safe first and keeps the bishop pin from g5 for later, as in 9.Bg5, when Black can no longer take on c3 with check.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 7.a3 asks the bishop at once, but 7...Bxc3+ 8.bxc3 doubles your c-pawns with check, and Black develops calmly with 8...b6 and 9...Bb7.
alternatives.after: 7.O-O keeps your pawns whole for now; if Black trades on c3 later, you've already castled and developed.

2118572924932318|g7g6.headline: 4...g6 ignores 5.Ng5; develop the bishop with 4...Bc5.
2118572924932318|g7g6.why: White threatens 5.Ng5, attacking f7 together with the bishop on c4, and 4...g6 does nothing about it: after 5.Ng5 d5 6.exd5 Black loses a pawn. 4...Bc5 develops the bishop toward the centre and readies castling, transposing into the Giuoco Pianissimo.
2118572924932318|g7g6.principle: When a knight and the bishop on c4 can combine against f7, develop the pieces that let you castle instead of spending time on a pawn move.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nf6/3. d3

2122895618389281|c8f5.headline: Hit the d5 pawn at once with 3...c6
2122895618389281|c8f5.why: 3...Bf5 develops but doesn't touch the d5 pawn, so White keeps it. After 4.d4 e6 5.dxe6 fxe6 you are still a pawn down and your e-pawn is weak. 3...c6 attacks d5 a second time, and after 4.d4 cxd5 the pawn is back. With 5.Nc3 Nc6 6.Nf3 Bg4 you reach a Caro-Kann Panov-Botvinnik with your pieces pressing on d4.
2122895618389281|c8f5.principle: When the opponent props up an extra pawn, hit it with a pawn at once; the bishop can come out later.

Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Nf6

ideas.title: Undermine the d5 pawn
ideas.text: 3.c4 props up White's extra pawn. Strike it at once with a pawn: after 3...c6 4.d4 cxd5 the pawn is back.

ideas.title: Pawn first, bishop later
ideas.text: Usually your bishop comes out before ...c6 and ...e6. Here it waits: 3...Bf5 leaves d5 alone and White keeps the pawn.

ideas.title: Target d4
ideas.text: Once White has pawns on c4 and d4, aim your pieces at d4, as in 5.Nc3 Nc6 6.Nf3 Bg4.

ideas.title: White clings to d5
ideas.text: White's 3.c4 hopes to stay a pawn up. Against slow moves it works: 3...Bf5 4.d4 e6 5.dxe6 fxe6 leaves you a pawn short.

habit.why: 3...Bf5 develops but doesn't touch the d5 pawn, so White keeps it. After 4.d4 e6 5.dxe6 fxe6 you are still a pawn down and your e-pawn is weak.

strays.text: The bishop move leaves d5 alone, so White's extra pawn survives.

taught.why: 3...c6 attacks d5 a second time, and after 4.d4 cxd5 the pawn is back. With 5.Nc3 Nc6 6.Nf3 Bg4 you reach a Caro-Kann Panov-Botvinnik with your pieces pressing on d4.

enforces.text: The c-pawn hits d5 at once and wins the pawn back.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3...e6 is the Icelandic Gambit: after 4.dxe6 Bxe6 you give a pawn for a big lead in development. The engine marks it down, since after 5.Nf3 Qe7 6.Qe2 Nc6 7.d4 Bf5 8.Qxe7+ the queens come off and you are still a pawn short.
alternatives.after: 3...c6 wins the pawn back for sure, while 3...e6 keeps it a gambit. Masters play the two almost equally (53% and 47%) and books rate the Icelandic well, but the engine prefers 3...c6.

2162412998029713|f1c4.headline: 3...e6 prepares ...d5: put the bishop on d3, not c4
2162412998029713|f1c4.why: After 3...e6 Black is ready for ...d5, which hits a bishop on c4. In the line 4.Bc4 d5 5.exd5 exd5 6.Bd3 your bishop has to move again and Black has a free, equal centre, and most of your edge is gone. 4.Bd3 is the masters' top choice (28.9%): it develops the bishop toward the centre and defends e4 in advance, so after 4...Nc6 5.e5 White keeps space. 4.Nc3, 4.c3 and 4.Be2 also avoid the problem.
2162412998029713|f1c4.principle: Ask what your opponent's last move prepares; when ...e6 readies ...d5, develop your bishop to a square that the pawn push will not hit.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6/2. d4/2...Bg7

2173517444444160|b2b3.headline: Against the Pirc fianchetto, take the centre with 4.d4.
2173517444444160|b2b3.why: 4.b3 prepares a slow fianchetto and leaves the centre alone: after 4...Bg7 5.d4 O-O White plays the central move anyway, a move later, and Black hits back with 6...c5. 4.d4 sets up the two-pawn centre on e4 and d4 straight away and keeps the initiative, with 5.Be3 and 6.Qd2 to follow. Masters play 4.d4 in 87.5% of games.
2173517444444160|b2b3.principle: When the opponent fianchettoes and leaves the centre empty, occupy it with a second pawn before anything slower.

2179133986956493|f1c4.headline: e4 has no defender: develop with 5.Bd3, not 5.Bc4
2179133986956493|f1c4.why: Black threatens 5...Nxe4, and 5.Bc4 does nothing about it: the e4 pawn has no defender, so 5...Nxe4 wins it and Black is better. 5.Bd3, the masters' choice 84.3% of the time, develops the bishop toward the centre and guards e4 in the same move. After 5...O-O 6.O-O Nbd7 7.Re1 e5 8.h3 your centre of pawns on e4, d4 and c3 stands firm.
2179133986956493|f1c4.principle: Before picking a square for a developing piece, check what is loose: put the piece where it develops and also guards the undefended pawn.

2185074222383401|d2d3.headline: 4...Qe7 doesn't hold f7: take it with 5.Bxf7+
2185074222383401|d2d3.why: 5.d3 is too slow: Black kicks the knight with 5...h6, and after 6.Nf3 Nxe4 the e4 pawn is gone. 4...Qe7 does not really defend f7, which the bishop on c4 and the knight on g5 both attack. 5.Bxf7+ takes the pawn with check; after 5...Kd8 the knight on g5 protects the bishop, and Black's king has lost the right to castle.
2185074222383401|d2d3.principle: f7 is guarded mainly by the king, which cannot take a protected piece, so with bishop and knight both on it, the capture wins a pawn and castling rights.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5

2185074222383401|g5f7.headline: Take on f7 with the bishop, with check: 5.Bxf7+
2185074222383401|g5f7.why: 5.Nxf7 grabs the pawn and hits the rook, but lets Black open the game with 5...d5; after 6.Bxd5 Nxd5 7.exd5 Qxf7 the trades leave Black with active pieces and a safe king after 9...O-O. 4...Qe7 looks like it guards f7, but 5.Bxf7+ wins the pawn with check: the bishop is protected by the knight on g5, so neither the king nor the queen can take it. After 5...Kd8 Black's king is stuck in the centre and can no longer castle, and 6.Bb3 keeps the bishop safe.
2185074222383401|g5f7.principle: f7 is guarded only by the king and queen while the bishop on c4 and the knight on g5 both hit it; capture with the piece that gives check and stays protected.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5

2185447105552102|e1h1.headline: ...dxe4 forks d3 and f3: push 6.e5 before castling
2185447105552102|e1h1.why: 5...d5 threatens 6...dxe4, and that pawn would attack the bishop on d3 and the knight on f3 at once. 6.O-O ignores it: after 6...dxe4 7.Bxe4 Nxe4 you have lost a bishop, because once the d-pawn has gone the bishop on b7 also guards e4. 6.e5 (87.9% of masters games) takes the pawn out of the exchange, gains space by attacking the knight on f6 and leaves the b7 bishop blocked by Black's own pawn on d5; you keep a clear edge.
2185447105552102|e1h1.principle: Before a quiet move like castling, look at your opponent's captures; when a pawn capture would hit two of your pieces, resolve the central tension first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...b6/2. d4/2...Bb7/3. Bd3/3...Nf6

221633201643279|d2d4.headline: 1...b5 hangs a pawn: take it with 2.Bxb5
221633201643279|d2d4.why: 2.d4 declines the free pawn, and after 2...Bb7 Black gets the queenside fianchetto at no cost, which gives back part of your advantage. The b5 pawn is attacked by your bishop and defended by nothing: 2.Bxb5 wins it and develops at the same time. The theory lists Black's ideas afterwards, ...Bb7 against your centre and ...a6 to kick the bishop (2...a6 3.Bc4), and they gain Black only a little time.
221633201643279|d2d4.principle: Take a gambit pawn when you can consolidate easily; here the capture is also a developing move, so there is nothing to consolidate.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...b5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...b5/2. Bxb5

2219393363100507|f8d6.headline: Hit the centralised queen with 3...Nc6
2219393363100507|f8d6.why: 3...Bd6 leaves the pawn on g7 unprotected against the queen on d4, so 4.Qxg7 wins it, and the bishop also blocks Black's d-pawn. 3...Nc6 is the usual answer to the Centre Game: it develops with an attack on the queen, so White has to move it again and Black gains time.
2219393363100507|f8d6.principle: When the opponent's queen sits in the centre, develop a piece that attacks it and make it move again.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. Qxd4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. Qxd4/3...Nc6

2227650220427205|d7d5.headline: Don't push ...d5 into three attackers; 5...h6 is the quiet move
2227650220427205|d7d5.why: 5...d5 drops a pawn: d5 is hit by the pawn on e4, the knight on c3 and the bishop on c4, and after 6.Nxd5 Nxd5 7.Bxd5 White has won it. 5...h6 is a useful waiting move that takes g5 away from White's knight and bishop, so Black can castle with 6.O-O O-O without worrying about a pin or a hit on f7.
2227650220427205|d7d5.principle: Before pushing a central pawn, count the attackers on its square: here three white pieces cover d5 and Black has fewer defenders.

2264630549471820|a2a3.headline: Castle with 5.O-O; 5.a3 wastes time and loosens e4
2264630549471820|a2a3.why: 5.a3 spends a tempo inviting 5...Bxc3, and after 6.dxc3 Nxe4 the e4 pawn is gone; White wins the knight back with 7.Bxf7+ Kxf7 8.Qd5+ Ke8 9.Qxe4, but has traded off the attacking bishop and Black has the easier game. 5.O-O gets the king safe and keeps the tempo: after 5...Bxc3 6.bxc3 Nxe4 7.Bd5 Nf6 8.Bxc6 dxc6 9.Nxe5 White has the pawn back with active pieces. It is the most common master move here.
2264630549471820|a2a3.principle: A pawn move like 5.a3 that neither develops nor fights for the centre needs a concrete reason; castling finishes White's kingside development instead.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Bc4

2264630549471820|c3b5.headline: Castle with 5.O-O; the c3 knight is e4's only guard
2264630549471820|c3b5.why: 5.Nb5 moves a developed knight again and abandons the e4 pawn, so 5...Nxe4 wins it for nothing. 5.O-O is the most common master move: it tucks the king away first. After 5...Bxc3 6.bxc3 Nxe4 7.Bd5 Nf6 8.Bxc6 dxc6 9.Nxe5 White wins the pawn back.
2264630549471820|c3b5.principle: Before moving a piece, count what it defends: if it is the only guard of a centre pawn, leave it and improve another piece.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Bc4

2326611116094961|c1e3.headline: Check on f7 first: 6.Bxf7+ before you guard the knight
2326611116094961|c1e3.why: 6.Be3 guards the knight but lets Black off the hook: 6...Qf6 7.c3 Nge7 8.O-O O-O is a normal, level Scotch-type game with Black fully developed. The tempo Black lost with 3...h6 and the weak f7 square are no longer worth anything. 6.Bxf7+ wins a pawn with check, and taking with the king would drop the c5 bishop to a queen check on h5. After 6...Kf8 7.Nxc6 Qh4 8.Qf3 dxc6 9.Bg6+ Qf6 10.Qxf6+ Nxf6 you are a clean pawn up and Black can never castle.
2326611116094961|c1e3.principle: Before you answer a threat, look for your own forcing move: 6.Bxf7+ wins a pawn with check, and the threat on d4 can wait a move.

ideas.title: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
ideas.text: 6.Bxf7+ takes a pawn with check. If the king takes, a queen check from h5 also hits the loose c5 bishop.

ideas.title: Check before you answer the threat
ideas.text: Black threatens 6...Bxd4. A check that wins a pawn comes first; the knight can be dealt with next move, as in 7.Nxc6.

ideas.title: A king that can't castle
ideas.text: After 6...Kf8 Black's king can never castle, and you keep the extra pawn even after the queens come off with 10.Qxf6+ Nxf6.

ideas.title: Black's pieces aim at f2
ideas.text: The c5 bishop already aims at f2. Given a free move, 6...Qf6 adds the queen and threatens mate there.

habit.why: 6.Be3 guards the knight but lets Black off the hook: 6...Qf6 7.c3 Nge7 8.O-O O-O is a normal, level Scotch-type game with Black fully developed. The tempo Black lost with 3...h6 and the weak f7 square are no longer worth anything.

strays.idea: Check before you answer the threat

taught.why: 6.Bxf7+ wins a pawn with check, and taking with the king would drop the c5 bishop to a queen check on h5. After 6...Kf8 7.Nxc6 Qh4 8.Qf3 dxc6 9.Bg6+ Qf6 10.Qxf6+ Nxf6 you are a clean pawn up and Black can never castle.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 6.Nxc6 removes the attacker but lets 6...Qf6 in, threatening mate on f2 with the c5 bishop; after 7.O-O dxc6 Black develops freely.
alternatives.after: 6.Bxf7+ comes first with check and wins a pawn; 7.Nxc6 can follow next move, when Black's king has already lost castling.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 6.c3 adds a guard to d4 but does nothing for f2 or e4: 6...Nf6 7.Nxc6 bxc6 8.e5 Ne4 9.O-O Nxf2 breaks into f2 with the c5 bishop's help.
alternatives.after: 6.Bxf7+ strikes first with check instead of defending, so Black never gets time for 6...Nf6 and the raid on f2.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 6.Nf5 saves the knight but moves it a third time: after 6...d6 7.Nxg7+ Kf8 8.Nh5 Qh4 it is stranded on the rim while Black's queen hits f2 and e4.
alternatives.after: 6.Bxf7+ forces matters with check instead of spending a third knight move; you win a pawn and Black's king loses castling.

2326611116094961|d4c6.why: 6.Nxc6 answers the threat on d4 but lets 6...Qf6 in, threatening mate on f2 together with the c5 bishop. You must spend 7.O-O on defence, and after 7...dxc6 Black develops freely and the shot on f7 is gone. 6.Bxf7+ wins a pawn with check, and taking with the king would drop the c5 bishop to a queen check on h5. 2385998627357413|b2b4.headline: Gain queenside space with 7.a4; 7.b4 just hangs a pawn
2385998627357413|b2b4.why: 7.b4 puts a pawn where the c6 knight and c5 bishop both hit it and only the c3 pawn guards it, so 7...Nxb4 wins it. Taking back with the c-pawn opens the long diagonal for the bishop to hit your a1 rook, and after 8.a4 d5 9.exd5 Nxd5 Black is simply a pawn up. 7.a4 gains queenside space at no cost, prepares a later b4 or a5 and gives your bishop a retreat on a2. After 7...a5 8.h3 Kh8 9.Qh5 the game is level, and h3 comes only now that Black has castled.
2385998627357413|b2b4.principle: Count attackers and defenders before you push: b4 is hit twice and guarded once, while 7.a4 gains space safely.
sources: Georgios Souleidis and Karsten Müller, Winning with the Slow (but Venomous!) Italian (New in Chess), pp. 11-13 | https://www.sjakkbutikken.no/media/productimages/preview-winning-with-the-slow-but-venomous-italian.pdf

ideas.title: Count the b4 pawn's guards
ideas.text: On b4 the pawn is hit by the c6 knight and the c5 bishop and guarded only by c3, so 7...Nxb4 wins it.

ideas.title: Slow Italian: build first
ideas.text: Gain space with a4 first: it costs nothing, gives your bishop a retreat on a2 and prepares b4 or a5 later.

ideas.title: Ng5 needs a real target
ideas.text: Black has castled and the h6 knight guards f7, so your g5 knight has no target. Build up around it instead of adding the queen.

ideas.title: Guard f7, chase the bishop
ideas.text: Black's knight wants a5 to hit your c4 bishop, as after 7.Qf3 Na5, so keep a retreat ready.

habit.why: 7.b4 puts a pawn where the c6 knight and c5 bishop both hit it and only the c3 pawn guards it, so 7...Nxb4 wins it. Taking back with the c-pawn opens the long diagonal for the bishop to hit your a1 rook, and after 8.a4 d5 9.exd5 Nxd5 Black is simply a pawn up.

strays.text: Two black pieces hit b4 and only the c3 pawn defends it.

taught.why: 7.a4 gains queenside space at no cost, prepares a later b4 or a5 and gives your bishop a retreat on a2. After 7...a5 8.h3 Kh8 9.Qh5 the game is level, and h3 comes only now that Black has castled.

enforces.text: Queenside space without giving up a pawn.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7.O-O gets your king safe and keeps the g5 knight's options; after 7...Kh8 8.h3 a5 9.Qh5 knight and queen press on f7 and h7. It's fully sound.
alternatives.after: The engine rates the two moves equally. 7.a4 grabs queenside space first and 7.O-O castles first; in the 7.O-O line you play 10.a4 a few moves later anyway.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.Nf3 brings the knight back, admitting the trip to g5 cost two moves. Black uses the time for 7...Kh8 and a later ...f5 break, as in 9.O-O f5.
alternatives.after: 7.a4 spends the move on useful queenside space; the g5 knight isn't attacked, so there's no need to spend a move bringing it back.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.Qf3 brings the queen out early, and 7...Na5 hits your bishop. After 8.Bd5 c6 it's kicked again and Black gains time.
alternatives.after: 7.a4 keeps the queen home and frees a2 as a retreat for your bishop if the knight comes to a5.

2446703153094283|b8c6.headline: Against 1.Nf3, keep your options open with 1...Nf6
2446703153094283|b8c6.why: 1...Nc6 blocks the c-pawn, and after 2.d4 d5 3.c4 White gets a Queen's Gambit in which Black cannot use the c-pawn to support d5 or to strike back with ...c5. 1...Nf6 is the most flexible reply and the most popular among masters at 46%: it develops, stops White from playing e4, and keeps every pawn free, so Black can choose a setup such as 1...Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.g3 g6.
2446703153094283|b8c6.principle: The knight on f6 controls e4 and d5 without committing a pawn, while a knight on c6 in front of the c-pawn takes away Black's usual way to fight for d5.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3
Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3/1...Nf6

2446703153094283|e7e5.headline: After 1.Nf3, e5 just hangs; play 1...Nf6
2446703153094283|e7e5.why: 1...e5 puts a pawn where the knight on f3 attacks it and nothing defends it, so 2.Nxe5 wins it; theory calls it the dubious Ross Gambit. 1...Nf6 is the most flexible reply: it keeps the position symmetrical and leaves Black free to choose a setup later. Masters choose it in 46.4% of games.
2446703153094283|e7e5.principle: Before putting a pawn on a square, count: e5 is attacked by the knight and defended by nothing.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3/1...e5
Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3/1...Nf6

2463215796795915|f1e2.headline: Take the undefended c5 pawn before Black trades it off: 6.dxc5
2463215796795915|f1e2.why: 6.Be2 lets Black release the tension with 6...cxd4 7.cxd4, which is what the theory says Black wants here, and your edge is gone. The c5 pawn is attacked once and defended by nothing, and the theory points out that 5...Bg4 does not stop you taking it: 6.dxc5. In the main line Black wins back the e5 pawn with 7...Nxe5, but 10.b4 then supports your pawn on c5 and gains space on the queenside, and you keep a small edge.
2463215796795915|f1e2.principle: Ask what your opponent wants: here Black wants ...cxd4 to free the position, so take on c5 first, which stops it and wins the undefended pawn.

2463215796795915|h2h3.headline: Don't spend a move on h3: take on c5 with 6.dxc5
2463215796795915|h2h3.why: 6.h3 invites 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3, and once the f3 knight is gone d4 has lost a defender: 7...cxd4 wins a pawn and Black is better. The pin on your knight does not need an answer yet; the theory points out that 5...Bg4 does not stop you taking on c5. The c5 pawn is attacked once and defended by nothing, so 6.dxc5 grabs it, and in the main line 10.b4 later supports it and gains queenside space.
2463215796795915|h2h3.principle: In the Advance, Black's play is aimed at the base of your chain, d4; don't help by inviting the exchange of its defender, and remove Black's c5 lever instead.

2465468553870240|c8f5.headline: Knight first: 5...Nc6, because ...Bf5 leaves b7 and d5 short
2465468553870240|c8f5.why: 5...Bf5 takes the bishop away from b7, and 6.Qb3 hits b7 and d5 at once: 6...Qb6 saves b7 but stops guarding d5, and 7.Nxd5 Nxd5 8.Qxd5 wins a pawn. 5...Nc6 is the main move (93% of master games): it develops toward the centre, adds pressure on d4, and keeps the bishop home until it can come out safely. The theory's line 5...Nc6 6.Bf4 Bf5 7.e3 e6 shows the bishop still reaches f5 a move later, and the game stays equal.
2465468553870240|c8f5.principle: In symmetrical positions the knight's square is obvious and the bishop's depends on the pawns, so develop the knight first and keep the bishop guarding b7 until its square is safe.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. cxd5/3...cxd5/4. Nc3/4...Nf6

2466581236058373|c8d7.headline: Block 5.Bb5+ with 5...Nc6: the bishop block runs into 6.Qe2+
2466581236058373|c8d7.why: 5...Bd7 blocks with the bishop, so 6.Qe2+ checks you again down the open e-file. After 6...Qe7 7.Bxd7+ Nxd7 8.Nxd5 the queen no longer guards d5 and White wins the pawn. 5...Nc6 blocks with a developing piece, so your c8 bishop isn't traded and the queen keeps guarding d5. After 6.O-O Nf6 7.d4 Bd6 8.Bg5 O-O you have castled, and after 10.dxc5 your active pieces have to make up for the isolated d5 pawn.
2466581236058373|c8d7.principle: Develop with every move: block the check with a piece that wants to come out anyway.
sources: Sicilian-phobia Part Two - Closed Sicilian (chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/article/view/sicilian-phobia-part-two---closed-sicilian
Playing the Grand Prix Attack Against the Sicilian (Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/grand-prix-attack/

ideas.title: Checks on e2 and b5
ideas.text: With the e-file open and your king on e8, 5.Bb5+ and 6.Qe2+ pin your pieces, and the d5 pawn drops.

ideas.title: Block with a developing piece
ideas.text: Answer the check with 5...Nc6: it develops, keeps your c8 bishop for later, and leaves the queen guarding d5.

ideas.title: Castle quickly
ideas.text: With the e-file open, get your king off e8 fast: 6...Nf6, 7...Bd6 and 8...O-O, as in the main line.

ideas.title: The isolated d5 pawn
ideas.text: Once the c-pawns are traded, d5 stands alone. White aims pieces at it; you answer with active pieces.

habit.why: 5...Bd7 blocks with the bishop, so 6.Qe2+ checks you again down the open e-file. After 6...Qe7 7.Bxd7+ Nxd7 8.Nxd5 the queen no longer guards d5 and White wins the pawn.

strays.text: The bishop block gets traded off, and the e-file check follows.

taught.why: 5...Nc6 blocks with a developing piece, so your c8 bishop isn't traded and the queen keeps guarding d5. After 6.O-O Nf6 7.d4 Bd6 8.Bg5 O-O you have castled, and after 10.dxc5 your active pieces have to make up for the isolated d5 pawn.

enforces.text: The knight develops while blocking, and the queen keeps guarding d5.

2471617853961957|e8e7.headline: Take the bishop on f7 with your king; nothing defends it
2471617853961957|e8e7.why: 7...Ke7 leaves White's bishop alive: after 8.Bxg8 Qxg8 White has traded it for a knight, kept the pawn it took on f7, and Black's king has lost the right to castle. The bishop on f7 is attacked by the king and defended by nothing, so 7...Kxf7 wins it. White's trick 8.Nxe5+ is a check that opens the queen's path to g4, but after 8...dxe5 9.Qxg4 Black has still won a knight for a pawn.
2471617853961957|e8e7.principle: When a piece lands on f7 with check, count its defenders before stepping aside: with none, take it and then meet the follow-up.

2480011064030415|f3g5.headline: Build with 5.c3; 5.Ng5 just loses time
2480011064030415|f3g5.why: 5.Ng5 moves the knight again, but 5...O-O covers f7 with the rook, and grabbing it would give two minor pieces for a rook and pawn. After 6.a4 Ne7 7.Nf3 c6 8.Bb3 Ng6 the knight is back on f3 and Black has used the time to castle and regroup. 5.c3 starts the slow Italian plan and keeps d4 for later. After 5...a6 6.a4 d6 7.O-O Ba7 8.Re1 O-O 9.Nbd2 you have the standard c3, d3 and a4 set-up, the most common choice of masters (42%).
2480011064030415|f3g5.principle: When Black can castle and cover f7, don't move the f3 knight twice: build up with c3, a4 and castling.
sources: NM Jeremy Kane, Bad Trades Amateurs Make In Chess | https://www.chess.com/article/view/bad-trades-amateurs-make-in-chess

ideas.title: Ng5 needs a real target
ideas.text: f7 is guarded by the king only until Black castles. After 5...O-O, taking on f7 gives two pieces for a rook and pawn.

ideas.title: Slow Italian: c3, d3, a4, then d4
ideas.text: Play c3 and a4, castle and bring the b1 knight out via d2. Push d4 only once you are ready.

ideas.title: Black: a retreat for the bishop
ideas.text: Black answers a4 with ...a6 and ...Ba7, so the c5 bishop can't be trapped or kicked with gain of time.

ideas.title: Don't move a piece twice
ideas.text: Your b1 knight and c1 bishop are still at home. Moving the f3 knight again gives Black free time.

habit.why: 5.Ng5 moves the knight again, but 5...O-O covers f7 with the rook, and grabbing it would give two minor pieces for a rook and pawn. After 6.a4 Ne7 7.Nf3 c6 8.Bb3 Ng6 the knight is back on f3 and Black has used the time to castle and regroup.

strays.text: Black castles, f7 is covered, and the knight has to go back.

taught.why: 5.c3 starts the slow Italian plan and keeps d4 for later. After 5...a6 6.a4 d6 7.O-O Ba7 8.Re1 O-O 9.Nbd2 you have the standard c3, d3 and a4 set-up, the most common choice of masters (42%).

enforces.idea: Slow Italian: c3, d3, a4, then d4
enforces.text: c3 first, then a4, castling and the knight via d2.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.O-O is a good move: your king is safe, and the build-up goes on with 7.Re1 and 8.Nbd2. Masters play it in 34% of games; one other move is a bit more popular.
alternatives.after: Both moves are good and usually transpose: 5.c3 (42%) commits to the pawn set-up first, while 5.O-O (34%) castles and plays 6.c3 next.
alternatives.idea: Slow Italian: c3, d3, a4, then d4

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.Bg5 develops with a pin on the f6 knight. After 5...h6 6.Be3 Bb6 you offer a bishop trade on the a7-g1 diagonal; it's sound, but masters prefer a more flexible plan.
alternatives.after: 5.c3 keeps the c1 bishop's options open and builds the pawn set-up, with a4 and d4 to come. Masters choose it 42% of the time, 5.Bg5 only 5%.
alternatives.idea: Slow Italian: c3, d3, a4, then d4

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.Nc3 develops and eyes d5: after 5...a6 6.Nd5 h6 the knight sits on a central square. It's sound, but masters prefer another move.
alternatives.after: 5.c3 keeps the c-pawn free so d4 can come later; with the knight on c3, its line has to move it again with 6.Nd5 before the pawn can advance.
alternatives.idea: Slow Italian: c3, d3, a4, then d4

2566699904980904|f8g7.headline: Play 3...d6 so e5 never kicks your knight
2566699904980904|f8g7.why: After 3...Bg7, 4.e5 kicks the knight on f6 and it has to go all the way back with 4...Ng8, leaving White with lots of space and Black undeveloped. 3...d6 covers e5, so the knight stays on f6 and the game transposes into the Pirc defence, the choice in about three quarters of master games. Black then follows with ...Bg7 and castles.
2566699904980904|f8g7.principle: A knight on f6 is a target for White's e-pawn; control e5 with a pawn first so the pawn can't chase the knight and gain space.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. Nc3

2583228623150903|d7d5.headline: Against 3.Bc4, develop with 3...Nc6 before pushing ...d5
2583228623150903|d7d5.why: 3...d5 opens the centre while d5 is hit by the c3 knight and the c4 bishop and guarded only by your queen. After 4.exd5 exd5 5.Qe2+ Be7 6.Nxd5 the check on the e-file wins the pawn. 3...Nc6 develops and prepares 4...Nf6 and a supported ...d5 later, the plan Ikeda and Astle give against 3.Bc4. After 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bb5 White moves the bishop again to avoid ...d5, and 6.Bxc6 Qxc6 leaves you the two bishops.
2583228623150903|d7d5.principle: Count attackers and defenders: d5 is hit twice and guarded once, so prepare ...d5 before pushing it.
sources: How I play against the Closed Sicilian (IM Junta Ikeda) | https://juntaikeda.substack.com/p/how-i-play-against-the-closed-sicilian

ideas.title: ...e6 blunts the c4 bishop
ideas.text: Your e6 pawn shuts the c4 bishop out of f7 and makes it a target for a later ...d5 or ...b5.

ideas.title: d5 is attacked twice
ideas.text: Right now the c3 knight and the c4 bishop both hit d5; after 4.exd5 exd5 5.Qe2+ there is no time to defend it.

ideas.title: Develop before ...d5
ideas.text: Bring out 3...Nc6 and 4...Nf6 first; then ...d5 comes with support and gains time on the bishop.

ideas.title: Chase the bishop with ...b5
ideas.text: The other main plan: 3...a6 and 4...b5 gain queenside space and chase the bishop, as in 4.Bb3 b5.

habit.why: 3...d5 opens the centre while d5 is hit by the c3 knight and the c4 bishop and guarded only by your queen. After 4.exd5 exd5 5.Qe2+ Be7 6.Nxd5 the check on the e-file wins the pawn.

strays.text: The pawn goes forward before any piece supports it.

taught.why: 3...Nc6 develops and prepares 4...Nf6 and a supported ...d5 later, the plan Ikeda and Astle give against 3.Bc4. After 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bb5 White moves the bishop again to avoid ...d5, and 6.Bxc6 Qxc6 leaves you the two bishops.

enforces.text: The knight adds a piece to the centre before the pawn moves.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3...a6 is a main move (43% of master games): it prepares ...b5 to chase the bishop, as in 4.Bb3 b5 5.d3 Bb7. It is fully sound, and the move this card teaches is just as good.
alternatives.after: Both are main moves (48% and 43% of master games). 3...Nc6 develops at once and readies ...Nf6 and ...d5, while 3...a6 first gains queenside space.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3...Nf6 develops and hits e4, with ...d5 to follow; after 4.Nf3 a6 5.Be2 Qc7 6.e5 Ng4 the knight hops out and keeps hitting the centre. It is sound, but masters choose it only 7% of the time.
alternatives.after: 3...Nc6 develops the other knight first, so an early e5 push has nothing to chase, and masters prefer it (48% to 7%).

2615425569294719|c8f5.headline: ...Bf5 leaves b7 loose to Qb3: develop with 4...Nf6 first
2615425569294719|c8f5.why: 4...Bf5 takes the bishop off c8, where it was the only guard of b7, and 5.Qb3 attacks b7 and d5 together: after 5...Nc6 6.Nf3 Nf6 7.Qxb7 the b-pawn falls. 4...Nf6 is the main move (75.9% of master games): it develops toward the centre and adds a defender to d5. The bishop can still come to f5 later, as in 4...Nf6 5.Bf4 Nc6 6.Nf3 Bf5, once the knights are out.
2615425569294719|c8f5.principle: Before moving a piece, check what it stops guarding: the c8 bishop is b7's only defender, so it stays home until Qb3 no longer wins a pawn.

2615583540108407|b8c6.headline: Answer 2.f3 with 2...d5 so that e4 costs White a pawn.
2615583540108407|b8c6.why: 2...Nc6 lets White carry out the plan: 3.e4 builds a big centre and after 4.e5 Ng8 Black's knight is pushed back home. 2.f3 weakens White's kingside and takes the knight's natural square just to prepare e4, and 2...d5 makes that push fail: if 3.e4 dxe4 4.fxe4 Nxe4, Black is a pawn up.
2615583540108407|b8c6.principle: When White prepares e4 with a weakening pawn move, add a second guard of e4 with your d-pawn so the advance costs material.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. f3

2615583540108407|g7g6.headline: Answer 2.f3 with 2...d5 so e4 never comes
2615583540108407|g7g6.why: 2.f3 prepares 3.e4, and 2...g6 lets it happen: after 3.e4 d5 4.e5 the knight is kicked to d7 and White has a big pawn centre. 2...d5 adds a second guard to e4, so White cannot push the e-pawn without losing it: if 3.e4 anyway, 3...dxe4 4.fxe4 Nxe4 leaves Black a pawn up. Masters play it in 83% of games, and White's f-pawn move is left looking weakening.
2615583540108407|g7g6.principle: When White prepares a central pawn advance, add a pawn guard to that square at once so the advance loses material.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. f3

2671625836318681|b8c6.headline: Release the tension with 5...dxe4 before 6.exd5 wins d5
2671625836318681|b8c6.why: 5...Nc6 doesn't stop 6.exd5: after 6...exd5 7.Bb5 the c6 knight is pinned and your d5 pawn has only the queen to guard it. After 7...Bd7 8.Nxd5 the pawn is gone, since your queen can't take back while White's queen stands behind the d4 knight. 5...dxe4 swaps off the pawn White was about to win, and after 6.Nxe4 you have no weak pawns. In the line 6...a6 7.Bd3 Be7 8.O-O Nf6 you develop calmly and castle next.
2671625836318681|b8c6.principle: Check the opponent's threats first: 6.exd5 and 7.Bb5 win d5, so 5...dxe4 removes the target before you develop.
sources: How I play against the Closed Sicilian (IM Junta Ikeda) | https://juntaikeda.substack.com/p/how-i-play-against-the-closed-sicilian

ideas.title: White threatens exd5
ideas.text: Your d5 pawn is hit by e4 and the c3 knight; after 6.exd5 exd5 the pawn is isolated and 7.Bb5 follows.

ideas.title: Checks on e2 and b5
ideas.text: 7.Bb5 pins a knight on c6, or checks your king, while the e-file and the a4-e8 diagonal are open.

ideas.title: Take on e4, keep no weakness
ideas.text: 5...dxe4 swaps off the attacked pawn; after 6.Nxe4 you have no weak pawn and can develop calmly.

ideas.title: Develop and castle
ideas.text: Then come 7...Be7 and 8...Nf6, and castling, before White's pieces find a target.

habit.why: 5...Nc6 doesn't stop 6.exd5: after 6...exd5 7.Bb5 the c6 knight is pinned and your d5 pawn has only the queen to guard it. After 7...Bd7 8.Nxd5 the pawn is gone, since your queen can't take back while White's queen stands behind the d4 knight.

strays.text: The knight develops but leaves d5 to 6.exd5 and 7.Bb5.

taught.why: 5...dxe4 swaps off the pawn White was about to win, and after 6.Nxe4 you have no weak pawns. In the line 6...a6 7.Bd3 Be7 8.O-O Nf6 you develop calmly and castle next.

enforces.idea: Take on e4, keep no weakness
enforces.text: Trading the attacked pawn ends all play against d5.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 5...Bb4 pins the c3 knight but doesn't save d5: after 6.exd5 Qxd5 7.Be2 Nc6 8.Nxc6 Qxd1+ 9.Bxd1 bxc6 your queenside pawns are split.
alternatives.after: 5...dxe4 trades the attacked pawn at once, so White never gets 6.exd5 and your pawns stay healthy.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 5...Bc5 hits the d4 knight but leaves d5 and the bishop loose: after 6.exd5 exd5 7.Bb5+ Bd7 8.Nf5 Bxb5 9.Nxb5 Qa5+ 10.Nc3 White's knights are active and d5 soon falls.
alternatives.after: 5...dxe4 takes the attacked pawn off the board, so there is no 6.exd5 and no check on b5 to fear.

2692473875865858|c8f5.headline: In the Slav, 3...Nf6 first: an early ...Bf5 drops a pawn
2692473875865858|c8f5.why: Once the bishop leaves c8, b7 is undefended and a queen on b3 hits b7 and d5 together. Theory calls 3...Bf5 a grave mistake here: 4.cxd5 cxd5 5.Qb3 wins a pawn, and the engine's 4.Qb3 Qb6 5.Qxb6 axb6 6.cxd5 does the same. 3...Nf6, Black's most common reply by far, defends d5 and keeps the balance; the bishop can come out once ...e6 and the knight make it safe.
2692473875865858|c8f5.principle: Before developing a piece, check what it was guarding; in the Slav the c8 bishop holds b7, and Qb3 punishes it for leaving early.

269926073920586|c1e3.headline: Question the pinning bishop at once with 6.h3
269926073920586|c1e3.why: 6.Be3 lets Black keep the pin on f3 and develop with 6...e6 and 7...c6. After 8.h3 Bh5 9.Bd3 Nbd7 10.Qe2 Bb4 the bishop is still on the board, 10...Bb4 adds to the pin on your c3-knight, and most of your edge is gone. 6.h3, the choice in 90% of master games, makes the bishop decide now. After 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 c6 8.Bd2 Nbd7 9.O-O-O you have both bishops, an active queen and no pin on c3.
269926073920586|c1e3.principle: A pin ties your knight down; break it while that costs Black something, by hitting the pinning bishop with the h-pawn before Black can support it.

ideas.title: Ask the Bg4 question with h3
ideas.text: h3 makes the g4-bishop decide now: after 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 you have the bishop pair and your queen is already active.

ideas.title: Bd2, long castling, pawn storm
ideas.text: Then 8.Bd2 unpins the c3-knight and 9.O-O-O follows; if the bishop retreats instead, g4 chases it to g6.

ideas.title: Black's pressure on d4
ideas.text: The g4-bishop eyes your f3-knight, a defender of d4; with ...Nc6 and ...O-O-O Black can pile up on the pawn.

ideas.title: The pin on c3
ideas.text: Black's queen on a5 pins your c3-knight to the king. A bishop on d2 breaks the pin; 6.Be3 does not.

habit.why: 6.Be3 lets Black keep the pin on f3 and develop with 6...e6 and 7...c6. After 8.h3 Bh5 9.Bd3 Nbd7 10.Qe2 Bb4 the bishop is still on the board, 10...Bb4 adds to the pin on your c3-knight, and most of your edge is gone.

strays.idea: Ask the Bg4 question with h3
strays.text: h3 comes two moves late, and the bishop simply drops back to h5.

taught.why: 6.h3, the choice in 90% of master games, makes the bishop decide now. After 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 c6 8.Bd2 Nbd7 9.O-O-O you have both bishops, an active queen and no pin on c3.

enforces.idea: Ask the Bg4 question with h3
enforces.text: Black must trade on f3 or retreat right now.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.Be2 is passive: after 6...Nbd7 7.a3 c6 Black develops calmly, then trades with 8...Bxf3 9.Bxf3 e6, and your edge shrinks.
alternatives.after: 6.h3 makes Black decide right away instead of two moves later. Masters play it in 90% of games, 6.Be2 in 5%.
alternatives.idea: Ask the Bg4 question with h3

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.Bd2 breaks the pin on c3, but 6...Qf5 7.Bd3 Bxf3 8.gxf3 wrecks your kingside pawns, and after 8...Qd7 9.Ne4 Qxd4 Black has won the d4 pawn.
alternatives.after: 6.h3 settles the bishop first, so after 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 you take back with the queen and your pawns stay whole.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: After 6.Bc4 Nc6 the knight joins the bishop against d4. Black trades on f3, castles long with 8...O-O-O, and after 9.d5 Ne5 the knight hits your queen and bishop. Your edge is gone.
alternatives.after: 6.h3 settles the bishop before Black's knight and rook join the attack on d4; masters play it in 90% of games, 6.Bc4 in only 2%.

269926073920586|f1e2.headline: Ask the g4 bishop at once with 6.h3
269926073920586|f1e2.why: 6.Be2 lets Black finish ...Nbd7 and ...c6 before deciding about the bishop. After 6...Nbd7 7.a3 c6 8.h3 Bxf3 9.Bxf3 you play h3 anyway, but two moves later. 269926073920586|f1e2.principle: A bishop that a pawn can attack is a target: hit it with the h-pawn right away, while the trade on f3 still costs Black something.

2731765578959899|c4b3.headline: Retreat 6.Bf1: guard g2 and stay out of the knight's reach
2731765578959899|c4b3.why: 6.Bb3 walks into 6...Nd4: the knight hits the bishop, guards b5, and a later c3 would just let it take on b3. After 7.d3 Bc5 8.Nc3 O-O 9.Nge4 Nxe4 10.Nxe4 Black is fully developed and your knight has been pushed back. 6.Bf1 guards g2, so if 6...Qxd5, 7.Nc3 gains time on the queen. After 6...Nxd5 7.Bxb5 Bb7 8.d4 exd4 9.O-O you have taken b5 with no queen fork, as masters do in 84% of games.
2731765578959899|c4b3.principle: Before you retreat, ask what Black wants: ...Qxd5 and ...Nd4. 6.Bf1 answers both, since g2 is guarded and ...Nd4 hits nothing.

27382415154004|d3d4.headline: Count the guards on d4 before you push
27382415154004|d3d4.why: 6.d4 pushes onto a square Black hits three times, with the pawn on e5, the knight on c6 and the bishop on c5, while White covers it only twice, so 6...exd4 simply wins a pawn. 6.Na4 goes after the bishop on c5 first: after 6...Bb6 7.O-O Nge7 8.Nxb6 axb6 one of d4's attackers is gone, and 9.d4 comes once it can be supported.
27382415154004|d3d4.principle: In the quiet Italian, push d4 only when you guard it as often as Black attacks it; otherwise trade off one of the attackers first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. d3

275585188789254|f3d4.headline: 5.e5 kicks the f6 knight before you collect d4
275585188789254|f3d4.why: 5.Nxd4 recaptures, but your e4 pawn has no defender and 5...Nxe4 takes it; after 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.Qe2 Qe7 8.O-O Nd6 Black trades queens and is slightly better. Theory points out that Black is a pawn up here but has weaknesses: the e5 square, the knight on f6 and the f7 square. 5.e5, the masters' choice 70% of the time, uses them: it attacks the knight, and after 5...d5 6.Bb5 Ne4 7.Nxd4 you have won the pawn back with more space in the centre.
275585188789254|f3d4.principle: When your opponent's extra pawn comes with weaknesses, play on the weaknesses first; the pawn can usually be won back afterwards.

2781218480891122|g1f3.headline: Kick the e5 knight with 4.f4 and take the centre
2781218480891122|g1f3.why: 4.Nf3 lets Black trade the badly placed knight with 4...Nxf3+ 5.Qxf3, so Black's cramp eases. You keep some space after 5...d6 6.g4 h6, but the chance to drive the knight back with gain of time is gone. 4.f4 attacks the knight, and after 4...Ng6 5.Nf3 d6 6.Nc3 you have a big centre and a lead in development. Then 7.f5 kicks the knight again, and 7...Ne5 8.Nxe5 dxe5 leaves Black cramped behind your d5 and f5 pawns.
2781218480891122|g1f3.principle: A centralised knight without pawn support is a target: 4.f4 drives it back and gains space with tempo.
