ideas.title: Chase the knight with pawns
ideas.text: The e5 knight has no pawn support. 4.f4 drives it back with tempo and grabs space at the same time.

ideas.title: Don't swap Black's bad knight
ideas.text: Black's knight is short of squares. 4.Nf3 lets it trade itself off with 4...Nxf3+, and Black's cramp eases.

ideas.title: The big centre
ideas.text: Pawns on d5, e4 and f4 give you a big centre. In 19th-century games Steinitz and Bird followed up with c4, Steinitz with e5 too.

habit.why: 4.Nf3 lets Black trade the badly placed knight with 4...Nxf3+ 5.Qxf3, so Black's cramp eases. You keep some space after 5...d6 6.g4 h6, but the chance to drive the knight back with gain of time is gone.

strays.text: Black's misplaced knight gets traded off for your good one.

taught.why: 4.f4 attacks the knight, and after 4...Ng6 5.Nf3 d6 6.Nc3 you have a big centre and a lead in development. Then 7.f5 kicks the knight again, and 7...Ne5 8.Nxe5 dxe5 leaves Black cramped behind your d5 and f5 pawns.

enforces.text: The f-pawn hits the knight and gains space at the same time.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 4.Bf4 lets Black defend with 4...d6, and after 5.Bxe5 dxe5 you've swapped your dark bishop for the knight without gaining any time.
alternatives.after: 4.f4 hits the knight with a pawn: it has to retreat, you gain space, and you keep both bishops.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4.Nc3 develops but gives Black time: after 4...d6 the knight can drop back to d7, and Black sets up with ...g6 and ...Bg7.
alternatives.after: 4.f4 kicks the knight at once and gains space with tempo; with 4.Nc3 first, Black uses the move for 4...d6 and the knight finds d7.

2782228191759896|g1f3.headline: ...dxe4 is threatened: settle the centre with 5.e5 first
2782228191759896|g1f3.why: The pawn on d5 attacks e4, and nothing defends it, so 5.Nf3 simply loses it: 5...dxe4 6.Ne5 Bb4+ 7.Nc3 Ne7 and Black is a pawn up. 5.e5 (66.3% of masters games) takes the pawn out of the capture and claims space: backed by d4, it takes the f6 square from Black's knight, which has to go the long way with 6...Nge7 and 7...Nf5, and White keeps a small edge. 5.exd5 also keeps the material level.
2782228191759896|g1f3.principle: Before developing, check your opponent's captures: when a pawn attacks one of your central pawns, resolve the tension by advancing, exchanging or defending.

2790758909279175|d1e2.headline: Jump 8.Nb5 at the d6 hole before Black plays ...a6
2790758909279175|d1e2.why: 8.Qe2 is the standard Morra move, but it threatens nothing, and 8...a6 takes b5 from your knight at once. After 9.a4 Qc7 10.h3 Nge7 11.Rd1 O-O Black has castled and keeps the extra pawn. 8.Nb5 threatens a knight check on d6, and since ...e6 and ...Bg7 no pawn or bishop guards that square. After 8...a6 9.Nd6+ Kf8 Black can't castle any more; Wikibooks also gives 8...Nf6 9.Qd6, threatening a knight fork on c7.
2790758909279175|d1e2.principle: When your opponent leaves a hole, hit it at once: ...g6 and ...e6 left d6 unguarded, so 8.Nb5 aims there before 8...a6 closes the door.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3/4...Nc6/5. Nf3/5...g6
Hannes Langrock, The Modern Morra Gambit (sample pages) | https://www.newinchess.com/media/wysiwyg/product_pdf/2702.pdf

ideas.title: Knight jump to d6
ideas.text: Black played ...e6 and ...Bg7 without ...d6, so no pawn or bishop guards d6. From b5 your knight checks there and Black loses castling.

ideas.title: ...a6 shuts the door
ideas.text: Black's answer is ...a6, taking b5 from your knight. One quiet move from you, and 8...a6 makes d6 safe.

ideas.title: Morra setup on autopilot
ideas.text: Queen to e2 and rook to d1 is the standard Morra setup, but against ...g6 with ...e6 a concrete hit beats finishing it.

ideas.title: Gambit pawn buys time
ideas.text: You are a pawn down for quick development and open lines. Spend that time on threats, or Black catches up and keeps the pawn.

habit.why: 8.Qe2 is the standard Morra move, but it threatens nothing, and 8...a6 takes b5 from your knight at once. After 9.a4 Qc7 10.h3 Nge7 11.Rd1 O-O Black has castled and keeps the extra pawn.

strays.text: It gives Black the one move, 8...a6, that makes d6 safe.

taught.why: 8.Nb5 threatens a knight check on d6, and since ...e6 and ...Bg7 no pawn or bishop guards that square. After 8...a6 9.Nd6+ Kf8 Black can't castle any more; Wikibooks also gives 8...Nf6 9.Qd6, threatening a knight fork on c7.

enforces.text: The knight heads for d6 before ...a6 can stop it.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 8.Bg5 attacks the queen, but 8...Nge7 blocks with a developing move. After 9.Qd2 a6 Black has taken b5 from your knight and keeps the extra pawn.
alternatives.after: 8.Nb5 makes a threat no developing move can meet: 8...a6 comes too late, because 9.Nd6+ follows anyway.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 8.Bf4 eyes d6, but it gives Black a free move: 8...a6 takes b5 from your knight, and after 9.Bb3 Nge7 10.e5 b5 Black is ready to castle.
alternatives.after: 8.Nb5 goes for d6 straight away; the bishop can come later, once Black's king is already stuck on f8.

2797760506254471|d2d3.headline: Refute the Latvian with 3.Nxe5: take the undefended pawn
2797760506254471|d2d3.why: 3.d3 defends e4 but lets Black keep the initiative in the centre: after 3...Nc6 4.d4 fxe4 5.Nxe5 Nf6 Black has the e4 pawn and easy development, and the game is level. Theory calls the Latvian utterly unsound: 2...f5 leaves the e5 pawn attacked once and not defended at all and opens the e8-h5 diagonal to Black's king. 3.Nxe5, played by masters 76.4% of the time, takes it, and Black dare not answer 3...fxe4 because of 4.Qh5+; after the main 3...Qf6 4.d4 d6 5.Nc4 fxe4 6.Nc3 Black has spent moves on the queen and pawns while you develop, and White is clearly better.
2797760506254471|d2d3.principle: Meet an unsound gambit by taking the material when your opponent's counterattack fails tactically, here because Black's king is exposed on the e8-h5 diagonal.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5/3. Nxe5

2797760506254471|f1c4.headline: Refute the Latvian by taking e5 at once with 3.Nxe5
2797760506254471|f1c4.why: 3.Bc4 declines the gambit and lets Black carry out the idea behind 2...f5: after 3...fxe4 4.Nxe5 Qg5 the queen hits the knight on e5 and the pawn on g2 at once, and 5.d4 Qxg2 wins the pawn with a level game. 3.Nxe5 (76.4% of masters games) takes the undefended e-pawn right away. Black dare not reply 3...fxe4 because of 4.Qh5+, winning an exchange or more, so the main line is 3...Qf6 4.d4 d6 5.Nc4 fxe4 6.Nc3, and you keep a clear edge.
2797760506254471|f1c4.principle: Check captures first: when a gambit leaves a central pawn undefended and the capture also opens a check on the weakened e8-h5 diagonal, take it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5/3. Bc4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5/3. Nxe5

2816849754100076|g8f6.headline: Hit the bishop that aims at f7
2816849754100076|g8f6.why: 3...Nf6 attacks the queen but leaves f7 guarded only by the king: 4.Qxf7# is mate. 3...d5 breaks the attack at its source by hitting the bishop on c4 with a pawn and opening the way for the c8-bishop; after 4.Bb3 Be6 that bishop covers f7 and Black has the better centre.
2816849754100076|g8f6.principle: Answer a threat with a move that also gains time: attacking the piece that aims at f7 removes the danger and frees your own development.

2823299714850307|b8c6.headline: Hit the base of White's pawn chain with 3...c5
2823299714850307|b8c6.why: 3...Nc6 blocks Black's own c-pawn, the one lever against White's chain, and the theory says it gives White an easy game; after 4.Nf3 f6 5.Bb5 White piles on the knight. 3...c5 attacks the base of the chain on d4 and is played in 95.8% of master games. Black follows up with ...Nc6 and ...Qb6 to add pressure on d4, and once the chain is gone the kingside pieces find good squares.
2823299714850307|b8c6.principle: When White's pawns lock the centre on d4 and e5, strike the base of the chain with your c-pawn and keep that pawn free to move.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. d4/2...d5/3. e5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. d4/2...d5/3. e5/3...c5

283181713049681|g7g5.headline: 2...g5 hangs a pawn; mirror White with 2...g6
283181713049681|g7g5.why: 2...g5 simply loses a pawn: the knight on f3 takes it with 3.Nxg5 and Black gets nothing for it. 2...g6 mirrors White's setup: Black prepares ...Bg7 and castling, and after 3.c4 Bg7 4.Bg2 the game is balanced. It is the masters' most common reply, at 42%.
283181713049681|g7g5.principle: Before pushing a pawn, count who attacks its new square: g5 is hit by the knight on f3 and defended by nothing.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3/1...Nf6/2. g3

2861143771416580|e7e6.headline: 4.Bg5 leaves c4 hanging: take it with 4...dxc4
2861143771416580|e7e6.why: 4...e6 lets White keep a comfortable position: after 5.e3 h6 6.Bxf6 Qxf6 White's centre stands and White is slightly better. 4.Bg5 develops the bishop but leaves c4 attacked once and defended by nothing, so 4...dxc4, the most common master move (43.4%), wins a pawn. After 5.e3 b5 the pawn is backed by your queenside pawns, and 6...Qb6 and 7...a6 keep it supported, so Black is better.
2861143771416580|e7e6.principle: Accept a pawn when you can consolidate: here ...b5, ...a6 and ...Qb6 hold c4, and you finish developing afterwards.

2885293173565302|d2d3.headline: Play 4.c3 to prepare d4 against Black's c5 and e5 pawns
2885293173565302|d2d3.why: 4.d3 is passive: the d-pawn takes one step, so challenging Black's centre with d4 later costs another move. After 4...Be7 5.Nc3 Nc6 6.a4 Nf6 7.Bg5 Bg4 8.h3 Be6 Black has developed freely, the e6-bishop challenges yours and the game is level. 4.c3 prepares d4 and opens b3 for your queen. After 4...Nf6 5.Qb3 Qc7 6.d4 Nc6 7.d5 Ne7 8.Qc2 you have hit f7 and b7, gained space with the d-pawn and pushed Black's knight back.
2885293173565302|d2d3.principle: Fight for the centre: Black's c5 and e5 pawns control d4, so 4.c3 prepares d4 to challenge them, while 4.d3 settles for a passive setup.
sources: IM Kushager Krishnater, Dangerous System against the Sicilian: the Concept with 3.Bc4 (Modern Chess) | https://www.modern-chess.com/course/dangerous-system-against-the-sicilian-the-concept-with-3-bc4/64692/
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4
Andre Schulz, Beating the Sicilian with 3.Bc4 - seriously? (ChessBase) | https://en.chessbase.com/post/beating-the-sicilian-with-3-bc4

ideas.title: c3 and d4 against ...c5 and ...e5
ideas.text: Black's pawns on c5 and e5 hold d4. c3 prepares d4 to challenge them, the plan IM Krishnater uses against ...e5.

ideas.title: Qb3 hits f7 and b7
ideas.text: Once c3 is in, the queen can go to b3, joining the bishop against f7 and hitting b7, as in 5.Qb3.

ideas.title: Italian-style setup
ideas.text: d3, c3, castling and a rook to the e-file is the quiet 3.Bc4 plan. Against ...e5, an early d3 means d4 costs a second move.

habit.why: 4.d3 is passive: the d-pawn takes one step, so challenging Black's centre with d4 later costs another move. After 4...Be7 5.Nc3 Nc6 6.a4 Nf6 7.Bg5 Bg4 8.h3 Be6 Black has developed freely, the e6-bishop challenges yours and the game is level.

strays.text: The d-pawn takes one step, so challenging Black's centre costs another move.

taught.why: 4.c3 prepares d4 and opens b3 for your queen. After 4...Nf6 5.Qb3 Qc7 6.d4 Nc6 7.d5 Ne7 8.Qc2 you have hit f7 and b7, gained space with the d-pawn and pushed Black's knight back.

enforces.text: 4.c3 gets 6.d4 in, then 7.d5 gains space.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 4.Nc3 blocks your c-pawn, so it can't support a d4 push against Black's c5 and e5 pawns. After 4...Be7 5.d3 the game is quiet and Black is comfortable.
alternatives.after: 4.c3 keeps the d4 break: after 6.d4 Nc6 7.d5 you gain space and push the knight back to e7.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 4.O-O is natural, but Black develops freely with 4...Be7 and ...Nf6. After 6.d3 O-O 7.Nc3 Nc6 you have no central break and 8...Nb4 hits your bishop.
alternatives.after: 4.c3 first prepares d4 and opens b3 for the queen: 5.Qb3 hits b7 and f7 before Black has castled.

2927847296126403|e7e6.headline: Take on f3 with 4...exf3 and keep the gambit pawn
2927847296126403|e7e6.why: White's f3 pawn attacks your e4 pawn, and 4.fxe4 would win back the gambit pawn. 4...e6 does nothing about it: after 5.fxe4 material is level, White has a broad pawn centre, and White is better. 4...exf3, the master choice in 78.7% of games, keeps the extra pawn; after 5.Nxf3 White has development for it, but you fianchetto with ...g6 and ...Bg7, castle, and stay a pawn up with the better game. 4...Bf5 and 4...e3 are also playable.
2927847296126403|e7e6.principle: Accept a gambit only if you can hold on to the pawn: here capturing on f3 keeps it, and a quick fianchetto and castling consolidate.

2927859860869340|f3g5.headline: After 3...d6, the queen covers g5; strike with 4.d4 instead.
2927859860869340|f3g5.why: With Black's e-pawn gone from e7, the queen on d8 sees g5, so 4.Ng5 just loses the knight to 4...Qxg5. 3...d6 is a passive move that blocks Black's own bishop and concedes space, and 4.d4 takes that space: after 4...exd4 5.Nxd4 White has a centralised knight, open lines and an easy lead in development.
2927859860869340|f3g5.principle: When the opponent shuts in a bishop with a passive pawn move, claim the centre with your d-pawn instead of launching a lone piece attack.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...d6

2939336997955700|b8c6.headline: Win back the c5-pawn with 3...e6 and the bishop
2939336997955700|b8c6.why: 3...Nc6 lets White keep the extra pawn: 4.a3 and then 6.b4 support the c5-pawn with pawns, and Black has no easy way to regain it. 3...e6 opens the diagonal for the king's bishop so it can recapture: after 4.c4 Bxc5 Black has the pawn back with an active bishop.
2939336997955700|b8c6.principle: When a pawn of yours has been taken, prefer the developing move that also wins it back: here the e-pawn frees the bishop to recapture on c5.

2949088022019168|g7g6.headline: When 3.Bc4 leaves e4 undefended, take it with 3...Nxe4.
2949088022019168|g7g6.why: 3...g6 ignores the loose pawn and lets White use it: 4.e5 dxe5 5.Nxe5 threatens a bishop mate on f7, and Black spends the next moves defending instead of developing. White's 3.Bc4 left e4 attacked once and not defended at all, so 3...Nxe4 wins a clean pawn. After 4.d4 g6 Black still gets the usual fianchetto, just a pawn up.
2949088022019168|g7g6.principle: Your knight on f6 hits e4 from move two, so every time White develops without covering that pawn, count its defenders and take it if there are none.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6/2. Nf3

2973368771887475|f3e5.headline: Kick the knight with 5.c3; 5.Nxe5 runs into 5...Qf6
2973368771887475|f3e5.why: 5.Nxe5 runs into 5...Qf6, which hits the e5 knight and threatens mate on f2. After 6.O-O Qxe5 you have lost the knight for the e5 pawn, and Black keeps an extra piece. 5.c3 kicks the b4 knight, so you gain time instead of a pawn: after 5...Nc6 6.d4 exd4 7.cxd4 Bb6 you have pawns on e4 and d4. That is the same position as the usual 4...Bxb4 5.c3 Bc5, the normal Evans centre for one pawn.
2973368771887475|f3e5.principle: Before grabbing a pawn, check what the opponent's queen can hit: here 5...Qf6 hits the e5 knight and f2 at once.
sources: Evans Gambit 4...Nxb4: Kaan and Chess Life (Google Books snippets) | https://www.google.com/books/feeds/volumes?q=Evans+Gambit+%224...Nxb4%22
Bruce Pandolfini, The Winning Way (Google Books snippet) | https://www.google.com/books/feeds/volumes?q=%22Nxb4%22+%22Nxe5+Qf6%22
GM John Nunn, Learn to play the Evans Gambit (ChessBase) | https://en.chessbase.com/post/john-nunn-learn-to-play-the-evans-gambit

ideas.title: Watch the queen counter-hit
ideas.text: If your knight takes on e5, 5...Qf6 hits it and threatens mate on f2 at the same time.

ideas.title: Evans: the centre is the payment
ideas.text: You gave the b-pawn so that c3 and d4 come with tempo. 5.c3 kicks the knight, then 6.d4 builds your centre.

ideas.title: Black threatens ...d5
ideas.text: Black's next idea is 5...d5, hitting your c4 bishop and the e4 pawn to win a second pawn.

habit.why: 5.Nxe5 runs into 5...Qf6, which hits the e5 knight and threatens mate on f2. After 6.O-O Qxe5 you have lost the knight for the e5 pawn, and Black keeps an extra piece.

strays.text: The e5 knight is loose, and 5...Qf6 hits it with a mate threat.

taught.why: 5.c3 kicks the b4 knight, so you gain time instead of a pawn: after 5...Nc6 6.d4 exd4 7.cxd4 Bb6 you have pawns on e4 and d4. That is the same position as the usual 4...Bxb4 5.c3 Bc5, the normal Evans centre for one pawn.

enforces.idea: Evans: the centre is the payment
enforces.text: Kicking the knight, then 6.d4, gets your centre with tempo.

2977407816810866|a7a6.headline: After White castles, Bxc6 and Nxe5 is a real threat
2977407816810866|a7a6.why: With White castled, 4...a6 no longer holds e5: 5.Bxc6 removes its defender and 6.Nxe5 wins the pawn, because the old ...Qd4 counter fails now that the rook on f1 guards f2. 4...Nd4 attacks the bishop on b5 and takes the knight out of the exchange; after 5.Nxd4 Bxd4 Black recaptures with the bishop. Masters choose it in 43.4% of games.
2977407816810866|a7a6.principle: Ask what your opponent's last move threatens: castling made Bxc6 and Nxe5 work, so move the knight with a counterattack instead of a slow pawn move.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Bc5/4. O-O

3001047939008470|e7e5.headline: e5 has no defender here: play the solid 5...e6
3001047939008470|e7e5.why: 5...e5 puts a pawn where the d4 pawn and the f3 knight both attack it and nothing defends it: 6.dxe5 wins it and also kicks the knight on f6 back to d7. White then follows with 7.Nd4 against the bishop on f5 and 8.f4, and Black is close to lost. 5...e6 is the main move (58.1% of master games): your light-squared bishop is already outside the pawn chain on f5, so ...e6 supports d5 and opens the way for ...Be7, keeping the game level.
3001047939008470|e7e5.principle: Before a pawn break, count who attacks and who defends the square it lands on; a break that is attacked twice and defended zero times just loses the pawn.

3021266198007975|d8f6.headline: Develop with 5...Nf6; 5...Qf6 runs into 6.Nd5
3021266198007975|d8f6.why: 5...Qf6 brings the queen out early, and 6.Nd5 hits it and c7 at once. After 6...Qd8 7.c3 Bb6 8.d4 White has gained time for a big centre, and 10.Nxb6 takes your bishop pair. 5...Nf6 develops toward the centre, hits e4 and gets you ready to castle, as 6...O-O does in the line. After 6.a3 O-O 7.d3 a5 you have a normal slow Italian with the ...a5 plan Wesley So favours for Black.
3021266198007975|d8f6.principle: Bring the knights out before the queen: a queen on f6 takes the knight's square and gives White's knight a target.
sources: IM Roven Vogel reviews Wesley So's Modern Italian (ChessBase) | http://en.chessbase.com/post/roven-vogel-reviews-the-modern-italian-by-wesley-so

ideas.title: Knights before the queen
ideas.text: A knight on f6 develops, hits e4 and prepares castling. A queen there takes the knight's square and gives White a target.

ideas.title: White's knight jumps to d5
ideas.text: The c3 knight can jump to d5, hitting f6 and c7, and gain time for c3 and d4.

ideas.title: Give the bishop a retreat
ideas.text: White's knight can chase your c5 bishop from a4; ...a6 makes a7 a safe retreat.

ideas.title: Swap off the Italian bishop
ideas.text: ...Be6 offers to trade White's c4 bishop. It's safe here: the d8 queen covers g5, so after the trade White's knight can't reach e6 that way.

habit.why: 5...Qf6 brings the queen out early, and 6.Nd5 hits it and c7 at once. After 6...Qd8 7.c3 Bb6 8.d4 White has gained time for a big centre, and 10.Nxb6 takes your bishop pair.

strays.text: The queen takes the knight's square and becomes a target for 6.Nd5.

taught.why: 5...Nf6 develops toward the centre, hits e4 and gets you ready to castle, as 6...O-O does in the line. After 6.a3 O-O 7.d3 a5 you have a normal slow Italian with the ...a5 plan Wesley So favours for Black.

enforces.text: The knight develops, hits e4 and clears the way to castle.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...h6 keeps White's pieces off g5 and is sound, but 6.Na4 goes straight for your c5 bishop. A developing move is a touch more useful.
alternatives.after: 5...Nf6 develops a piece instead. The engine rates the two about equal, but after 5...h6 6.Na4 Qf6 the queen still comes out early.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...Be6 offers to trade White's c4 bishop; after 6.Bxe6 fxe6 you get the half-open f-file and an extra guard on d5. It's sound, though 7.Na4 then chases your other bishop.
alternatives.after: 5...Nf6 develops the kingside first. After 5...Be6 6.Bxe6 fxe6 7.Na4 Bb6 White can win the bishop pair; both moves keep the balance.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...a6 gives your bishop a7 as a retreat against a knight on a4, and if 6.Nd5 you can trade it off with 7...Nxd5. It's sound; a developing move is a touch more useful.
alternatives.after: 5...Nf6 develops at once; 5...a6 is a useful waiting move, and both keep the balance. After 5...a6 6.Nd5 the knight still comes out with 6...Nf6.

3024364401435985|g8h6.headline: Grab the centre with d5 against the early queen
3024364401435985|g8h6.why: 2...Nh6 does nothing for the centre or for the pawn on e5, and after 3.d4 d5 4.dxe5 White has won it. 2...d5 takes the centre with a second pawn while White's queen sits in front of its own knight; after 3.Qg3 the queen has moved twice, and 3...Nc6 develops while guarding e5.
3024364401435985|g8h6.principle: An early queen blocks its own pieces and wastes time; answer it by taking the centre with pawns and developing, not with a knight on the rim.

3047838571696673|d7d5.headline: Develop with 2...Bc5 and aim at the d4 hole
3047838571696673|d7d5.why: 2...d5 is the Bavarian gambit, and the theory marks it as a mistake: 3.cxd5 wins a pawn. 2.c4 is slow and leaves White with a permanent hole on d4. 2...Bc5, the most common master reply, develops the bishop to a square that aims at d4 and f2.
3047838571696673|d7d5.principle: When your opponent's pawn moves leave a square that no pawn can cover, point your pieces at it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. c4

3047838571696673|d8g5.headline: Develop with 2...Bc5; an early queen just gets chased
3047838571696673|d8g5.why: 2...Qg5 brings the queen out with four minor pieces still at home, and White develops by attacking it: 3.Nf3 sends it back to e7, and Black has lost time. 2.c4 left a permanent hole on d4 and blocked White's own king's bishop, and 2...Bc5 exploits that: the bishop takes an active diagonal aimed at d4 and f2.
3047838571696673|d8g5.principle: An early queen sortie invites knights and bishops to come out with tempo; develop a minor piece toward the squares your opponent has weakened instead.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. c4

3078274341826662|f3e5.headline: The d6 pawn guards e5: recapture on d4 instead
3078274341826662|f3e5.why: 6.Ne5 puts the knight where the pawn on d6 takes it: 6...dxe5, and 7.Qh5+ Kd7 8.Qxe5 does not win it back, leaving you a knight down. The Qh5+ trick that wins the rook on h8 in the 3...f5 line does not work here: Black answers 7.Qh5+ with 7...Kd7. Meanwhile d4 is attacked twice and not defended at all, so 6.Nxd4 (95.7% of masters games) wins the pawn back and centralises the knight, with a small edge for White.
3078274341826662|f3e5.principle: Moving a developed piece again is only worth it when it wins something concrete: here the knight's second move should collect the free pawn on d4, not walk into a pawn capture.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4

3087437353600707|d1e2.headline: Kick the f6-knight with 7.e5 before Black can pin
3087437353600707|d1e2.why: 7.Qe2 lets Black play 7...Bg4, pinning your knight now that the f6-knight covers g4. After 8.Be3 Rc8 9.h3 Bxf3 10.Qxf3 Black has traded off one of your attackers and stays a pawn up. 7.e5 hits the f6-knight before Black can pin or castle: after 7...Ng4 8.exd6 exd6 9.O-O Be7 10.h3 the knight must go back and Black's d6 pawn is isolated. It is the masters' main move here (57%).
3087437353600707|d1e2.principle: You lead in development and Black's king is in the centre, so open the game now with 7.e5 instead of a quiet setup move that allows the pin.

ideas.title: The e4-e5 break
ideas.text: e4-e5 hits the f6-knight and the d6 pawn and opens lines while Black's king is still on e8.

ideas.title: Bc4 eyes f7
ideas.text: With Black's e-pawn still on e7, your c4-bishop aims at f7, so opening the centre is risky for Black.

ideas.title: The ...Bg4 pin
ideas.text: With the f6-knight covering g4, Black can pin your f3-knight with a bishop on g4 and trade it off, freeing Black's game.

ideas.title: No autopilot setup
ideas.text: The usual setup with the queen on e2 and a rook on d1 doesn't fit every defence; check what Black is ready for first.

habit.why: 7.Qe2 lets Black play 7...Bg4, pinning your knight now that the f6-knight covers g4. After 8.Be3 Rc8 9.h3 Bxf3 10.Qxf3 Black has traded off one of your attackers and stays a pawn up.

strays.text: The routine queen move gives Black time for 7...Bg4 and a trade on f3.

taught.why: 7.e5 hits the f6-knight before Black can pin or castle: after 7...Ng4 8.exd6 exd6 9.O-O Be7 10.h3 the knight must go back and Black's d6 pawn is isolated. It is the masters' main move here (57%).

enforces.text: The pawn kicks the f6-knight before Black can pin your f3-knight.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7.O-O is a good, natural move, played in 40% of master games. After 7...a6 8.Bf4 e6 Black reaches a solid setup; there's a slightly stronger move.
alternatives.after: 7.e5 is the masters' main choice (57%): it strikes before Black can set up with ...a6, ...Bg4 and ...e6. After 7.O-O a6 Black has time for that.

3087437353600707|f3g5.headline: 7.e5, not 7.Ng5: Black's 7...e6 shuts out the knight's target
3087437353600707|f3g5.why: 7.Ng5 moves the knight again, but 7...e6 shuts the c4-bishop off from f7 and the knight has nothing to hit. After 8.O-O Be7 9.Qe2 O-O 10.Nf3 it goes back home, two moves lost in a gambit where time is everything. 7.e5 hits the f6-knight while Black's king is still on e8, and 7...Nxe5 8.Nxe5 dxe5 9.Bxf7+ Kxf7 10.Qxd8 wins the queen. Black's best is 7...Ng4 8.exd6 exd6 9.O-O Be7 10.h3, when the knight must retreat and the d6 pawn is isolated.
3087437353600707|f3g5.principle: Don't move the same piece twice without a target: after 7.Ng5 e6 the knight hits nothing and goes back, while 7.e5 hits the f6-knight.
sources: IM John Watson, Watson on Trent: The Smith-Morra Gambit | https://en.chessbase.com/post/watson-on-trent-the-smith-morra-gambit

ideas.title: The e4-e5 break
ideas.text: e4-e5 hits the f6-knight and the d6 pawn and opens lines while Black's king is still on e8.

ideas.title: Bc4 eyes f7
ideas.text: Your c4-bishop aims at f7: after 7.e5, 7...Nxe5 8.Nxe5 dxe5 9.Bxf7+ Kxf7 10.Qxd8 wins Black's queen.

ideas.title: ...e6 shuts out the bishop
ideas.text: One pawn move, ...e6, cuts your c4-bishop off from f7. Then a knight on g5 has nothing to attack.

ideas.title: The ...Bg4 pin
ideas.text: With the f6-knight covering g4, Black can pin your f3-knight with a bishop on g4 and trade it off, freeing Black's game.

habit.why: 7.Ng5 moves the knight again, but 7...e6 shuts the c4-bishop off from f7 and the knight has nothing to hit. After 8.O-O Be7 9.Qe2 O-O 10.Nf3 it goes back home, two moves lost in a gambit where time is everything.

strays.text: One pawn move by Black makes the knight's trip pointless.

taught.why: 7.e5 hits the f6-knight while Black's king is still on e8, and 7...Nxe5 8.Nxe5 dxe5 9.Bxf7+ Kxf7 10.Qxd8 wins the queen. Black's best is 7...Ng4 8.exd6 exd6 9.O-O Be7 10.h3, when the knight must retreat and the d6 pawn is isolated.

enforces.text: The pawn kicks the f6-knight and opens lines toward Black's king.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7.O-O is a good, natural move, played in 40% of master games. After 7...a6 8.Bf4 e6 Black reaches a solid setup; there's a slightly stronger move.
alternatives.after: 7.e5 is the masters' main choice (57%): it strikes before Black can set up with ...a6, ...Bg4 and ...e6. After 7.O-O a6 Black has time for that.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.Qe2 allows 7...Bg4, pinning your knight now that the f6-knight covers g4. After 8.O-O e6 9.h3 Bxf3 10.Qxf3 Black has traded off an attacker and is solid.
alternatives.after: 7.e5 hits the f6-knight first, so Black is busy answering threats instead of pinning and trading on f3.

3105714547729451|c8g4.headline: Develop 2...Nf6 and hit e4 before pinning with the bishop
3105714547729451|c8g4.why: 2...Bg4 develops the bishop before the knights and lets White strike with 3.d4: after 3...e5 4.dxe5 Black loses a pawn. 2...Nf6 develops the knight toward the centre and attacks the pawn on e4 right away, so White answers 3.Nc3 to defend it. It is the choice of 62.4% of masters.
3105714547729451|c8g4.principle: Bring the knights out before the bishops: the knight's square on f6 is clear and hits e4 now, while the bishop's best square isn't clear yet.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6/2. Nf3

3119368342174684|e7e6.headline: Strike at e5 with d6 before it gets support
3119368342174684|e7e6.why: 3...e6 is slow: it lets White shore up the advanced pawn with 4.Nc3 and 5.f4, leaving Black cramped behind it. 3...d6 attacks e5 together with the bishop on g7 before it can be supported; after 4.exd6 Qxd6 the queen and bishop both bear on d4, and 5...c5 attacks White's centre again.
3119368342174684|e7e6.principle: When White pushes a centre pawn to the fifth rank early, hit it with a pawn at once, before other pawns arrive to support it.

3179485995949204|c1f4.headline: Kick the f6 knight with 6.e5 once ...Be7 blocks its retreat
3179485995949204|c1f4.why: 6.Bf4 lets Black strike back with 6...c5, and after 7.Nc3 cxd4 8.Nxd4 your d4 pawn is traded off and much of your advantage goes with it. 5...Be7 was slow, and with the bishop on e7 the knight on f6 can no longer drop back to e7. 6.e5 gains space with tempo on the knight, which goes all the way back to g8 in the engine line, and after 7.O-O you are far ahead in development with a big advantage.
3179485995949204|c1f4.principle: A knight on f6 in front of an advanced e-pawn is a target: push the pawn when the knight has no good square, and you gain space and time together.

3179485995949204|e1h1.headline: Use your lead: 6.e5 sends the f6 knight back home
3179485995949204|e1h1.why: Black's 5...Be7 is passive and does nothing about the e4-e5 advance. 6.O-O is the most common move (83.3% of masters games), but it gives Black time for 6...O-O 7.c4 d5, and your large edge is cut in half. 6.e5 claims the centre and attacks the knight on f6; after 6...Ng8 the knight has to undo its development, and you keep a large advantage.
3179485995949204|e1h1.principle: When your opponent's quiet move hands you a clear advantage, act on it at once with a forcing advance; a routine move gives them the time to catch up.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...b6/2. d4/2...Bb7/3. Bd3

3191630614517678|f2f3.headline: Punish 2...Nh6 by developing 3.Nc3, not with f3
3191630614517678|f2f3.why: 3.f3 props up e4 but takes f3 from White's knight and doesn't hold: after 3...c6 4.d4 d5 5.Bb3 dxe4 Black wins a pawn. 2...Nh6 put Black's knight on the rim, away from the centre; 3.Nc3 simply develops, defends e4 and controls d5, and White keeps the lead in development.
3191630614517678|f2f3.principle: When your opponent puts a knight on the rim, just develop toward the centre; a pawn move like f3 needs a concrete reason and takes your knight's best square.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4

3244175099892819|f7f6.headline: Against 1.g4, take the centre and hit g4 with 1...d5.
3244175099892819|f7f6.why: 1...f6 weakens Black's own king and does nothing against the g4 pawn, so White settles in comfortably with 2.d4 d5 3.h3. The theory calls 1.g4 one of the worst first moves because it loosens White's kingside and leaves the pawn on g4 hard to defend. 1...d5 takes central space and attacks g4 at once with the bishop on c8, and masters play it in 66.9% of games.
3244175099892819|f7f6.principle: Answer a flank opening by occupying the centre, ideally with a move that also hits the flank pawn, as ...d5 does to g4.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. g4
Chess Opening Theory/1. g4/1...d5

3244175099892819|g8f6.headline: Against the Grob, take the centre with 1...d5
3244175099892819|g8f6.why: 1...Nf6 eyes the g4 pawn, but 2.g5 kicks the knight, which has no good square besides h5 and its starting square; after 2...Nh5 it sits on the rim while White builds a centre with 3.e4 and 5.d4. 1...d5, played in 66.9% of master games, takes central space and opens the line of the bishop on c8 to g4, so the pawn is attacked at once. After 2.c4 d4 Black gains even more space.
3244175099892819|g8f6.principle: A knight on f6 is exactly what White's g-pawn wants to chase, so take the centre with a pawn first and make the advanced pawn the target.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. g4
Chess Opening Theory/1. g4/1...Nf6
Chess Opening Theory/1. g4/1...d5

3249639623522672|c7c6.headline: Use the fork trick: 6...Nxe4 and 7...d5
3249639623522672|c7c6.why: 6...c6 is slow, and 7.e5 kicks the knight back to 7...Ne8, leaving White with a big centre and Black cramped. 6...Nxe4, the masters' most common move at 36.1%, uses a fork: after 7.Nxe4 d5 the pawn attacks both the bishop on c4 and the knight on e4, and 8.Bd3 dxe4 9.Bxe4 wins the piece back. The trade removes White's e-pawn and frees Black's game.
3249639623522672|c7c6.principle: When White's centre pawn is guarded only by a piece that a pawn fork can hit, trade it off before it advances and cramps you.

3253136195144505|f7f6.headline: Develop with 3...Nf6; 3...f6 weakens your king and wastes time
3253136195144505|f7f6.why: 3...f6 is a third pawn move that takes the f6 square from your own knight and opens the diagonal from the bishop on c4 toward g8, so castling kingside becomes risky. After 4.d4 Nc6 5.Be3 White has a strong centre and a lead in development. 3...Nf6 develops toward the centre and attacks the pawn on e4, which gains time; after 4.Nc3 Be7 Black is ready to castle.
3253136195144505|f7f6.principle: With two pawn moves already played and the bishop on c4 eyeing your king, every extra pawn move costs time and loosens the king; develop a piece instead.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4

3294566395905444|f1c4.headline: Punish 3...Bd6 with 4.Nxe5 and a pawn fork
3294566395905444|f1c4.why: 4.Bc4 lets Black off the hook: after 4...Nc6 e5 is defended and the game is normal. 3...Bd6 puts the bishop beside the knight where White's centre pawns can reach them both, and 4.Nxe5 exploits it: after 4...Bxe5 5.d4 Bd6 6.e5 the pawn hits bishop and knight together, and after 6...Bb4 7.exf6 Qxf6 White has won back the piece and is a pawn up.
3294566395905444|f1c4.principle: When an enemy bishop and knight stand side by side within reach of your centre pawns, check the capture that clears the way for a pawn fork.

3294907482050607|f3g5.headline: Guard e4 with 4.Nc3 instead of moving the knight twice
3294907482050607|f3g5.why: 4.Ng5 moves the knight again, and 4...e6 covers f7 and blunts your bishop. After 5.d3 Be7 6.O-O O-O 7.Nc3 Nc6 8.Re1 a6 the g5-knight has no target and Black has the easier game. 4.Nc3 develops a new piece and guards e4 against 4...Nxe4. After 4...e6 5.d4 cxd4 6.Nxd4 a6 7.a4 you have an Open Sicilian with your bishop on c4 and a level game.
3294907482050607|f3g5.principle: Develop a new piece rather than moving one twice: 4.Nc3 guards e4 and develops, while 4.Ng5 spends a second knight move that 4...e6 answers.
sources: IM Kushager Krishnater, Dangerous System against the Sicilian: the Concept with 3.Bc4 (Modern Chess) | https://www.modern-chess.com/course/dangerous-system-against-the-sicilian-the-concept-with-3-bc4/64692/
Bowdler Attack - An Advanced Study Guide (Chess Klub) | https://chessklub.com/bowdler-attack/

ideas.title: Guard e4 first
ideas.text: 3...Nf6 attacks e4. 4.Nc3 or 4.d3 defends it; castling first allows 4...Nxe4.

ideas.title: No time for knight raids
ideas.text: 4.Ng5 moves a piece twice; 4...e6 covers f7 and the knight has nothing to hit.

ideas.title: Open Sicilian with Bc4
ideas.text: Pushing d4 can give an Open Sicilian with your bishop already on c4, as in 5.d4 cxd4 6.Nxd4.

ideas.title: Italian-style setup
ideas.text: The quiet alternative from IM Krishnater's course: d3, castling and c3, later a rook to e1, a4 and the bishop back to b3.

habit.why: 4.Ng5 moves the knight again, and 4...e6 covers f7 and blunts your bishop. After 5.d3 Be7 6.O-O O-O 7.Nc3 Nc6 8.Re1 a6 the g5-knight has no target and Black has the easier game.

strays.text: The knight jumps to g5, but 4...e6 leaves it nothing to hit.

taught.why: 4.Nc3 develops a new piece and guards e4 against 4...Nxe4. After 4...e6 5.d4 cxd4 6.Nxd4 a6 7.a4 you have an Open Sicilian with your bishop on c4 and a level game.

enforces.text: The knight defends e4 and develops in one move.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.d3 guards e4 and is the main line in IM Krishnater's course. After 4...e6 5.O-O Be7 6.a4 O-O 7.Bb3 you keep a solid Italian-style position. It's fully sound.
alternatives.after: 4.Nc3 also guards e4 but heads for an open game with d4; 4.d3 is the slower plan with c3 and a rook on e1. The engine rates them the same.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4.O-O leaves e4 hanging: after 4...Nxe4 5.d4 cxd4 6.Nxd4 e6 you're a pawn down without enough for it.
alternatives.after: 4.Nc3 defends e4 first; you can castle later, once Black can no longer take the pawn.

3297019676720294|d8e7.headline: 5...Qg5 hits the knight on e5 and the g2 pawn at once
3297019676720294|d8e7.why: 5...Qe7 does attack the knight, but it lets White play 6.d4 with gain of time against the bishop on c5, which the theory warns can be kicked by d4. Black only wins the pawn back after 8.O-O Bxe5 9.dxe5 Qxe5, having traded the bishop for the knight while White has castled and kept developing. 5...Qg5 attacks the knight on e5 and the pawn on g2 together, and after 6.Ng4 d5 7.d4 Qxg4 8.Qxg4 Bxg4 9.dxc5 dxe4 Black has the pawn back with the queens off.
3297019676720294|d8e7.principle: When you need to win back a pawn, do it with a move that makes two threats, so the opponent spends the move answering instead of developing with gain of time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Bc5

3303598185152393|d1d5.headline: Develop with 4.Nc3; the early 4.Qd5 just gets chased
3303598185152393|d1d5.why: 4.Qd5 brings the queen out with three minor pieces still at home, and Black develops by attacking it: 4...Nc6, then 5...Be6 hits the queen again, and after 6.Qd2 dxe5 Black has won back the pawn. 4.Nc3 develops and, as the theory notes, adds a defender to the queen on d1, which takes the sting out of the Derek Wu trap that 3...d6 sets up. In the line White keeps the extra pawn: 6.exd6 cxd6 only swaps the e-pawn for Black's d-pawn.
3303598185152393|d1d5.principle: Keep the queen at home while the minor pieces are undeveloped; in the centre it only gives Black's knights and bishops targets to develop against.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...e5/2. dxe5/2...Bc5

3324621583464853|c6e5.headline: Develop with 5...Bb4 instead of moving the c6 knight again
3324621583464853|c6e5.why: 5...Ne5 moves the knight a second time and puts it where White's pawns can chase it: 6.f4 kicks it back to c6 and 7.e5 sends the other knight home to g8, so White gains a lot of time. 5...Bb4 develops a bishop, pins the knight on c3 and prepares to castle. After 6.Bd2 O-O 7.Bd3 d5 Black strikes in the centre, the break that White's queen retreat 4.Qd1 allows.
3324621583464853|c6e5.principle: With both bishops still at home, a second knight move needs a concrete gain; this one has none and only gives White's pawns a target.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. Qxd4/3...Nc6

3337365835027440|d2d3.headline: Punish the early 3...Qf6 by opening the centre with 4.d4.
3337365835027440|d2d3.why: 4.d3 is too modest: after 4...Be6 Black trades off the bishop on c4, and the queen goes home with 6...Qd8 having lost little. Black's 3...Qf6 brings the queen out early and takes f6 from the king's knight, so White should open the centre while Black is behind. 4.d4 attacks the pawn on e5 at once, and after 4...Nc6 5.d5 Nb8 the knight is driven home; by 6...Qd8 the queen has gone back too, and White is well ahead in development.
3337365835027440|d2d3.principle: When your opponent brings the queen out early, open the centre and gain time against it rather than making quiet moves.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4

3350501418691275|a7a6.headline: Stop e4-e5 with 5...d6 before it kicks your knight
3350501418691275|a7a6.why: 5...a6 does nothing about e4-e5, and 6.e5 Ng8 sends your knight back home. After 7.Bf4 Ne7 8.Bd3 Ng6 9.Bg3 your knight has moved four times while White has space and a big lead in development. 5...d6 covers e5, so your knight stays on f6. After 6.g4 h6 7.Rg1 Nc6 8.Be3 Bd7 9.Be2 d5 you meet the Keres Attack with the central ...d5 break once your pieces are out.
3350501418691275|a7a6.principle: A piece a pawn can attack is a target: 5...d6 controls e5, while 5...a6 lets 6.e5 chase your knight home.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...e6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...Nf6

ideas.title: The e4-e5 kick
ideas.text: With your knight on f6 and no pawn on d6, e4-e5 drives it away: 6.e5 sends it back to g8.

ideas.title: Control e5 with ...d6
ideas.text: 5...d6 stops e4-e5 for good and gives a Scheveningen, the most common choice here (55% of master games).

ideas.title: White's Keres Attack
ideas.text: Against the Scheveningen, White's sharpest try is 6.g4, aiming g5 at your knight; Semkov names it, with White's f4 and queen-to-f3 system, as the Scheveningen's biggest problem.

habit.why: 5...a6 does nothing about e4-e5, and 6.e5 Ng8 sends your knight back home. After 7.Bf4 Ne7 8.Bd3 Ng6 9.Bg3 your knight has moved four times while White has space and a big lead in development.

strays.text: Without ...d6, nothing stops 6.e5 from kicking the knight.

taught.why: 5...d6 covers e5, so your knight stays on f6. After 6.g4 h6 7.Rg1 Nc6 8.Be3 Bd7 9.Be2 d5 you meet the Keres Attack with the central ...d5 break once your pieces are out.

enforces.text: The d6 pawn holds e5, so the f6-knight can't be kicked.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 5...Bb4, the Pin Variation, hits e4 at once, but 6.e5 Nd5 7.Qg4 attacks g7 and 7...Kf8 costs you castling.
alternatives.after: 5...d6 stops 6.e5 before it happens. The pin works better when a knight on c6 is ready to meet e5.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5...Nc6 is the Sicilian Four Knights, played in 41% of master games and judged sound by Willis and Kotronias. The engine grades it lower: 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.e5 Nd5 8.Ne4 leaves you a dark-square hole that the e5 pawn and the e4-knight eye.
alternatives.after: 5...d6 is a little more popular (55% to 41%) and stops e4-e5 at once. Both are normal; the engine just prefers 5...d6.

3383188774541308|d8f6.headline: After 5.Nxe5, 5...Qg5 forks the knight and g2.
3383188774541308|d8f6.why: 5...Qf6 attacks only the knight, and 6.Ng4 hits the queen while White keeps the pawn. 5...Qg5 attacks the knight on e5 and the pawn on g2 together, and after 6.Ng4 h5 7.Ne3 Nxb5 8.Nxb5 Bxe3 Black wins a knight for a pawn.
3383188774541308|d8f6.principle: When a knight grabs a pawn, look for the queen move that attacks it and a second target at once; a double attack beats a single one.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Bc5

3400735200665154|g5e4.headline: Don't recapture on e4: 5.Bxf7+ comes first, with check
3400735200665154|g5e4.why: 5.Nxe4 walks into 5...d5, a pawn fork of your knight and c4 bishop. After 6.Bd3 dxe4 7.Bxe4 Bd7 material is level, but Black has a free centre and easy development, and your attack is gone. 5.Bxf7+ Ke7 wins back the pawn with check, and Black's king can never castle. 6.d4 stops Black taking on g5, since your c1 bishop would recapture with check and win the queen; after 6...h6 7.Nxe4 Kxf7 8.d5 the king stays exposed.
3400735200665154|g5e4.principle: Look for checks before recaptures: 5.Bxf7+ forces Black's king to move, while the natural 5.Nxe4 runs into the 5...d5 fork.
sources: Jan Pinski, The Two Knights Defence (Everyman, 2004) | https://masterinchess.com/Media/2024/07/The%20Two%20Knights%20Defence.pdf
Two Knights Defense (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two_Knights_Defense

ideas.title: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
ideas.text: 5.Bxf7+ takes f7 with check: the king must go to e7, can never castle, and 6.d4 follows with tempo.

ideas.title: Black's counter-threats
ideas.text: Black's e4 knight hits your g5 knight and f2. A queen on h4 would add a second attacker on f2.

ideas.title: The skewer on g5
ideas.text: After 5.Bxf7+ Ke7 6.d4, taking on g5 fails: your c1 bishop recaptures with check and wins the queen behind the king.

ideas.title: Watch the d5 fork
ideas.text: If your knight takes on e4, the pawn jump to d5 forks it and the c4 bishop, and Black wins the piece back.

habit.why: 5.Nxe4 walks into 5...d5, a pawn fork of your knight and c4 bishop. After 6.Bd3 dxe4 7.Bxe4 Bd7 material is level, but Black has a free centre and easy development, and your attack is gone.

strays.text: Recapturing on e4 lets 5...d5 fork knight and bishop.

taught.why: 5.Bxf7+ Ke7 wins back the pawn with check, and Black's king can never castle. 6.d4 stops Black taking on g5, since your c1 bishop would recapture with check and win the queen; after 6...h6 7.Nxe4 Kxf7 8.d5 the king stays exposed.

enforces.idea: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
enforces.text: The bishop takes with check, and the e4 knight can wait.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 5.Nxf7 forks queen and rook, but 5...Qh4 threatens mate on f2. After 6.Qe2 Nd4 7.g3 Nxe2 8.gxh4 Nd4 9.Nxh8 Nxc2+ Black forks back, and you have no edge.
alternatives.after: 5.Bxf7+ takes the same pawn with check, so Black never gets time for 5...Qh4, and the king can never castle.

3400735200665154|g5f7.headline: Take on f7 with the bishop and check, not the knight
3400735200665154|g5f7.why: 5.Nxf7 forks queen and rook, but 5...Qh4 hits f2 with the queen and the e4 knight and threatens mate. After 6.Qe2 Nd4 7.g3 Nxe2 8.gxh4 Nd4 9.Nxh8 Nxc2+ Black forks your king and rook, and you have no advantage left. 5.Bxf7+ Ke7 wins back the pawn with check, and Black's king can never castle. 6.d4 stops Black taking on g5, since your c1 bishop would recapture with check and win the queen; after 6...h6 7.Nxe4 Kxf7 8.d5 the king stays exposed.
3400735200665154|g5f7.principle: Check the opponent's threats before grabbing material, and prefer captures with check: 5.Bxf7+ moves the king before Black has time for 5...Qh4.

ideas.title: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
ideas.text: 5.Bxf7+ takes f7 with check: the king must go to e7, can never castle, and 6.d4 follows with tempo.

ideas.title: Black's counter-threats

habit.why: 5.Nxf7 forks queen and rook, but 5...Qh4 hits f2 with the queen and the e4 knight and threatens mate. After 6.Qe2 Nd4 7.g3 Nxe2 8.gxh4 Nd4 9.Nxh8 Nxc2+ Black forks your king and rook, and you have no advantage left.

strays.idea: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
strays.text: The knight takes without check, so Black strikes first with 5...Qh4.

enforces.idea: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
enforces.text: The bishop takes with check, so Black never gets time for 5...Qh4.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 5.Nxe4 takes the knight back, but 5...d5 forks your e4 knight and c4 bishop. After 6.Bd3 dxe4 7.Bxe4 Black has a free centre and the better game.
alternatives.after: 5.Bxf7+ comes first, with check, and you take the e4 knight later with 7.Nxe4, when your bishop is no longer on c4 to be forked.

3408833361615716|e2e3.headline: A pawn up, develop with 3.Nc3 and keep the e5 pawn
3408833361615716|e2e3.why: 3.e3 blocks the bishop's pressure on f2 but is slow, and Black wins the e5 pawn back: after 3...Nc6 4.Nf3 Qe7 5.Bd2 d6 6.exd6 Bxd6 material is level. 2...Bc5 did nothing to attack e5, so White can keep the extra pawn by developing quickly. 3.Nc3 develops a piece and, as the theory notes, adds another defender to the queen to defuse Black's tricks; later 5.Ne4 hits the bishop on c5.
3408833361615716|e2e3.principle: When you are a pawn up, develop quickly and with threats so your opponent never gets the time to win it back.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...e5/2. dxe5/2...Bc5

3415269394174453|b2b4.headline: No Evans here: 5.d3 develops, 5.b4 just drops a pawn
3415269394174453|b2b4.why: 5.b4 offers an Evans-style pawn, but the follow-up of hitting the bishop with c3 is impossible with your knight already on c3: 5...Bxb4 simply wins a pawn, and after 6.Nd5 O-O 7.Nxb4 Nxb4 Black stays a pawn up and is better. 5.d3, the masters' choice 88.4% of the time, guards e4 and opens the diagonal for your c1 bishop. After 5...a6 6.O-O d6 7.a4 you have a solid position with the game level.
3415269394174453|b2b4.principle: In the opening, play the pawn moves that free your pieces and support the centre; a flank pawn push that neither develops nor gains time just costs material.

3415269394174453|f3e5.headline: The fork trick fails here; play the quiet 5.d3.
3415269394174453|f3e5.why: 5.Nxe5 Nxe5 6.d4 hopes to fork the knight and the bishop on c5, but the knight answers 6...Nxc4 by taking White's own bishop. After 7.dxc5 White has given a knight for a pawn. 5.d3 is the hallmark of the Giuoco Pianissimo: it defends e4, opens a line for the dark-squared bishop, and prepares a slow build-up.
3415269394174453|f3e5.principle: Before a capture that relies on a follow-up fork, check what your own loose pieces can be taken in reply.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5

3415269394174453|f3g5.headline: Support e4 with 5.d3 and develop; Ng5 gets nowhere
3415269394174453|f3g5.why: 5.Ng5 moves the knight again, and 5...O-O puts a rook behind f7, so the attack has no target; after 6.d3 Nd4 the knight goes back with 7.Nf3, and Black takes over the centre with ...c6 and ...d5. 5.d3, played in 88.4% of master games, shores up e4, which the theory names as the weak point of this Italian variation because of ...Nxe4 tricks, and opens the bishop on c1 before 6.O-O.
3415269394174453|f3g5.principle: A knight that jumps to g5 must win something at once; once Black castles and covers f7, the trip only gives Black time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nc3/3...Nc6

3420590449456095|c1e3.headline: Pin the c6-knight with 6.Bb5 before it hits d4
3420590449456095|c1e3.why: 6.Be3 adds a defender to d4 but leaves the c3-knight pinned and the c6-knight free. After 6...Bg4 7.h3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3 O-O-O 9.O-O-O e5 10.d5 Nd4 Black's knight lands in the centre with active play. 6.Bb5 develops and pins the c6-knight to your king, so it can't take part in the fight for d4. After 6...Nd5 7.Rb1 a6 8.Bxc6+ bxc6 9.O-O Black's c-pawns are doubled and isolated, and you have castled.
3420590449456095|c1e3.principle: A pin ties a piece down: pin the knight that would attack d4, and Black's pressure on your centre loses its key piece.
sources: IM John Bartholomew, Main Line Scandinavian (Chessiverse) | https://chessiverse.com/resources/openings/main-line-scandinavian

ideas.title: Pin the c6-knight
ideas.text: 6.Bb5 pins the c6-knight to your king, so it can't join ...Bg4 and ...O-O-O against d4. It's the masters' top choice (48%).

ideas.title: Black's pressure on d4
ideas.text: Black's knight, a bishop on g4 and a rook after ...O-O-O can all hit d4; only your queen and f3-knight defend it.

ideas.title: The pin on c3
ideas.text: Black's queen on a5 pins your c3-knight to the king. A bishop on d2 breaks the pin; 6.Be3 does not.

ideas.title: Broken pawns for Black
ideas.text: If Black chases the bishop with ...a6, 8.Bxc6+ bxc6 leaves Black with doubled, isolated c-pawns.

habit.why: 6.Be3 adds a defender to d4 but leaves the c3-knight pinned and the c6-knight free. After 6...Bg4 7.h3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3 O-O-O 9.O-O-O e5 10.d5 Nd4 Black's knight lands in the centre with active play.

strays.text: The c6-knight stays free and lands on d4 in the end.

taught.why: 6.Bb5 develops and pins the c6-knight to your king, so it can't take part in the fight for d4. After 6...Nd5 7.Rb1 a6 8.Bxc6+ bxc6 9.O-O Black's c-pawns are doubled and isolated, and you have castled.

enforces.text: While the pin lasts, the c6-knight can't jump to d4 or e5.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 6.Bd2 breaks the pin on c3 and is the masters' second choice (33%). It's sound, but d4 needs watching: after 6...a6 7.Bc4 Nxd4 the c6-knight joins in with a tactic.
alternatives.after: 6.Bb5 takes the c6-knight out of play first, so a trick like 7...Nxd4 can't happen while the pin lasts. Masters play 6.Bb5 in 48% of games, 6.Bd2 in 33%.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: After 6.Bc4 Bg4 7.h3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3 O-O-O Black's pieces pile up on d4, and after 9.d5 Ne5 the knight hits your queen and bishop. Your edge is gone.
alternatives.after: 6.Bb5 pins the c6-knight, so it can't join the attack on d4 or jump to e5.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.Be2 is too quiet: 6...Bg4 7.h3 Bxf3 8.Bxf3 e5 lets Black strike at d4 at once.
alternatives.after: 6.Bb5 pins the c6-knight, the piece that supports ...e5 and hits d4. Masters prefer it, 48% to 4%.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.d5 chases the knight, but after 6...Nb4 7.Bc4 e6 8.dxe6 Bxe6 9.Bxe6 fxe6 Black is developed and comfortable. Masters play it in 7% of games, but the engine doesn't like it.
alternatives.after: 6.Bb5 develops a piece and keeps your pawn on d4, while 6.d5 spends a move and then trades it off.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 6.h3 stops ...Bg4 before it comes, so the f3-knight keeps guarding d4; after 6...a6 7.Bc4 b5 8.Bb3 Black gains queenside space. Sound, but another move does more.
alternatives.after: 6.Bb5 develops and deals with the c6-knight directly, while 6.h3 spends a pawn move on prevention. Masters prefer 6.Bb5, 48% to 6%; the engine rates both close.

3420590449456095|f1d3.headline: Black is eyeing d4: pin the c6-knight with 6.Bb5
3420590449456095|f1d3.why: 6.Bd3 blocks your queen's guard of d4, leaving only the f3-knight to defend it. Black goes after that knight: 6...Bg4 7.Bd2 O-O-O 8.Nb5 Qb6 9.a4 Bxf3 10.Qxf3 Nxd4 wins the pawn. 6.Bb5 develops and pins the c6-knight to your king, so it can't take part in the fight for d4. After 6...Nd5 7.Rb1 a6 8.Bxc6+ bxc6 9.O-O Black's c-pawns are doubled and isolated, and d4 is safe.
3420590449456095|f1d3.principle: Count the defenders before you develop: 6.Bd3 blocks the queen's guard of d4 just as Black lines up the knight, the g4-bishop and a rook against it.
sources: IM John Bartholomew, Main Line Scandinavian (Chessiverse) | https://chessiverse.com/resources/openings/main-line-scandinavian

3428826784804820|d7d5.headline: Against the Bishop's Opening, attack e4 with 2...Nf6.
3428826784804820|d7d5.why: The bishop on c4 already watches d5, so 2...d5 just gives up a pawn after 3.exd5. Black gets some activity, but not enough for the pawn. 2...Nf6 develops and attacks the pawn on e4, and it also covers h5, ruling out the early 3.Qh5 aimed at f7.
3428826784804820|d7d5.principle: Before pushing a pawn to a central square, count how many enemy pieces and pawns already attack it.

3428826784804820|d7d6.headline: Answer the Bishop's Opening with 2...Nf6, developing with a threat
3428826784804820|d7d6.why: 2...d6 overprotects a pawn that isn't attacked, since White has not played Nf3, and it shuts in Black's own king's bishop. 2...Nf6 develops with a threat to the pawn on e4, and it also controls h5, so White can't aim the queen at f7 with 3.Qh5. It is the choice in 83.2% of master games.
3428826784804820|d7d6.principle: When the e4-pawn is unprotected, develop the knight to f6 so your developing move also gains time by attacking it.

3428826784804820|d8e7.headline: Against 2.Bc4, develop 2...Nf6 instead of the queen
3428826784804820|d8e7.why: 2...Qe7 guards e5 and f7 with the queen and blocks the bishop on f8 while all four minor pieces are still at home; White just develops with 3.Nf3 and 4.O-O and then strikes with 5.d4. 2...Nf6 develops the king's knight with an attack on e4 and takes h5 away from White's queen, ruling out 3.Qh5. Masters choose it in 83.2% of games.
3428826784804820|d8e7.principle: Meet early pressure with a developing move that attacks, not with the queen, which only blocks your own pieces and becomes a target.

3428826784804820|d8f6.headline: Develop with 2...Nf6, which attacks e4 and guards h5
3428826784804820|d8f6.why: 2...Qf6 brings the queen out with four minor pieces still at home and takes the knight's natural square. White develops calmly, and in the engine line the knight jumps to d5 with 7.Nd5, gaining time on your queen. 2...Nf6, played in 83% of master games, develops while attacking the e4 pawn and controls h5, so the scholar's-mate idea 3.Qh5 is off the table.
3428826784804820|d8f6.principle: Bring the knights out first and let them do the defending; the queen on f6 blocks the knight and becomes a target.

3428826784804820|d8h4.headline: Answer 2.Bc4 with 2...Nf6, not an early queen raid
3428826784804820|d8h4.why: 2...Qh4 brings the queen out with four minor pieces still at home; after 3.Nc3 Bc5 4.Qe2 d6 5.Nf3 the knight hits the queen and it goes back with 5...Qd8, so Black has spent two moves for nothing. 2...Nf6 develops, attacks the pawn on e4 and controls h5, which rules out White's own queen raid. It is the master choice in 83% of games.
3428826784804820|d8h4.principle: An early queen only gives White targets to develop against with gain of time; bring out the knight that attacks e4 instead.

3428826784804820|f7f5.headline: Answer 2.Bc4 with 2...Nf6, not a risky f-pawn push
3428826784804820|f7f5.why: 2...f5 is the Calabrese Countergambit, a risky system that loosens Black's king before any piece is out, while the bishop on c4 already aims at f7. White opens lines with 3.d4 exd4 and gets active pieces, as in 4.Nh3 Nc6 5.Ng5. 2...Nf6 develops with an attack on e4 and covers h5, which rules out 3.Qh5; masters choose it in 83.2% of games.
3428826784804820|f7f5.principle: With White's bishop on c4 aiming at f7, keep the f-pawn home and develop the knight to f6, which also covers h5.

3428826784804820|f7f6.headline: Put the knight on f6, not the pawn
3428826784804820|f7f6.why: 2...f6 takes the g8-knight's best square and opens the diagonal from c4 to your king, while White calmly builds the centre with 3.d4 and develops with 4.Nf3 and 5.O-O. 2...Nf6 develops with an attack on the pawn on e4 and covers h5, so it fights for the centre and keeps White's queen out at the same time.
3428826784804820|f7f6.principle: The bishop on c4 already aims at f7 and g8, so never loosen that diagonal further; meet it with pieces, not pawn moves around your king.

3428826784804820|g8h6.headline: Knight to f6, not the rim: hit e4 and cover h5
3428826784804820|g8h6.why: 2...Nh6 puts the knight on the rim, where it neither attacks e4 nor contests d5, and White gets a free hand in the centre with 3.Nf3 and 4.d4. 2...Nf6 develops the same knight to its natural square, attacks the pawn on e4 and covers h5, so the scholar's-mate idea 3.Qh5 is off the table.
3428826784804820|g8h6.principle: A knight on f6 controls central squares and hits e4, while on h6 it controls nothing central; pick the square that fights for the middle.

3450965353871567|d8f6.headline: Develop with 3...Nf6, which also stops 4.Qg4
3450965353871567|d8f6.why: 3...Qf6 guards g7 against 4.Qg4, but it brings the queen out with three minor pieces still at home and takes the best square from your knight. In the engine line the knight has to settle for 4...Ne7, and White's knight jumps to b5 with 6.Nb5 to go after c7. 3...Nf6 is the most popular move in master games: it develops toward the centre and covers g4, so the queen can't come there to attack g7.
3450965353871567|d8f6.principle: Meet a threat with a developing move when you can; the queen should stay home while the minor pieces are still undeveloped.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3/2...Bc5

3450965353871567|f7f6.headline: Develop with 3...Nf6; 3...f6 opens the king to checks.
3450965353871567|f7f6.why: 3...f6 weakens the squares around Black's king. After 4.Qh5+ g6 5.Qh4 Black has a loose kingside, and the bishop on c4 eyes g8, so castling is uncomfortable. White was also threatening 4.Qg4 to win a pawn. 3...Nf6 develops the knight to its natural square, covers g4 and h5, and prepares to castle.
3450965353871567|f7f6.principle: When the bishop on c4 aims at your king's side, protect it by developing pieces, not by moving the f-pawn.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3/2...Bc5

3451177064254537|d8b6.headline: Don't bring the queen out: strike with 6...d5 instead
3451177064254537|d8b6.why: 6...Qb6 brings the queen out with three minor pieces still at home, and White simply castles and breaks. After 7.O-O Nf6 8.Nc3 Be7 9.d5 exd5 10.exd5 the c6 knight is driven off and the e-file opens with your king still on e8. 6...d5 hits the c4 bishop and the e4 pawn and rules out 7.d5 for good. After 7.exd5 exd5 8.Bb3 Bb4+ 9.Nc3 Nf6 you have an isolated d-pawn but free, quick development.
3451177064254537|d8b6.principle: Don't bring the queen out early: 6...Qb6 hits d4 but leaves three minor pieces at home while White castles and breaks with 9.d5.

ideas.title: Strike with ...d5
ideas.text: 6...d5 hits the c4 bishop and the e4 pawn at once and stops d4-d5 for good.

ideas.title: ...e6 blunts the c4 bishop
ideas.text: Your e6 pawn keeps the c4 bishop off f7 and prepares ...d5 with gain of time.

ideas.title: White's broad centre
ideas.text: Given time, White keeps pawns on d4 and e4, castles and pushes 8.e5 to cramp your d6 and e6 pawns.

habit.why: 6...Qb6 brings the queen out with three minor pieces still at home, and White simply castles and breaks. After 7.O-O Nf6 8.Nc3 Be7 9.d5 exd5 10.exd5 the c6 knight is driven off and the e-file opens with your king still on e8.

strays.text: The queen hits d4, but White pushes 9.d5 anyway and opens the centre.

taught.why: 6...d5 hits the c4 bishop and the e4 pawn and rules out 7.d5 for good. After 7.exd5 exd5 8.Bb3 Bb4+ 9.Nc3 Nf6 you have an isolated d-pawn but free, quick development.

enforces.text: The pawn hits the bishop and e4 together, gaining time.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 6...Nf6 develops, but after 7.Qe2 Be7 8.e5 Nd5 the e5 pawn gains space and cramps your d6 and e6 pawns. It is only slightly worse, but there is a more direct move.
alternatives.after: 6...d5 stops the e5 push and hits the c4 bishop, the most direct way to fight White's centre.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6...a6 is a useful waiting move in many Sicilians, but here it ignores the centre: after 7.Nc3 Nf6 8.Bd3 Be7 9.O-O O-O 10.Bf4 White keeps the big centre and a free hand.
alternatives.after: 6...d5 challenges the centre at once and gains time on the c4 bishop instead of waiting.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6...Be7 is solid but passive: after 7.Bd3 a6 8.Nc3 Nf6 9.O-O O-O 10.Bf4 White keeps the broad e4/d4 centre.
alternatives.after: 6...d5 strikes at e4 and the bishop before White has finished developing.

3451177064254537|g8f6.headline: Hit the c4 bishop and e4 with 6...d5 before developing
3451177064254537|g8f6.why: 6...Nf6 develops but lets White gain space: after 7.Qe2 Be7 8.e5 Nd5 the e5 pawn cramps your d6 and e6 pawns. White castles with 9.O-O and builds up with 10.Re1 and 11.Bd2 while your pieces have little room. 6...d5 hits the c4 bishop and the e4 pawn and rules out 7.d5 for good. After 7.exd5 exd5 8.Bb3 Bb4+ 9.Nc3 Nf6 you have an isolated d-pawn but free, quick development.
3451177064254537|g8f6.principle: Contest the centre White has built: 6...d5 attacks e4 and the c4 bishop before White can push e5 or d5.

ideas.text: 7.d5 would hit your c6 knight and e6 pawn; after 7...exd5 8.exd5 Ne5 9.Qe2 White wins a pawn.

3453954165498770|g7g6.headline: Hit the queen and e4 at once with 3...Nf6.
3453954165498770|g7g6.why: 3...g6 does chase the queen, but it develops nothing and ignores e4. After 4.Qd1 White has lost nothing, and Black has weakened the kingside. 3.Bb5 left the pawn on e4 without a defender, and 3...Nf6 attacks the queen on h5 and that pawn at the same time. After 4.Qd1 Nd4 5.a4 Nxe4 Black wins the pawn while developing.
3453954165498770|g7g6.principle: When the opponent's queen comes out early, chase it with a developing piece that also attacks something else.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qh5/2...Nc6

3462820906204562|d7d6.headline: 4...Nd4 counterattacks; 4...d6 leaves Black cramped and passive.
3462820906204562|d7d6.why: 4...d6 shuts in the bishop on f8 and lets White open the centre with 5.d4 exd4 6.Nxd4, leaving Black cramped and a step behind. 4...Nd4 is the Rubinstein variation: the knight jumps to the centre, where it attacks the bishop on b5 and the knight on f3, and after 5.Nxd4 exd4 6.e5 dxc3 7.exf6 Qxf6 Black's pieces come alive.
3462820906204562|d7d6.principle: Answer a developing move with a centralising move that attacks something, rather than a pawn move that only defends.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Nf6/4. Nc3

3464521704326894|e1h1.headline: Defend e4 with 4.d3 before castling
3464521704326894|e1h1.why: 4.O-O leaves e4 hanging, and after 4...Nxe4 White has to spend time getting the pawn back: 5.Bd5 Nf6 6.Bxc6 dxc6 7.Nxe5 Bc5 gives up the strong bishop and leaves Black with free, active development. 4.d3 simply defends e4 and opens the diagonal for the dark-squared bishop, leading to the calm Giuoco Pianissimo structure that masters choose in 74.6% of games.
3464521704326894|e1h1.principle: Before castling, check whether your e4-pawn is attacked and defended; protect it first, since castling can wait a move.

3472532178632675|f1b5.headline: 5...e5 left f7 weak: your bishop belongs on c4
3472532178632675|f1b5.why: 6.Bb5 pins a knight that is easy to cover, and the bishop no longer aims at f7. After 6...Be7 7.Qa4 Nf6 8.O-O d6 Black is developed, and 9.Bxc6+ bxc6 10.Qxc6+ Bd7 wins the pawn back only by handing Black the two bishops. 6.Bc4 aims at f7, which Black can no longer shield with ...e6 after 5...e5. If 6...Nf6, then 7.Ng5 hits f7 twice and 7...d5 8.exd5 wins the pawn back with Black's king still in the centre.
3472532178632675|f1b5.principle: Put the bishop where it hits a weakness: after ...e5 Black can no longer shield f7 with ...e6, so the bishop goes to c4, not b5.

ideas.title: Aim at f7 and d5
ideas.text: 5...e5 means Black can't block the a2-g8 diagonal with ...e6. Your bishop belongs on c4 aiming at f7, with 7.Ng5 to follow.

ideas.title: Strike before Black castles
ideas.text: Black needs ...Nf6, ...Be7 and castling to make f7 safe. Wade calls 6...Be7 a mistake because your queen jumps to d5 against f7.

ideas.title: The d5 hole
ideas.text: After 5...e5 the d5 square is weak for good: Black's c-pawn is gone and the e-pawn can't go back to e6.

ideas.title: Black's ...d5 block
ideas.text: Black shuts a c4 bishop with ...d5, but against 7.Ng5 it costs the pawn: 6.Bc4 Nf6 7.Ng5 d5 8.exd5.

habit.why: 6.Bb5 pins a knight that is easy to cover, and the bishop no longer aims at f7. After 6...Be7 7.Qa4 Nf6 8.O-O d6 Black is developed, and 9.Bxc6+ bxc6 10.Qxc6+ Bd7 wins the pawn back only by handing Black the two bishops.

strays.text: On b5 the bishop leaves the diagonal toward f7.

taught.why: 6.Bc4 aims at f7, which Black can no longer shield with ...e6 after 5...e5. If 6...Nf6, then 7.Ng5 hits f7 twice and 7...d5 8.exd5 wins the pawn back with Black's king still in the centre.

enforces.text: The bishop goes where ...e5 left f7 open, with 7.Ng5 next.

347661827882589|b8a6.headline: Play 3...e6 first; 3...Na6 lets White double your pawns.
347661827882589|b8a6.why: 3...Na6 guards c7 before it is threatened, and after 4.e3 Bf5 5.Bxa6 bxa6 White trades the bishop for the knight and leaves Black with doubled, isolated a-pawns. 3...e6 reinforces the centre and opens the dark-squared bishop; only after 4.Nb5 threatens the fork on c7 does Black play 4...Na6, and then ...c6 kicks the knight back so Black's knight can reroute via c7.
347661827882589|b8a6.principle: Make the useful developing move first and meet the c7 threat only once it exists, so your knight's placement answers White's actual choice.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. Nc3/2...d5/3. Bf4
Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. Nc3/2...d5/3. Bf4/3...e6

3481634403483951|f7f6.headline: Trade on c4 so the knight has nothing to win on e6
3481634403483951|f7f6.why: White threatens 6.Nxe6 fxe6 7.Bxe6, trading on e6 and then taking the pawn. 5...f6 makes it worse: the f-pawn no longer guards e6, so 6.Nxe6 wins the bishop outright. 5...Bxc4 removes the bishop on c4 that backs up the attack, and after 6.dxc4 h6 7.Nf3 the knight has to retreat and Black is fine.
3481634403483951|f7f6.principle: The bishop on e6 is attacked twice, by the knight on g5 and the bishop on c4, and defended once, by the f7 pawn; remove an attacker rather than weaken the defender.

3516647903289485|f8d6.headline: Knight to f6 first: 6...Bd6 gets hit by e4 and d4
3516647903289485|f8d6.why: After 6...Bd6 7.e4 the pawn hits your bishop and d5 together, and 8.d4 opens the centre while your pieces are still loose; after 9.exd5 cxd5 10.Nb5 Bb8 11.dxe5 your centre has broken up and White is clearly better. 6...Ngf6 develops the knight toward the centre and adds a guard against e4. After 7.e4 dxe4 8.Nxe4 Nxe4 9.dxe4 Be6 pieces come off and the game stays level.
3516647903289485|f8d6.principle: Bring out the knight whose square is obvious before committing a bishop that can become a target for the opponent's central pawns.

3520598348324233|d2d3.headline: Punish the early queen: 3.Nc3 heads for d5 with tempo
3520598348324233|d2d3.why: 2...Qf6 brought the queen out early and took f6 away from Black's knight, and 3.d3 lets Black off with a pawn move instead of attacking it. 3.Nc3 develops and threatens 4.Nd5, centralising the knight with tempo on the queen. After 3...Nc6 4.Nd5 Qd8 the queen has gone back home and White is clearly ahead in development, with Bc4 and castling to follow.
3520598348324233|d2d3.principle: When the opponent's queen comes out early, develop your pieces to squares where they attack it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Qf6

3540159667319526|b7b6.headline: Develop with 5...Nc6; 5...b6 invites 6.dxc5 and 7.b4
3540159667319526|b7b6.why: 5...b6 develops nothing, and White uses the time: 6.dxc5 Bxc5 7.b4 chases the bishop, and after 7...Be7 8.Bb5+ Kf8 you have lost the right to castle. Blocking the check with a piece instead lets White take on d5 and hit your a8 rook down the long diagonal that ...b6 opened. 5...Nc6 develops and adds pressure on d4, so White usually pins it with 6.Bb5 before taking on c5. After 6...Bd6 7.dxc5 Bxc5 8.O-O Nf6 your pieces are out and you get an active isolated-pawn position, as in French Tarrasch lines.
3540159667319526|b7b6.principle: Develop a piece before moving more pawns: 5...Nc6 brings a knight out and presses d4, while 5...b6 only loosens your queenside.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...e6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. c3/2...e6
The Alapin Variation (Matthew Astle, Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/the-alapin-variation/

ideas.title: Develop toward d4
ideas.text: 5...Nc6 brings a piece out and hits d4, the pawn White's centre rests on. Pawn moves here only lose time.

ideas.title: Keep the tension on d4
ideas.text: Swapping with ...cxd4 frees White's pieces and leaves you an isolated d5 pawn to defend. Keep your c5 pawn pressing d4.

ideas.title: Watch the b5 check
ideas.text: Your king is still on e8 and the e-file is open, so White's bishop checks on b5 the moment you allow it.

ideas.title: White's dxc5 and b4
ideas.text: If nothing covers c5, White takes with 6.dxc5 and after 6...Bxc5 chases your bishop with 7.b4.

habit.why: 5...b6 develops nothing, and White uses the time: 6.dxc5 Bxc5 7.b4 chases the bishop, and after 7...Be7 8.Bb5+ Kf8 you have lost the right to castle. Blocking the check with a piece instead lets White take on d5 and hit your a8 rook down the long diagonal that ...b6 opened.

strays.text: A pawn move instead of a piece: c5 stays loose and your king stuck.

taught.why: 5...Nc6 develops and adds pressure on d4, so White usually pins it with 6.Bb5 before taking on c5. After 6...Bd6 7.dxc5 Bxc5 8.O-O Nf6 your pieces are out and you get an active isolated-pawn position, as in French Tarrasch lines.

enforces.text: The knight comes out and hits d4 at once, chosen in 70% of master games.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...Nf6 is natural development and fine: after 6.Bd3 Be7 7.O-O O-O you have castled safely. Masters prefer another move here, though.
alternatives.after: 5...Nc6 is the masters' choice (70% to 13%) because the knight presses d4 at once. Both are sound; 5...Nf6 just lets White pick the moment for 10.dxc5.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5...c4 gives up the pressure on d4 and hands White a target: 6.b3 cxb3 7.axb3 opens the a-file, and 10.b4 later gains space.
alternatives.after: 5...Nc6 keeps your c5 pawn pressing d4, so White's centre stays under fire instead of being left alone.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 5...cxd4 releases the tension and lets White develop with checks: 6.Bb5+ Bd7 7.Bxd7+ Qxd7 8.O-O and 9.Re1+ come while your king is still in the centre.
alternatives.after: 5...Nc6 keeps the tension and blocks the b5 diagonal in advance, so a bishop on b5 meets a knight, not your king.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 5...Bd6 develops, but White checks first with 6.Bb5+, and after 7.dxc5 Bxc5 8.O-O a6 9.Re1+ Ne7 your king is stuck in the centre a while longer.
alternatives.after: 5...Nc6 first means 6.Bb5 is only a pin, and after 6...Bd6 you reach the same structure on your terms.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 5...a6 stops the bishop check but costs a tempo in an open position: after 6.Bd3 and 7.O-O White is a move ahead in development.
alternatives.after: 5...Nc6 develops instead and is still fine against 6.Bb5, so you don't need a pawn move to prevent it.

3541436241248924|c4f7.headline: Bxf7+ with no follow-up is just a lost bishop
3541436241248924|c4f7.why: 5.Bxf7+ gives up a bishop for one pawn: after 5...Kxf7 no other white piece can join in, because the knight on f3 is pinned against the queen by the bishop on g4. Black's 3...Bg4 delayed castling and knight development, so White should keep building instead: 5.c3 prepares 6.b4 and castling, and White keeps the easier position.
3541436241248924|c4f7.principle: f7 is attacked only by the bishop and defended by the king, so the capture just trades a bishop for a pawn; take on f7 only when a second piece also hits it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4/3...Bg4

3557627017946811|b7b5.headline: In the Pirc, play 3...g6 and fianchetto; 3...b5 just drops a pawn.
3557627017946811|b7b5.why: 3...b5 puts a pawn where the bishop on f1 can take it with check, and after 4.Bxb5+ c6 5.Be2 Black is simply a pawn down. 3...g6 is the main move: it prepares ...Bg7 to press on White's centre from the long diagonal, followed by castling kingside, in the hypermodern style. Masters play it in 49.1% of games.
3557627017946811|b7b5.principle: Before pushing a pawn, check which enemy pieces see its new square; b5 is covered by White's bishop on f1.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6/2. d4/2...Nf6/3. Nc3
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6/2. d4/2...Nf6/3. Nc3/3...g6

3562880418201798|b8c6.headline: Control d4 with a pawn: 1...c5 stops White's two-pawn centre
3562880418201798|b8c6.why: 1...Nc6 eyes d4 but doesn't stop White's two-pawn centre: after 2.d4 the queen also guards d4, and 2...d5 3.e5 gains White space. 1...c5, the Sicilian, controls d4 with a pawn and is the most popular reply among masters (45.9%). When White plays d4, Black trades the c-pawn for White's d-pawn and is left with two central pawns to one.
3562880418201798|b8c6.principle: Against 1.e4, put a pawn where it controls d4, so White can't keep two pawns side by side in the centre.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4

3562880418201798|g8f6.headline: Fight for d4 with 1...c5 instead of inviting e5
3562880418201798|g8f6.why: 1...Nf6 invites 2.e5, and after 2...Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb6 5.f4 White's pawns chase the knight around and take over the centre with gain of time. 1...c5, the Sicilian and the masters' most common reply at 45.9%, controls d4 with a pawn so White can't keep a two-pawn centre. After 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Black has traded a flank pawn for a centre pawn and keeps two central pawns to White's one.
3562880418201798|g8f6.principle: Contest d4 with a pawn from move one, so White can never set up pawns on both e4 and d4 and kick your pieces.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nf6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5

3563738946985954|d1f3.headline: Retreat with 6.Nf3: f7 is covered, so the queen sortie fails
3563738946985954|d1f3.why: 6.Qf3 adds the queen to the f7 attack, but the h6 knight and the king already guard f7, and 6...Nd4 hits your queen and c2 at once. After 7.Qd1 Qf6 8.Nf3 Qg6 your queen is back home and Black has gained time. 6.Nf3 admits f7 is covered and brings the knight back to the slow plan. After 6...Ng4 7.O-O h6 8.c3 a5 9.Nbd2 you have the normal c3 set-up, and castling has covered the f2 pawn that 6...Ng4 eyed.
3563738946985954|d1f3.principle: An early queen becomes a target: with f7 covered, 6.Qf3 walks into 6...Nd4, while 6.Nf3 keeps building.
sources: Georgios Souleidis and Karsten Müller, Winning with the Slow (but Venomous!) Italian (New in Chess), pp. 11-13 | https://www.sjakkbutikken.no/media/productimages/preview-winning-with-the-slow-but-venomous-italian.pdf
