ideas.title: Ng5 needs a real target
ideas.text: 5.Ng5 only works when Black can't cover f7 in time. After 5...Nh6 it is covered, so go back with 6.Nf3 and build up.

ideas.title: Guard f7, chase the bishop
ideas.text: 5...Nh6 develops and guards f7. Black then hits whatever comes out early, as with 6...Nd4 or 6...Bg4.

ideas.title: An early queen is a target
ideas.text: With your b1 knight and c1 bishop at home, a queen on f3 or h5 gets hit: 6...Nd4 attacks it and c2 at once.

ideas.title: Slow Italian: build first
ideas.text: Castle, play c3 and keep d4 until it's prepared, as in 6.Nf3 Ng4 7.O-O h6 8.c3 a5 9.Nbd2.

habit.why: 6.Qf3 adds the queen to the f7 attack, but the h6 knight and the king already guard f7, and 6...Nd4 hits your queen and c2 at once. After 7.Qd1 Qf6 8.Nf3 Qg6 your queen is back home and Black has gained time.

strays.idea: An early queen is a target
strays.text: The queen comes out with two minor pieces at home and gets chased by 6...Nd4.

taught.why: 6.Nf3 admits f7 is covered and brings the knight back to the slow plan. After 6...Ng4 7.O-O h6 8.c3 a5 9.Nbd2 you have the normal c3 set-up, and castling has covered the f2 pawn that 6...Ng4 eyed.

enforces.text: With f7 covered, the knight goes back and you build up.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 6.O-O tucks your king away and keeps the knight on g5 for now, in the spirit of the slow plan. After 6...O-O 7.a4 Bg4 Black's pressure makes the knight decide anyway, so it's slightly less accurate.
alternatives.after: 6.Nf3 makes that decision at once, before 7...Bg4 can force it. In the 6.O-O line the knight goes back with 8.Nf3 anyway.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.Qh5 also adds the queen to the f7 attack, but f7 is already covered, and 6...Bg4 7.Qh4 Nd4 lets Black develop by hitting your queen.
alternatives.after: 6.Nf3 keeps your queen home and returns to the slow plan; with f7 covered, a queen sortie only gives Black targets.
alternatives.idea: An early queen is a target

3586492073419954|g7g6.headline: In the Sozin, develop with 6...Be7 and castle
3586492073419954|g7g6.why: 6...g6 leaves d6 and f6 with no pawn cover, and 7.Bg5 pins your f6-knight to the queen. After 7...Nbd7 8.Qe2 h6 9.Be3 e5 you have moved the e-pawn twice and your king is still in the centre. 6...Be7 develops and gets castling ready, which is what the Sozin demands. After 7.Be3 a6 8.Bb3 b5 9.f3 O-O your king is safe and ...b5 has gained queenside space.
3586492073419954|g7g6.principle: Against the Sozin, get your king safe fast: 6...Be7 prepares castling, while 6...g6 spends a move and leaves d6 and f6 weak.
sources: Wikibooks: Sozin vs Scheveningen 6.Bc4 | https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Chess_Opening_Theory/1._e4/1...c5/2._Nf3/2...d6/3._d4/3...cxd4/4._Nxd4/4...Nf6/5._Nc3/5...e6/6._Bc4

ideas.title: Pick one pawn setup
ideas.text: With ...e6 played, ...g6 leaves d6 and f6 without pawn cover. The Scheveningen setup wants ...Be7 and castling.

ideas.title: Castle before the attack
ideas.text: In the Sozin, delaying ...Be7 and castling invites a dangerous attack; 6...Be7 and 9...O-O get your king out of the centre.

ideas.title: The Sozin bishop
ideas.text: White's c4-bishop aims at e6 and f7. ...a6 and ...b5 push it back, as in 7.Be3 a6 8.Bb3 b5.

ideas.title: Bg5 pins the knight
ideas.text: After ...g6, 7.Bg5 pins your f6-knight to the queen, and you have to untangle with ...Nbd7 and ...h6.

habit.why: 6...g6 leaves d6 and f6 with no pawn cover, and 7.Bg5 pins your f6-knight to the queen. After 7...Nbd7 8.Qe2 h6 9.Be3 e5 you have moved the e-pawn twice and your king is still in the centre.

strays.text: ...g6 mixes a Dragon into the Scheveningen and leaves dark-square holes.

taught.why: 6...Be7 develops and gets castling ready, which is what the Sozin demands. After 7.Be3 a6 8.Bb3 b5 9.f3 O-O your king is safe and ...b5 has gained queenside space.

enforces.text: The bishop clears f8, and you castle before White's attack arrives.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 6...a6 is sound (35% of master games): it prepares ...b5 to chase the c4-bishop, as after 7.Be3 b5 8.Bb3. One move is still a little more precise.
alternatives.after: 6...Be7 and 6...a6 usually reach the same position, as here after 9.f3 O-O; 6...Be7 gets castling ready first, as Wikibooks advises in the Sozin.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 6...Nc6 is sound and leads to a Classical Sozin. White can answer with 8.Qe2 and 9.O-O-O, the sharp Velimirovic-style setup. A slightly more precise move exists.
alternatives.after: 6...Be7 is more common (55% to 9%) and gets castling ready at once; both are fine moves.

3598575371397628|b1c3.headline: Kick the knight with 3.e5; 3.Nc3 lets Black equalise
3598575371397628|b1c3.why: 3.Nc3 lets Black transpose into a comfortable open game with 3...e5, where Black's pieces develop freely, as in 4.d4 exd4 5.Nxd4 Bb4. 2...Nf6 put the knight where White's e-pawn can kick it, and 3.e5 exploits that: it gains space with tempo and drives the knight back to g8, then White takes the centre with 4.d4. Masters choose 3.e5 in 84.6% of games.
3598575371397628|b1c3.principle: When an enemy knight on f6 can be hit by your e-pawn, the push gains space and costs the knight time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nc6/2. Nf3

3598575371397628|d2d3.headline: Push e5 and kick the knight
3598575371397628|d2d3.why: 3.d3 is passive: it holds e4 but gives Black an easy game, and after 3...e5 4.g3 Black has a free hand in the centre. 3.e5 attacks the knight on f6 and takes the pawn out of danger in one move; after 3...Ng8 4.d4 Black's pieces are back home while White owns the centre.
3598575371397628|d2d3.principle: A knight on f6 that your e-pawn can reach with one push is a target: kick it to gain space and time.

3598575371397628|d2d4.headline: Kick the f6 knight with 3.e5; 3.d4 drops the e4 pawn
3598575371397628|d2d4.why: 2...Nf6 attacks e4, and 3.d4 ignores it: 3...Nxe4 wins the pawn, and after 4.d5 Nb8 White has little for it. 3.e5, the master choice in 85% of games, gains space with tempo, and the knight retreats with 3...Ng8. After 4.d4 d6 White has a big centre and a lead in development.
3598575371397628|d2d4.principle: A knight on f6 that your e-pawn can reach is a target: push to gain space and time instead of leaving e4 to be taken.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nc6/2. Nf3

3598575371397628|f1c4.headline: Kick the knight with 3.e5 instead of leaving e4 hanging
3598575371397628|f1c4.why: 3.Bc4 leaves e4 undefended, and 3...Nxe4 simply takes it; after 4.d4 d5 Black keeps the extra pawn and blocks the bishop. 3.e5 punishes the knight's arrival on f6: the pawn gains space with tempo and drives the knight back to g8, after which White builds the centre with 4.d4. Masters play 3.e5 in 84.6% of games here.
3598575371397628|f1c4.principle: When a knight on f6 attacks your e-pawn and your pawn can advance with tempo, push it: you gain space and the knight loses time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nc6/2. Nf3

3601332546328408|f3g5.headline: Castle and play d4; Ng5 only gets kicked back
3601332546328408|f3g5.why: 5.Ng5 moves the knight again, but 5...O-O puts the rook on f8 behind f7 and the attack has no target. After 6.d4 h6 7.Nf3 the knight has gone back, and 7...Nxe4 8.Nxe4 d5 strikes at White's centre, forking bishop and knight to win back the piece. 5.O-O, the most common master move (55%), tucks the king away and prepares 6.d4, building the centre the Pirc lets White have.
3601332546328408|f3g5.principle: A knight that jumps to g5 must win something at once; once Black castles and covers f7, the trip only gives Black time.

3610881811711296|d7d5.headline: Defend e5 with 2...Nc6, not the Elephant Gambit
3610881811711296|d7d5.why: 2...d5 is the Elephant Gambit, and it is unsound: after 3.exd5 e4 4.Qe2 Black is a pawn down without enough to show for it, and in the game line 6.Nxe4 picks off the advanced pawn as well. 2...Nc6 develops a piece while defending e5 and controlling d4, which is why it is about five times more popular than everything else combined.
3610881811711296|d7d5.principle: When the knight on f3 attacks e5, defend it with a developing move instead of giving up a pawn for activity you don't have yet.

3610881811711296|d8f6.headline: Defend e5 with 2...Nc6, not the queen.
3610881811711296|d8f6.why: 2...Qf6 brings the queen out with four minor pieces still at home and takes f6 away from the king's knight. White develops with gain of time, for example 3.Nc3 with the idea Nd5 hitting the queen, and Black falls behind. 2...Nc6 defends e5 while developing and also controls d4, which is why it is about five times more popular than everything else combined.
3610881811711296|d8f6.principle: Defend attacked pawns with developing pieces; a queen used as a defender becomes a target for White's next knight move.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Qf6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6

3610881811711296|f7f5.headline: Defend e5 with 2...Nc6; the Latvian gambit 2...f5 is unsound
3610881811711296|f7f5.why: 2...f5 leaves e5 hanging and opens the diagonal from h5 to your king: after 3.Nxe5 you can't grab e4 with 3...fxe4 because of 4.Qh5+, and in the engine line 3...Qf6 4.d4 d6 5.Nc4 fxe4 6.Nc3 White is simply better developed. The theory calls the gambit utterly unsound. 2...Nc6 is the main line, chosen in 86% of master games: it develops a piece, defends e5 and also controls d4.
3610881811711296|f7f5.principle: Answer an attack on e5 with a developing move that defends it, not with a pawn move that leaves the pawn loose and weakens your king.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3

3610881811711296|f7f6.headline: Defend e5 with 2...Nc6; 2...f6 only seems to defend it
3610881811711296|f7f6.why: 2...f6 only seems to defend e5: 3.Nxe5 takes the pawn anyway, because 3...fxe5 runs into 4.Qh5+ g6 5.Qxe5+, forking the king and the rook on h8. It also takes f6 away from the knight and opens the diagonal to Black's king. 2...Nc6 develops a piece while defending e5 and controlling d4, and is played in 86% of master games.
3610881811711296|f7f6.principle: Defend a centre pawn with a developing piece, not with a pawn move that weakens your king.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6

3610881811711296|f8c5.headline: 2.Nf3 attacks e5: defend it with 2...Nc6 before developing elsewhere
3610881811711296|f8c5.why: 2...Bc5 develops but ignores the attack on e5, so 3.Nxe5 just wins a pawn. The theory calls this Busch-Gass gambit unsound: Black hopes for play with 3...Qh4, but gets no real compensation if White keeps their head. 2...Nc6, the main line and 86% of master games, develops the knight while defending e5 and controlling d4.
3610881811711296|f8c5.principle: Before choosing a developing move, check what your opponent's last move attacks: 2.Nf3 hit e5, so the developing move should also defend it.

3610881811711296|f8d6.headline: Defend e5 with 2...Nc6, not a bishop that blocks your d-pawn
3610881811711296|f8d6.why: 2...Bd6 defends e5 but blocks Black's d-pawn, so the queen's bishop stays shut in, and White can open the centre with 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4, aiming at f7 before Black is organised. 2...Nc6 develops a piece while defending e5 and controlling d4; it is about five times more popular than everything else combined.
3610881811711296|f8d6.principle: Defend attacked pawns with pieces developing toward the centre, without blocking the pawns that free your other pieces.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6

3610922251931051|c1d2.headline: The c3 knight is pinned: guard e4 with 4.Bd3
3610922251931051|c1d2.why: Black threatens 4...Qxe4+, and the c3 knight can't really defend e4 because the b4 bishop pins it. 4.Bd2 doesn't help: 4...Bxc3 5.Bxc3 Qxe4+ removes the defender and takes the pawn with check. 4.Bd3 develops a bishop that defends e4 directly, and in the engine line Black's queen has to go back with 5...Qd8 while White castles.
3610922251931051|c1d2.principle: A pinned piece is not a real defender; protect what it guards with a piece that is free to recapture.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. d4

3610922251931051|c1e3.headline: Defend e4 with a piece the pin can't remove
3610922251931051|c1e3.why: Black's queen attacks e4 and the bishop on b4 pins its only defender, the knight on c3: after 4.Be3 Bxc3+ 5.bxc3 Qxe4 the knight is gone and so is the pawn. 4.Bd3 develops a bishop that guards e4 directly, and after 4...d5 5.Nf3 White develops with an attack on the queen, which has to retreat with 5...Qd8.
3610922251931051|c1e3.principle: When a pinned piece is the only guard of a pawn, give the pawn a second defender that the pin can't take away.

3610922251931051|g2g3.headline: Guard e4 first: 4.Bd3 develops and defends the pawn
3610922251931051|g2g3.why: 4.g3 attacks the queen but leaves e4 hanging: Black's 3...Bb4 pins the knight on c3, so after 4.g3 Qxe4+ the queen checks and hits the rook on h1 as well, and 5.Qe2 Qxh1 costs White a whole rook. 4.Bd3 develops a piece and protects e4, and after 4...d5 5.Nf3 Qd8 Black's queen has to retreat while White keeps a clear lead in development.
3610922251931051|g2g3.principle: Before kicking the queen, check what your move leaves loose: with the knight pinned, e4 has no real defender.

361821916697346|f3g5.headline: Gain queenside space with 7.a4, not 7.Ng5
361821916697346|f3g5.why: 7.Ng5 moves the knight again, but 7...O-O covers f7 with the rook, and grabbing it would give two minor pieces for a rook and pawn. After 8.a4 a5 9.b5 Ne7 10.Qb3 Qe8 11.Nf3 the knight is back home and Black has castled for free. 7.a4 gains space and threatens a5 against the b6 bishop, so Black answers 7...a5. Then 8.b5 Ne7 9.O-O Ng6 10.Nbd2 follows Mestel-Pinter, a White win, and masters choose 7.a4 69% of the time.
361821916697346|f3g5.principle: When Black can castle and cover f7, use the move to gain space with your pawns instead of moving the f3 knight twice.

ideas.title: Ng5 needs a real target
ideas.text: f7 is guarded by the king only until Black castles. After 7...O-O, taking on f7 gives two pieces for a rook and pawn.

ideas.title: Slow Italian: c3, d3, a4, then d4
ideas.text: a4 gains queenside space and threatens a5 against the b6 bishop. Then castle and bring the b1 knight out via d2.

ideas.title: Push b5 only when it can't go to a5
ideas.text: After 7.a4 a5, 8.b5 kicks the c6 knight, and with a pawn on a5 it can't jump there to hit your bishop.

ideas.title: Don't move a piece twice
ideas.text: Your b1 knight and c1 bishop are still at home. Moving the f3 knight again gives Black free time.

habit.why: 7.Ng5 moves the knight again, but 7...O-O covers f7 with the rook, and grabbing it would give two minor pieces for a rook and pawn. After 8.a4 a5 9.b5 Ne7 10.Qb3 Qe8 11.Nf3 the knight is back home and Black has castled for free.

strays.text: Black castles, f7 is covered, and the knight has to go back.

taught.why: 7.a4 gains space and threatens a5 against the b6 bishop, so Black answers 7...a5. Then 8.b5 Ne7 9.O-O Ng6 10.Nbd2 follows Mestel-Pinter, a White win, and masters choose 7.a4 69% of the time.

enforces.idea: Slow Italian: c3, d3, a4, then d4
enforces.text: a4 gains space with a threat, then castle and develop.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7.O-O is a sound move that gets your king safe before play starts; after 7...Ne7 Black heads for ...Ng6. Masters choose a different move more often (69% to 20%).
alternatives.after: 7.a4 first threatens a5 against the bishop and forces 7...a5; 7.O-O usually comes back to the same plan after 7...Ne7 8.a4.
alternatives.idea: Slow Italian: c3, d3, a4, then d4

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 7.Qb3 aims at f7, but 7...O-O covers it and Black gets ...a5 in. Once your queenside pawns advance, the queen on b3 becomes a target.
alternatives.after: 7.a4 uses the move for space and forces 7...a5, so 8.b5 kicks the knight without letting it reach a5; 7.Qb3 hits f7 just as Black is ready to castle.
alternatives.idea: Slow Italian: c3, d3, a4, then d4

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7.h3 takes g4 from Black's pieces, and the engine rates it fine. Souleidis' guideline is to wait with h3 until Black has castled, since it can invite ...g5-g4.
alternatives.after: 7.a4 does something on the queenside straight away, while 7.h3 waits; its line comes back to 10.a4 a5 11.b5 anyway.
alternatives.idea: Slow Italian: c3, d3, a4, then d4

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7.Nbd2 starts the standard regrouping: the knight heads for f1 and g3, or c4. After 7...Ne7 Black also reroutes a knight toward g6.
alternatives.after: 7.a4 forces the issue on the queenside first; after 7.Nbd2 Black gets 7...Ne7 and 8...c6, and your bishop has to drop back with 9.Bb3.
alternatives.idea: Slow Italian: c3, d3, a4, then d4

362391570447215|c5d4.headline: 4.d4 left e4 hanging: take it with 4...dxe4
362391570447215|c5d4.why: 4...cxd4 releases the tension when White's e4 pawn was simply hanging. After 5.exd5 exd5 6.Bb5+ Nc6 7.Nxd4 Bd7 8.Qe2+ you have an isolated d5 pawn, a pinned knight and a king stuck in the centre. 4...dxe4 wins a pawn, because 4.d4 left e4 attacked once and defended zero times. After 5.Ne5 Nf6 6.Bb5+ Bd7 7.Nxd7 Nbxd7 8.O-O you keep the extra pawn and your pieces are out.
362391570447215|c5d4.principle: Check what is loose before releasing the tension: 4.d4 left e4 attacked and undefended, so take it.
sources: The Alapin Variation (Matthew Astle, Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/the-alapin-variation/
Sicilian Defence, Alapin Variation (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicilian_Defence,_Alapin_Variation

ideas.title: Take the loose e4 pawn
ideas.text: After 4.d4, e4 is attacked by your d5 pawn and defended by nothing, so 4...dxe4 wins it.

ideas.title: Keep the tension on d4
ideas.text: Swapping with ...cxd4 frees White's pieces and, after 5.exd5 exd5, leaves you an isolated d5 pawn to defend.

ideas.title: Watch the b5 check
ideas.text: Your king is still on e8, so once the centre opens 6.Bb5+ and 8.Qe2+ come with gain of time.

ideas.title: A French Advance if White pushes
ideas.text: After 4...Nc6 5.e5 the centre locks as in the French Advance, and 5...Bd7 6.Be2 Nge7 aims your pieces at d4.

habit.why: 4...cxd4 releases the tension when White's e4 pawn was simply hanging. After 5.exd5 exd5 6.Bb5+ Nc6 7.Nxd4 Bd7 8.Qe2+ you have an isolated d5 pawn, a pinned knight and a king stuck in the centre.

strays.text: 4...cxd4 lets White rescue e4 by trading it off on d5.

taught.why: 4...dxe4 wins a pawn, because 4.d4 left e4 attacked once and defended zero times. After 5.Ne5 Nf6 6.Bb5+ Bd7 7.Nxd7 Nbxd7 8.O-O you keep the extra pawn and your pieces are out.

enforces.text: Count it: e4 is attacked once and defended by nothing.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.idea: A French Advance if White pushes
alternatives.before: 4...Nc6 is solid: after 5.e5 Bd7 6.Be2 Nge7 you have a standard French Advance setup. There is a stronger move here, though.
alternatives.after: 4...dxe4 simply wins the pawn that 4.d4 left undefended; 4...Nc6 lets White push 5.e5 and keep everything.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...c4 gains queenside space and keeps the centre closed, which is playable. There is a more direct move.
alternatives.after: 4...dxe4 takes the pawn at once; 4...c4 gives up the pressure on d4 and only grabs e4 a move later with 5...dxe4.

3649736493107135|b7b6.headline: Castle before queenside moves; e5 is coming
3649736493107135|b7b6.why: 5...b6 is a slow wing move with the king still in the centre: 6.e5 hits the knight on f6, and after 6...dxe5 7.dxe5 Nfd7 8.e6 the pawn breaks into Black's position. 5...O-O completes the Pirc plan from the theory: fianchetto the bishop to pressure White's centre, then castle kingside, and after 6.O-O Nc6 Black starts working on the centre. Masters castle here in 85% of games.
3649736493107135|b7b6.principle: With White's pawn ready to advance to e5 and open lines, castle before spending moves on the queenside.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6/2. d4/2...Nf6/3. Nc3/3...g6

3678353102233444|g8f6.headline: Recapture at once with 3...exd5 in the Exchange QGD
3678353102233444|g8f6.why: 3...Nf6 lets White capture again: after 4.dxe6 Bxe6 White has taken two pawns for one. d5 is attacked twice and not defended, so 3...exd5 recaptures at once, keeps a pawn on d5 and opens the diagonal for the light-squared bishop that 2...e6 had blocked.
3678353102233444|g8f6.principle: Recapture toward the centre straight away: the pawn on d5 holds your share of the centre and frees the bishop on c8.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6

3692429315258999|c4e2.headline: Ask the bishop with 6.h3 before Black wins e5 back
3692429315258999|c4e2.why: 6.Be2 doesn't stop 6...dxe5, so Black wins the pawn back at once, and after 7.Nbd2 Nf6 8.c3 a5 the game is level. It also moves your bishop a second time while the b1 knight and c1 bishop wait. 6.h3 asks the bishop first: after 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 your queen comes out with a threat on f7. Black wins the pawn back only with 7...Nxe5 8.Qe2 Nxc4 9.Qxc4, giving up the c6 knight for your bishop while you stay ahead in development.
3692429315258999|c4e2.principle: Deal with the pin with tempo: 6.h3 makes the bishop decide while you're still a pawn up, instead of retreating your own bishop.
sources: Semi-Italian Opening (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-Italian_Opening

ideas.title: Ask the bishop with h3
ideas.text: 6.h3 makes the g4 bishop decide. After 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 your queen and c4 bishop threaten mate on f7.

ideas.title: Black wins e5 back
ideas.text: You're a pawn up only for now: Black threatens 6...dxe5, and a quiet move just lets it happen.

ideas.title: Develop, don't retreat
ideas.text: Your b1 knight and c1 bishop are still at home. Moving the c4 bishop again with 6.Be2 hands Black the time.

habit.why: 6.Be2 doesn't stop 6...dxe5, so Black wins the pawn back at once, and after 7.Nbd2 Nf6 8.c3 a5 the game is level. It also moves your bishop a second time while the b1 knight and c1 bishop wait.

strays.text: The bishop moves twice and Black regains the pawn with 6...dxe5.

taught.why: 6.h3 asks the bishop first: after 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 your queen comes out with a threat on f7. Black wins the pawn back only with 7...Nxe5 8.Qe2 Nxc4 9.Qxc4, giving up the c6 knight for your bishop while you stay ahead in development.

enforces.text: The bishop must decide, and 7.Qxf3 develops your queen with a threat.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 6.exd6 gives the pawn back on your terms: after 6...Bxd6 the centre is open and Black's 4...h6 was a lost move. It's sound, and 72% of club players choose it.
alternatives.after: The engine rates both moves the same. 6.h3 makes Black trade the c6 knight for your bishop to regain the pawn; after 6.exd6 Bxd6 you ask the bishop a move later with 7.h3 Bh5.

3699514865674152|d1e2.headline: Hit f7 at once with 7.Ng5 before Black castles
3699514865674152|d1e2.why: 7.Qe2 threatens nothing, so Black develops with 7...Be7, 8...d6 and 9...O-O, and f7 is covered for good. After 10.h3 Be6 Black has every piece out and still keeps the extra pawn. 7.Ng5 hits f7 twice, with knight and bishop, so Black blocks the bishop with 7...d5 and gives the pawn back. After 8.Bxd5 Nxd5 9.exd5 material is level, your d5 pawn hits the c6 knight and Black's king is still in the centre.
3699514865674152|d1e2.principle: After ...e5, f7 is guarded only by the king, so hit it at once with 7.Ng5 before Black castles; a quiet 7.Qe2 gives that time away.

ideas.title: Aim at f7 and d5
ideas.text: 5...e5 means Black can't block your c4 bishop with ...e6. Bishop and a knight jump to g5 both hit f7.

ideas.title: Strike before Black castles
ideas.text: Black needs ...Be7 and castling to make f7 safe. Quiet moves like 7.Qe2 or castling give Black exactly that time, and the pawn stays.

ideas.title: The d5 hole
ideas.text: After 5...e5 the d5 square is weak for good: Black's c-pawn is gone and the e-pawn can't go back to e6.

ideas.title: Black's ...d5 block
ideas.text: Black shuts the c4 bishop with ...d5, but against 7.Ng5 it costs the pawn: 7...d5 8.Bxd5 Nxd5 9.exd5.

habit.why: 7.Qe2 threatens nothing, so Black develops with 7...Be7, 8...d6 and 9...O-O, and f7 is covered for good. After 10.h3 Be6 Black has every piece out and still keeps the extra pawn.

strays.text: The queen move threatens nothing, so Black castles and keeps the pawn.

taught.why: 7.Ng5 hits f7 twice, with knight and bishop, so Black blocks the bishop with 7...d5 and gives the pawn back. After 8.Bxd5 Nxd5 9.exd5 material is level, your d5 pawn hits the c6 knight and Black's king is still in the centre.

enforces.text: Knight and bishop both hit f7, so Black must return the pawn.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: Castling is natural but threatens nothing. After 7...Be7 8.Bg5 d6 9.Bxf6 Bxf6 10.Nd5 O-O Black has castled, kept the pawn and has the two bishops.
alternatives.after: 7.Ng5 uses the move while Black's king is still in the centre: f7 is hit twice and 7...d5 gives the pawn back.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: The pin is slow: after 7...Be7 8.Bxf6 Bxf6 you've given up a bishop for the knight, and 9.Qd6 Qe7 10.Qd3 d6 only sends your queen back.
alternatives.after: 7.Ng5 makes a real threat against f7, so Black has no time for ...Be7 and castling and must return the pawn.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.Qb3 hits f7 too, but 7...Na5 attacks queen and bishop at once. After 8.Qa4 Nxc4 9.Qxc4 your best attacker is gone and f7 is safe.
alternatives.after: 7.Ng5 attacks f7 with a piece Black can't chase with tempo, so the c4 bishop stays and Black must play 7...d5 to block it.

3699514865674152|e1h1.headline: 7.Ng5 hits f7 and forces Black to give back the pawn
3699514865674152|e1h1.why: 7.O-O threatens nothing, so Black develops with 7...Be7 and castles soon, and f7 is safe. After 8.Bg5 d6 9.Bxf6 Bxf6 10.Nd5 O-O Black has the bishop pair and the extra pawn. 7.Ng5 threatens to take on f7, and Black's only decent answer, 7...d5, gives up a pawn: 8.Bxd5 Nxd5 9.exd5 hits the c6-knight. After 9...Nd4 10.O-O Be7 11.f4 material is level and Black's king is still in the centre.
3699514865674152|e1h1.principle: Attack f7 while only Black's king guards it: 7.Ng5 makes Black give back the pawn, while castling lets Black develop and castle first.
sources: IM Hannes Langrock, The Modern Morra Gambit (excerpt) | https://www.newinchess.com/media/wysiwyg/product_pdf/2702.pdf
Morra Gambit Accepted (ianchessgambits) | http://www.ianchessgambits.com/morra-gambit-accepted.html

ideas.title: Hit f7 early
ideas.text: After ...e5, f7 is guarded only by the king. Knight on g5 and the c4-bishop threaten to take there before Black can castle.

ideas.title: Use the d5 hole
ideas.text: After ...e5, d5 is a weak spot. If Black blocks the bishop with 7...d5, that pawn falls: 8.Bxd5 Nxd5 9.exd5.

ideas.title: Strike before Black castles
ideas.text: Black's king is still on e8. Quiet moves give Black time for ...Be7 and castling, and then f7 is safe.

ideas.title: Black hunts the c4-bishop
ideas.text: Black's c6-knight can jump to a5 to trade off your best attacking bishop, especially when it also hits a queen on b3.

habit.why: 7.O-O threatens nothing, so Black develops with 7...Be7 and castles soon, and f7 is safe. After 8.Bg5 d6 9.Bxf6 Bxf6 10.Nd5 O-O Black has the bishop pair and the extra pawn.

strays.text: Castling gives Black the move needed for 7...Be7 and castling.

taught.why: 7.Ng5 threatens to take on f7, and Black's only decent answer, 7...d5, gives up a pawn: 8.Bxd5 Nxd5 9.exd5 hits the c6-knight. After 9...Nd4 10.O-O Be7 11.f4 material is level and Black's king is still in the centre.

enforces.text: Knight and bishop hit f7 together, forcing Black to give back the pawn.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.Bg5 pins the knight but makes no threat. After 7...Be7 8.Bxf6 Bxf6 9.Qd6 Qe7 10.Qd3 Black has the bishop pair and an easy game.
alternatives.after: 7.Ng5 makes a direct threat against f7, so Black has no time for 7...Be7 and has to give back the pawn with 7...d5.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.Qb3 lines up on f7 and b7, but 7...Na5 hits the queen. After 8.Qa4 Nxc4 9.Qxc4 your best attacking bishop is gone.
alternatives.after: 7.Ng5 keeps the queen at home, so there is no 7...Na5 with tempo, and the threat on f7 leaves Black little better than 7...d5.

3708088433535320|f1b5.headline: Take the whole centre with d4 against 1...b6
3708088433535320|f1b5.why: 2.Bb5 develops the bishop to a square with no target: Black hits e4 with 2...Bb7 and chases the bishop with 3...a6 and 4...b5. 1...b6 lets White take the centre for free, and 2.d4 does so: both centre pawns stand side by side and both bishops are ready to come out.
3708088433535320|f1b5.principle: When the opponent's first move ignores the centre, occupy it with a second pawn before sending pieces to squares without a purpose.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...b6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...b6/2. d4

3725666597101221|c2c3.headline: Develop with 3.Bb5; 3.c3 leaves e4 loose
3725666597101221|c2c3.why: 3.c3 prepares d4 but takes the c3 square from White's own knight, so the pawn on e4 is loose and Black can hit it at once with 3...d5 or 3...Nf6. 3.Bb5, the Ruy Lopez, is the master choice (65%): it develops, gets White ready to castle, and pressures the knight on c6 that defends e5.
3725666597101221|c2c3.principle: Develop a piece with pressure before spending a move on pawn preparation like c3.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. c3
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5

3725666597101221|d2d3.headline: Develop with 3.Bb5 rather than the passive 3.d3
3725666597101221|d2d3.why: 3.d3 defends e4 before it is attacked and shuts in the bishop on f1, so Black takes free play in the centre, as in 3...Nf6 4.g3 d5. 3.Bb5, the Ruy Lopez, develops the bishop instead, gets White ready to castle, and puts pressure on the knight on c6, the defender of e5. Masters choose it in 65% of games.
3725666597101221|d2d3.principle: When nothing of yours is attacked, develop a piece that pressures the opponent rather than a pawn move that guards what is already safe.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5

3726374757153429|f1c4.headline: 5.Bg5 pins the e7 knight and stops 5...Nec6
3726374757153429|f1c4.why: 5.Bc4 lets Black untangle at once with 5...Nec6, and after 6.Nc3 Be7 7.Nd5 Nxd4 8.Qxd4 O-O the knights are traded and Black is comfortable, so half your edge is gone. 4...Ne7 blocks the f8 bishop, and 5.Bg5 pins that knight to the queen on d8, so it cannot move without losing the queen. Black spends 5...h6 chasing the bishop, and after 6.Be3 Nec6 7.Nc3 Be7 8.Nd5 O-O 9.Nb5 your knights take over d5 and b5 while Black's knight ends up on a6.
3726374757153429|f1c4.principle: Develop your bishop to a square where it pins or attacks, so the opponent has to spend a move answering it instead of carrying out their plan.

3729547871689507|f1c4.headline: Answer 1...Nc6 with 2.Nf3; a c4 bishop runs into ...d5
3729547871689507|f1c4.why: 2.Bc4 puts the bishop where Black's centre pawns can hit it: after 2...e6 3.d4 d5 4.exd5 exd5 it has to move again with 5.Bb3, and 6...Na5 chases it once more. 2.Nf3 develops the knight to its best square and is the most popular master move at 60%. If Black answers 2...e5 the game is a normal Open Game, and other replies leave Black's knight awkwardly placed.
3729547871689507|f1c4.principle: The knight's best square, f3, is clear already, while the bishop's depends on how Black's pawns settle; Black can still choose ...e6 and ...d5, which would hit a bishop on c4.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nc6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nc6/2. Nf3

3729547871689507|f2f4.headline: Develop the king's knight; save pawn moves for the centre
3729547871689507|f2f4.why: 2.f4 develops nothing, and after 2...d5 3.e5 d4 Black gains space and White's edge is gone. 2.Nf3 develops the knight to its most active square and invites 2...e5, a normal Open Game; if Black avoids it, the knight on c6 gets in the way of Black's usual pawn breaks.
3729547871689507|f2f4.principle: With no reason yet to commit pawns, bring the king's knight out first; its best square is already clear.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nc6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nc6/2. Nf3

3747843569338814|d2d4.headline: After 3...Bc5, use the fork trick: 4.Nxe5 and 5.d4
3747843569338814|d2d4.why: 4.d4 loses a pawn after 4...exd4, and 5.Nd5 does not win it back. 4.Nxe5 takes the e5 pawn because the knight on c6 is not really defending it: after 4...Nxe5 5.d4 the pawn forks the bishop on c5 and the knight on e5, and White wins the piece back. Material stays level, but White gets the freer game and the centre.
3747843569338814|d2d4.principle: Look at captures first: e5 looks defended, but after the capture 5.d4 forks two pieces, so the defence is an illusion.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Bc5

3772385141189769|d2d4.headline: Prepare d4 with 2.Nf3 so a knight, not the queen, recaptures.
3772385141189769|d2d4.why: 2.d4 cxd4 leaves an awkward choice: 3.Qxd4 lets Black develop 3...Nc6 with tempo on the queen, and 3.Nf3 allows 3...e5, keeping the extra pawn. Playing 2.Nf3 first means that after 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 White recaptures with the knight and keeps the tempo, and Black has no time to defend the d4 pawn.
3772385141189769|d2d4.principle: Prepare the central break so a knight recaptures on d4; a queen there is chased by ...Nc6.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3

3772385141189769|f1c4.headline: Play 2.Nf3 against the Sicilian; 2.Bc4 runs into ...e6 and ...d5.
3772385141189769|f1c4.why: 2.Bc4 aims at f7, but Black answers 2...e6 and later ...d5, blunting the bishop and gaining time on it with an easy central position. 2.Nf3 adds control of d4 and prepares 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4, opening the position while Black, whose 1...c5 did nothing for development, is still catching up.
3772385141189769|f1c4.principle: Against the Sicilian, put your pieces where they support the d4 break, not on squares Black can hit with a central pawn.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Bc4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3

3772385141189769|f2f4.headline: Against the Sicilian, develop with 2.Nf3 and prepare d4
3772385141189769|f2f4.why: 2.f4 starts a kingside attack before White has developed, and Black answers by striking in the centre: after 2...e6 3.Nf3 d5 White has to commit with 4.Bb5+ Nd7 5.e5, and Black's position is fine. 2.Nf3 develops and prepares 3.d4; after the pawn trade White recaptures with the knight and gets open lines for both bishops and the queen. It is the choice in 83% of master games.
3772385141189769|f2f4.principle: 1...c5 does nothing for Black's development, so develop and open the centre with d4 rather than spend a move on a flank pawn.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. f4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3

3800718395256466|c6d5.headline: Recapture 7...Nxd5 and keep c6 guarding b5
3800718395256466|c6d5.why: 7...cxd5 removes the pawn that kept White's knight out of b5: 8.Nb5 threatens a fork on c7, Black has to answer 8...Kd8, and after 9.Ne5 Bg6 10.Nxa7 White's rook on a1 helps win the a7 pawn, leaving White clearly better. 7...Nxd5 takes back the pawn, which was attacked twice and defended only by the knight on c3, and leaves the c6 pawn in place. After 8.e4 Nxc3 9.exf5 Nd5 material is level and White's edge is small.
3800718395256466|c6d5.principle: In a queenless position judge the differences: 7.axb3 gave White a half-open a-file against a7, so keep the c6 pawn covering b5 and recapture with a piece.

3815488023003540|b8c6.headline: Take on d4 before White's pawn can push to d5
3815488023003540|b8c6.why: 5...Nc6 leaves the c5 and d4 pawns facing each other, and 6.d5 gains space with a hit on the knight. After 6...Na5 7.O-O d6 8.c4 Nxc4 9.a4 Bd7 10.Nc3 you are a pawn up, but your knight is stuck on c4 and White's lead in development and pressure on b5 count for more. 5...cxd4 takes White's centre pawn before it can advance. After 6.a4 b4 7.Nxd4 Qc7 8.Bd3 Nf6 your b-pawn has gained space, your pieces develop freely and the game is level.
3815488023003540|b8c6.principle: Resolve pawn tension on your terms: 5...cxd4 trades your flank pawn for White's centre pawn, while 5...Nc6 lets 6.d5 gain space with tempo.
sources: The Bowlder Attack: Bold move or beginner's folly? (Matthew Astle, Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/bowlder-attack/
countering 2. Bc4 in the Sicilian (chess.com forum) | https://www.chess.com/forum/view/chess-openings/countering-2-bc4-in-the-sicilian
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Bc4

ideas.title: Settle the d4 tension
ideas.text: White's d4 pawn and your c5 pawn hit each other. Taking with 5...cxd4 clears the centre before White can push past.

ideas.title: White's d5 space grab
ideas.text: If the tension stays, the d-pawn advances, gains space and kicks a knight on c6, as in 6.d5 Na5.

ideas.title: Chase the bishop with ...a6 and ...b5
ideas.text: Your ...a6 and ...b5 gained space and drove the bishop back to e2. If White hits b5 with a4, push on, as in 6.a4 b4.

ideas.title: Kan-style setup
ideas.text: After 7.Nxd4 you have an Open Sicilian with ...e6, ...a6 and ...b5 already played: develop with 7...Qc7 and 8...Nf6.

habit.why: 5...Nc6 leaves the c5 and d4 pawns facing each other, and 6.d5 gains space with a hit on the knight. After 6...Na5 7.O-O d6 8.c4 Nxc4 9.a4 Bd7 10.Nc3 you are a pawn up, but your knight is stuck on c4 and White's lead in development and pressure on b5 count for more.

strays.text: The tension stays, so 6.d5 gains space and chases your knight.

taught.why: 5...cxd4 takes White's centre pawn before it can advance. After 6.a4 b4 7.Nxd4 Qc7 8.Bd3 Nf6 your b-pawn has gained space, your pieces develop freely and the game is level.

enforces.text: Trading on d4 removes the pawn that wanted to push to d5.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5...c4 releases the pressure on d4 instead of trading. After 6.b3 cxb3 7.axb3 Bb7 8.Bd3 Nf6 9.e5 Nd5 White's centre stays whole and your knight has been pushed around.
alternatives.after: 5...cxd4 removes White's d-pawn instead. The ...c4 push is a known trap when White's bishop retreats to b3, but here it stands on e2 and nothing is trapped.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5...Bb7 develops and eyes e4, a plan club players like against 2.Bc4. After 6.a4 the queenside opens up, as in 7.axb5 Bxe4 8.bxa6; it stays level, though a more precise move exists.
alternatives.after: 5...cxd4 settles the centre first, so 6.a4 can be met by 6...b4 and your queenside pawns stay. Both moves keep the game level.

3815955546086349|d8f6.headline: Take the centre with 2...d5; a queen on f6 is a target.
3815955546086349|d8f6.why: 2...Qf6 brings the queen out with four minor pieces still at home, and White gains time on it: after 3.c4 c6 4.Bg2 the queen has to move again with 4...Qe6. 2.g3 is slow, and 2...d5 punishes it by building a full pawn centre, as in 3.d4 Nc6 4.Nf3 e4, where Black gains space with tempo on the knight.
3815955546086349|d8f6.principle: Against a slow flank setup like e3 and g3, occupy the centre with both pawns; that is worth more than an early queen sortie.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e3/1...e5

3842365322435851|b8c6.headline: Take the free pawn: 3...Nxe4 punishes 3.Nf3
3842365322435851|b8c6.why: 3...Nc6 is a decent move, but it gives White time to cover e4 with 4.d3, and the game becomes a quiet Italian where Black's chance is gone. White's 3.Nf3 left the pawn on e4 attacked by your knight and defended by nothing. After 3...Nxe4 4.Nxe5 d5 Black's pawn attacks the bishop on c4 and takes the centre; the bishop retreats with 5.Be2 and Black develops with 5...Bd6.
3842365322435851|b8c6.principle: Every time your opponent moves, check what they left undefended: here the e4 pawn was hanging to the f6 knight.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nf6/3. Nf3

3842365322435851|d7d5.headline: 3.Nf3 left e4 hanging: take it with 3...Nxe4
3842365322435851|d7d5.why: 3...d5 gives up a pawn for nothing: 4.exd5 takes it, and after 4...e4 5.Ne5 White's knight is active while Black is a pawn down. 3.Nf3 left the pawn on e4 attacked by the knight and defended by nothing, so 3...Nxe4 simply takes it. After 4.Nxe5 d5 Black hits the bishop on c4 and shuts it off from f7.
3842365322435851|d7d5.principle: Before each move, check what is loose: White's e4 pawn has no defender, so take it before anything else.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nf6/3. Nf3

3842365322435851|d7d6.headline: 3.Nf3 left e4 undefended: take it with 3...Nxe4
3842365322435851|d7d6.why: 3...d6 defends e5 but passes up a free central pawn, and after 4.Nc3 White has covered e4 and the chance is gone. White's 3.Nf3 left the pawn on e4 attacked by your knight and defended by nothing. 3...Nxe4 takes it; White can only win back e5 with 4.Nxe5, and then 4...d5 attacks the bishop on c4 and builds a strong centre, with 5...Bd6 hitting the knight on e5 next.
3842365322435851|d7d6.principle: Check what is loose after every opponent move: White's third move developed a piece but left the e4 pawn hanging.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nf6/3. Nf3

3842365322435851|f6h5.headline: 3.Nf3 left e4 hanging: take it with 3...Nxe4
3842365322435851|f6h5.why: 3...Nh5 moves the knight a second time to the rim and leaves e5 unprotected: 4.Nxe5 wins the pawn, and after 4...Qg5 5.Bxf7+ Kd8 6.Qxh5 the knight on h5 falls too. 3.Nf3 left e4 attacked and not defended at all, so 3...Nxe4 simply takes it, and after 4.Nxe5 d5 Black has a solid centre and easy development.
3842365322435851|f6h5.principle: Check what is loose on both sides before moving: White's e4 pawn was free, and taking it also gets your knight out of trouble.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nf6/3. Nf3

3881559155902992|d7d5.headline: Guard e5 with 4...d6; 4...d5 just drops a pawn.
3881559155902992|d7d5.why: White threatens 5.Nxe5, and 4...d5 doesn't help: d5 is attacked by the e4 pawn, the knight on c3 and the bishop on c4, more times than Black can defend it, so 5.Nxd5 wins it. 4...d6 calmly defends e5 and opens the c8 bishop, and Black castles next, as in 5.O-O O-O.
3881559155902992|d7d5.principle: Before pushing a pawn into the centre, count: d5 is hit three times by White and covered only twice by Black.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3/2...Bc5

3903276797068408|a2a3.headline: Take on c5 now: 7.dxc5 wins a pawn
3903276797068408|a2a3.why: 7.a3 is too slow: after 7...Bxf3 8.Qxf3 Qb6 Black's queen hits b2 and backs up the attack on d4, and the position tips slightly in Black's favour. The theory notes explain that White threatens to take on c5 and that ...Bg4 does not stop it, so Black should have released the tension with ...cxd4. 7.dxc5 takes the pawn while it is there, and after 7...Bxf3 8.Qxf3 you are a pawn up with a small edge.
3903276797068408|a2a3.principle: In the Advance structure Black aims every break at the base of your chain on d4; when the pawn attacking it can be captured for free, take it instead of letting the pressure build.

3903276797068408|h2h3.headline: Take on c5 with 7.dxc5 before Black liquidates
3903276797068408|h2h3.why: 7.h3 invites 7...Bxf3, and after 8.gxf3 Qb6 your kingside pawns are doubled, Black's queen hits b2 and Black is better. Theory notes that in this line White keeps threatening to take on c5, which is why Black should liquidate the tension with ...cxd4. 6...e6 didn't, so take now: 7.dxc5 wins a pawn, and after 7...Bxf3 8.Qxf3 you recapture with the queen and keep your pawn structure intact.
3903276797068408|h2h3.principle: Look at captures before quiet moves: when your opponent leaves the central tension in place, the capture may simply win a pawn.

3931450314873962|d2d3.headline: Black's light-squared bishop is gone: hit b7 with Qb3
3931450314873962|d2d3.why: 6.d3 is solid but slow: it leaves the queen on f3 with nothing to do and lets Black catch up in development. Black's 3...Bg4 traded off the bishop that guarded b7, so 6.Qb3 attacks the pawn on b7 and lines up behind the bishop on c4 against f7. After 6...d5 7.Qxb7 White wins a pawn.
3931450314873962|d2d3.principle: When the opponent gives up the bishop that guards a pawn, check whether your queen can reach that loose pawn while keeping pressure elsewhere.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4/3...Bg4

3931450314873962|g2g4.headline: Black's light-squared bishop is gone: hit b7 with Qb3
3931450314873962|g2g4.why: 6.g4 weakens White's own kingside and achieves nothing: Black just develops with 6...Nc6 and later castles long. Black's 3...Bg4 traded off the bishop that guarded b7, so 6.Qb3 attacks the pawn on b7 straight away; after 6...d5 7.Qxb7 White is a pawn up and ahead in development.
3931450314873962|g2g4.principle: Once the opponent gives up the bishop that guarded b7, check whether your queen can reach that pawn before starting a pawn storm.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4/3...Bg4

3941407114211180|a2a3.headline: Castle first, so e5 later hits the queen with tempo
3941407114211180|a2a3.why: 5.a3 is a slow pawn move: after 5...d6 6.d4 Bxd4 7.Nxd4 exd4 the pawn on d4 attacks the knight on c3, and White ends up a pawn down. 5.O-O tucks the king away first, so in the same sequence 8.e5 attacks the queen on f6 with gain of time and White stays ahead in development. Black's early queen and 4...c6 have cost time, and castling keeps that lead alive.
3941407114211180|a2a3.principle: Black's queen came out on move two; keep developing and castle, so that central pawn moves gain time by attacking it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Qf6/3. Bc4

397857285398425|d5d4.headline: After 4.e5, hit the chain with 4...Nc6 instead of 4...d4
397857285398425|d5d4.why: 4...d4 pushes past the c3 knight and hands it the e4 square: after 5.Ne4 it eyes d6 and f6. Following 5...Nc6 6.d3 f5 7.exf6 Nxf6 8.g3 your d4 pawn is a target and White develops freely. 4...Nc6 develops and eyes d4, where White's chain will need support. After 5.Nf3 Bd7 6.d4 Nh6 7.Ne2 Qb6 8.c3 f6 your knights, queen and f-pawn all press on White's centre.
397857285398425|d5d4.principle: Attack a pawn chain with pieces and pawn breaks instead of pushing past it: 4...Nc6, ...Qb6 and ...f6 hit d4 and e5.
sources: Playing the Grand Prix Attack Against the Sicilian (Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/grand-prix-attack/
How I play against the Closed Sicilian (IM Junta Ikeda) | https://juntaikeda.substack.com/p/how-i-play-against-the-closed-sicilian
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nc3/2...e6

ideas.title: Attack the e5/f4 chain
ideas.text: Your e6/d5 pawns face White's e5/f4 chain, French style: pressure it with 4...Nc6, 7...Qb6 and 8...f6.

ideas.title: Knight to f5
ideas.text: Your g8 knight heads for f5 via h6 or e7, where it presses on d4 and covers the kingside.

ideas.title: Don't hand over e4
ideas.text: 4...d4 lets the c3 knight jump to e4, eyeing d6 and f6; chasing it with ...f5 allows 7.exf6.

ideas.title: White's kingside space
ideas.text: 3.f4 and 4.e5 grab kingside space; White follows with 5.Nf3 and 6.d4 to support the chain.

habit.why: 4...d4 pushes past the c3 knight and hands it the e4 square: after 5.Ne4 it eyes d6 and f6. Following 5...Nc6 6.d3 f5 7.exf6 Nxf6 8.g3 your d4 pawn is a target and White develops freely.

strays.text: Pushing past the chain leaves e5 alone and gives White e4.

taught.why: 4...Nc6 develops and eyes d4, where White's chain will need support. After 5.Nf3 Bd7 6.d4 Nh6 7.Ne2 Qb6 8.c3 f6 your knights, queen and f-pawn all press on White's centre.

enforces.text: The knight is the first piece aimed at the d4 square.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...Ne7 is the other master move (18%): the knight heads for f5, as in 5.Nf3 Nbc6 6.d4 Nf5, pressing on d4. It is sound and close to the best move.
alternatives.after: 4...Nc6 is the masters' choice (77%) and keeps the g8 knight free for h6 or e7; both plans aim at d4 and f5.

3987932696906099|d1f3.headline: Castle with 5.O-O; a queen on f3 only becomes a target.
3987932696906099|d1f3.why: 5.Qf3 brings the queen out with two minor pieces still at home, and Black meets it with 5...Qf6, offering a trade, so White's queen has to retreat with 6.Qe2 having achieved nothing. 5.O-O tucks the king away first and prepares Re1 behind the e4 pawn, as in 5...Nf6 6.d3 c6 7.Re1, keeping the lead in development the trade on d4 gave White.
3987932696906099|d1f3.principle: With the knights traded, finish development and castle before bringing the queen out, so Black gets nothing to develop against.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nd4/4. Nxd4

399137672893272|f1b5.headline: Take the pawn with 4.exd5; 4.Bb5+ lets Black push ...d4.
399137672893272|f1b5.why: 4.Bb5+ c6 5.Be2 wastes time, and 5...d4 drives the knight back to b1, after which Black takes on e4 with 6...Nxe4 and has the active game. 3...d5 is a loose pawn break, and 4.exd5 wins the pawn and claims the centre. After 4...Bd6 Black spends a move defending e5, and White can still give the check 5.Bb5+ once it gains something.
399137672893272|f1b5.principle: Among forcing moves, look at captures before checks: a check that wins nothing only helps the opponent improve.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nc3

399137672893272|f1c4.headline: Take the offered pawn with 4.exd5; c4 is covered by d5
399137672893272|f1c4.why: 4.Bc4 puts the bishop where the d5 pawn takes it: 4...dxc4 wins a piece, and 5.Nxe5 gets back only a pawn. 3...d5 was a loose pawn push, and 4.exd5 simply takes it while claiming the centre. After 4...Bd6 5.Bb5+ c6 6.dxc6 Nxc6 White still has the extra pawn.
399137672893272|f1c4.principle: Before developing a piece, check which squares enemy pawns attack: the d5 pawn covers c4, and it is itself the loose target.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nc3

3996150506658750|f3g5.headline: Castle and hit e5: 6.O-O, not 6.Ng5
3996150506658750|f3g5.why: 6.Ng5 attacks f7 with the knight alone, since the d5 knight blocks your c4 bishop, and 6...f6 kicks it while guarding e5. After 7.Nc3 Bb4 8.Ne4 Nb6 9.Bb3 Bf5 that knight has moved three times, and Black develops with gain of time. 6.O-O gets your king safe and lets the rook join the fight for e5: after 6...Be7 7.Re1 f6 8.c3 Be6 9.d4 you strike in the centre. Masters choose 6.O-O 88% of the time; Emms says Black's early 4...d5 shouldn't really work because e5 can be hit so quickly.
3996150506658750|f3g5.principle: With Black's knight on d5 blocking your c4 bishop, f7 is no target: castle and pressure e5 instead of moving the f3 knight again.
sources: John Emms, Beating 1e4 e5 (Google Books snippet) | https://www.google.com/books/feeds/volumes?q=inauthor:Emms+%22shouldn%27t+really+work%22

ideas.title: Ng5 needs a real target
ideas.text: The d5 knight blocks your c4 bishop, so 6.Ng5 hits f7 with the knight alone, and 6...f6 sends it on its way.

ideas.title: Pressure e5: castle, then Re1
ideas.text: You haven't spent time on c3 or a bishop retreat to b3, so go after e5 at once: castle, then 7.Re1.

ideas.title: Black's ...f6 holds e5
ideas.text: One pawn move guards e5 and takes g5 from your knight and bishop. Black then develops with ...Bf5 or ...Be6.

ideas.title: Don't move a piece twice
ideas.text: Your b1 knight and c1 bishop are still at home. Moving the f3 knight again gives Black free time.

habit.why: 6.Ng5 attacks f7 with the knight alone, since the d5 knight blocks your c4 bishop, and 6...f6 kicks it while guarding e5. After 7.Nc3 Bb4 8.Ne4 Nb6 9.Bb3 Bf5 that knight has moved three times, and Black develops with gain of time.

strays.text: Black covers f7 and kicks the knight with one pawn move.

taught.why: 6.O-O gets your king safe and lets the rook join the fight for e5: after 6...Be7 7.Re1 f6 8.c3 Be6 9.d4 you strike in the centre. Masters choose 6.O-O 88% of the time; Emms says Black's early 4...d5 shouldn't really work because e5 can be hit so quickly.

enforces.text: Castling first brings the rook to e1 against e5.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 6.Bxd5 gives up your Italian bishop for the knight, and 6...Qxd5 puts Black's queen on a strong central square. After 7.Nc3 Qd6 Black follows with 8...Bf5 and castles long, with the two bishops.
alternatives.after: 6.O-O keeps the bishop and puts pressure on e5 with 7.Re1, so Black's queen never gets a free central post.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 6.Bg5 develops, but 6...f6 hits the bishop at once and guards e5 too. After 7.Bd2 Bf5 8.Nh4 Be6 Black gains time and later trades your c4 bishop with 10...Bxc4.
alternatives.after: 6.O-O is a move Black can't kick, and 7.Re1 keeps e5 under pressure before Black finishes developing.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.h3 does nothing against e5, and Souleidis' guideline is to wait with h3 until Black has castled. After 6...Bf5 Black adds 7...Qd7 and castles long.
alternatives.after: Masters do play 6.h3 (5.5%), but 6.O-O (88%) spends the move on king safety and brings the rook to e1 against e5.

4040334401902569|c4e2.headline: Ask the bishop with 5.h3; 5.Be2 drops the d4 pawn
4040334401902569|c4e2.why: 5.Be2 breaks the pin but leaves d4 short of guards: 5...Bxf3 6.Bxf3 Nxd4 removes the defender and wins the pawn. It also moves your bishop a second time while your b1 knight and c1 bishop are still at home. 5.h3 hits the bishop before Black can win d4: after 5...Bh5 6.d5 Nb8 your pawn gains space with tempo on the c6 knight and closes the centre. Black then gives up the bishop with 7.Be3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3, leaving you the bishop pair.
4040334401902569|c4e2.principle: Count who guards d4: once the f3 knight is traded off, 5.Be2 can't hold the pawn, so ask the bishop first with 5.h3.
sources: Semi-Italian Opening (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-Italian_Opening
Légal Trap (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9gal_Trap
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...d6

ideas.title: Ask the bishop with h3
ideas.text: 5.h3 makes the g4 bishop decide now: take on f3 and hand you the bishop pair, or retreat and allow 6.d5 with tempo.

ideas.title: The pin hits d4
ideas.text: The g4 bishop pins your f3 knight to the queen, so it can't really guard d4: Black threatens 5...Nxd4, winning a pawn.

ideas.title: Keep d4 and your space
ideas.text: 3...d6 gave you more space. Keep the d4 pawn standing, by asking the bishop, adding c3 or pushing d5, rather than trading on e5.

ideas.title: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
ideas.text: A bishop sacrifice on f7 pays only when a check or fork wins it back. Here 5.Bxf7+ Kxf7 just gives a bishop for a pawn.

habit.why: 5.Be2 breaks the pin but leaves d4 short of guards: 5...Bxf3 6.Bxf3 Nxd4 removes the defender and wins the pawn. It also moves your bishop a second time while your b1 knight and c1 bishop are still at home.

strays.text: The bishop retreats instead of guarding d4, and 6...Nxd4 takes it.

taught.why: 5.h3 hits the bishop before Black can win d4: after 5...Bh5 6.d5 Nb8 your pawn gains space with tempo on the c6 knight and closes the centre. Black then gives up the bishop with 7.Be3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3, leaving you the bishop pair.

enforces.text: The bishop must decide now, and 6.d5 comes with tempo.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5.dxe5 dxe5 saves the pawn but releases the tension: the centre turns symmetrical, your space is gone and Black's bishop stays active, as in 6.Nbd2 Bd6.
alternatives.after: 5.h3 keeps the d4 pawn and your space, and makes the bishop decide first. Only 6% of master games trade on e5.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5.d5 gains space and hits the c6 knight, but 5...Nd4 jumps into the hole and the pin stops you chasing it cheaply: 6.Qd3 Nxf3+ 7.gxf3 wrecks your kingside pawns.
alternatives.after: 5.h3 asks the bishop first; after 5...Bh5 6.d5 Nb8 the space gain sends Black's knight home. Masters choose 5.d5 in 11% of games, 5.h3 in 33%.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 5.Bxf7+ Kxf7 gives a bishop for one pawn with no follow-up. Even after 7.Qxf3+ Nf6 Black's king is safe enough and Black stays a piece up.
alternatives.after: 5.h3 keeps all your pieces and makes the g4 bishop decide. A bishop check on f7 only works when a fork or a knight follows to win the material back.
alternatives.idea: Hit f7 only with a follow-up

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5.c3 shores up d4, so 5...Nxd4 no longer wins a pawn, and it's the most common master move (44%). The engine rates it a little lower: after 5...Nf6 6.d5 Nb8 7.Bd3 Black gets a solid set-up.
alternatives.after: Masters and the engine disagree here: masters prefer 5.c3 (44% to 33%), while the engine prefers 5.h3 because it makes the bishop decide at once instead of leaving the pin in place.

4040334401902569|d4e5.headline: Ask the bishop with 5.h3 instead of trading on e5
4040334401902569|d4e5.why: 5.dxe5 releases the tension: after 5...dxe5 the centre is symmetrical, your space is gone and the pin on f3 is still there. In 6.Nbd2 Bd6 7.h3 Bd7 8.c3 Nf6 Black's bishop just steps back and Black is comfortable. 5.h3 hits the bishop before Black can win d4: after 5...Bh5 6.d5 Nb8 your pawn gains space with tempo on the c6 knight and closes the centre. Black then gives up the bishop with 7.Be3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3, leaving you the bishop pair.
4040334401902569|d4e5.principle: When a pinning bishop is about to win a pawn, ask it to decide at once: 5.h3 keeps your d4 pawn and your space, 5.dxe5 gives them up.
sources: Semi-Italian Opening (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-Italian_Opening
Légal Trap (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9gal_Trap

strays.text: Trading on e5 gives back the space that 3...d6 handed you.

4084843176360845|f8e8.headline: Use the fork trick: 6...Nxe4, then ...d5 hits two pieces
4084843176360845|f8e8.why: 6...Re8 is slow: 7.e5 kicks the knight on f6, and after 7...d5 8.Bd3 Nh5 it sits on the edge while White has more space. 6...Nxe4 is the fork trick: after 7.Nxe4 d5 the pawn attacks both the bishop on c4 and the knight on e4, so Black regains the piece with 8.Bd3 dxe4 9.Bxe4. Then 9...c5 strikes at d4, and White's centre is broken up.
4084843176360845|f8e8.principle: Look at captures first: ...Nxe4 works whenever ...d5 can then fork a bishop on c4 and a knight on e4.

4111926581298046|d6e5.headline: Against 5.e5, retreat 5...Nfd7 and hit d4 with ...c5
4111926581298046|d6e5.why: 5...dxe5 opens the d-file with the queens facing each other, and after 6.dxe5 Qxd1+ 7.Kxd1 Ng4 the e5 pawn is still held by the f4 pawn, so Black wins nothing. 9.Nd5 then hits c7, and Black's king has to step to 9...Kd8. 5...Nfd7, the masters' choice 59.2% of the time, keeps the tension and prepares to attack the centre from the side: after 6.Nf3 c5 Black hits d4.
4111926581298046|d6e5.principle: White's pawns on d4 and e5 form a chain; aim your pawn break at its base on d4 rather than swapping at the head.

4120112958252679|f6d7.headline: Trade queens with check first, then move the knight
4120112958252679|f6d7.why: 6...Nfd7 dodges 7.exf6 but walks into 7.e6: after 7...fxe6 8.Ng5 Ne5 9.Qxd8+ Kxd8 10.f4 the knight on e5 is chased and lost to 11.fxe5. 6...Qxd1+ trades queens with check, so after 7.Nxd1 Black has a free move to rescue the knight, and 7...Ng4 puts it where it attacks the e5 pawn. Black wins that pawn back by 10...fxe6 and ends up a pawn ahead.
4120112958252679|f6d7.principle: When a pawn attacks your knight, look at checks and captures first: a capture with check buys the tempo to move the knight to an active square.

4120112958252679|f6g4.headline: Trade queens with check first, then hunt e5 with the knights
4120112958252679|f6g4.why: 6...Ng4 moves the knight a second time and lets White trade first: 7.Qxd8+ Kxd8 costs Black the right to castle, and after 8.Bf4 and 9.Rd1+ White's pieces swarm around the exposed king. 6...Qxd1+ captures first with check, so 7.Nxd1 pulls White's knight back, and then 7...Ng4 and 8...Nc6 both attack the pawn on e5. The line ends with Black a pawn up after 10.e6 fxe6.
4120112958252679|f6g4.principle: When queens face each other on an open file, capture first with check so your king keeps its shelter and the opponent's pieces are pulled back.

4138915868453329|b7b5.headline: Develop the light-squared bishop before starting queenside play
4138915868453329|b7b5.why: 4...b5 is a flank pawn move while White already has a full centre and two knights out; after 5.Bd3 b4 6.Ne2 the pawns run forward, but Black's kingside is still at home and White simply castles. 4...Bg4 develops the bishop outside the pawn chain and pins the knight on f3, which defends d4. After 5.h3 Bxf3 6.Qxf3 e6 Black has a solid pawn chain and can still expand with ...b5 later, as in the line; masters choose it in 77% of games.
4138915868453329|b7b5.principle: Before starting play on the wing, bring out the pieces still at home; the light-squared bishop belongs outside the pawn chain before ...e6 shuts it in.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6

4140088474015032|e7e5.headline: Finish the fianchetto with 2...Bg7; 2...e5 abandons the plan.
4140088474015032|e7e5.why: 2...e5 mixes two setups: after 3.d4 exd4 4.Qxd4 White's queen sits in the centre, and the dark squares on Black's kingside, weakened by 1...g6, have no bishop to guard them. 2...Bg7 completes the fianchetto that 1...g6 prepared: Black lets White build a centre and undermines it later with ...d6 and ...Nf6, as in 2...Bg7 3.d4 d6 4.Nc3 Nf6.
4140088474015032|e7e5.principle: Complete the setup your first move committed to: after 1...g6, the bishop on g7 is the piece that makes that pawn move worthwhile.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6

4141510809291242|d7d5.headline: 1.c4 targets d5: develop with 1...Nf6 instead
4141510809291242|d7d5.why: 1.c4 discourages 1...d5, and the theory notes say that capturing the pawn gives White a small advantage: after 2.cxd5 Nf6 3.d4 c6 4.dxc6 Nxc6 White has traded the c-pawn for your centre pawn and is a pawn up. 1...Nf6 is the most popular reply (27.7% of masters games): it develops toward the centre, controls d5 and e4 with a piece, and keeps your options open; after 2.d4 the game can turn into an Indian defence. 1...e5, 1...e6 and 1...c5 are also good.
4141510809291242|d7d5.principle: Your king's knight's best square is clear from move one, while the right pawn setup depends on what White does next; so develop the knight first and choose the pawn moves later.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. c4
Chess Opening Theory/1. c4/1...d5
Chess Opening Theory/1. c4/1...Nf6

4149741967394205|c1f4.headline: Knight first: 4.Nc3 before deciding where the bishop goes
4149741967394205|c1f4.why: 4.Bf4 lets Black take on c4: after 4...dxc4 5.Qa4+ Nbd7 White spends queen moves regaining the pawn, and 6...Nd5 7.Bxc4 Nxf4 8.exf4 swaps off the early bishop and doubles White's f-pawns. 4.Nc3 develops the knight toward the centre and adds pressure on d5. It is one of White's main moves here and the choice of 61.7% of masters.
4149741967394205|c1f4.principle: The knight's best square on c3 is clear now, while the queen's bishop's best square depends on how Black's pawns settle, so bring the knight out first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nf3/3...Nf6

4149982820903367|e8h8.headline: Release the tension with 7...dxc4 before White strips d5's defenders
4149982820903367|e8h8.why: White threatens to win a pawn on d5, and 7...O-O doesn't stop it: after 8.Bxf6 Bxf6 9.Bxf5 exf5 10.cxd5 White's two bishop trades remove the knight and pawn that guarded d5, and you are a pawn down. 7...dxc4 takes the target away first and makes the d3 bishop move a second time with 8.Bxc4. Then 8...h6 9.Bh4 Ne4 forces trades that free your position, and after 10.Nxe4 Bxe4 11.Bxe7 Qxe7 the game is level.
4149982820903367|e8h8.principle: Count the defenders of a centre pawn under pressure, including pieces your opponent can exchange off, and release the tension before a routine move like castling.

4150297190773573|e7e5.headline: In the Pirc, finish the fianchetto with 4...Bg7 before playing ...e5.
4150297190773573|e7e5.why: 4...e5 opens the d-file with Black's king still in the centre: after 5.dxe5 dxe5 6.Qxd8+ Kxd8 Black has lost the right to castle, 7.Bg5 pins the knight on f6 to the king, and after 7...Be7 8.Nxe5 the e5 pawn falls. 4...Bg7 is the Pirc plan: the bishop presses on the centre from the long diagonal and Black castles next, as in 5.Be2 O-O 6.O-O. Masters choose it in 97.5% of games.
4150297190773573|e7e5.principle: Don't open the centre while your king is still on e8: castle first, then challenge White's pawns.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6/2. Nf3

4164085910631465|c1g5.headline: Retake with 8.cxd4: the centre is what your pawns paid for
4164085910631465|c1g5.why: 8.Bg5 develops but leaves both centre pawns hanging: 8...dxc3 9.Nxc3 h6 10.Bh4 d6 and Black is two pawns up with no weaknesses. After 11.Nd5 Qd7 12.Rc1 O-O Black has castled and your attack has nothing to hit. 8.cxd4 wins a pawn back, rebuilds e4 and d4, and hits the c5 bishop, so 8...Bb6 costs Black a tempo. Then 9.Ng5 hits f7 twice, and after 9...d5 10.exd5 Na5 11.d6 Nxc4 12.Qa4+ c6 your queen wins back the piece on c4.
4164085910631465|c1g5.principle: In a gambit your pawns buy a centre and time, so take the centre when you can: 8.cxd4 restores pawns on e4 and d4 with gain of time.

ideas.title: Rebuild the centre with cxd4
ideas.text: Your pawns paid for c3 and d4. With your king castled, 8.cxd4 puts pawns back on e4 and d4 and hits the c5 bishop.

ideas.title: Quiet moves cost the centre
ideas.text: 8.Bg5 and other quiet moves leave d4 and c3 to Black. After 8...dxc3 9.Nxc3 you are two pawns down with no centre.

ideas.title: Ng5 needs a real target
ideas.text: Once 8.cxd4 has kicked the c5 bishop, 9.Ng5 joins the c4 bishop against f7, and Black must block with 9...d5.

ideas.title: Black's knight prepares ...d5
ideas.text: 7...Nge7 covers d5 and gets ready for ...d5, giving a pawn back so Black's pieces come out easily.

habit.why: 8.Bg5 develops but leaves both centre pawns hanging: 8...dxc3 9.Nxc3 h6 10.Bh4 d6 and Black is two pawns up with no weaknesses. After 11.Nd5 Qd7 12.Rc1 O-O Black has castled and your attack has nothing to hit.

strays.text: A developing move, but d4 and c3 are left to Black.

taught.why: 8.cxd4 wins a pawn back, rebuilds e4 and d4, and hits the c5 bishop, so 8...Bb6 costs Black a tempo. Then 9.Ng5 hits f7 twice, and after 9...d5 10.exd5 Na5 11.d6 Nxc4 12.Qa4+ c6 your queen wins back the piece on c4.

enforces.text: Pawns back on e4 and d4, with a tempo on the c5 bishop.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 8.Ng5 hits f7 at once, but 8...d5 9.exd5 Ne5 blocks and hits your bishop. A few moves later 12...Qxd1 trades the queens, and your attack is gone.
alternatives.after: 8.cxd4 first kicks the c5 bishop to b6, so when the knight jumps in with 9.Ng5 Black is a tempo behind. With Black's bishop retreated to a5 instead, the knight jump is a main try that roughly levels.

4164085910631465|c4f7.headline: No follow-up after the f7 sacrifice here: retake with 8.cxd4
4164085910631465|c4f7.why: 8.Bxf7+ Kxf7 gives your bishop for one pawn, and no queen check follows because the d4 pawn and the e7 knight cover d5. After 9.cxd4 Bb6 10.d5 Na5 11.e5 d6 12.e6+ Kg8 Black is a whole piece up and the king is safe. 8.cxd4 wins a pawn back, rebuilds e4 and d4, and hits the c5 bishop, so 8...Bb6 costs Black a tempo. Then 9.Ng5 hits f7 twice, and after 9...d5 10.exd5 Na5 11.d6 Nxc4 12.Qa4+ c6 your queen wins back the piece on c4.
4164085910631465|c4f7.principle: A sacrifice on f7 needs a concrete follow-up; with no queen check to come, rebuild the centre with 8.cxd4 instead.

ideas.title: Rebuild the centre with cxd4
ideas.text: Your pawns paid for c3 and d4. With your king castled, 8.cxd4 puts pawns back on e4 and d4 and hits the c5 bishop.

ideas.title: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
ideas.text: 8.Bxf7+ pays only when a check follows. Here the d4 pawn and the e7 knight stop any queen check on d5, so nothing follows.

ideas.title: Ng5 needs a real target
ideas.text: Once 8.cxd4 has kicked the c5 bishop, 9.Ng5 joins the c4 bishop against f7, and Black must block with 9...d5.

ideas.title: Black's knight prepares ...d5
ideas.text: 7...Nge7 covers d5 and gets ready for ...d5, giving a pawn back so Black's pieces come out easily.

habit.why: 8.Bxf7+ Kxf7 gives your bishop for one pawn, and no queen check follows because the d4 pawn and the e7 knight cover d5. After 9.cxd4 Bb6 10.d5 Na5 11.e5 d6 12.e6+ Kg8 Black is a whole piece up and the king is safe.

strays.idea: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
strays.text: No check follows on d5, so the bishop is simply lost.

taught.why: 8.cxd4 wins a pawn back, rebuilds e4 and d4, and hits the c5 bishop, so 8...Bb6 costs Black a tempo. Then 9.Ng5 hits f7 twice, and after 9...d5 10.exd5 Na5 11.d6 Nxc4 12.Qa4+ c6 your queen wins back the piece on c4.

enforces.text: Pawns back on e4 and d4, with a tempo on the c5 bishop.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 8.Ng5 hits f7 at once, but 8...d5 9.exd5 Ne5 blocks and hits your bishop. A few moves later 12...Qxd1 trades the queens, and your attack is gone.
alternatives.after: 8.cxd4 first kicks the c5 bishop to b6, so when the knight jumps in with 9.Ng5 Black is a tempo behind. With Black's bishop retreated to a5 instead, the knight jump is a main try that roughly levels.

4175344914430296|e7e5.headline: Nothing defends e5: play the solid 4...e6
4175344914430296|e7e5.why: 4...e5 puts a pawn where the knight on f3 attacks it and nothing of yours defends it, so 5.Nxe5 simply wins it, and after 5...Bd6 6.Nf3 Nf6 White is clearly better. 4...e6, the masters' top choice (43.2%), backs up d5, opens the way for the f8 bishop and keeps the game level. 4...Nf6 and 4...h6 are also fine.
4175344914430296|e7e5.principle: Before pushing a pawn into the centre, count who attacks the square and who defends it; a pawn on e5 facing a knight with no defender is just lost.

4211428648959227|c5d4.headline: Take back on d5 with 4...exd5
4211428648959227|c5d4.why: 4...cxd4 leaves White's pawn on d5 alive and lets 5.Bb5+ in. After 5...Bd7 6.dxe6 fxe6 7.cxd4 your e6 pawn is isolated, your king is exposed and White is clearly better. 4...exd5 takes back at once and opens the diagonal for your c8-bishop; masters choose it 90% of the time. After 5.Nf3 Nf6 6.Bd3 Bd6 you develop quickly and the game is level.
4211428648959227|c5d4.principle: Fight for the centre: recapture on d5 with 4...exd5, while 4...cxd4 releases the tension and lets White's d5 pawn and 5.Bb5+ hurt you.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. c3/2...e6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. c3/2...d5/3. exd5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. d4/2...d5/3. Nd2/3...c5/4. exd5
