6833062692676193|d1f3.headline: Against Alekhine's, chase the knight with 2.e5
6833062692676193|d1f3.why: 2.Qf3 guards e4 with the queen, but it takes f3 from White's knight and becomes a target: in the line 2...Nc6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Bd3 Nd4 Black hits it, and 5.Qg3 has to move it again. 2.e5 is played in 84.9% of master games: it attacks the knight on f6, gains space and makes it move, usually with 2...Nd5, where 3.c4 kicks it once more.
6833062692676193|d1f3.principle: A knight that attacks your centre pawn from f6 can be chased with e5, gaining space and time instead of defending passively.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nf6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nf6/2. e5

6833062692676193|d2d3.headline: Kick the knight with 2.e5 and take space.
6833062692676193|d2d3.why: 2.d3 saves the pawn on e4 but shuts in the bishop on f1, and after 2...e5 Black has an easy, equal game. 1...Nf6 put a knight where White's e-pawn can attack it. 2.e5 gains space with tempo: the knight has to move, usually to d5, and after 3.c4 Nb6 4.d4 White builds a big centre. Masters play it 85% of the time.
6833062692676193|d2d3.principle: When an enemy knight stands in front of your centre pawns, push a pawn to gain space and time by chasing it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nf6

6833062692676193|f2f3.headline: Answer 1...Nf6 with 2.e5, not 2.f3.
6833062692676193|f2f3.why: 2.f3 protects e4 but takes the f3 square from the knight and weakens the king. After 2...e5 3.d4 exd4 4.Qxd4 Nc6 Black develops while chasing White's queen. 1...Nf6 put a knight where the e-pawn can hit it, and 2.e5 does exactly that: the knight must move, usually to d5. After 3.c4 Nb6 4.d4 White builds a big centre.
6833062692676193|f2f3.principle: When an enemy knight sits in front of your centre pawns, kick it with a pawn rather than defending with a pawn move that weakens your king.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nf6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nf6/2. e5

6833062692676193|f2f4.headline: Against the Alekhine, 2.e5 gains space and kicks the knight
6833062692676193|f2f4.why: 2.f4 ignores the attack on e4, and 2...Nxe4 wins the pawn outright. 2.e5 is the main move: it gains space and kicks the knight, usually to d5, where 3.c4 chases it again and White keeps taking central space with tempo. Masters choose 2.e5 in 84.9% of games.
6833062692676193|f2f4.principle: When a knight on f6 attacks your e-pawn, the pawn advance that hits the knight defends nothing and attacks something, so it gains time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nf6

6849990694088956|b2b4.headline: 3...Bc5 leaves e5 loose: take it with 4.Nxe5, not 4.b4
6849990694088956|b2b4.why: 4.b4 hands Black a pawn: after 4...Bxb4 5.Nxe5 O-O 6.Nc4 Re8 Black is castled with a rook bearing down on e4 while your king is still on e1, and Black is clearly better. 4.Nxe5 takes the e5 pawn, which nothing defends, while the knight on c3 still covers e4. Black has to spend moves to regain it, as in 4...Bd4 5.Nf3 Bxc3 6.dxc3 Nxe4 7.Bd3 d5 8.Bxe4 dxe4, and White stays clearly better.
6849990694088956|b2b4.principle: Before reaching for a wing gambit, check what is loose in the centre: an undefended e5 pawn is the simplest gain on the board.

6849990694088956|d2d4.headline: 3...Bc5 left e5 undefended: take it with 4.Nxe5
6849990694088956|d2d4.why: 4.d4 exd4 5.Nxd4 trades off the pawn you could have taken for free, and after 5...O-O Black develops easily and the game is level. 3...Bc5 left e5 attacked once and defended by nothing, so 4.Nxe5 wins it. In the engine line Black hits back with 4...Bd4 5.Nf3 Bxc3 6.dxc3 Nxe4 to regain the pawn, but after 7.Bd3 d5 8.Bxe4 dxe4 White keeps a clear edge.
6849990694088956|d2d4.principle: After every opponent move check what has become loose: when a developing move leaves a centre pawn undefended, take it before following your own plan.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nc3

6849990694088956|f1c4.headline: 3...Bc5 leaves e5 loose: take it with 4.Nxe5
6849990694088956|f1c4.why: The usual replies to 3.Nc3 are 3...Nc6, reaching the Four Knights, or 3...Bb4; 3...Bc5 develops but leaves the e5 pawn undefended. 4.Nxe5 takes it, and in the main line Black gives up the dark-squared bishop to win material back with 4...Bd4 5.Nf3 Bxc3 6.dxc3 Nxe4. 4.Bc4 lets Black cover e5 with 4...d6 5.d3, and the position is level.
6849990694088956|f1c4.principle: Check every developing move by the opponent for what it stopped defending; an undefended centre pawn in front of your knight is often simply free.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nc3

6850591830216347|g8h6.headline: Develop the knight to f6, toward the centre.
6850591830216347|g8h6.why: From h6 the knight controls none of the central squares, so 6.Nd5 lands on d5 with no knight to challenge it. 5...Nf6 develops toward the centre: it attacks e4, covers d5 and lets Black castle. After 6.Na4 a6 7.Nxc5 dxc5 Black has a comfortable game.
6850591830216347|g8h6.principle: Put your knights where they control the centre, normally f6 and c6; a knight on the edge leaves central squares to the opponent.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nc6

6863144374799225|f3d4.headline: Hit the early queen first: 5.Bg5, then take on d4
6863144374799225|f3d4.why: 5.Nxd4 recaptures at once and lets Black develop calmly with 5...Bb4, so a large part of your advantage disappears. 5.Bg5 develops the bishop with an attack on the queen on f6, so Black has to spend the move on the queen (5...Qd6) instead of playing 5...dxc3, and only then 6.Nxd4 takes the pawn back with your bishop already developed and a big edge. This is the theory's point against 2...Qf6: the queen blocks the knight's best square and hands you developing moves with tempo.
6863144374799225|f3d4.principle: When the opponent's queen sits on an exposed square, look for a developing move that attacks it before you recapture material.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Qf6

6886380190448217|f3d5.headline: The d5 knight is loose: take it with the bishop, with check
6886380190448217|f3d5.why: 8.Qxd5+ wins the knight but brings your queen into the centre with two minor pieces still at home. After 8...Ke8 9.Bb5 Bd7 10.Nc3 Rd8 Black develops with gain of time, the queen on f6 hits f2, and most of your advantage is gone. 8.Bxd5+ wins the same knight with check and keeps your queen on f3, facing Black's. After 8...Be6 9.Bxc6 bxc6 10.Qxc6 you win a pawn too, and your queen hits the a8 rook.
6886380190448217|f3d5.principle: Check what is loose: the d5 knight has no defender, so take it with a minor piece and keep your queen out of reach.

ideas.title: Take the loose knight with the bishop
ideas.text: 7...Qf6 leaves the d5 knight attacked twice and defended by nothing. 8.Bxd5+ wins it with check.

ideas.title: Keep the queens on
ideas.text: Black's king on f7 can't castle; that is your attack. Keep your queen on f3, because trading queens lets the king walk to safety.

ideas.title: Take off the defenders
ideas.text: Once your bishop reaches d5, taking on c6 removes Black's other knight and 10.Qxc6 picks up a pawn.

ideas.title: Black wants trades and tempo
ideas.text: Black's queen offers a trade on f3 and hits f2 once your queen leaves. A queen in the centre gives Black free moves.

habit.why: 8.Qxd5+ wins the knight but brings your queen into the centre with two minor pieces still at home. After 8...Ke8 9.Bb5 Bd7 10.Nc3 Rd8 Black develops with gain of time, the queen on f6 hits f2, and most of your advantage is gone.

strays.idea: Take the loose knight with the bishop
strays.text: Takes with the queen, which then gets chased around the centre.

taught.why: 8.Bxd5+ wins the same knight with check and keeps your queen on f3, facing Black's. After 8...Be6 9.Bxc6 bxc6 10.Qxc6 you win a pawn too, and your queen hits the a8 rook.

enforces.idea: Take the loose knight with the bishop
enforces.text: A minor piece takes, with check, and the queen stays on f3.

6931592131044425|c6d4.headline: Develop the bishop instead of moving the knight again
6931592131044425|c6d4.why: 3...Nd4 moves the knight a second time while three minor pieces are still at home; after 4.Nxd4 exd4 5.O-O and 6.Re1 White is ahead in development, and the pawn on d4 falls to 7.c3 and 8.cxd4. 3...Bc5, the Giuoco Piano, develops the bishop to its best diagonal and keeps control of d4 and g5, ready for ...Nf6 and castling.
6931592131044425|c6d4.principle: With three minor pieces still at home, each move should bring a new one out; a second knight move needs a concrete gain.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nc6/3. Nf3

6931592131044425|f7f5.headline: Develop before touching the f-pawn in the Italian
6931592131044425|f7f5.why: 3...f5 opens the diagonal from c4 toward your king while you are undeveloped, and after 4.d4 exd4 5.Ng5 Ne5 6.Qxd4 Qe7 7.Bxg8 White wins a knight. 3...Bc5, the Giuoco Piano, develops the bishop to its best diagonal, keeps control of g5 until Black is ready to castle and adds a third guard to d4, so White's central break needs preparation.
6931592131044425|f7f5.principle: Against a bishop on c4, bring out a minor piece before moving the f-pawn; pawn moves near the king only weaken f7 and the diagonal toward g8.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4

6931592131044425|f7f6.headline: Develop a piece against the Italian; don't spend a move on ...f6
6931592131044425|f7f6.why: 3...f6 guards e5, which the knight on c6 already defends, and in exchange it takes the f6 square from Black's own knight and loosens the king. White opens the centre with 4.d4 exd4 5.O-O and develops quickly while Black's kingside is still at home. 3...Bc5, the Giuoco Piano, develops the bishop to an active diagonal, adds control of d4 and gets Black ready to castle.
6931592131044425|f7f6.principle: When a pawn is already protected by a piece, defending it again with a pawn only costs time and a good square for your knight.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5

6931592131044425|g8h6.headline: Develop toward the centre with 3...Bc5, not a knight on the rim
6931592131044425|g8h6.why: 3...Nh6 puts the knight on the edge, where it neither pressures e4 nor helps fight for the centre. In the engine line White plays 5.d4 and the knight has to move again with 6...Ng4, and after 7.Bb3 Nxd4 8.Qxd4 White's queen dominates the centre. 3...Bc5, the Giuoco Piano, puts the bishop on its most active diagonal and keeps the queen's control of g5, so 4...Nf6 and castling follow safely.
6931592131044425|g8h6.principle: Bring each piece to a square that fights for the centre; a knight on the rim controls half as much and usually has to move again.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5

6936096123661830|c8e6.headline: After 5.Nxe5, 5...Qd4 wins the pawn back.
6936096123661830|c8e6.why: 5...Be6 develops but lets White keep the extra pawn: 6.Nf3 retreats the knight, and Black has nothing for it. 5.Nxe5 left the knight on e5 and the pawn on e4 loose. 5...Qd4 attacks both and threatens mate on f2 with the bishop on c5, so after 6.Nd3 Qxe4+ Black regains the pawn with check.
6936096123661830|c8e6.principle: When you are a pawn down after a trade, look for a forcing queen move that hits two loose targets before you develop quietly.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Bc5

6936096123661830|d8e7.headline: Punish 5.Nxe5 with 5...Qd4, hitting knight, pawn and f2
6936096123661830|d8e7.why: 5...Qe7 gives White time: 6.d4 defends the knight and takes the centre, and after 6...Bb4+ 7.c3 Black has nothing to show for the lost pawn. 5...Qd4 is a multiple attack: it hits the knight on e5 and the pawn on e4 and, with the bishop on c5, threatens mate on f2. After 6.Nd3 Qxe4+ Black has the pawn back, and after 7.Qe2 Qxe2+ 8.Kxe2 White's king is stuck in the centre.
6936096123661830|d8e7.principle: With your bishop on c5 already aiming at f2, a queen move to d4 can add a mating threat to attacks on loose pieces in the centre.

6936096123661830|d8f6.headline: After 5.Nxe5, 5...Qd4 hits the knight, e4 and f2 at once.
6936096123661830|d8f6.why: 5...Qf6 lets White keep the extra pawn: 6.d4 gains time on the bishop, and Black has nothing to show for the pawn. 5...Qd4 exploits what the knight on e5 left behind: it attacks the knight and the e4 pawn and threatens mate on f2. After 6.Nd3 Qxe4+ Black has the pawn back.
6936096123661830|d8f6.principle: After a knight grabs a pawn on e5, check what it left loose: e4 and f2 are unguarded, and one queen move can hit them together with the knight.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Bc5

6936096123661830|f7f6.headline: Answer 5.Nxe5 with 5...Qd4, forking the knight and e4.
6936096123661830|f7f6.why: 5...f6 opens the e8-h5 diagonal: 6.Qh5+ g6 7.Nxg6 hxg6 8.Qxh8 and Black loses a rook and a pawn for a knight. 5.Nxe5 took a pawn but left the knight on e5 and the pawn on e4 loose. 5...Qd4 attacks both and threatens mate on f2 with the bishop on c5, so after 6.Nd3 Qxe4+ Black wins the pawn back with check.
6936096123661830|f7f6.principle: When the opponent grabs a pawn with a piece, look for a queen move that attacks the piece, a loose pawn and f2 together.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Bc5

6936096123661830|g8f6.headline: Fork with 5...Qd4 before White can protect e4.
6936096123661830|g8f6.why: 5...Nf6 attacks e4 only once, and 6.Qe2 defends it, so White keeps the extra pawn. 5.Nxe5 left the knight on e5 and the pawn on e4 loose. 5...Qd4 hits both and threatens mate on f2 with the bishop on c5. After 6.Nd3 Qxe4+ Black wins the pawn back with check.
6936096123661830|g8f6.principle: When you can attack two loose targets and threaten mate in one move, do that before a single attack the opponent can parry.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Bc5

695832176392433|g7g6.headline: Kick the pinning bishop with h6
695832176392433|g7g6.why: The bishop on g5 pins the knight on f6 to your queen, and 6...g6 does nothing about it: 7.Nd5 adds a second attacker, and after 7...Nxd5 8.Bxd8 Black has given the queen for a knight. 6...h6 puts the question to the bishop at once; after 7.Bxf6 Qxf6 the pin is gone, and 8.Nd5 is met by 8...Qd8.
695832176392433|g7g6.principle: When a bishop pins your f6-knight to the queen, challenge it with the h-pawn before White can bring another attacker to d5.

6967288124345715|g1f3.headline: Defend e4 with 3.d3; 3.Nf3 leaves it hanging
6967288124345715|g1f3.why: 3.Nf3 leaves e4 undefended, and 3...Nxe4 takes it; after 4.Nxe5 d5 the pawn hits the bishop and Black has the easier game. 3.d3 defends e4 with a pawn and opens the diagonal for the queen's bishop. It is the main line, played in 86.4% of master games.
6967288124345715|g1f3.principle: When the knight on f6 attacks your e4-pawn, defend it before developing elsewhere, ideally with a move that also frees a piece.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nf6

6980672627372882|d7d5.headline: Develop with 4...Nf6; ...d5 here just drops a pawn
6980672627372882|d7d5.why: 4...d5 opens the centre before Black is ready, and 5.exd5 wins a pawn, since d5 is hit by the pawn on e4, the knight on c3 and the bishop on c4. 4...Nf6 develops toward the centre, attacks e4 and prepares castling; masters choose it in 82.9% of games.
6980672627372882|d7d5.principle: Before pushing ...d5 here, count: White's pawn, knight and bishop all hit d5, so develop the knight first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5

6980672627372882|f7f6.headline: In the Giuoco Piano, bring out 4...Nf6, not the f-pawn
6980672627372882|f7f6.why: 4...f6 develops nothing, takes the f6 square from Black's own knight and weakens the light squares near Black's king, which White's bishop on c4 already aims at. 4...Nf6 develops the last kingside piece, adds pressure on e4 and gets Black ready to castle; masters choose it in 82.9% of games.
6980672627372882|f7f6.principle: With White's pieces out and aimed at your king, finish developing so you can castle; a pawn move like f6 has no concrete reason.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5

6994580878022218|b7b6.headline: Develop and clear the centre with 5...cxd4, not 5...b6
6994580878022218|b7b6.why: 5...b6 spends a move on a pawn while your kingside pieces wait. After 6.Nc3 Nf6 7.Be3 c4 8.a3 b5 9.Ne5 White's knight lands on e5, and after 9...b4 10.axb4 your queenside pawns are loose. 5...cxd4 settles the centre, and after 6.Nxd4 Nf6 7.Bb5+ Bd7 8.Bxd7+ Qxd7 you have traded White's active bishop and developed quickly. Your d5 pawn is isolated, but with fewer pieces on the board it is less of a target.
6994580878022218|b7b6.principle: Develop before you push side pawns: 5...cxd4 settles the centre and gets your pieces out, while 5...b6 spends a move that White's 7.Be3 and 8.a3 punish.
sources: Shaun Sedice, Playing the Grand Prix Attack (Chessable) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/grand-prix-attack/

ideas.title: Keep a pawn in the centre
ideas.text: Your pawn on d5 is your share of the centre. Keep it supported by pieces: ...Nf6 and ...Nc6 cover it.

ideas.title: Bb5 against d5
ideas.text: White's plan against your d5 pawn is a bishop check from b5 and piece pressure. Develop fast and trade pieces, as with 7...Bd7.

ideas.title: Develop before pawn moves
ideas.text: With your king still on e8, bring out pieces first. Slow pawn moves like ...b6 let White develop with threats on your queenside.

habit.why: 5...b6 spends a move on a pawn while your kingside pieces wait. After 6.Nc3 Nf6 7.Be3 c4 8.a3 b5 9.Ne5 White's knight lands on e5, and after 9...b4 10.axb4 your queenside pawns are loose.

strays.text: A pawn move instead of a piece, and it loosens your queenside.

taught.why: 5...cxd4 settles the centre, and after 6.Nxd4 Nf6 7.Bb5+ Bd7 8.Bxd7+ Qxd7 you have traded White's active bishop and developed quickly. Your d5 pawn is isolated, but with fewer pieces on the board it is less of a target.

enforces.text: You meet the check with 7...Bd7 and trade White's bishop.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.idea: Keep a pawn in the centre
alternatives.before: 5...Nf6 is a sound developing move: the knight guards d5 and prepares castling. There is a slightly more accurate move.
alternatives.after: 5...Nf6 usually transposes: 6.Nc3 cxd4 7.Nxd4 Nc6 reaches a similar position. Both are fine.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.idea: Keep a pawn in the centre
alternatives.before: 5...Nc6 develops and adds pressure on d4. After 6.Nc3 Nf6 7.Be3 your pieces are ready; it's a fine choice, though not the most accurate.
alternatives.after: Similar plans: in the line 7...cxd4 8.Bxd4 Be7 9.Qd3 O-O 10.O-O-O White castles long, while 5...cxd4 at once lets you trade White's bishop after 7.Bb5+ Bd7.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.idea: Keep a pawn in the centre
alternatives.before: 5...c4 gains queenside space and avoids an isolated pawn. White answers 6.b3 cxb3 7.axb3 and gets the open a-file, so it's fine but not the most accurate.
alternatives.after: 5...cxd4 keeps your pawns flexible; after 5...c4 6.b3 White undermines the chain at once and the a-file opens for White's rook.

7050462614834999|c1b2.headline: Hit b7 and f7 with 9.Qb3 while Black's bishop is away
7050462614834999|c1b2.why: 9.Bb2 points the bishop at your own d4-pawn and makes no threat. Black gets 9...Nf6, and after 10.h3 Bh5 11.d5 Bxf3 12.Qxf3 Ne5 the knight hits your queen and bishop while you are still a pawn down. With the bishop gone from c8, 9.Qb3 hits b7 and f7 at once. After 9...Bxf3 10.Qxf3 the queen recaptures along the third rank, so your kingside pawns stay intact and you keep the bishop pair.
7050462614834999|c1b2.principle: Make threats while you are a pawn down: 9.Qb3 attacks b7 and f7, while 9.Bb2 lets Black develop in peace.

ideas.title: The centre is the payment
ideas.text: You are a pawn down for the e4-d4 centre and quicker development. Keep the centre and make moves that create threats.

ideas.title: Qb3 hits f7 and b7
ideas.text: With Black's light bishop gone from c8, a queen on b3 attacks b7 and joins the c4-bishop against f7.

ideas.title: Black trades your knight
ideas.text: The g4-bishop pins your f3-knight; Black wants to take it, then use e5 for a knight.

habit.why: 9.Bb2 points the bishop at your own d4-pawn and makes no threat. Black gets 9...Nf6, and after 10.h3 Bh5 11.d5 Bxf3 12.Qxf3 Ne5 the knight hits your queen and bishop while you are still a pawn down.

strays.text: A quiet move: no threat, so Black finishes developing for free.

taught.why: With the bishop gone from c8, 9.Qb3 hits b7 and f7 at once. After 9...Bxf3 10.Qxf3 the queen recaptures along the third rank, so your kingside pawns stay intact and you keep the bishop pair.

enforces.text: The double attack makes Black give up the g4-bishop for your knight.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 9.h3 asks the g4-bishop to decide at once and keeps a good game. There is a slightly stronger move.
alternatives.after: 9.Qb3 hits b7 and f7 right away; after 9.h3 Bh5 10.Qb3 you reach the same idea a move later.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 9.Nbd2 blocks your c1-bishop and makes no threat: 9...Nf6 10.h3 Bh5 and Black castles in time with 11...O-O, then trades on f3.
alternatives.after: 9.Qb3 makes threats on b7 and f7 first, so Black must trade on f3 at once instead of developing.

7062831770535036|c1e3.headline: Push 7.d5 first and keep Black's knight off c6
7062831770535036|c1e3.why: 7.Be3 lets Black develop with 7...Nc6, hitting your d4 pawn. After 8.d5 O-O-O 9.Nf4 Qxd1+ 10.Rxd1 Ne5 the queens are off, the knight is centralised and most of your lead is gone. 7.d5 takes c6 and e6 from Black's knights before 7...Nc6 can hit d4, so after 7...Nf6 8.Qd3 the b8 knight has to go to d7. After 8...Nbd7 9.Be3 O-O-O 10.O-O-O you keep the queens on, more space, and 11.Nf4 to hit the queen again.
7062831770535036|c1e3.principle: With a lead in development and the opponent's king in the centre, gain central space at once rather than make quiet moves.
sources: Jeremy Silman, First Verbalize, Then Analyze (chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/article/view/first-verbalize-then-analyze-plus-one-from-the-rule-books
Scandinavian Defense Guide (Control The Center) | https://openings.controlthecenter.com/openings/scandinavian-defense/?side=white

ideas.title: Push d5 while you lead
ideas.text: Black's king is still on e8 and the queen is offside on h5. Push 7.d5 before Black is ready for it.

ideas.title: Take c6 and e6 from the knights
ideas.text: A pawn on d5 controls c6 and e6, so Black's b8 knight must go to d7 or a6 instead.

ideas.title: Develop with tempo on the queen
ideas.text: The queen on h5 is still a target: your e2 knight can hit her from f4, as in 11.Nf4 Qg4.

ideas.title: Black's pressure on d4
ideas.text: Given time, 7...Nc6 and ...O-O-O hit your d4 pawn, and 9...Qxd1+ can trade queens.

habit.why: 7.Be3 lets Black develop with 7...Nc6, hitting your d4 pawn. After 8.d5 O-O-O 9.Nf4 Qxd1+ 10.Rxd1 Ne5 the queens are off, the knight is centralised and most of your lead is gone.

strays.text: 7...Nc6 hits d4 and lets Black trade queens with check.

taught.why: 7.d5 takes c6 and e6 from Black's knights before 7...Nc6 can hit d4, so after 7...Nf6 8.Qd3 the b8 knight has to go to d7. After 8...Nbd7 9.Be3 O-O-O 10.O-O-O you keep the queens on, more space, and 11.Nf4 to hit the queen again.

enforces.text: The pawn gains space while Black's queen is offside on h5.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.O-O is safe and the most common club move (74%), but it gives Black time for 7...e6 and 9...c6. Black's pawns are then ready for any central push, and the knight jumps in with 10...Nb4.
alternatives.after: 7.d5 comes before ...e6 and ...c6: it takes c6 and e6 from the knights while Black's queen is still offside on h5.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7.Bf4 is one of the best moves here: the bishop takes an active diagonal and hits c7, so Black has to guard it with 7...Na6, putting the knight on the edge.
alternatives.after: 7.d5 and 7.Bf4 are about equally strong. 7.d5 takes c6 and e6 from the knights at once; 7.Bf4 develops first and pushes 8.d5 next move.

7062831770535036|e1h1.headline: Grab space with 7.d5 before Black builds ...e6 and ...c6
7062831770535036|e1h1.why: 7.O-O is safe, but it gives Black time for 7...e6 and later 9...c6. After 8.Bf4 Na6 9.Qd3 c6 10.d5 Nb4 Black's pawns are ready for your d5 push and the knight jumps in on b4, so much of your lead is gone. 7.d5 takes c6 and e6 from Black's knights before 7...Nc6 can hit d4, so after 7...Nf6 8.Qd3 the b8 knight has to go to d7. After 8...Nbd7 9.Be3 O-O-O 10.O-O-O you keep the queens on, more space, and 11.Nf4 to hit the queen again.
7062831770535036|e1h1.principle: With a lead in development and the opponent's king in the centre, gain central space at once rather than make quiet moves.
sources: Jeremy Silman, First Verbalize, Then Analyze (chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/article/view/first-verbalize-then-analyze-plus-one-from-the-rule-books

ideas.title: Take c6 and e6 from the knights
ideas.text: A pawn on d5 controls c6 and e6, so Black's b8 knight must go to d7 or a6 instead.

ideas.title: Develop with tempo on the queen
ideas.text: The queen on h5 is still a target: your e2 knight can hit her from f4, as in 11.Nf4 Qg4.

ideas.title: Black's ...e6 and ...c6 wall
ideas.text: Given time, Black sets up 7...e6 and 9...c6, and your d5 push no longer gains space.

habit.why: 7.O-O is safe, but it gives Black time for 7...e6 and later 9...c6. After 8.Bf4 Na6 9.Qd3 c6 10.d5 Nb4 Black's pawns are ready for your d5 push and the knight jumps in on b4, so much of your lead is gone.

strays.text: Castling gives Black time to meet your d5 push with pawns.

taught.why: 7.d5 takes c6 and e6 from Black's knights before 7...Nc6 can hit d4, so after 7...Nf6 8.Qd3 the b8 knight has to go to d7. After 8...Nbd7 9.Be3 O-O-O 10.O-O-O you keep the queens on, more space, and 11.Nf4 to hit the queen again.

enforces.text: The pawn gains space while Black's queen is offside on h5.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 7.Bf4 is one of the best moves here: the bishop takes an active diagonal and hits c7, so Black has to guard it with 7...Na6, putting the knight on the edge.
alternatives.after: 7.d5 and 7.Bf4 are about equally strong. 7.d5 takes c6 and e6 from the knights at once; 7.Bf4 develops first and pushes 8.d5 next move.

7121051583391236|f3c3.headline: Put the queen where it attacks: 6.Qb3 hits b7 and f7.
7121051583391236|f3c3.why: 6.Qc3 hits nothing Black needs to worry about, so Black catches up in development with 6...Nd7 and 7...Ne7. The theory calls 3...Bg4 dubious because it delays development, and after giving up that bishop b7 is left loose: 6.Qb3 attacks the pawn on b7, and the queen also lines up behind the bishop on c4 against f7. Black has to spend 6...b6 on defence, and White develops with 7.Nc3 and 9.Nd5, when the knight hits the queen on f6.
7121051583391236|f3c3.principle: When your queen must move anyway, put it where it attacks something, so the opponent answers your threat instead of developing.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4/3...Bg4

7121051583391236|f3d3.headline: The b7 pawn is loose: hit it with 6.Qb3
7121051583391236|f3d3.why: 6.Qd3 puts the queen on a passive square and gives Black time: after 6...Nc6 Black develops and castles long with 7...O-O-O. The bishop that guarded b7 was traded on f3, so 5...Qf6 left that pawn with no defender, and 6.Qb3 attacks it. Black has to weaken the queenside with 6...b6, while White keeps developing with 7.Nc3 and 8.O-O.
7121051583391236|f3d3.principle: After every exchange, check which pawns lost their defender; a loose pawn gives your queen a move with a threat.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4/3...Bg4

7127830528967939|e7e6.headline: Grab space with 3...d4 against the Grob's wing pawns
7127830528967939|e7e6.why: 3...e6 is solid but passive: it shuts in your c8 bishop, and after 4.d4 White's odd first move hardly matters any more and the game is level. 3...d4 takes space instead: in the engine line your pawns follow up with ...e5 and ...e4, driving White's knight back home with 7.Ng1, while 4...h5 makes the advanced g-pawn commit with 5.g5, and Black has a clear advantage. 3...dxc4 is also fine; the theory notes White then has to spend a move on Qa4 to win the pawn back.
7127830528967939|e7e6.principle: When White spends their first moves on wing pawns like g4 and c4, claim the centre with your pawns and use the space to push White's pieces back.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. g4/1...d5/2. Bg2/2...c6

7139051363978185|e7e5.headline: Prepare ...e5 with 3...d6; pushed at once, it just drops a pawn
7139051363978185|e7e5.why: 3...e5 puts a pawn on a square hit twice, by the d4 pawn and the knight on f3, and defended only by the bishop on g7, so 4.dxe5 simply wins it. 3...d6 is the normal move in the Modern, played in 81% of master games: it covers e5 so that ...e5 can follow with support, as in 4.h3 Nf6 5.Bd3 Nc6 6.c3 e5.
7139051363978185|e7e5.principle: Before pushing a pawn to a contested square, count its attackers and defenders, and add a defender first if it comes up short.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6/2. d4/2...Bg7

7139051363978185|g8f6.headline: In the Modern, play 3...d6 first so e5 can't kick the knight.
7139051363978185|g8f6.why: After 3...Nf6, White pushes 4.e5 and the knight has to move again. On e4 it is attacked by 5.Bd3, and Black has to spend 5...d5 propping it up. 3...d6, played 81% of the time, controls e5 first. After 4.h3 the knight can come to f6 safely.
7139051363978185|g8f6.principle: Against a pawn centre on e4 and d4, control e5 before putting a knight on f6 where the e-pawn can chase it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6/2. d4/2...Bg7

7152453611816462|c1f4.headline: Win back c4 first: 4.e3 frees the bishop on f1
7152453611816462|c1f4.why: 4.Bf4 develops but does nothing about the pawn on c4, and Black gets time to keep it: after 4...a6 5.Nc3 Bb4 6.a4 Nc6 7.e3 Na5 the knight guards c4. 4.e3 opens the diagonal for the bishop on f1, and 5.Bxc4 wins back the gambit pawn while developing. That is why 74.4% of masters play it.
7152453611816462|c1f4.principle: In the Queen's Gambit Accepted, recover the c4 pawn first by freeing the king's bishop; develop the rest afterwards.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...dxc4/3. Nf3

7172083930230506|d2d3.headline: Punish the slow 3...h6 by striking the centre with 4.d4
7172083930230506|d2d3.why: 4.d3 is solid but passive: after 4...Nf6 5.O-O Bc5 6.c3 d6 Black has developed exactly as planned. The tempo Black spent on 3...h6 goes unpunished. 4.d4 hits e5 at once, and 4...Nf6 would just lose the pawn. After 4...exd4 5.O-O Nf6 6.e5 d5 7.Bb5 Ne4 8.Nxd4 your pieces are active and the pawn is back, and masters choose 4.d4 in 54% of games.
7172083930230506|d2d3.principle: When the opponent spends a move on a slow pawn push, open the centre while you are ahead in development.

ideas.title: Punish the slow 3...h6
ideas.text: 3...h6 stops a knight jump to g5 but costs Black a tempo. Open the centre while you are ahead in development.

ideas.title: Hit e5 first
ideas.text: 4.d4 attacks e5 at once. If Black plays 4...Nf6 anyway, the e5 pawn is lost.

ideas.title: Black wants 4...Nf6 in peace
ideas.text: The point of 3...h6 is to play 4...Nf6 with no knight jump to g5. A slow move gives Black exactly that.

ideas.title: Castling and c3 come back to d4
ideas.text: Masters' other choices usually push the d-pawn two squares a move later, as in 4.O-O Nf6 5.d4 or 4.c3 Nf6 5.d4.

habit.why: 4.d3 is solid but passive: after 4...Nf6 5.O-O Bc5 6.c3 d6 Black has developed exactly as planned. The tempo Black spent on 3...h6 goes unpunished.

strays.text: A quiet pawn move lets Black's lost tempo go unpunished.

taught.why: 4.d4 hits e5 at once, and 4...Nf6 would just lose the pawn. After 4...exd4 5.O-O Nf6 6.e5 d5 7.Bb5 Ne4 8.Nxd4 your pieces are active and the pawn is back, and masters choose 4.d4 in 54% of games.

enforces.text: The pawn strikes the centre while Black is a tempo behind.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: Castling is sound and popular, played in 36% of master games, and it usually transposes to the same kind of game. There is a slightly more direct move.
alternatives.after: 4.d4 is the masters' first choice (54%) and hits e5 at once; 4.O-O mostly plays it a move later, as in 4.O-O Nf6 5.d4.
alternatives.idea: Castling and c3 come back to d4

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 4.Nc3 develops but doesn't challenge the centre: after 4...Bc5 5.Na4 you spend time chasing the bishop to win the bishop pair.
alternatives.after: 4.d4 opens the centre while Black is a tempo behind; 4.Nc3 lets Black develop at leisure, and masters play it in only 4% of games.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.c3 is sound and leads to Giuoco Piano-style play; masters play it in 7% of games. There is a more direct option.
alternatives.after: 4.d4 strikes at once; 4.c3 prepares the same push with pawn support, as in 4.c3 Nf6 5.d4 exd4 6.O-O Nxe4 7.Qb3. Masters prefer the direct move, 54% to 7%.
alternatives.idea: Castling and c3 come back to d4

7232835087865144|d2d3.headline: Develop and attack e5 with 2.Nf3, not the passive 2.d3
7232835087865144|d2d3.why: 2.d3 defends e4, which was not attacked, shuts in the bishop on f1 and brings out no piece; Wikibooks calls it insipid and notes it gives Black easy equality with 2...Nc6 or 2...Nf6 followed by 3...d5. 2.Nf3 develops the knight, controls d4 and attacks the undefended pawn on e5, so Black has to spend the next move defending it. Masters choose it in 92% of games.
7232835087865144|d2d3.principle: When nothing of yours is attacked, bring out a piece that makes a threat rather than a pawn move that guards what is already safe.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d3
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3

7232835087865144|d2d4.headline: Develop first with 2.Nf3; 2.d4 opens the centre too early
7232835087865144|d2d4.why: 2.d4 opens the centre before any piece is out: after 2...exd4 White must either spend a queen move on Qxd4, which ...Nc6 then attacks with tempo, or play a gambit to get the pawn back. Masters play it in under 1% of games. 2.Nf3 develops the knight, controls d4 and attacks the undefended pawn on e5, keeping White's first-move initiative without giving anything away.
7232835087865144|d2d4.principle: Open the centre only once your pieces are ready to use the open lines; until then develop with a threat.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3

7232835087865144|f2f3.headline: Develop with 2.Nf3, attacking e5; 2.f3 only weakens your king
7232835087865144|f2f3.why: The theory calls 2.f3 one of the worst second moves: it defends e4 but takes the f3 square from your knight and weakens your king, and in the line 2...Bc5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Na4 Be7 5.d4 exd4 you end up a pawn down. 2.Nf3, played in 92.2% of master games, develops a piece and attacks the undefended e5 pawn, so Black has to react. It also controls d4 and makes room to castle.
7232835087865144|f2f3.principle: Every opening move should develop a piece or fight for the centre; a pawn move that does neither, and blocks a knight's best square, just hands your opponent time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. f3
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3

7232835087865144|f2f4.headline: Develop the knight and hit e5; the King's Gambit drops a pawn.
7232835087865144|f2f4.why: 2.f4 gives up a pawn after 2...exf4, and it weakens White's own king: in the line 3.Nf3 g5 4.d4 g4 5.Ne5 Qh4+ 6.g3 fxg3 Black keeps the extra pawn and uses the e1-h4 diagonal for a queen check. 2.Nf3 attacks the undefended pawn on e5 while developing a piece, controls d4 for a later d4, and starts to clear the way to castle. That is why masters choose it 92% of the time.
7232835087865144|f2f4.principle: When the opponent's centre pawn is undefended, attack it with a developing move instead of a pawn move that loosens your king.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. f4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3

7232835087865144|g2g3.headline: Develop with a threat: the knight attacks e5
7232835087865144|g2g3.why: 2.g3 spends a move preparing a fianchetto although the bishop could already come out, and 2...d5 hits e4 at once; after 3.exd5 Qxd5 the queen attacks the rook on h1 along the diagonal that g3 opened. 2.Nf3 develops a piece, controls d4 and attacks the pawn on e5, so Black has to spend the next move defending it.
7232835087865144|g2g3.principle: A developing move that attacks something forces a reply; a quiet pawn move gives Black a free hand to strike in the centre.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. g3
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3

7273207378554101|d7d5.headline: Trade off the attacked pawn with 2...exd4
7273207378554101|d7d5.why: 2...d5 leaves the pawn on e5 attacked by the d4 pawn and undefended, so 3.dxe5 wins it. 2...exd4 removes the attacker first and is the most common master reply. After 3.exd4 d5 Black has an equal share of the centre and open lines for both bishops.
7273207378554101|d7d5.principle: When your pawn is attacked and undefended, deal with it before making a new move; capturing the attacker is the simplest way.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e3/1...e5/2. d4

7273207378554101|e5e4.headline: Trade with 2...exd4, then claim the centre with 3...d5
7273207378554101|e5e4.why: 2...e4 pushes the pawn past the centre, where it gives up d4 and becomes a target: in the engine line White takes space with 3.c4 and 5.d5 and Black is cramped. 2...exd4, played in 79% of master games, trades off the attacked pawn; after 3.exd4 d5 Black has an equal share of the centre and open lines for both bishops.
7273207378554101|e5e4.principle: When your centre pawn is attacked, trade it if pushing it would hand your opponent the squares it was controlling.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e3/1...e5/2. d4

7276016824343167|c8e6.headline: Take on d4 before the pawn forks knight and bishop
7276016824343167|c8e6.why: 4...Be6 puts the bishop next to the knight on c6, both in reach of White's d-pawn, so 5.d5 attacks them at once; after 5...Bc8 6.dxc6 bxc6 Black has lost a knight for a pawn. 4...exd4 removes the d-pawn before it can advance, and after 5.Nxd4 Nf6 Black develops normally.
7276016824343167|c8e6.principle: Don't line up pieces where an enemy pawn can attack two at once; with White's d-pawn able to advance, trade it off first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nc6

7292743344203540|f1c4.headline: Open the Sicilian with 3.d4; 3.Bc4 hits a wall
7292743344203540|f1c4.why: 3.Bc4 aims at f7, but Black blunts it with ...e6 and then hits it with ...d5, as in 3...e6 4.O-O d5 5.exd5 exd5 6.Bb5, and the bishop has spent two moves for little. 3.d4 is the Open Sicilian, played in 58% of master games: it takes space in the centre, and after 3...cxd4 4.Nxd4 White has open lines for all the pieces to develop.
7292743344203540|f1c4.principle: Fight for the centre with your pawns first; a bishop aimed at a square the opponent can easily close loses time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4

7319360163413787|f3g5.headline: Ng5 hits nothing here: castle and keep developing
7319360163413787|f3g5.why: 6.Ng5 moves the knight again for a one-move attack on f7, and 6...e6 shuts it down by blocking your c4-bishop. After 7.O-O a6 8.Re1 Be7 9.Bf1 O-O 10.Nf3 Nd4 your knight and bishop have walked back, Black's knight lands on d4, and your edge is gone. 6.O-O brings your king to safety and keeps the lead in development that Black's ...Qd8 gave you. After 6...Bg4 7.h3 Bh5 8.d4 you take the centre, and 9.d5 drives the c6-knight to the edge.
7319360163413787|f3g5.principle: Black's queen went back to d8, so you lead in development: keep adding pieces and castle instead of spending moves on one knight.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qd8

ideas.title: Develop, castle, then d4
ideas.text: Black's queen went back to d8, so you're ahead in development: castle, then take the centre with 8.d4.

ideas.title: Black's ...e6 shuts the door
ideas.text: A knight and bishop against f7 achieve nothing once ...e6 blocks your c4-bishop's path to f7.

ideas.title: Move each piece once
ideas.text: 6.Ng5 moves the knight a second time, and after 6...e6 it has to walk back with 10.Nf3 while Black catches up.

habit.why: 6.Ng5 moves the knight again for a one-move attack on f7, and 6...e6 shuts it down by blocking your c4-bishop. After 7.O-O a6 8.Re1 Be7 9.Bf1 O-O 10.Nf3 Nd4 your knight and bishop have walked back, Black's knight lands on d4, and your edge is gone.

strays.text: The knight goes to g5 and back while Black develops.

taught.why: 6.O-O brings your king to safety and keeps the lead in development that Black's ...Qd8 gave you. After 6...Bg4 7.h3 Bh5 8.d4 you take the centre, and 9.d5 drives the c6-knight to the edge.

enforces.text: Castle first, then 8.d4 takes the centre.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 6.d3 is solid but slow: after 6...a6 7.a3 Bf5 8.d4 you have spent two moves to get the pawn to d4.
alternatives.after: 6.O-O castles and later reaches d4 in one step with 8.d4, a full move ahead of the 6.d3 line.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 6.d4 grabs the centre at once and is sound, but in the engine line Black later takes on f3 and grabs the pawn with 9...Qxd4, and you play 10.Bb3 a pawn down for development. Another move keeps your edge without giving a pawn.
alternatives.after: Both moves are equally good by the engine. 6.O-O castles first and takes the centre a little later with 8.d4; 6.d4 at once gives the d-pawn back for quick development.

7372822453560713|d1b3.headline: Castle with 9.O-O: you're a pawn up, so get your king safe
7372822453560713|d1b3.why: 9.Qb3 lines up on f7, but Black has castled and 9...d5 blocks the bishop while opening the e-file. After 10.exd5 Ng6 11.Nf3 Re8+ 12.Kf1 you can no longer castle, and 12...a6 13.d4 axb5 wins the pawn back with Black's attack still coming. 9.O-O gets your king off the e-file before Black can open it. After 9...d6 10.Nf3 Re8 11.Re1 d5 12.exd5 Nexd5 13.Rxe8+ Qxe8 the rooks come off on the open file and you stay a pawn up.
7372822453560713|d1b3.principle: When you grab a pawn with your king still in the centre, castle before the lines open: 9.O-O, not 9.Qb3.

ideas.title: Castle before the centre opens
ideas.text: You've taken the e5 pawn, so Black wants ...d5 and a rook on e8 against your king on e1. Castle first.

ideas.title: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
ideas.text: Black has castled, so a queen and bishop battery on f7 has no follow-up, and 9...d5 simply blocks the c4 bishop.

ideas.title: Black opens the e-file
ideas.text: Black gave the e5 pawn to open lines: 9...d5 blocks your bishop and opens the e-file toward your king.

ideas.title: Two pieces beat a rook here
ideas.text: Taking on f7 trades your knight and bishop for a rook and pawn; with most pieces still on, the two minor pieces are worth more.

habit.why: 9.Qb3 lines up on f7, but Black has castled and 9...d5 blocks the bishop while opening the e-file. After 10.exd5 Ng6 11.Nf3 Re8+ 12.Kf1 you can no longer castle, and 12...a6 13.d4 axb5 wins the pawn back with Black's attack still coming.

strays.text: The king stays on e1 while 9...d5 opens the e-file.

taught.why: 9.O-O gets your king off the e-file before Black can open it. After 9...d6 10.Nf3 Re8 11.Re1 d5 12.exd5 Nexd5 13.Rxe8+ Qxe8 the rooks come off on the open file and you stay a pawn up.

enforces.text: The king is safe before Black's rook reaches e8.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 9.Nxf7 Rxf7 10.Bxf7+ Kxf7 gives two minor pieces for a rook and pawn, and after 11.Nd2 d5 12.e5 Nh7 Black's pieces come out fast. The two pieces are worth more here.
alternatives.after: 9.O-O keeps your knight and bishop and simply makes the king safe; you're already a pawn up and don't need to force anything.
alternatives.idea: Two pieces beat a rook here

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 9.Qf3 attacks nothing new, and 9...d6 hits your knight, which has no good square: 10.Nxf7 Rxf7 11.Bxf7+ Kxf7 is the same bad trade, with your queen exposed on f3.
alternatives.after: 9.O-O makes your king safe first, and after 9...d6 10.Nf3 the knight retreats to the square your queen would have blocked.
alternatives.idea: Two pieces beat a rook here

7372822453560713|d1f3.headline: Castle, and keep f3 free for the e5 knight
7372822453560713|d1f3.why: 9.Qf3 defends nothing important and takes f3 away from your knight. After 9...d6 the e5 knight has no safe square, so 10.Nxf7 Rxf7 11.Bxf7+ Kxf7 is forced and Black gets two minor pieces for rook and pawn, with your king still in the centre. 9.O-O gets your king safe and keeps f3 free. After 9...d6 10.Nf3 Re8 11.Re1 d5 12.exd5 Nexd5 13.Rxe8+ Qxe8 your king is safe when the e-file opens, and you keep the pawn you won on e5.
7372822453560713|d1f3.principle: Castle before the centre opens, and don't block the square your advanced knight needs to retreat to.

ideas.title: Keep a retreat for the knight
ideas.text: Your knight on e5 will be kicked by 9...d6. Keep f3 free so it can go back with 10.Nf3.

ideas.title: Castle before the e-file opens
ideas.text: Your king is still on e1 and Black has castled. Black can open the e-file with checks, as in 9.Qb3 d5 10.exd5 Ng6 11.Nf3 Re8+.

ideas.title: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
ideas.text: Once Black has castled, 9.Nxf7 Rxf7 10.Bxf7+ Kxf7 gives two minor pieces for rook and pawn with no attack to follow.

ideas.title: Black hits the b5 pawn
ideas.text: Black threatens 9...c6, attacking your b5 pawn and opening the c-file.

habit.why: 9.Qf3 defends nothing important and takes f3 away from your knight. After 9...d6 the e5 knight has no safe square, so 10.Nxf7 Rxf7 11.Bxf7+ Kxf7 is forced and Black gets two minor pieces for rook and pawn, with your king still in the centre.

strays.idea: Keep a retreat for the knight
strays.text: Your queen takes f3, the knight's only retreat from 9...d6.

taught.why: 9.O-O gets your king safe and keeps f3 free. After 9...d6 10.Nf3 Re8 11.Re1 d5 12.exd5 Nexd5 13.Rxe8+ Qxe8 your king is safe when the e-file opens, and you keep the pawn you won on e5.

enforces.text: Your king is on g1 before Black opens the e-file with 11...d5.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 9.Qb3 aims at f7, but Black opens the e-file at once: 9...d5 10.exd5 Ng6 11.Nf3 Re8+ 12.Kf1 and your king can no longer castle.
alternatives.after: 9.O-O puts the king on g1 first, so when Black opens the e-file there is no check to fear.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 9.Nxf7 Rxf7 10.Bxf7+ Kxf7 gives two minor pieces for rook and pawn with no attack behind it; after 11.Nd2 d5 12.e5 Nh7 Black's pieces are more active.
alternatives.after: 9.O-O keeps your pieces and the extra pawn; the knight goes back to f3 when 9...d6 comes.
alternatives.idea: Hit f7 only with a follow-up

7413259852066043|h7h6.headline: Meet the knight on g5 by blocking the bishop with 4...d5
7413259852066043|h7h6.why: 4...h6 is too slow: 5.Nxf7 takes the pawn and forks the queen on d8 and the rook on h8, and after 5...d5 6.Nxd8 Black ends up giving the queen for a bishop and a knight. 4...d5 shuts the bishop on c4 off from f7 and attacks it at the same time. After 5.exd5 h6 6.Nf3 the knight has to go back, and Black gains more time with 6...e4.
7413259852066043|h7h6.principle: Your f7 pawn is guarded only by the king, and the knight on g5 and the bishop on c4 both aim at it, so break that attack at once instead of preparing to.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4

741393967202585|e4f5.headline: Castle with 5.O-O and leave the f5 tension to Black
741393967202585|e4f5.why: 5.exf5 gives up your hold on the centre: 5...d5 hits the c4-bishop, and after 6.Bb3 Bxf5 Black has the pawn back and free development. Then 7.O-O Bg4 pins your knight, and Black's pawns rule the centre. 5.O-O tucks your king away and leaves the f5 tension for Black; Morphy played it against Rousseau in 1849. After 5...Bb4 6.c3 fxe4 7.dxe4 Bc5 8.b4 Bb6 9.a4 your pawns gain queenside space with tempo.
741393967202585|e4f5.principle: With the centre tense, castle first and let Black release the tension, instead of opening lines yourself with 5.exf5.

ideas.title: Castle and let Black decide
ideas.text: Castle first and leave the f5 tension. If Black takes on e4, you recapture with the d-pawn and keep a solid centre.

ideas.title: Taking on f5 frees Black
ideas.text: After exf5, ...d5 hits your c4-bishop and ...Bxf5 wins the pawn back with a big centre and free development.

ideas.title: Black aims for ...f4
ideas.text: Black sets up like a Giuoco Piano, waits for you to castle, then pushes ...f4 against your king; you play in the centre.

ideas.title: Ng5 needs a real target
ideas.text: A knight jump to g5 hits f7 only once. Black answers ...d5, blocks the bishop and chases your pieces, as in the Two Knights.

habit.why: 5.exf5 gives up your hold on the centre: 5...d5 hits the c4-bishop, and after 6.Bb3 Bxf5 Black has the pawn back and free development. Then 7.O-O Bg4 pins your knight, and Black's pawns rule the centre.

strays.text: The capture frees Black's c8-bishop and lets ...d5 come with tempo.

taught.why: 5.O-O tucks your king away and leaves the f5 tension for Black; Morphy played it against Rousseau in 1849. After 5...Bb4 6.c3 fxe4 7.dxe4 Bc5 8.b4 Bb6 9.a4 your pawns gain queenside space with tempo.

enforces.text: You castle, and recapture on e4 with the d-pawn if Black takes.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5.Bg5 pins the knight only to the queen, and 5...Be7 ends that. After 6.Nc3 d6 7.Bxf6 Bxf6 you have given up the bishop, and 9...f4 gains Black kingside space.
alternatives.after: 5.O-O keeps your bishop and gets the king safe before Black's ...f4 push arrives.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 5.Ng5 moves the knight again to hit f7 once. After 5...d5 6.exd5 Na5 7.Bb5+ c6 8.dxc6 bxc6 9.Ba4 Bd6 Black has a big centre and quick development.
alternatives.after: 5.O-O develops instead of moving a piece twice, and leaves Black to resolve the f5 tension.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 5.Nc3 develops and guards e4, but 5...Bb4 pins the knight and 6...Bxc3 7.bxc3 doubles your pawns. There is a slightly more accurate move.
alternatives.after: 5.O-O keeps c3 for a pawn: after 5...Bb4 6.c3 the bishop is kicked instead of trading for your knight.

741414726801315|c1f4.headline: Black took on c4, so take the whole centre with 5.e4
741414726801315|c1f4.why: 5.Bf4 develops but leaves the c4 pawn in Black's hands: after 5...c6 6.a4 Bb4 Black keeps the pawn for now and pins the knight on c3. 5.e4 claims the centre with both pawns while Black's pawn sits on c4, and 6.Bxc4 then regains it with the bishop developed. If Black takes on e4 with 6...Nxe4, White castles with 7.O-O and has active pieces; 54.8% of masters choose 5.e4.
741414726801315|c1f4.principle: When Black has given up the centre to take on c4, occupy it with both pawns, then win the c4 pawn back with a developing move.

7422621539281278|c1g5.headline: 7.Nb5, not 7.Bg5: hit the d6 hole before ...a6
7422621539281278|c1g5.why: 7.Bg5 attacks the queen, but 7...Ne7 blocks with a developing move and the bishop has nothing else to hit. After 8.O-O Nbc6 9.Qd2 a6 b5 is covered and the d6 hole can't be used. 7.Nb5 threatens 8.Nd6+, and since ...e6 and ...Bg7 no pawn or bishop guards d6. After 7...Nf6 8.Nd6+ Ke7 9.e5 Ne8 10.Bg5+ f6 Black's king is stuck in the centre.
7422621539281278|c1g5.principle: When your opponent leaves a hole, hit it at once: ...g6 and ...e6 left d6 unguarded, so 7.Nb5 aims there before ...a6 closes the door.
sources: Hannes Langrock, The Modern Morra Gambit (sample pages) | https://www.newinchess.com/media/wysiwyg/product_pdf/2702.pdf

ideas.title: Knight jump to d6
ideas.text: Black played ...e6 and ...Bg7 but no d-pawn move, so nothing guards d6. From b5 your knight checks there and Black loses castling.

ideas.title: ...a6 shuts the door
ideas.text: Black's answer is ...a6, taking b5 from your knight. Neither ...a6 nor ...Nc6 is in yet, so the jump works now.

ideas.title: The e4-e5 break
ideas.text: Against the fianchetto, e5 blocks the g7 bishop and takes f6 from Black's knight. With ...e6 in, Black just develops the knight to e7.

ideas.title: Gambit pawn buys time
ideas.text: You are a pawn down for quick development and open lines. Spend that time on threats, or Black catches up and keeps the pawn.

habit.why: 7.Bg5 attacks the queen, but 7...Ne7 blocks with a developing move and the bishop has nothing else to hit. After 8.O-O Nbc6 9.Qd2 a6 b5 is covered and the d6 hole can't be used.

strays.text: It lets Black develop and play 9...a6 before the knight gets to b5.

taught.why: 7.Nb5 threatens 8.Nd6+, and since ...e6 and ...Bg7 no pawn or bishop guards d6. After 7...Nf6 8.Nd6+ Ke7 9.e5 Ne8 10.Bg5+ f6 Black's king is stuck in the centre.

enforces.text: The knight heads for d6 before ...a6 can stop it.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: Castling is natural, but 7...a6 takes b5 from your knight. After 8.Qd6 Nc6 9.Bg5 f6 Black covers the dark squares and castles soon.
alternatives.after: 7.Nb5 uses d6 before ...a6 can cover it; castling can wait a move.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 7.e5 blocks the g7 bishop, but with ...e6 in, Black develops with 7...Ne7. After 8.O-O b6 9.Ne4 O-O Black has castled and is still a pawn up.
alternatives.after: 7.Nb5 hits d6 first; the push comes later with more force, as in 7...Nf6 8.Nd6+ Ke7 9.e5.

7422621539281278|e1h1.headline: Don't castle yet: 7.Nb5 aims at the hole on d6
7422621539281278|e1h1.why: Castling is natural, but it gives Black time for 7...a6, which takes b5 from your knight. After 8.Qd6 Nc6 9.Bg5 f6 10.Bf4 Nge7 11.Bb3 O-O Black has castled and keeps the extra pawn. 7.Nb5 threatens 8.Nd6+, and since ...e6 and ...Bg7 no pawn or bishop guards d6. After 7...Nf6 8.Nd6+ Ke7 9.e5 Ne8 10.Bg5+ f6 Black's king is stuck in the centre.
7422621539281278|e1h1.principle: When your opponent leaves a hole, hit it at once: ...g6 and ...e6 left d6 unguarded, so 7.Nb5 aims there before ...a6 closes the door.
sources: Hannes Langrock, The Modern Morra Gambit (sample pages) | https://www.newinchess.com/media/wysiwyg/product_pdf/2702.pdf

ideas.text: Black played ...e6 and ...Bg7 but no d-pawn move, so nothing guards d6. From b5 your knight checks there and Black loses castling.

744743001475587|b1c3.headline: Play the Queen's Gambit 2.c4 to challenge d5
744743001475587|b1c3.why: 2.Nc3 is sound but blocks your c-pawn, so it can no longer challenge Black's d5 pawn, and in the engine line Black develops freely with 2...Nf6 and 3...e6. That's why masters play it in only 1% of games. 2.c4, the Queen's Gambit, is the main line at 77%: it attacks d5 from the flank, and if Black takes, their pawn is pulled away from the centre and White takes a bigger share of it.
744743001475587|b1c3.principle: Use a flank pawn to attack your opponent's central pawn before your pieces block that pawn's path.

744743001475587|e2e3.headline: After 1.d4 d5, challenge the centre with 2.c4
744743001475587|e2e3.why: 2.e3 is solid but passive: it shuts in White's dark-squared bishop and puts no pressure on d5, so Black develops freely with 2...Nf6. 2.c4, the Queen's Gambit, is played in 76.9% of master games: White offers a pawn to challenge d5 at once, and if 2...dxc4 White can take a bigger share of the centre with 3.e4.
744743001475587|e2e3.principle: With 1.d4 d5, attack Black's centre pawn with the c-pawn: trading a flank pawn for a centre pawn wins you central control.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5

7494602145104629|d2d3.headline: The Elephant Gambit is unsound: take the pawn with 3.exd5
7494602145104629|d2d3.why: 3.d3 turns down the gambit and lets Black open the centre on equal terms: after 3...dxe4 4.Nxe5 Nf6 5.Be2 exd3 6.Nxd3 the material is level and so is the game. The theory notes call 2...d5 unsound and say that taking either pawn wins for White; 3.exd5 is the main move. Black's best try is 3...e4, and 4.Qe2 defends the knight by pinning the pawn, keeping your extra pawn and a clear edge. 3.Nxe5 and 3.d4 are also good.
7494602145104629|d2d3.principle: Take a gambit pawn when you can consolidate; here 4.Qe2 shows you can, so declining with a passive pawn move just hands Black the open game they wanted.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d5/3. exd5

7494602145104629|f1d3.headline: Against the Elephant Gambit, take on d5.
7494602145104629|f1d3.why: 3.Bd3 doesn't stop 3...dxe4, and it blocks the d-pawn. After 3...dxe4 4.Bxe4 f5 5.Bd3 e4 the bishop is chased and the pawn forks the bishop on d3 and the knight on f3. 2...d5 is an unsound gambit, and 3.exd5 accepts it. If 3...Qxd5, 4.Nc3 gains time on the queen, and against 3...e4 White has 4.Qe2, pinning the pawn.
7494602145104629|f1d3.principle: When the opponent offers an unsound gambit, take the pawn that removes the threat and develop with tempo against whatever recaptures.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d5/3. exd5

7498080805028408|f3b3.headline: Take the c6 knight with check before it reaches d4
7498080805028408|f3b3.why: 9.Qb3 moves your queen again with two minor pieces still at home, and 9...Nd4 hits it at once. After 10.Qd3 Bg4 11.h3 Bh5 12.c3 Rd8 13.cxd4 Rxd5 Black wins your bishop back and your advantage is gone. 9.Bxc6+ removes the knight with check before it can join in, and 9...bxc6 leaves Black's pawns split. Then 10.Qh5+ g6 11.Qe2 keeps the queens on, and Black's king stays stuck in the centre while you stay a pawn up.
7498080805028408|f3b3.principle: When the enemy king is stuck in the centre, remove its defenders with check instead of moving your queen again.

ideas.title: Keep the queens on
ideas.text: Black's king can't castle and stands in the centre; that is your attack. Trading queens lets it walk to safety.

ideas.title: Take off the defenders
ideas.text: 9.Bxc6+ removes the knight with check before it can jump to d4, and 9...bxc6 splits Black's pawns.

ideas.title: Check, then keep the queen safe
ideas.text: After the trade on c6, 10.Qh5+ g6 11.Qe2 forces a pawn forward and keeps your queen on the board.

ideas.title: Black wants trades and tempo
ideas.text: Black's queen on f6 offers a trade, and a knight jump to d4 would hit your queen and c2 with gain of time.

habit.why: 9.Qb3 moves your queen again with two minor pieces still at home, and 9...Nd4 hits it at once. After 10.Qd3 Bg4 11.h3 Bh5 12.c3 Rd8 13.cxd4 Rxd5 Black wins your bishop back and your advantage is gone.

strays.text: The c6 knight stays and jumps to d4 with gain of time.

taught.why: 9.Bxc6+ removes the knight with check before it can join in, and 9...bxc6 leaves Black's pawns split. Then 10.Qh5+ g6 11.Qe2 keeps the queens on, and Black's king stays stuck in the centre while you stay a pawn up.

enforces.text: Removes the knight with check, so Black never gets 9...Nd4.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 9.Qxf6 gxf6 trades off your best attacker, and Black's king later walks to f7 in safety (13...Kf7). Most of your advantage is gone.
alternatives.after: 9.Bxc6+ bxc6 10.Qh5+ keeps the queens on and the king stuck on e8; trading them first throws that away.

7498080805028408|f3f6.headline: Keep the queens on: Black's stuck king is your target
7498080805028408|f3f6.why: 9.Qxf6 gxf6 trades off the queen that pressures Black's king, which can no longer castle. After 10.Bxc6+ bxc6 11.d3 Rg8 Black's rook uses the open g-file, the king walks to f7 by 13...Kf7, and most of your advantage is gone. 9.Bxc6+ removes the knight with check, and after 9...bxc6 10.Qh5+ g6 11.Qe2 the queens stay on. Black's king is stuck in the centre behind split pawns, and you stay a pawn up.
7498080805028408|f3f6.principle: Play to your trump: Black's king can't castle, so keep the queens on and trade minor pieces instead.

7498176079464762|g1f3.headline: 5.d4 threatens d5, hitting queen and knight at once
7498176079464762|g1f3.why: 5.Nf3 is natural but doesn't touch the queen, so Black regroups with 5...Qd7. After 6.d4 e6 7.O-O Nf6 Black has a solid position and part of your lead is gone. 5.d4 threatens 6.d5, hitting the queen and the knight together, so Black must react at once. After 5...Qd6 6.d5 Ne5 7.Qd4 c5 8.Qe3 you keep chasing Black's pieces and gain more time.
7498176079464762|g1f3.principle: When a pawn push can fork two pieces, threaten it: the opponent must spend moves avoiding it while you gain space.
sources: Jeremy Silman, First Verbalize, Then Analyze (chess.com) | https://www.chess.com/article/view/first-verbalize-then-analyze-plus-one-from-the-rule-books

ideas.title: Develop with tempo on the queen
ideas.text: The queen on e6 blocks Black's e-pawn and must move again. 5.d4 makes her go now.

ideas.title: Push d5 while you lead
ideas.text: With the knight on c6 and the queen on e6, a pawn on d5 hits both, so Black must react to 5.d4 at once.

ideas.title: Mind the pin on e2
ideas.text: The queen on e6 pins your e2 bishop to your king, so the bishop can't move yet.

ideas.title: Black's queen regroups
ideas.text: After a slow move, Black tucks the queen on d7 and follows with ...e6 and ...Nf6, as in 5.Nf3 Qd7 6.d4 e6.

habit.why: 5.Nf3 is natural but doesn't touch the queen, so Black regroups with 5...Qd7. After 6.d4 e6 7.O-O Nf6 Black has a solid position and part of your lead is gone.

strays.text: It gives Black a free move to tuck the queen on d7.

taught.why: 5.d4 threatens 6.d5, hitting the queen and the knight together, so Black must react at once. After 5...Qd6 6.d5 Ne5 7.Qd4 c5 8.Qe3 you keep chasing Black's pieces and gain more time.

enforces.text: The threat of 6.d5 forces Black's pieces to move again.

7521748049854142|b8c6.headline: Against 2.e3, put the knight on f6 and keep the c-pawn free
7521748049854142|b8c6.why: 2...Nc6 blocks the c-pawn, so Black loses the natural ways to challenge d4 or support d5 with it, and the knight becomes a target, as in 3.Nf3 Bf5 4.Bb5 where it gets pinned. 2...Nf6 is the natural developing move, played in three quarters of master games: it controls e4 so White can't push there freely, and prepares ...e6 and castling, as in 3.Nf3 e6 4.Bd3 Be7 5.O-O O-O.
7521748049854142|b8c6.principle: In closed d-pawn openings, develop the king's knight to f6 to guard e4 and leave the c-pawn free for the fight against d4.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5

7521748049854142|e7e5.headline: Develop with 2...Nf6; 2...e5 just drops a pawn
7521748049854142|e7e5.why: 2...e5 puts a pawn where the d4 pawn attacks it and nothing defends it, so 3.dxe5 wins it. 2...Nf6 is the most common master reply: it develops the knight toward the centre, and Black's d5 pawn is already defended by the queen.
7521748049854142|e7e5.principle: Before pushing a pawn into contact, count attackers and defenders: e5 would be attacked once and defended zero times.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5

7528031277512488|c1e3.headline: Develop with 6.Bc4 and keep d2 for the other bishop
7528031277512488|c1e3.why: 6.Be3 doesn't break the pin on c3, since the bishop stands off the a5-e1 diagonal, and it gives Black's pieces a target. After 6...Bf5 7.Nh4 Nbd7 8.Nxf5 Qxf5 9.Bd3 Qg4 10.Qxg4 Nxg4 the queens are off and the knight hits your e3-bishop, so little of your edge remains. 6.Bc4 develops toward the centre and keeps d2 free, so after 6...Bf5 7.Bd2 the pin is broken. 6.Bc4 Bf5 is the Classical Line, which Lorenzini's survey treats as good for White; 8.Qe2 and 9.O-O-O can follow.
7528031277512488|c1e3.principle: Develop each piece to the square the plan gives it, here Bc4 and then Bd2, instead of a square that leaves the pin and gives Black a target.

ideas.title: The pin on c3
ideas.text: Black's queen on a5 pins your c3-knight to the king. A bishop on d2 breaks the pin; 6.Be3 does not.

ideas.title: Bd2, long castling, pawn storm
ideas.text: A good plan: bishops to c4 and d2, queen to e2, then long castling, as in 7.Bd2 Nbd7 8.Qe2 Qc7 9.O-O-O.

ideas.title: Bishop out before ...e6/...c6
ideas.text: Black brings the bishop to f5 before ...e6, and the queen can drop back to c7 through the hole ...c6 made.

ideas.title: Hunt the f5 bishop
ideas.text: Once Black's bishop sits on f5, a knight on h4 or e5 and the g4 push can chase it, as in 10.Nh4 Bg6.

habit.why: 6.Be3 doesn't break the pin on c3, since the bishop stands off the a5-e1 diagonal, and it gives Black's pieces a target. After 6...Bf5 7.Nh4 Nbd7 8.Nxf5 Qxf5 9.Bd3 Qg4 10.Qxg4 Nxg4 the queens are off and the knight hits your e3-bishop, so little of your edge remains.

strays.text: The bishop goes to e3, so the c3-knight stays pinned.

taught.why: 6.Bc4 develops toward the centre and keeps d2 free, so after 6...Bf5 7.Bd2 the pin is broken. 6.Bc4 Bf5 is the Classical Line, which Lorenzini's survey treats as good for White; 8.Qe2 and 9.O-O-O can follow.

enforces.text: 6.Bc4 first keeps d2 free for the bishop that unpins the knight.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 6.Bd2 breaks the pin at once, so any knight move now uncovers an attack on the queen. It's fully sound; masters play it in 12% of games and prefer another move.
alternatives.after: 6.Bd2 and 6.Bc4 usually meet: 6...Bf5 7.Bc4 reaches the same main line. Masters start with 6.Bc4 (66%) far more often.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 6.Bd3 develops and prepares castling, but after 6...Bg4 7.h3 Bh5 8.Bd2 e6 Black has the bishop outside the pawn chain. It's sound, though masters rarely play it (2%).
alternatives.after: 6.Bc4 puts the bishop on a more active diagonal and is the masters' main move (66% to 2%); the engine rates the two close.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 6.Be2 is quiet and safe; after 6...Bf5 7.O-O e6 8.Ne5 you still get the knight jump and 9.g4 against the bishop. Masters play it in 3% of games.
alternatives.after: 6.Bc4 puts the bishop on its most active square and is the masters' main choice (66% to 3%).

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 6.Ne5 jumps in at once: the knight can go on to c4 to hit the queen, and after 6...Be6 7.f4 a pawn backs it up. Masters play it in 14% of games.
alternatives.after: Masters prefer 6.Bc4, 66% to 14%: it develops a new piece first, and the knight jump to e5 can still come later.

7560471072032627|b1c3.headline: Take on d5 with 2.exd5, then develop with tempo
7560471072032627|b1c3.why: 1...d5 attacks e4, and 2.Nc3 lets Black kick the knight with 2...d4, so it has to go back with 3.Nb1 and Black has gained space for free. 2.exd5 is played in 97% of master games: it trades off Black's central pawn, and after 2...Qxd5 3.Nc3 your knight develops with gain of time on the queen, which has to move again.
7560471072032627|b1c3.principle: Trading on d5 draws Black's queen into the centre, where your pieces can develop by attacking it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5

7560471072032627|d2d3.headline: Meet 1...d5 with 2.exd5, not the timid 2.d3
7560471072032627|d2d3.why: 2.d3 looks like it defends e4, but after 2...dxe4 3.dxe4 Qxd1+ 4.Kxd1 the queens come off and White's king has lost the right to castle; Wikibooks calls the move timid. 2.exd5 is played in 97% of master games: it removes Black's central pawn, and if Black takes back with 2...Qxd5, 3.Nc3 develops with gain of time on the queen.
7560471072032627|d2d3.principle: When a pawn challenges your centre pawn, capture it so that your opponent's recapture brings a piece out where you can attack it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5

7560471072032627|d2d4.headline: Take on d5: 2.d4 just hands Black the e4 pawn.
7560471072032627|d2d4.why: After 1...d5 the pawn on e4 is attacked, and 2.d4 does nothing about it: 2...dxe4 wins a pawn and you are in the Blackmar-Diemer gambit, a line considered suspect at a high level. 2.exd5 trades the attacked pawn, and if Black recaptures with 2...Qxd5 the queen stands exposed in the centre, so 3.Nc3 develops with tempo against it. That is why 2.exd5 is played in 96.9% of master games.
7560471072032627|d2d4.principle: Answer the opponent's threat first: when a pawn attacks your centre pawn, capture rather than add a pawn that doesn't defend it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5

7560471072032627|f1d3.headline: Against the Scandinavian, trade with 2.exd5 and chase the queen
7560471072032627|f1d3.why: 2.Bd3 blocks White's d-pawn, and after 2...dxe4 3.Bxe4 e5 4.Nc3 Nf6 the bishop is hit and must move again with 5.Bf3, while Black has a free hand in the centre. 2.exd5 is played in 96.9% of master games: White trades the attacked pawn, and after 2...Qxd5 3.Nc3 White develops with tempo against the queen.
7560471072032627|f1d3.principle: When your centre pawn is attacked, the trade that brings the opponent's queen out lets you develop with threats, Nc3 hitting the queen.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5

7560471072032627|f2f3.headline: Trade on d5 and gain time on the queen
7560471072032627|f2f3.why: 2.f3 defends e4 at the cost of the g1-knight's best square and a weaker king, and Black simply adds 2...e5 for a fine centre. 2.exd5 trades the pawn, and when Black recaptures with 2...Qxd5, 3.Nc3 develops with an attack on the queen, which has to move again.
7560471072032627|f2f3.principle: When the opponent can only recapture with the queen, trade: a queen in the centre lets you develop with gain of time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5

7560471072032627|f2f4.headline: Against 1...d5, take the pawn: 2.exd5.
7560471072032627|f2f4.why: Black is threatening 2...dxe4, and 2.f4 does nothing about it, so the e-pawn is simply lost: 2.f4 dxe4. 2.exd5 trades the attacked pawn off at once and keeps the centre balance. If Black takes back with 2...Qxd5, 3.Nc3 develops a knight while chasing the queen, which is the main drawback of the Scandinavian.
7560471072032627|f2f4.principle: When a centre pawn is attacked by a pawn, deal with the threat first, and prefer the capture that leaves the opponent's queen exposed to your developing moves.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5

7560471072032627|g1f3.headline: Trade with 2.exd5; 2.Nf3 just hands Black the e4 pawn
7560471072032627|g1f3.why: 2.Nf3 is the Tennison Gambit, and it doesn't stop 2...dxe4, which wins a pawn with a hit on your knight. After 3.Ng5 e5 4.h4 h6 5.Nxe4 Be6 you get the pawn back, but Black has a strong centre and the easier game. 2.exd5 removes Black's attacker, and after 2...Qxd5 3.Nc3 gains a tempo on the queen. After 3...Qd8 4.d4 Nf6 5.Nf3 you have the freer development; masters choose 2.exd5 in 97% of games.
7560471072032627|g1f3.principle: When a centre pawn is attacked, trade it or defend it; leaving it hanging gives the opponent a free pawn with tempo.
sources: Matthew Astle, The Tennison Gambit (Chessable blog) | https://www.chessable.com/blog/tennison-gambit/
Anton Shuravin, How to Play the Tennison Gambit (ChessDoctrine) | https://chessdoctrine.com/chess-openings/flank/tennison-gambit/
Scandinavian Defense (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scandinavian_Defense
