ideas.title: Trade on d5 first
ideas.text: Black's pawn hits e4. 2.exd5 is almost always played, because trading pawns suits White.

ideas.title: Develop with tempo on the queen
ideas.text: If Black takes back with 2...Qxd5, then 3.Nc3 develops with a hit on the queen.

ideas.title: Black's pawn hits e4
ideas.text: After 2.Nf3 dxe4 Black wins the pawn with a hit on your knight.

ideas.title: Bishop out before ...e6/...c6
ideas.text: If you push past to e5, Black brings the bishop to f5 first and plays ...e6 after, as in 5...Bf5 6.Nf3 e6.

habit.why: 2.Nf3 is the Tennison Gambit, and it doesn't stop 2...dxe4, which wins a pawn with a hit on your knight. After 3.Ng5 e5 4.h4 h6 5.Nxe4 Be6 you get the pawn back, but Black has a strong centre and the easier game.

strays.text: Ignoring the pawn lets Black take e4 with tempo.

taught.why: 2.exd5 removes Black's attacker, and after 2...Qxd5 3.Nc3 gains a tempo on the queen. After 3...Qd8 4.d4 Nf6 5.Nf3 you have the freer development; masters choose 2.exd5 in 97% of games.

enforces.idea: Develop with tempo on the queen
enforces.text: Taking first means 3.Nc3 later develops with a hit on the queen.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 2.e5 avoids the trade but poses Black no problems: 2...c5 clamps down on d4, and Black's bishop comes out to f5 before ...e6, as in 5...Bf5 6.Nf3 e6. Masters play it in only 0.4% of games.
alternatives.after: 2.exd5 keeps the game open and gains time on Black's queen with 3.Nc3, instead of a French-type structure where Black's bishop is already outside the chain.

7590461919375344|b8c6.headline: Against the London, play 2...Nf6 and keep the c-pawn free.
7590461919375344|b8c6.why: 2...Nc6 puts the knight in front of the c-pawn, so Black can no longer play the ...c5 break, one of the two main ways of fighting the London. 2...Nf6 is Black's most common reply: it develops, controls e4, and keeps both plans open, ...c5 with pressure on b2 or ...e6 with ...Bd6, as in 2...Nf6 3.e3 c5.
7590461919375344|b8c6.principle: In queen's pawn openings, don't block the c-pawn with a knight before you've decided whether you need the ...c5 break.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. Bf4
Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. Bf4/2...Nf6

7590461919375344|f7f6.headline: Against the London, develop with 2...Nf6; leave the f-pawn home
7590461919375344|f7f6.why: 2...f6 takes the best square from Black's own king's knight and loosens the squares around the black king, all to stop a knight that hasn't reached e5 yet. 2...Nf6 develops toward the centre, controls e4 and keeps the f-pawn home; Black then counters the London with ...c5 or ...e6, as in 3.e3 c5.
7590461919375344|f7f6.principle: Develop the king's knight to f6 before touching the f-pawn; a pawn move here fixes nothing and takes the knight's square.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. Bf4
Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. Bf4/2...Nf6

7617223119001726|f3g5.headline: Castle first; the knight raid to g5 only loses time
7617223119001726|f3g5.why: 4.Ng5 moves the knight again and threatens nothing that 4...e6 doesn't cover. After 5.d3 Bg7 6.Bb3 Nge7 7.O-O O-O 8.Nf3 the knight is back on f3, so you have lost two moves and Black is the one who is comfortable. 4.O-O tucks your king away and keeps both c3 and d4 ready, as masters do in 51% of games. If 4...Nf6 5.e5 d5 6.Bb5 Nd7 7.Bxc6 bxc6 8.Re1 you have gained time on the knight and left Black with doubled c-pawns.
7617223119001726|f3g5.principle: Don't move a piece twice in the opening: 4.O-O adds to your development, while 4.Ng5 spends two moves on a knight that 4...e6 sends back.
sources: IM Kushager Krishnater, Dangerous System against the Sicilian: the Concept with 3.Bc4 (Modern Chess) | https://www.modern-chess.com/course/dangerous-system-against-the-sicilian-the-concept-with-3-bc4/64692/
Andre Schulz, Beating the Sicilian with 3.Bc4 - seriously? (ChessBase) | https://en.chessbase.com/post/beating-the-sicilian-with-3-bc4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Bc4

ideas.title: Castle, then prepare d4
ideas.text: Castle first, then build c3 and d4. Castling gets your king safe and keeps both options open.

ideas.title: No time for knight raids
ideas.text: 4.Ng5 moves a piece twice. One move, 4...e6, covers f7 and blunts your bishop, and the knight must go back.

ideas.title: Black's ...d5 hits your bishop
ideas.text: ...e6 blunts the c4-bishop and prepares ...d5, which attacks it with gain of time.

habit.why: 4.Ng5 moves the knight again and threatens nothing that 4...e6 doesn't cover. After 5.d3 Bg7 6.Bb3 Nge7 7.O-O O-O 8.Nf3 the knight is back on f3, so you have lost two moves and Black is the one who is comfortable.

strays.text: The knight goes to g5 and back while Black develops.

taught.why: 4.O-O tucks your king away and keeps both c3 and d4 ready, as masters do in 51% of games. If 4...Nf6 5.e5 d5 6.Bb5 Nd7 7.Bxc6 bxc6 8.Re1 you have gained time on the knight and left Black with doubled c-pawns.

enforces.text: Your king is safe first; c3 and d4 can follow.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.c3 prepares d4 at once, the plan IM Krishnater gives against ...g6: after 4...e6 and 6.d4 cxd4 7.Nxd4 you have an Open Sicilian. Masters play it in 39% of games.
alternatives.after: 4.O-O, the masters' main move (51%), does the same job one step at a time: castle first and keep c3 or d4 for later. Both are sound.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.d4 offers a pawn: after 4...cxd4 5.c3 dxc3 6.Nxc3 Bg7 7.e5 you get quick development and Morra-style play. It's playable, but Black gets an equal game.
alternatives.after: 4.O-O keeps the pawn and prepares c3 and d4 calmly; masters prefer it, 51% to 4%.

7623551723116652|f3g5.headline: g5 belongs to Black's queen; play 6.d4 instead
7623551723116652|f3g5.why: 6.Ng5 loses a knight: the queen on d8 sees g5 along the open diagonal and nothing of White's defends the square, so 6...Qxg5 wins a piece. Black is also threatening 6...Bxe4, since the bishop on g6 is aimed at the pawn on e4. 6.d4 claims the centre and challenges e5, and 7.Nc3 follows to cover e4.
7623551723116652|f3g5.principle: Before landing a piece on a square, count who covers it: g5 is attacked by the queen on d8 and defended by nothing.

7652733641084001|b8c6.headline: Against the Colle, play 3...e6 and keep the c-pawn free
7652733641084001|b8c6.why: 3...Nc6 blocks Black's c-pawn, so the natural ...c5 break against White's centre is off, and after 4.c4 e6 5.Nc3 White fights for d5 with the c-pawn while Black cannot. 3...e6 is the most common reply: it opens the dark-squared bishop and prepares 4...c5, with the queen's knight coming out later.
7652733641084001|b8c6.principle: In queen's pawn games keep the c-pawn free: ...c5 is Black's main way to challenge d4, so develop the queen's knight after it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. e3

7701337958463963|d7d6.headline: Follow 1...e6 with 2...d5 and challenge e4
7701337958463963|d7d6.why: 2...d6 leaves both of White's centre pawns unchallenged: after 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bd3 White develops freely and later gains more space with 7.d5. 2...d5 is the point of 1...e6: it claims the centre and attacks the pawn on e4 at once. 98.8% of masters play it, and however White answers, Black has a share of the centre.
7701337958463963|d7d6.principle: Use the support that 1...e6 gives to put the d-pawn on d5 and challenge e4, instead of settling for a small, passive centre.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. d4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. d4/2...d5

7701337958463963|f8b4.headline: In the French, strike at e4 with 2...d5.
7701337958463963|f8b4.why: 2...Bb4+ achieves nothing: 3.c3 blocks with a useful move that supports d4, and the bishop has to retreat with 3...Be7. Meanwhile White keeps two pawns in the centre. 2...d5, played 99% of the time, challenges e4 at once and threatens ...dxe4. That is the point of 1...e6.
7701337958463963|f8b4.principle: When the opponent builds a two-pawn centre, challenge it with a pawn right away instead of giving a check that can be blocked with gain of time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...e6/2. e4

7739923539884250|b7b6.headline: Answer 5.d4 with 5...c4, not 5...b6: the checks win d5
7739923539884250|b7b6.why: 5...b6 does nothing about 6.dxc5 and loosens the a4-e8 diagonal while your king sits on the open e-file. After 6.Bb5+ Bd7 7.Qe2+ Be7 8.Nxd5 the two checks pin your pieces and the d5 pawn falls. 5...c4 sidesteps 6.dxc5 and keeps your c-pawn, so the d5 pawn is never isolated. White's plan is 6.g3 and 7.Bg2 against d5; you develop with 7...Nf6, block 8.Qe2+ with 8...Be7 and add 9...Nc6.
7739923539884250|b7b6.principle: Look at the opponent's forcing moves first: 6.dxc5, Bb5+ and Qe2+ decide this position before any plan does.

ideas.title: White threatens dxc5
ideas.text: 5.d4 hits c5: 6.dxc5 wins a pawn or leaves your d5 pawn isolated, as in 6...Nf6 7.Bb5+ Nc6.

ideas.title: Checks on e2 and b5
ideas.text: With the e-file open and your king on e8, 6.Bb5+ and 7.Qe2+ pin your pieces, and then d5 falls.

ideas.title: Space with ...c4
ideas.text: 5...c4 keeps your c-pawn out of the swap on d4, so d5 never becomes isolated, and gains queenside space.

ideas.title: White aims at d5
ideas.text: Against 5...c4, White plays 6.g3 and 7.Bg2 to press on d5 down the long diagonal, adding 8.Qe2+.

habit.why: 5...b6 does nothing about 6.dxc5 and loosens the a4-e8 diagonal while your king sits on the open e-file. After 6.Bb5+ Bd7 7.Qe2+ Be7 8.Nxd5 the two checks pin your pieces and the d5 pawn falls.

strays.text: 5...b6 opens the diagonal for 6.Bb5+, and 7.Qe2+ follows on the e-file.

taught.why: 5...c4 sidesteps 6.dxc5 and keeps your c-pawn, so the d5 pawn is never isolated. White's plan is 6.g3 and 7.Bg2 against d5; you develop with 7...Nf6, block 8.Qe2+ with 8...Be7 and add 9...Nc6.

enforces.text: The pawn steps past d4, so it can't be taken and d5 keeps a neighbour.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 5...Nf6 is the masters' most common move (36%), but the engine rates it a mistake: after 6.Bb5+ Nc6 7.O-O Bg4 8.Bg5 both your knights are pinned. Following 9.Bxf6 Bxf6 10.Re1+ your king is checked on the open e-file.
alternatives.after: 5...c4 deals with the c5 pawn first, so White gets no dxc5 and no isolated d5 pawn to aim at. Masters play the two about equally often; the engine clearly prefers 5...c4.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 5...Nc6 develops, but 6.Bb5 pins the knight and 8.Bg5 pins the other one too. In the line 7.O-O Be6 8.Bg5 Be7 9.dxc5 O-O 10.Bxc6 White wins the c5 pawn and splits your pawns.
alternatives.after: 5...c4 removes the c5 target before White's pins arrive, and keeps your c-pawn beside d5.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 5...cxd4 opens the a4-e8 diagonal at once: after 6.Bb5+ Nc6 7.Nxd4 Bd7 8.Nxd5 White wins the isolated d5 pawn.
alternatives.after: 5...c4 keeps your c-pawn on the board, so d5 is not isolated and White's pieces have no easy target.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 5...Be6 guards d5, but after 6.Bb5+ Nc6 7.O-O Nf6 8.Bg5 both knights are pinned. Then 9.dxc5 and 10.Bxc6 win the c5 pawn and split your pawns.
alternatives.after: 5...c4 settles the c5 pawn before White's checks and pins, while 5...Be6 still leaves 6.dxc5 in the air.

7739923539884250|g8f6.headline: 5...Nf6 lets White pin both knights; push 5...c4 first
7739923539884250|g8f6.why: 5...Nf6 leaves 6.dxc5 in the air and lets White develop with checks and pins: 6.Bb5+ Nc6 7.O-O Bg4 8.Bg5 pins both knights. After 9.Bxf6 Bxf6 10.Re1+ your king is checked on the open e-file and d5 is weak. 5...c4 sidesteps 6.dxc5 and keeps your c-pawn, so the d5 pawn is never isolated. White's plan is 6.g3 and 7.Bg2 against d5; you develop with 7...Nf6, block 8.Qe2+ with 8...Be7 and add 9...Nc6.
7739923539884250|g8f6.principle: Deal with pins before they bite: 5...Nf6 walks into 6.Bb5+ and 8.Bg5, which pin both knights while c5 still hangs.

7780638886141553|c2c4.headline: Castle first: 6.O-O guards g2 and tucks your king away
7780638886141553|c2c4.why: 6.c4 hits the queen, but nothing guards c4, so 6...Qxc4 wins a pawn and attacks your knight on e2. After 7.Na3 Qa6 8.Qb3 Nc6 9.Nb5 O-O-O Black is a pawn up, castled, while your king is still in the centre. 6.O-O puts your king on g1, where it guards g2 against ...Qxg2. Then 7.Nd2 covers c4, so 8.c4 Qd6 gains space with tempo on the queen.
7780638886141553|c2c4.principle: Castle before you open the centre, especially when the opponent leads in development.

ideas.title: Castle before opening the centre
ideas.text: Your king is still in the middle and Black is ahead in development. Castle first; open the centre with c4 later.

ideas.title: Guard g2
ideas.text: With the light bishops traded, Black's queen on d5 eyes g2. If you ignore it, 6...Qxg2 7.Rg1 Qxh2 takes two pawns.

ideas.title: Nothing guards c4
ideas.text: c4 attacks the queen, but no white piece covers that square, so 6...Qxc4 takes the pawn and hits your e2 knight.

ideas.title: Develop with tempo on the queen
ideas.text: Once 7.Nd2 covers c4, 8.c4 gains space with tempo on the queen, as in the main line.

habit.why: 6.c4 hits the queen, but nothing guards c4, so 6...Qxc4 wins a pawn and attacks your knight on e2. After 7.Na3 Qa6 8.Qb3 Nc6 9.Nb5 O-O-O Black is a pawn up, castled, while your king is still in the centre.

strays.text: You open the centre while your king is still on e1.

taught.why: 6.O-O puts your king on g1, where it guards g2 against ...Qxg2. Then 7.Nd2 covers c4, so 8.c4 Qd6 gains space with tempo on the queen.

enforces.text: Castling defends g2, and c4 follows once the square is covered.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 6.Nbc3 develops with tempo on the queen but leaves g2 unguarded: 6...Qxg2 7.Rg1 Qh3 wins a pawn, and with the rook gone from h1 you can no longer castle short.
alternatives.after: 6.O-O guards g2 first; masters castle here in 97% of games. The knight can come out later.

7782133965544018|f1c4.headline: Against 2...c6, take the free pawn with 3.Nxe5.
7782133965544018|f1c4.why: 2...c6 leaves the e5 pawn attacked once and not defended at all, and 3.Bc4 lets Black play 3...d5, hitting the bishop and taking the centre at no cost. 3.Nxe5 wins the pawn, and 2...c6 has also taken the c6 square from Black's queen's knight, so there is little compensation. After 3...Nf6 4.Bc4 d5 5.exd5 White keeps developing; the theory warns only that 4.d3 loses to 4...Qa5+, forking king and knight.
7782133965544018|f1c4.principle: After each opponent move, check what was left undefended; an unprotected centre pawn next to your knight is usually a free pawn.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...c6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...c6/3. Nxe5

7803977633029211|c8e6.headline: Guard f7 with 6...Nh6; 6...Be6 loses to 7.Bxe6 fxe6 8.Nxe6
7803977633029211|c8e6.why: 6...Be6 lets White trade on e6: 7.Bxe6 fxe6 8.Nxe6 wins a pawn and forks your queen and the c5 bishop. After 8...Bxf2+ 9.Kf1 Qd7 10.Qg4 your kingside falls apart, as 11.Nxg7+ shows. 6...Nh6 develops your last minor piece and adds a defender to f7. If 7.Qh5 you castle with 7...O-O so the rook guards f7 too, and 8...Na5 and 9...Nxc4 later remove the Italian bishop.
7803977633029211|c8e6.principle: When a knight and bishop both aim at f7, guard it with a developing move before starting your own plans.

ideas.title: White's attack on f7
ideas.text: The g5 knight and c4 bishop both hit f7, and White threatens 7.Qh5 to add the queen.

ideas.title: Guard f7 with a piece
ideas.text: A knight on h6 covers f7, and castling then adds the rook, as in 6...Nh6 7.Qh5 O-O.

ideas.title: Swap off the Italian bishop
ideas.text: Trading White's c4 bishop is a good plan, as 8...Na5 and 9...Nxc4 do in the main line. 6...Be6 fails here: 7.Bxe6 fxe6 lets the knight into e6.

habit.why: 6...Be6 lets White trade on e6: 7.Bxe6 fxe6 8.Nxe6 wins a pawn and forks your queen and the c5 bishop. After 8...Bxf2+ 9.Kf1 Qd7 10.Qg4 your kingside falls apart, as 11.Nxg7+ shows.

strays.text: Here 7...fxe6 opens e6 to the g5 knight, so the trade backfires.

taught.why: 6...Nh6 develops your last minor piece and adds a defender to f7. If 7.Qh5 you castle with 7...O-O so the rook guards f7 too, and 8...Na5 and 9...Nxc4 later remove the Italian bishop.

enforces.text: The knight on h6 covers f7 and clears the way to castle.

7827708463373629|c2c3.headline: Block with 5.Nc3; 5.c3 hands the b2 pawn to the queen
7827708463373629|c2c3.why: 4...Qb4+ checks the king and eyes the pawn on b2. 5.c3 blocks the check but lets 5...Qxb2 take that pawn, and after 6.Nbd2 Qxc3 the queen grabs a second one, so White ends up a pawn down instead of a pawn up. 5.Nc3 blocks with a developing move and keeps the extra pawn: after 5...Qa5 6.Qd5 White offers the queen trade, and after 7.Qxa5 Bxa5 Black's queen can no longer go pawn hunting.
7827708463373629|c2c3.principle: Block a check with a piece you want to develop anyway, not with a pawn move that leaves new targets for the queen.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...e5/2. dxe5

7832135918552384|d2d3.headline: Black gives you the centre: take it with 2.d4
7832135918552384|d2d3.why: 1...g6 is a hypermodern opening: Black allows White a big centre and hopes to undermine it later. 2.d3 declines the offer, and after 2...c5 3.g3 Nc6 4.Bg2 Bg7 Black has an easy, equal game. 2.d4 (95.1% of masters games) puts a second pawn in the centre while Black has not contested it, gains space and opens the way for your pieces; you keep a small edge.
7832135918552384|d2d3.principle: When the opponent lets you build a two-pawn centre, build it: pawns on e4 and d4 take space and give your pieces room before Black can challenge them.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6/2. d4

7832135918552384|f2f4.headline: Take the full centre with 2.d4 when Black allows it
7832135918552384|f2f4.why: 2.f4 doesn't develop anything and leaves d4 unsupported: Black strikes with 2...d5, and after 3.e5 c5 4.d4 cxd4 White has lost a pawn. 1...g6 is a hypermodern move that lets White build a classical centre and hopes to undermine it later. 2.d4, played in 95% of master games, accepts the invitation: two pawns in the centre, more space, and lines open for both bishops.
7832135918552384|f2f4.principle: When your opponent doesn't contest the centre, occupy it with both centre pawns before anything else.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6/2. d4

7839204652261332|f1c4.headline: Against the Caro-Kann, put a second pawn in the centre
7839204652261332|f1c4.why: 1...c6 prepares 2...d5, and 2.Bc4 puts the bishop right where that pawn hits it: after 2...d5 3.exd5 cxd5 it has to move again with 4.Bb3, and Black has swapped the c-pawn for White's central e-pawn. 2.d4, played in 80.5% of master games, takes the two-pawn centre that Black's quiet first move allowed. After 2...d5 3.e5 White gains space and keeps the pawn out of harm's way.
7839204652261332|f1c4.principle: If your opponent's first move doesn't stop d4, claim the centre with pawns first; bishops go out once you know which squares the enemy pawns will hit.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. Bc4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4

7839204652261332|f2f4.headline: Against the Caro-Kann, put the second pawn on d4
7839204652261332|f2f4.why: 2.f4 doesn't defend e4 against 2...d5, and after 3.d3 dxe4 4.dxe4 Qxd1+ 5.Kxd1 the queens are gone and your king has lost the right to castle. 1...c6 neither makes a threat nor controls d4, so 2.d4 builds a two-pawn centre; it is the choice in over 80% of master games. After 2...d5 3.e5 White gains space and Black has to find a home for the bishop with 3...Bf5.
7839204652261332|f2f4.principle: When the opponent's first move doesn't contest d4, occupy it: two centre pawns give your pieces room and take squares from Black's.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4

7896021651424943|f1e2.headline: Against 3...Bg4, open the centre at once with 4.d4.
7896021651424943|f1e2.why: 4.Be2 is too slow: Black answers 4...Nc6 and sets up comfortably with no pressure on e5. The Philidor is a passive defence whose pawn on d6 blocks Black's own bishop, and the main plan against it is the d4 break. 4.d4 strikes at e5 at once; after 4...Nc6 5.Bb5 exd4 6.Qxd4 White's queen is centralised and Black has given up the centre.
7896021651424943|f1e2.principle: When the opponent's setup is passive, open the centre with d4 while your pieces are the more active ones.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6

7902974846795865|b4b5.headline: Play 8.a4 first; 8.b5 sends Black's knight to a5
7902974846795865|b4b5.why: 8.b5 drives the knight to a5, where it hits your c4-bishop, and 9.Nxe5 doesn't help: 9...Qe8 hits the knight at once. After 10.Ng4 Nxg4 11.Qxg4 Nxc4 12.dxc4 d6 Black has your bishop, your c-pawns are doubled and the c8-bishop now hits your queen. 8.a4 gains space and threatens a5 against the b6-bishop, so Black spends 8...a6 on a retreat. After 9.Nbd2 d6 10.Re1 Be6 11.Bxe6 fxe6 you have built up calmly and left Black with doubled e-pawns.
7902974846795865|b4b5.principle: Ask what your push allows: 8.b5 hands the knight a5 with tempo on your bishop, while 8.a4 gains space without a gift.
sources: Souleidis & Müller, Winning with the Slow (but Venomous!) Italian (preview) | https://www.sjakkbutikken.no/media/productimages/preview-winning-with-the-slow-but-venomous-italian.pdf
Chess Life (2002) | https://books.google.com/books?id=XGJLAAAAYAAJ
Nick de Firmian, Modern Chess Openings, 15th ed. | https://books.google.com/books?id=oC3GNWHyrl0C

ideas.title: a4 before b5
ideas.text: a4 gains queenside space and threatens a5 against the b6-bishop. Push b5 only once the a-pawn supports it.

ideas.title: b5 sends the knight to a5
ideas.text: Push b5 too soon and the c6-knight jumps to a5, hitting your c4-bishop; Black can trade it off.

ideas.title: Build up, then d4
ideas.text: Bring the queen's knight via d2 and f1 to g3, and push d4 only after that preparation.

ideas.title: Black trades with ...Be6
ideas.text: Black often plays ...Be6 to trade your c4-bishop; taking on e6 leaves Black with doubled e-pawns.

habit.why: 8.b5 drives the knight to a5, where it hits your c4-bishop, and 9.Nxe5 doesn't help: 9...Qe8 hits the knight at once. After 10.Ng4 Nxg4 11.Qxg4 Nxc4 12.dxc4 d6 Black has your bishop, your c-pawns are doubled and the c8-bishop now hits your queen.

strays.text: Without a4 behind it, the b5-pawn just drives the knight to a5.

taught.why: 8.a4 gains space and threatens a5 against the b6-bishop, so Black spends 8...a6 on a retreat. After 9.Nbd2 d6 10.Re1 Be6 11.Bxe6 fxe6 you have built up calmly and left Black with doubled e-pawns.

enforces.text: a4 gains space and makes Black spend 8...a6 on the bishop.

7908463020324267|b8c6.headline: Hit e4 with 4...Nf6 before White gets in c4
7908463020324267|b8c6.why: 4...Nc6 attacks nothing, so White has time for 5.c4, putting pawns on c4 and e4 that clamp the d5 square. After 5...Nf6 6.Nc3 g6 7.f3 White holds the Maroczy bind and freeing your game with a pawn to d5 becomes very hard. 4...Nf6 attacks e4, so White has no time for 5.c4 and defends with 5.Nc3, which blocks the c-pawn. After 5...a6 6.Be3 e5 7.Nb3 you are in a Najdorf, the choice of 99.5% of masters at move 4.
7908463020324267|b8c6.principle: Develop with threats: 4...Nf6 attacks e4, so White must defend it instead of setting up the Maroczy bind with 5.c4.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4

ideas.title: Hit e4 with ...Nf6 early
ideas.text: 4...Nf6 attacks e4 at once, so White must spend the next move defending it, usually with 5.Nc3.

ideas.title: White wants the Maroczy bind
ideas.text: With pawns on c4 and e4, White clamps d5 and freeing your game with a pawn to d5 becomes very hard.

ideas.title: Nc3 blocks the c-pawn
ideas.text: Once 5.Nc3 guards e4, the knight stands in front of the c-pawn, so the c4 clamp is off for now.

ideas.title: The d5 hole after ...e5
ideas.text: An early ...e5, before ...Nf6 and ...a6, leaves d5 weak and lets the d4 knight jump to f5.

habit.why: 4...Nc6 attacks nothing, so White has time for 5.c4, putting pawns on c4 and e4 that clamp the d5 square. After 5...Nf6 6.Nc3 g6 7.f3 White holds the Maroczy bind and freeing your game with a pawn to d5 becomes very hard.

strays.text: No pressure on e4, so White has a free move for 5.c4.

taught.why: 4...Nf6 attacks e4, so White has no time for 5.c4 and defends with 5.Nc3, which blocks the c-pawn. After 5...a6 6.Be3 e5 7.Nb3 you are in a Najdorf, the choice of 99.5% of masters at move 4.

enforces.text: The knight develops with a threat, and White must spend 5.Nc3 on e4.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4...e5 kicks the knight, but you haven't prepared it: 5.Bb5+ Nd7 6.Nf5 puts the knight on a fine square and d5 becomes a lasting hole.
alternatives.after: 4...Nf6 first makes White commit with 5.Nc3, and then ...e5 comes once ...a6 has covered b5: 5...a6 6.Be3 e5.

7908463020324267|g7g6.headline: Play 4...Nf6 first: 4...g6 leaves e4 alone and White free
7908463020324267|g7g6.why: 4...g6 puts no pressure on e4, so White can choose freely: 5.c4 for the Maroczy bind, or 5.Be3 Nf6 6.Nc3 Nc6 7.f3 and 8.Qd2. That is a Yugoslav Attack setup against the Dragon, with White's pieces placed before you have any counterplay. 4...Nf6 attacks e4, and 5.c4 would just drop the pawn to 5...Nxe4. So White defends with 5.Nc3, blocking the c-pawn, and after 5...a6 6.Be3 e5 7.Nb3 you are in a Najdorf.
7908463020324267|g7g6.principle: Develop with threats: 4...Nf6 attacks e4, so White must defend it instead of choosing a setup freely.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4

strays.text: No threat to e4, so White sets up exactly as it likes.

enforces.text: The knight develops with a threat, and White must spend 5.Nc3 on e4.

7917889477711464|c6d4.headline: Develop the other knight; 4...Nd4 leaves e5 hanging.
7917889477711464|c6d4.why: 4...Nd4 moves the same knight again and stops guarding e5, so 5.Nxe5 wins a pawn, and after 5...Qf6 6.Bxf7+ Kd8 7.Bxg8 White's bishop on c4 also strikes at f7. 4...Nf6 develops a new piece to a good square where it pressures e4, controls d5 and prepares to castle. That calm setup is what the slow Giuoco Pianissimo calls for.
7917889477711464|c6d4.principle: In a quiet opening, bring out the pieces still at home rather than moving a developed piece again and abandoning what it guards.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. d3

7917889477711464|f7f6.headline: Knight to f6: develop and castle, don't play f6
7917889477711464|f7f6.why: 4...f6 takes the king knight's best square and weakens the diagonal from c4 toward g8; after 5.Nh4 g6 6.O-O Black ends up moving the king with ...Kf8 instead of castling. 4...Nf6 develops the knight to a good square where it pressures e4, controls d5 and prepares to castle kingside, and masters choose it in 91.7% of games.
7917889477711464|f7f6.principle: In the quiet Italian, finish developing and castle; a pawn move that blocks a knight and loosens the king costs more than it supports e5.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. d3

7920350690808360|f8c5.headline: Develop with 3...Nf6; 3...Bc5 runs into 4.d4
7920350690808360|f8c5.why: White wants 4.d4 anyway, and 3...Bc5 makes it stronger: the theory notes the pawn takes the centre, gains time on the bishop and opens the c1 bishop to win back the f4 pawn. After 4.d4 Be7 5.Bxf4 the gambit pawn is gone. 3...Nf6, the Schallopp defence, develops and attacks e4; if White pushes 4.e5, the theory recommends 4...Nh5 to keep defending f4.
7920350690808360|f8c5.principle: Don't put a piece where a pawn can attack it with gain of time; develop to squares where your piece attacks something instead.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. f4/2...exf4/3. Nf3

7994400733701852|d7d5.headline: Develop with 3...Nc6 and go after the c4 bishop
7994400733701852|d7d5.why: 3...d5 opens the centre while d5 is hit by the c4-bishop and, after 4.exd5 exd5, by the queen too. 5.Qxd5 wins the pawn and threatens mate on f7, so after 5...Qe7+ 6.Ne2 Nc6 7.Nc3 Be6 8.Qd3 you are simply a pawn down. 3...Nc6 develops and heads for e5, where the knight hits both the queen and the c4-bishop. After 4.Ne2 Ne5 5.Qc3 Nxc4 6.Qxc4 Nf6 you have both bishops and White's queen has moved three times.
7994400733701852|d7d5.principle: Count attackers before you push: d5 is hit by the bishop and, once the e-pawns trade, the queen, so develop with 3...Nc6 instead of losing the pawn to 5.Qxd5.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Bc4

ideas.title: ...Nc6 before ...d5
ideas.text: Develop before you push ...d5. With the c4-bishop and the queen both aiming at d5, an early 3...d5 just drops the pawn.

ideas.title: Hunt the c4 bishop
ideas.text: The bishop is White's best piece. 3...Nc6 and 4...Ne5 hit it and the queen together; ...a6 and ...b5 chase it too.

ideas.title: Queen and bishop aim at d5 and f7
ideas.text: 3.Qf3 joins the c4-bishop: both aim at d5, and the queen also eyes f7. Once the e-pawns are traded, 5.Qxd5 also threatens mate on f7.

habit.why: 3...d5 opens the centre while d5 is hit by the c4-bishop and, after 4.exd5 exd5, by the queen too. 5.Qxd5 wins the pawn and threatens mate on f7, so after 5...Qe7+ 6.Ne2 Nc6 7.Nc3 Be6 8.Qd3 you are simply a pawn down.

strays.text: The pawn goes to d5 before any piece can defend it.

taught.why: 3...Nc6 develops and heads for e5, where the knight hits both the queen and the c4-bishop. After 4.Ne2 Ne5 5.Qc3 Nxc4 6.Qxc4 Nf6 you have both bishops and White's queen has moved three times.

enforces.text: 4...Ne5 attacks queen and bishop, and you trade off the bishop.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3...a6 prepares ...b5 to chase the bishop, as in 4.d3 b5 5.Bb3 Bb7, and it's a sound choice. There is a more forcing one.
alternatives.after: 3...Nc6 goes after the bishop at once: 4...Ne5 hits it and the queen together, and 5...Nxc4 takes it. 3...a6 is also fine, just slower.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3...Nf6 develops and hits e4, so your ...d5 later comes with support, as in 5...d5. It's sound, but after 7.Bb5 and 8.Bxc6+ your c-pawns end up doubled.
alternatives.after: 3...Nc6 heads for e5 to win the bishop. Both moves develop before ...d5 and keep the game level.

8013895061699550|d5d6.headline: Keep the pawn: 7.Qe2 hits e5, don't push 7.d6
8013895061699550|d5d6.why: 7.d6 hands back your extra pawn: 7...Nxd6 takes it back and hits the c4-bishop. After 8.Be2 h6 9.Nf3 e4 10.Ne5 Qe7 Black's pieces chase yours and Black is the one pressing. 7.Qe2 attacks e5 and keeps the d5-pawn, so Black has to defend instead of recovering material. After 7...Nd6 8.Bb3 Be7 9.d3 you stay a pawn up with a solid position.
8013895061699550|d5d6.principle: You took Black's pawn, so consolidate: 7.Qe2 keeps it and makes Black defend, while 7.d6 just gives it back.

ideas.title: Keep the extra pawn
ideas.text: You are a pawn up on d5. Pushing it to d6 gives it back for nothing; keep it and develop.

ideas.title: Qe2 hits e5
ideas.text: 7.Qe2 attacks the e5-pawn, so Black must spend moves defending it instead of winning material back.

ideas.title: Retreat the knight in time
ideas.text: When ...h6 hits the g5-knight, pull it back to f3; after ...e4 it can jump on to e5.

ideas.title: Black gains time on your pieces
ideas.text: Black's knight hits your bishop from d6, and ...h6 and ...e4 drive your knight back; Black wants time, not just the pawn.

habit.why: 7.d6 hands back your extra pawn: 7...Nxd6 takes it back and hits the c4-bishop. After 8.Be2 h6 9.Nf3 e4 10.Ne5 Qe7 Black's pieces chase yours and Black is the one pressing.

strays.text: The push gives the pawn back and develops Black's knight.

taught.why: 7.Qe2 attacks e5 and keeps the d5-pawn, so Black has to defend instead of recovering material. After 7...Nd6 8.Bb3 Be7 9.d3 you stay a pawn up with a solid position.

enforces.text: The queen attacks e5, so Black defends instead of winning the pawn back.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: Castling is natural, but 7...h6 8.Nf3 e4 kicks your knight twice and Black gets active play for the pawn. There is a slightly more useful move.
alternatives.after: 7.Qe2 makes Black deal with e5 first. Nelson's engine check still rates 7.O-O as good for White.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.d4 opens the centre with your king on e1: after 7...exd4 8.O-O Nxd5 9.Re1+ Be7 Black has the pawn back, and you need a wild 10.g4 to keep going.
alternatives.after: 7.Qe2 keeps the centre closed and the d5-pawn guarded, so you never need a gamble like 11.Nxh7.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 7.Qf3 brings the queen out where Black gains time on it: 7...Nd6 hits the bishop, 8.Bd3 Bg4 hits the queen, and after 9.Qg3 h6 Black wins the d5-pawn back with the better game.
alternatives.after: 7.Qe2 also attacks e5, but after 7...Nd6 8.Bb3 the queen is not hit, and you stay a pawn up.
alternatives.idea: Black gains time on your pieces

8021519334015813|d2d3.headline: Take the free e5 pawn: 4.Nxe5 is the main line
8021519334015813|d2d3.why: 4.d3 leaves e5 alone and lets the bishop on b4 pin your knight on c3 to the king, which is what the theory says 3...Bb4 was hoping for; after 4...d5 Black takes over the centre and is slightly better. 4.Nxe5, played in 67% of master games, takes the pawn nothing defends, and e4 is safe for now: if 4...Bxc3 5.dxc3 Nxe4, then 6.Qg4 forks the knight on e4 and the g7 pawn. Black usually gets the pawn back later, as in 5.Be2 Re8 6.Nd3 Bxc3 7.dxc3 Nxe4 8.O-O, but you keep the bishop pair and a small edge.
8021519334015813|d2d3.principle: Count before you capture: e5 has no defender and the knight on c3 covers e4, so the pawn is free unless Black can remove that defender safely.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nc3/3...Bb4

8021519334015813|d2d4.headline: Take 4.Nxe5 first; 4.d4 pins your own knight and drops e4
8021519334015813|d2d4.why: As the theory says, 3...Bb4 threatens to pin your knight as soon as the d-pawn moves. 4.d4 does exactly that, so the knight on c3 can no longer take back on e4: 4...Nxe4 grabs the pawn, and after 5.Qd3 d5 6.dxe5 O-O 7.a3 Bxc3+ 8.bxc3 Re8 Black is better. 4.Nxe5, the main move (67% of master games), takes the free pawn while e4 is still covered; if 4...Bxc3 5.dxc3 Nxe4, then 6.Qg4 forks the knight on e4 and the g7 pawn. Black usually regains the pawn with 4...O-O and 7...Nxe4, but White keeps a small edge.
8021519334015813|d2d4.principle: Before moving the d-pawn, look at the bishop on b4: once d2 is empty your knight on c3 is pinned to the king and stops defending e4.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nc3/3...Bb4

8041898991527130|d1e2.headline: In the exchange French, play 4.d4, not an early queen check
8041898991527130|d1e2.why: 4.Qe2+ brings the queen out with three minor pieces still at home: 4...Be7 blocks the check while developing, the queen shuts in the bishop on f1, and after 5.d4 Nf6 she has to go back with 6.Qd1. 4.d4, chosen in 97.4% of master games, claims the centre and opens the bishop on c1, reaching the exchange French with a free hand for development such as 5.Bd3.
8041898991527130|d1e2.principle: A queen check that the opponent blocks with a developing move only helps the opponent; develop the minor pieces first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. Nf3/2...d5

8076559324931644|b1c3.headline: Punish 2...f6 with 3.Nxe5: the pawn on f6 can't defend e5
8076559324931644|b1c3.why: 2...f6 only seems to defend e5, and 3.Nc3 lets Black get away with it and develop normally. 3.Nxe5 takes the pawn, because 3...fxe5 4.Qh5+ g6 5.Qxe5+ forks the king and the rook on h8. Black's best try is 3...Qe7, and after 4.Nf3 White keeps a big lead in development; don't play 4.Qh5+ there, since 4...g6 leaves the queen with nowhere to go.
8076559324931644|b1c3.principle: Look at captures first and check what forcing reply follows: here the weakened diagonal to Black's king makes the capture safe.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f6/3. Nxe5

8144277447096351|f1c4.headline: Black gave up the c8 bishop: hit b7 with 6.Qb3
8144277447096351|f1c4.why: 6.Bc4 lets Black answer 6...Qf6, and after 7.Qb3 Nd7 8.Qxb7 Rb8 9.Qa6 Qxa6 10.Bxa6 the queens come off and Black's pieces get active, so you keep less of your edge. Theory calls 3...Bg4 dubious, and after 4...Bxf3 Black no longer has the light-squared bishop that guards b7. 6.Qb3 attacks the pawn on b7 at once, before Black's queen can help, and after 6...Nd7 7.Be3 Bc5 8.Bxc5 Nxc5 9.Qb5+ Nd7 10.Qxb7 you win the pawn with queens still on.
8144277447096351|f1c4.principle: When your opponent trades off a bishop, the squares it guarded become weak; aim your pieces at them, here the light squares b7 and f7.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Bg4

8151329472450239|d2d3.headline: Punish the slow 3...g6 by striking at once with 4.d4
8151329472450239|d2d3.why: 3...g6 is slow, with Black's kingside undeveloped and e5 held only by the d6 pawn. 4.d3 lets Black complete the fianchetto with 4...Bg7, and after 5.Ng5 Nh6 f7 is covered and most of White's edge is gone. 4.d4 strikes at e5 before the bishop reaches g7, so Black has to hold it with the queen, 4...Qe7, while White develops with 5.Nc3.
8151329472450239|d2d3.principle: With more pieces out, open the centre right away, before the opponent's slow setup catches up.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4

8153210382746448|f6g4.headline: When 4.e5 attacks your knight, capture with 4...dxe5 instead of retreating.
8153210382746448|f6g4.why: 4...Ng4 saves the knight but sends it toward the edge: 5.h3 Nh6 leaves it badly placed while White develops with 6.Bf4 and 7.Nf3. 4...dxe5 removes the pawn that attacked the knight, and after 5.dxe5 Qxd1+ 6.Nxd1 the knight lands on a central square with 6...Nd5. The queens are off and Black develops smoothly with 7...Bg7 to follow.
8153210382746448|f6g4.principle: When a pawn attacks your developed piece, look first for a capture that removes the attacker rather than spending a move retreating to a worse square.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6/2. d4/2...Nf6/3. Nc3/3...g6

8186436489067117|b5e2.headline: Play 8.d3: free the c1-bishop and keep the pin on c6
8186436489067117|b5e2.why: 8.Be2 moves the bishop again and drops the pin, and 8...h6 leaves the g5-knight short of squares: f3 runs into ...e4, and the c6-knight covers e5. After 9.Nh3 Bxh3 10.gxh3 Qc8 11.d3 Qxh3 Black has the pawn back and your kingside is wrecked. 8.d3 opens the c1-bishop, covers e4 against ...e4 and keeps the b5-bishop pinning c6. If 8...Qd5, 9.Bxc6+ Qxc6 10.O-O Bd6 11.Qf3 and you stay a clean pawn up.
8186436489067117|b5e2.principle: With a pawn in hand, bring out a new piece (8.d3 frees the c1-bishop) instead of moving the b5-bishop a second time.

ideas.title: Keep the extra pawn
ideas.text: You are still a pawn up after 7.dxc6 Nxc6. Develop the rest of your pieces without giving Black time to win it back.

ideas.title: Keep your active bishop
ideas.text: The b5-bishop pins the c6-knight. Moving it again costs time; take on c6 only when that wins time, as after 8...Qd5.

ideas.title: Retreat the knight in time
ideas.text: ...h6 and ...e4 will hit the g5-knight, and with the c6-knight covering e5 it has few good squares.

ideas.title: Black gains time on your pieces
ideas.text: Black wants ...h6 and ...e4 to drive your knight back, and develops with gain of time for the pawn.

habit.why: 8.Be2 moves the bishop again and drops the pin, and 8...h6 leaves the g5-knight short of squares: f3 runs into ...e4, and the c6-knight covers e5. After 9.Nh3 Bxh3 10.gxh3 Qc8 11.d3 Qxh3 Black has the pawn back and your kingside is wrecked.

strays.text: With e5 covered, ...h6 sends your knight to h3, where it gets taken.

taught.why: 8.d3 opens the c1-bishop, covers e4 against ...e4 and keeps the b5-bishop pinning c6. If 8...Qd5, 9.Bxc6+ Qxc6 10.O-O Bd6 11.Qf3 and you stay a clean pawn up.

enforces.text: You develop without weakening anything and stay a clean pawn up.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 8.Qf3 brings the queen out early. After 8...Be7 9.Bxc6+ bxc6 10.O-O O-O Black catches up in development, and your extra pawn counts for little.
alternatives.after: 8.d3 develops a pawn and frees the c1-bishop instead of the queen, so ...Ng4 and ...Be7 don't gain time on anything.
alternatives.idea: Black gains time on your pieces

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: Back to c4 aims at f7 again: after 8...Bc5 9.Bxf7+ Ke7 a sharp fight starts. A calmer move is a little stronger.
alternatives.after: 8.d3 keeps the pin on c6 and the extra pawn without the complications of 9.Bxf7+.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: Castling is fine: after 8...h6 9.Nf3 e4 10.Re1 the rook hits the e-pawn and your knight finds e5. There is a slightly more useful move.
alternatives.after: 8.d3 first covers e4 and frees the c1-bishop, so Black's ...e4 push can't kick your knight.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: Taking on c6 doubles Black's pawns and keeps your extra pawn, but it gives up the pin for nothing yet. Keeping the tension is a little better.
alternatives.after: 8.d3 keeps the choice: you take on c6 only when it wins time, as in 8...Qd5 9.Bxc6+.

8211444126196396|c1f4.headline: 5.e3 props up d4 and opens the f1 bishop toward c4
8211444126196396|c1f4.why: 5.Bf4 does nothing for the pawn on d4 or against the pawn on c4. After 5...a6, White's try to win back c4 with 6.Nd2 takes a defender away from d4 and blocks the queen's guard of it, so 6...Qxd4 picks up a second pawn. 5.e3, the most common master move (36% of 124 games), supports d4 and opens the way for the bishop on f1 to recapture on c4. After 5...b5 6.a4 White attacks Black's queenside at once, the theory's plan for disrupting Black's hold on the c-pawn.
8211444126196396|c1f4.principle: Pick the pawn move that does two jobs: e3 supports the centre pawn and frees the bishop that targets the gambit pawn.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...dxc4/3. Nc3

8224292196866816|b8c6.headline: Support d5 with 3...e6; 3...Nc6 lets White take the centre
8224292196866816|b8c6.why: 3...Nc6 blocks the c-pawn, so after 4.cxd5 Nxd5 Black has no pawn left on d5: 5.Bb5 pins the knight, and 7.Bxc6+ Qxc6 8.e4 lets White take the centre with gain of time on the queen. 3...e6 supports d5 with a pawn, so cxd5 can be answered by a pawn recapture, and it opens the bishop on f8 for development, as in 4.Nc3 Be7.
8224292196866816|b8c6.principle: When White attacks your d5 pawn with c4, support it with a pawn so you keep a foothold in the centre.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5

826798325202564|c2c3.headline: The d4 pawn is undefended: take it with 4.Nxd4
826798325202564|c2c3.why: 4.c3 gives up a pawn that had no defender at all. After 4...dxc3 5.Nxc3 Nc6 6.Be2 d6 7.O-O Nf6 Black has developed calmly and keeps the extra pawn. 4.Nxd4 regains the pawn with a developing move and gives a normal Open Sicilian. After 4...Nc6 5.Nc3 Qc7 6.Be3 a6 7.Qf3 you are in the sharp main-line Taimanov with material level.
826798325202564|c2c3.principle: Loose pawns drop off: nothing guards d4, so 4.Nxd4 takes it back with a developing move instead of gambiting it with 4.c3.
sources: Hannes Langrock, The Modern Morra Gambit (sample) | https://www.newinchess.com/media/wysiwyg/product_pdf/2702.pdf
Semko Semkov, The Taimanov-Scheveningen Hybrid (preview) | https://www.sjakkbutikken.no/media/productimages/preview-the-taimanov-scheveningen-hybrid.pdf

ideas.title: Take back the d4 pawn
ideas.text: Nothing guards d4, and your knight and queen both hit it. 4.Nxd4 wins it back and develops; 99.7% of masters play it.

ideas.title: Morra: pawn for development
ideas.text: After 4.c3 dxc3 5.Nxc3 you're in a Smith-Morra, a pawn down for development. Black answers ...Nc6, ...d6, ...Nf6 and ...Be7 and keeps it.

ideas.title: Queen out, knight hits it
ideas.text: Taking with the queen invites ...Nc6, which attacks it and gains Black a move, as in 4.Qxd4 Nc6 5.Qd1.

habit.why: 4.c3 gives up a pawn that had no defender at all. After 4...dxc3 5.Nxc3 Nc6 6.Be2 d6 7.O-O Nf6 Black has developed calmly and keeps the extra pawn.

strays.text: The undefended pawn was yours for free; now you're a pawn down.

taught.why: 4.Nxd4 regains the pawn with a developing move and gives a normal Open Sicilian. After 4...Nc6 5.Nc3 Qc7 6.Be3 a6 7.Qf3 you are in the sharp main-line Taimanov with material level.

enforces.text: The knight recaptures and develops in one move.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 4.Qxd4 takes the pawn back but brings the queen out early. After 4...Nc6 5.Qd1 it has gone home again, and after 6.Bd3 d5 Black develops freely.
alternatives.after: 4.Nxd4 recaptures with a piece that wants to stand in the centre anyway, so 4...Nc6 gains Black no time.

8290697107627463|f6d5.headline: Trade queens with check, then win the loose e5 pawn
8290697107627463|f6d5.why: 4...Nd5 saves the knight but spends a second move on it, and 5.Bc4 hits it at once, so Black has to prop it up with 5...c6 and 6...e6 while White develops freely. 4...Qxd1+ trades queens with check, so 5.Kxd1 costs White the right to castle. Then 5...Ng4 attacks the e5 pawn, which nothing defends, and after 6.Ke1 Nxe5 Black is a pawn ahead.
8290697107627463|f6d5.principle: Look at checks and captures first: a capture with check removes the threat to your knight and gives you time to attack what is loose.

8290697107627463|f6g4.headline: Trade queens with check first, then take e5 with the knight
8290697107627463|f6g4.why: 4...Ng4 leaves the queens facing each other, so White trades first with 5.Qxd8+ Kxd8 and it is Black's king that loses the right to castle, while the knight has moved twice and 6.Nf3 keeps e5 protected. 4...Qxd1+ captures first with check: after 5.Kxd1 White can no longer castle, and 5...Ng4 6.Ke1 Nxe5 wins the pawn on e5.
8290697107627463|f6g4.principle: When queens face each other on an open file, capture first with check so the opponent's king is the one dragged out of its corner.

8292354532353769|d2d3.headline: Trade on d4 and win the overextended pawn
8292354532353769|d2d3.why: 4.d3 lets Black trade with 4...Nxf3+ 5.Qxf3, so the double knight move becomes a harmless exchange and White's edge is gone. 4.Nxd4 removes the knight instead: after 4...exd4 the pawn on d4 is cut off, and 5.O-O, 6.Re1 and 7.c3 win it with 8.cxd4. Avoid the bait 4.Nxe5, which runs into 4...Qg5.
8292354532353769|d2d3.principle: The opponent's knight trip cost time; trade it off, castle and open the centre while you lead in development.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nd4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nd4/4. Nxd4

8292354532353769|f3e5.headline: Trade with 4.Nxd4; 4.Nxe5 walks into 4...Qg5
8292354532353769|f3e5.why: 4.Nxe5 walks into 4...Qg5, which hits the e5 knight and g2 at once, and saving the knight with 5.Nxf7 loses to 5...Qxg2. After 5.O-O Qxe5 you are a knight down for a pawn. 4.Nxd4 trades off the knight Black moved twice, and after 4...exd4 5.O-O Nf6 6.Re1 d6 7.c3 you go after the d4 pawn. 8.cxd4 wins it and leaves you a pawn up with a lead in development.
8292354532353769|f3e5.principle: When your opponent moves a piece twice to set a trap, don't grab the bait: check what is left loose, trade the piece off and keep your lead.
sources: Modern Chess Openings, 15th ed. (Google Books snippet) | https://www.google.com/books/feeds/volumes?q=%223...Nd4%22+%224.Nxd4%22+%22Qg5%22
Blackburne Shilling Gambit (Wikipedia) | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Game,_Blackburne_Shilling_Gambit

ideas.title: Watch the queen counter-hit
ideas.text: If your knight takes on e5, 4...Qg5 hits it and g2 at once. Saving it with 5.Nxf7 loses to 5...Qxg2.

ideas.title: Punish the twice-moved knight
ideas.text: 3...Nd4 moves a knight twice and leaves e5 bait. 4.Nxd4 trades it off and leaves you ahead in development.

ideas.title: Hit f7 only with a follow-up
ideas.text: After 4.Nxd4 exd4 5.O-O, a careless 5...Bc5 allows 6.Bxf7+ Kxf7 7.Qh5+ and 8.Qxc5+, picking up the loose bishop.

ideas.title: Black wants ...Nxf3+
ideas.text: If your knight stays on f3, 4...Nxf3+ 5.Qxf3 swaps Black's offside knight for your good one.

habit.why: 4.Nxe5 walks into 4...Qg5, which hits the e5 knight and g2 at once, and saving the knight with 5.Nxf7 loses to 5...Qxg2. After 5.O-O Qxe5 you are a knight down for a pawn.

strays.text: The e5 knight is loose, and the queen hits it and g2.

taught.why: 4.Nxd4 trades off the knight Black moved twice, and after 4...exd4 5.O-O Nf6 6.Re1 d6 7.c3 you go after the d4 pawn. 8.cxd4 wins it and leaves you a pawn up with a lead in development.

enforces.text: You trade the knight off on your terms and keep your lead.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4.c3 kicks the knight, but Black just trades with 4...Nxf3+ 5.Qxf3, swapping the offside knight for your good one. After 5...Nf6 6.d4 d6 Black's development problems are gone.
alternatives.after: 4.Nxd4 does the trading on your terms: Black has to take back with a pawn, and 4...exd4 leaves a target on d4. Silman rates 4.c3 good for White, but it lets Black off lightly.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 4.d3 guards e4 but lets Black trade with 4...Nxf3+ 5.Qxf3. After 5...Nf6 6.Be3 d6 7.Nc3 Be7 Black has caught up in development.
alternatives.after: 4.Nxd4 trades the knight before Black can swap it for yours, and the pawn left on d4 becomes a target for 7.c3 and 8.cxd4.

8292354532353769|f3g5.headline: Against 3...Nd4, trade knights with 4.Nxd4; 4.Ng5 drops a piece.
8292354532353769|f3g5.why: 4.Ng5 puts the knight where the queen on d8 can simply take it: 4...Qxg5, and the knight that moved twice is gone. 3...Nd4 is the Blackburne Shilling gambit, a trap that only works if White grabs e5 with 4.Nxe5, and its knight is misplaced. 4.Nxd4 exd4 trades it off and drags Black's pawn away from e5, and after 5.O-O Nf6 6.Re1 White ends up a pawn ahead with 8.cxd4.
8292354532353769|f3g5.principle: Before moving a piece, check whether it lands on a square an enemy piece already covers; g5 is on the diagonal of Black's queen.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nd4

8297553024226585|f3g5.headline: Castle first: 5.O-O, not 5.Ng5
8297553024226585|f3g5.why: 5.Ng5 moves the knight again, but 5...O-O covers f7 with the rook, and grabbing it would give two minor pieces for a rook and pawn. After 6.O-O Na5 7.Nc3 Nxc4 8.dxc4 h6 9.Nf3 Black has the two bishops and your knight is back where it started. 5.O-O gets your king safe and keeps every option for the build-up. After 5...d6 6.a3 O-O 7.Nc3 Bg4 8.h3 Bh5 9.Nd5 your knight takes a strong central square; masters choose 5.O-O 79% of the time.
8297553024226585|f3g5.principle: When Black can simply castle to cover f7, don't move the f3 knight twice: castle and build up.
sources: NM Jeremy Kane, Bad Trades Amateurs Make In Chess | https://www.chess.com/article/view/bad-trades-amateurs-make-in-chess

ideas.title: Ng5 needs a real target
ideas.text: f7 is guarded by the king only until Black castles. After 5...O-O, taking on f7 gives two pieces for a rook and pawn.

ideas.title: Castle, then build slowly
ideas.text: Black's set-up is solid, with nothing to attack yet. Castle, then build up with c3 or the knight to c3, as masters do.

ideas.title: Black: chase the bishop
ideas.text: Black wants to swap off your c4 bishop with ...Na5 and get the two bishops.

ideas.title: Don't move a piece twice
ideas.text: Your b1 knight and c1 bishop are still at home. Moving the f3 knight again gives Black free time.

habit.why: 5.Ng5 moves the knight again, but 5...O-O covers f7 with the rook, and grabbing it would give two minor pieces for a rook and pawn. After 6.O-O Na5 7.Nc3 Nxc4 8.dxc4 h6 9.Nf3 Black has the two bishops and your knight is back where it started.

strays.text: Black castles, f7 is covered, and the knight has to go back.

taught.why: 5.O-O gets your king safe and keeps every option for the build-up. After 5...d6 6.a3 O-O 7.Nc3 Bg4 8.h3 Bh5 9.Nd5 your knight takes a strong central square; masters choose 5.O-O 79% of the time.

enforces.text: King safe first, then the pieces come out.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.Nc3 develops a new piece and is a good move: after 5...d6 6.a4 and Black's 7...Bg4, 8.h3 Bh5 9.Nd5 puts your knight in the centre. Masters prefer another move by far, though.
alternatives.after: 5.O-O is the masters' choice (79%) and often reaches the same set-up, since 7.Nc3 follows in its main line. Castling first just keeps your king safe before play starts.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 5.c3 is the slow Italian set-up, preparing d4 for later. Once you spend a tempo on c3, though, 5...d5 is well timed: after 6.exd5 Nxd5 Black follows with 7...Bg4 and is comfortable.
alternatives.after: 5.O-O keeps the king safe first and doesn't yet invite ...d5; Emms notes that ...d5 is harder to justify before White has spent time on c3.

8308599203837326|e4f5.headline: Answer 3...f5 with 4.d4: hit e5, don't grab on f5
8308599203837326|e4f5.why: 4.exf5 lets 4...e4 kick your knight, and after 5.Nd4 Nf6 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.d4 d5 8.Be2 Bxf5 Black has the pawn back, a big centre and your bishop pushed back. Wikibooks calls 4.exf5 a common beginner mistake. 4.d4 hits e5 before Black is developed: after 4...fxe4 5.Nxe5 d5 6.Bb5 your knight is strong on e5 and the bishop pins c6. Wikipedia rates 4.d4 a clear advantage for White.
8308599203837326|e4f5.principle: When Black loosens the centre with an early ...f5, strike the centre at once with 4.d4 instead of grabbing the pawn.
sources: Tim Harding, Counter Gambits | https://books.google.com/books?id=iJarwg3VQowC

ideas.title: Strike back with d4
ideas.text: ...f5 loosens Black's centre and king. 4.d4 hits e5 at once and opens lines before Black is developed.

ideas.title: Taking on f5 frees Black
ideas.text: After exf5, Black's centre rolls with gain of time: ...e4 kicks your knight and ...Bxf5 later wins the pawn back.

ideas.title: Aim at the loose king
ideas.text: With the f-pawn gone, your c4-bishop eyes g8 and the king's side; Wikibooks says to attack there with this bishop.

ideas.title: Keep the light bishop
ideas.text: Wikibooks warns that trades involving your light-squared bishop help Black: it is your best attacker against the king.

habit.why: 4.exf5 lets 4...e4 kick your knight, and after 5.Nd4 Nf6 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.d4 d5 8.Be2 Bxf5 Black has the pawn back, a big centre and your bishop pushed back. Wikibooks calls 4.exf5 a common beginner mistake.

strays.text: The pawn grab hands Black ...e4 and ...d5 with tempo.

taught.why: 4.d4 hits e5 before Black is developed: after 4...fxe4 5.Nxe5 d5 6.Bb5 your knight is strong on e5 and the bishop pins c6. Wikipedia rates 4.d4 a clear advantage for White.

enforces.text: You attack e5 instead of defending e4.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4.d3 holds e4 solidly and gives a reversed King's Gambit Declined, a good choice. There is a more forcing option.
alternatives.after: 4.d4 asks more of Black: after 4...fxe4 5.Nxe5 Wikibooks calls it an improved Latvian Gambit for White. 4.d3 is a solid second choice, though Black can later push the f-pawn to f4.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 4.Nc3 doesn't hold e4: 4...fxe4 hits your knight, and after 5.Bxg8 exf3 6.Bd5 fxg2 7.Bxg2 Qh4 you are a pawn down with your king's cover gone.
alternatives.after: 4.d4 attacks e5 instead of defending e4, so 4...fxe4 costs Black the e5-pawn: 5.Nxe5.

8341087684859850|g5f7.headline: After 5...Nxd5, 6.Qh5 keeps the attack without giving a piece
8341087684859850|g5f7.why: 6.Nxf7 gives a knight for a pawn: after 6...Kxf7 7.Qf3+ Ke6 Black's king holds in the centre, and White has to keep attacking a piece down with much less of an edge. 5...Nxd5 took the knight away from f6, where it guarded h5, so 6.Qh5 comes in with a mate threat on f7, hit by both the queen and the knight on g5. Black has to weaken with 6...g6, and White keeps the pressure with 7.Qf3 while keeping all the material.
8341087684859850|g5f7.principle: f7 is guarded only by the king; when Black's knight leaves f6 it stops covering h5, so bring the queen there as a second attacker on f7.

8342193165505706|d7d6.headline: Play 4...a6 and keep ...d5 a one-step break
8342193165505706|d7d6.why: 4...d6 is passive: the d-pawn stops on d6, so ...d5 against the bishop now costs a second move. After 5.d4 cxd4 6.Nxd4 Nf6 7.Be3 a6 8.Qe2 Qc7 9.Nxc6 White has a free Open Sicilian with every piece developing easily. 4...a6, the masters' choice in 49% of games, prepares ...b5 against the bishop and keeps ...d5 in reserve. After 5.d4 cxd4 6.Nxd4 Qc7 7.Nxc6 dxc6 8.a4 White spends a move stopping ...b5, and the d-file is open for your rook and queen.
8342193165505706|d7d6.principle: Make only the pawn moves you need: 4...a6 prepares ...b5 against the bishop, while 4...d6 makes the ...d5 break cost an extra move.

ideas.title: Keep ...d5 in one step
ideas.text: With ...e6 played, ...d5 hits the c4-bishop with tempo, as in the Wikibooks line 5.O-O d5. After ...d6 that break takes two moves.

ideas.title: Chase the bishop with ...a6 and ...b5
ideas.text: ...a6 takes b5 away from White's pieces and prepares ...b5 to drive the bishop off its diagonal.

ideas.title: Open Sicilian with Bc4
ideas.text: After 5.d4 cxd4 6.Nxd4 you're in an Open Sicilian against a bishop on c4, where your e6 pawn already blunts it.

habit.why: 4...d6 is passive: the d-pawn stops on d6, so ...d5 against the bishop now costs a second move. After 5.d4 cxd4 6.Nxd4 Nf6 7.Be3 a6 8.Qe2 Qc7 9.Nxc6 White has a free Open Sicilian with every piece developing easily.

strays.text: The d-pawn stops on d6, so ...d5 now costs an extra move.

taught.why: 4...a6, the masters' choice in 49% of games, prepares ...b5 against the bishop and keeps ...d5 in reserve. After 5.d4 cxd4 6.Nxd4 Qc7 7.Nxc6 dxc6 8.a4 White spends a move stopping ...b5, and the d-file is open for your rook and queen.

enforces.text: ...b5 is ready, so White must spend 8.a4 to stop it.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 4...Nf6 develops and prepares ...d5; the Wikibooks and Chessable line 5.O-O d5 6.exd5 exd5 7.Bb3 is comfortable for Black. The engine rates it as good as anything here.
alternatives.after: 4...a6 is the masters' slight favourite (49% to 40%) and keeps ...b5 ready, while 4...Nf6 aims for a quick ...d5. Both are fully sound.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 4...Nge7 blocks your f8-bishop, and after 5.d4 cxd4 6.Nxd4 and 7.Bg5 the knight is pinned to your queen. After 7...Nxd4 8.Qxd4 White's pieces are the more active.
alternatives.after: 4...a6 keeps f6 for the knight and your f8-bishop free, and prepares ...b5 against the bishop.

8358083107211199|g7g6.headline: Hit the knight on e5 while you develop
8358083107211199|g7g6.why: 4...g6 is too slow with a white knight already on e5: after 5.Bc4 White threatens mate on f7, and Black has to answer 5...e6, shutting in the c8 bishop. 4...Nbd7 develops a piece and challenges the knight on e5 at once, so White must spend another move on it; after 5.Nc4 e5 6.Be2 Bc5 Black has a central pawn and active pieces.
8358083107211199|g7g6.principle: When an enemy knight sits in your half of the board, develop a piece that attacks it, so your development gains time instead of losing it.

8378513320650736|e1h1.headline: e4 is hit twice: add a defender with 5.Qe2
8378513320650736|e1h1.why: After 4...Nf6, e4 is attacked twice, by the bishop on b7 and the knight on f6, and defended only by the bishop on d3. 5.O-O ignores this and 5...Nxe4 wins a pawn. 5.Qe2, the most common master move (62.6%), adds a second defender; after 5...d5 6.e5 Nfd7 7.c3 you have a French-style space advantage and a clear edge. 5.Nbd2 also defends, and 5.e5 kicks the knight away.
8378513320650736|e1h1.principle: Each time your opponent adds an attacker to a pawn, count again: two attackers against one defender means you must add a defender or move the pawn before doing anything else.

8399621132422899|b1c3.headline: Start with a centre pawn to free your pieces
8399621132422899|b1c3.why: 1.Nc3 is sensible but blocks the c-pawn, and it doesn't stop 1...d5, which threatens 2...d4 to kick the knight and gain space. 1.e4 claims the centre and opens lines for the queen and the king's bishop at once, and with a pawn on e4 Black can't push a pawn there to chase a knight from f3.
8399621132422899|b1c3.principle: Begin by putting a pawn in the centre: it controls key squares and frees your pieces, while an early knight in front of the c-pawn can be chased.

8399621132422899|e2e3.headline: Start with a centre pawn: 1.e4 claims the centre
8399621132422899|e2e3.why: 1.e3 is not a mistake, but the theory calls it passive: it lets Black take over the centre with ...e5 and ...d5, and the pawn on e3 shuts in your queenside bishop, so White's first-move edge is gone. 1.e4 puts a pawn in the centre, opens lines for the queen and the king's bishop, and keeps a black pawn off e4, so your knight can go to f3 without being kicked. It is the most popular first move at every level (45.5% of master games); 1.d4, 1.Nf3 and 1.c4 are good too.
8399621132422899|e2e3.principle: The opening is a race for development and control of the centre, so the first move should put a pawn on a central square and open lines for your pieces.
sources: Chess Opening Theory

Chess Opening Theory/1. e4

8399621132422899|g2g3.headline: Start with 1.e4: put a pawn in the centre at once
8399621132422899|g2g3.why: 1.g3 doesn't touch the centre; it only prepares to fianchetto the bishop, so Black takes central space for free with 1...e5 and gets an easy game. 1.e4 occupies the centre, controls d5 and f5, and opens lines for the queen and the king's bishop at the same time. It is the most popular first move among masters, played in 45.5% of their games.
8399621132422899|g2g3.principle: On move one, a central pawn move both claims space and frees your pieces, so it does two jobs where a flank pawn move does neither.
sources: Chess Opening Theory

Chess Opening Theory/1. e4

8399621132422899|g2g4.headline: Start with 1.e4: take the centre, not the flank
8399621132422899|g2g4.why: 1.g4, Grob's Attack, is considered one of the worst first moves: it does nothing for the centre and loosens White's kingside, and after 1...d5 Black takes the centre while the g4-pawn becomes a target. 1.e4 controls d5 and f5, opens lines for the queen and the king's bishop, and is the most popular first move at every level, played in 45.5% of master games.
8399621132422899|g2g4.principle: The first moves should fight for the central squares and free your pieces; a flank pawn move does neither.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. g4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4

8425508266792292|f6g4.headline: Take back the bishop on c6 first.
8425508266792292|f6g4.why: The bishop on c6 is attacked twice and defended by nothing, yet 4...Ng4 leaves it there. After 5.Ba4 it escapes and White keeps the knight it captured, and 6.exf5 even adds a pawn. 4...dxc6 wins the bishop back and opens the c8 bishop's diagonal, and Black is fine in the reference line.
8425508266792292|f6g4.principle: After every capture, look first at recapturing: count what attacks the capturing piece before making any other plan.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Nf6

8425508266792292|f8d6.headline: Recapture on c6 before anything else.
8425508266792292|f8d6.why: 4...Bd6 develops but ignores the bishop on c6, which is attacked twice and defended by nothing. After 5.Ba4 the bishop retreats and White stays a whole piece up, and 5...Nxe4 only wins back a pawn. 4...dxc6 takes back the bishop and frees the c8 bishop, so the position is level again.
8425508266792292|f8d6.principle: When the opponent has just captured, recapture before developing; a developing move cannot make up for a missing piece.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Nf6

8432999302569785|c2c3.headline: Recapture with 4.Nxd4 instead of gambiting with 4.c3
8432999302569785|c2c3.why: 4.c3 offers a pawn your knight could take back for free. After 4...dxc3 5.Nxc3 e6 6.Be2 d6 7.O-O Be7 Black finishes developing and keeps the extra pawn. 4.Nxd4 wins the pawn back at once and gives a normal Open Sicilian. After 4...Nf6 5.Nc3 e5 6.Ndb5 d6 7.Nd5 your knight lands on the d5 square that ...e5 left without a pawn guard.
8432999302569785|c2c3.principle: Only gambit a pawn when you get something you couldn't have for free: 4.Nxd4 regains it with a developing move, so 4.c3 just hands Black a pawn.

ideas.title: Take back the d4 pawn
ideas.text: Your knight and queen both hit d4 and only Black's knight guards it. 4.Nxd4 wins it back; 99.8% of masters play it.

ideas.title: Morra: pawn for development
ideas.text: 4.c3 dxc3 5.Nxc3 is a Smith-Morra: a pawn for quick development. Black can calmly answer with ...e6, ...d6 and ...Be7.

ideas.title: Black hits e4 with ...Nf6
ideas.text: After 4.Nxd4, Black's 4...Nf6 attacks e4 at once and makes you play 5.Nc3 before choosing a setup.

ideas.title: The d5 square
ideas.text: After 5...e5 no black pawn can guard d5, and 7.Nd5 plants your knight there.

habit.why: 4.c3 offers a pawn your knight could take back for free. After 4...dxc3 5.Nxc3 e6 6.Be2 d6 7.O-O Be7 Black finishes developing and keeps the extra pawn.

strays.text: 4.c3 gives away a pawn your knight could recapture for nothing.

taught.why: 4.Nxd4 wins the pawn back at once and gives a normal Open Sicilian. After 4...Nf6 5.Nc3 e5 6.Ndb5 d6 7.Nd5 your knight lands on the d5 square that ...e5 left without a pawn guard.

8432999302569785|f1c4.headline: Take the d4 pawn back with 4.Nxd4
8432999302569785|f1c4.why: 4.Bc4 leaves the d4 pawn alone, so you are simply a pawn down. After 4...Nf6 5.Qe2 d5 6.exd5 Nxd5 7.h3 Bf5 8.O-O Ndb4 Black's pieces are out and the knight and bishop both hit c2. 4.Nxd4 wins the pawn back at once and gives a normal Open Sicilian. After 4...Nf6 5.Nc3 e5 6.Ndb5 d6 7.Nd5 your knight lands on the d5 square that ...e5 left without a pawn guard.
8432999302569785|f1c4.principle: Count attackers and defenders: d4 is hit twice and guarded once, so 4.Nxd4 simply wins the pawn back.

843339252523142|d2d4.headline: Kick the b4 knight before opening the centre
843339252523142|d2d4.why: 10.d4 gives Black time: 10...Qf6 hits your queen, and after 11.Qe2 Kd7 12.dxe5 Qg6 13.O-O Kc7 Black's king is safe. The b4 knight still guards d5, so 14.Nxd5+ Nxd5 wins nothing and Black's extra piece counts. 10.a3 hits the b4 knight, and 10...Na6 takes it away from d5. Then 11.Nxd5 cxd5 12.d4 opens the centre, and with d5 pinned, 12...e4 13.Qxe4+ and 14.Qxd5+ win two pawns with check.
843339252523142|d2d4.principle: Your compensation is the exposed king: remove its defenders before opening the centre, or the king walks to safety.

ideas.title: Take off the defenders
ideas.text: 10.a3 drives the b4 knight away from d5, then 11.Nxd5 removes the knight shielding Black's king.

ideas.title: The pin on d5
ideas.text: Your b3 bishop pins d5 to the king on e6. After 11.Nxd5 cxd5 the pinned pawn can't take on e4, so 13.Qxe4+ is safe.

ideas.title: Keep the queens on
ideas.text: Black's king on e6 is what you got for the piece. A queen trade or a slow move lets it walk to safety.

ideas.title: Black's king runs for c7
ideas.text: 10...Qf6 offers a trade, then 11...Kd7 and 13...Kc7 tuck Black's king away on the queenside.

habit.why: 10.d4 gives Black time: 10...Qf6 hits your queen, and after 11.Qe2 Kd7 12.dxe5 Qg6 13.O-O Kc7 Black's king is safe. The b4 knight still guards d5, so 14.Nxd5+ Nxd5 wins nothing and Black's extra piece counts.

strays.text: The b4 knight still guards d5 while Black's king escapes.

taught.why: 10.a3 hits the b4 knight, and 10...Na6 takes it away from d5. Then 11.Nxd5 cxd5 12.d4 opens the centre, and with d5 pinned, 12...e4 13.Qxe4+ and 14.Qxd5+ win two pawns with check.

enforces.text: Kicks the b4 knight first, so d5 falls before you open the centre.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: Castling is slow: 10...Qf6 offers a trade, and after 11.Qd1 Kd7 Black's king heads for safety while the b4 knight still guards d5.
alternatives.after: 10.a3 removes that defender first, so 11.Nxd5 and 12.d4 hit the king while it is still in the centre.

843339252523142|e1h1.headline: Kick the b4 knight first; castling gives Black time
843339252523142|e1h1.why: 10.O-O is slow: 10...Qf6 offers a queen trade, and after 11.Qd1 Kd7 Black's king heads for safety. The b4 knight still guards d5, and even after 12.a3 Na6 13.Bxd5 cxd5 14.Nxd5 Qc6 Black's extra piece counts. 10.a3 hits the b4 knight, and 10...Na6 takes it away from d5. Then 11.Nxd5 cxd5 12.d4 opens the centre, and with d5 pinned, 12...e4 13.Qxe4+ and 14.Qxd5+ win two pawns with check.
843339252523142|e1h1.principle: Your compensation is the exposed king: keep making threats against it, because a quiet move lets it walk to safety.

8455496353401048|c1g5.headline: 7.Ng5 hits f7 now; 7...d5 just drops a pawn
8455496353401048|c1g5.why: 7.Bg5 pins the knight but threatens nothing, so Black answers 7...Be7 8.O-O O-O and f7 is safe. Black keeps the extra pawn and your lead in development is gone. 7.Ng5 threatens to take on f7 with knight or bishop, and Black has no comfortable way to cover it. The best try, 7...d5, loses a pawn to 8.Nxd5, and after 8...Be6 9.Nxe6 fxe6 10.Nxf6+ Qxf6 Black also has doubled e-pawns.
8455496353401048|c1g5.principle: Attack f7 while only Black's king guards it: 7.Ng5 forces the issue before Black can play ...Be7 and castle.

ideas.title: Hit f7 early
ideas.text: After ...e5, f7 is guarded only by the king. Knight on g5 and the c4-bishop threaten it before Black can castle.

ideas.title: Use the d5 hole
ideas.text: With ...e5 played, no black pawn can hold d5. Your e4 pawn, c3-knight and c4-bishop all hit it, so 7...d5 loses a pawn to 8.Nxd5.

ideas.title: Strike before Black castles
ideas.text: Black's king is still on e8. Quiet moves give Black time for ...Be7 and castling, and then f7 is safe.

ideas.title: Black's ...d5 freeing push
ideas.text: Black would like ...d5 to block your c4-bishop and free the game, even at the cost of the extra pawn, as in 7.Qb3 d5.

habit.why: 7.Bg5 pins the knight but threatens nothing, so Black answers 7...Be7 8.O-O O-O and f7 is safe. Black keeps the extra pawn and your lead in development is gone.

strays.text: The pin gives Black time to castle, and the f7 target disappears.

taught.why: 7.Ng5 threatens to take on f7 with knight or bishop, and Black has no comfortable way to cover it. The best try, 7...d5, loses a pawn to 8.Nxd5, and after 8...Be6 9.Nxe6 fxe6 10.Nxf6+ Qxf6 Black also has doubled e-pawns.

enforces.text: Knight and bishop hit f7 together while Black's king is still on e8.

alternatives.label: blunder
alternatives.before: 7.O-O is natural but makes no threat. Black plays 7...Be7 and castles next, and f7 is no longer a target.
alternatives.after: 7.Ng5 uses the move while Black's king is still in the centre; castling first gives Black exactly the time needed to make f7 safe. About a third of club players castle here.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 7.Qb3 eyes f7 and b7, but 7...d5 hands back the pawn to block the c4-bishop. After 8.Nxd5 Bd6 9.Bg5 Qa5+ Black's pieces come out with tempo.
alternatives.after: With 7.Ng5, 7...d5 8.Nxd5 Be6 9.Nxe6 fxe6 leaves Black with doubled e-pawns and no free development; after 7.Qb3 d5 Black develops with checks and threats.

8465086871106005|f1d3.headline: Against the Philidor, strike with 3.d4 before developing the bishop
8465086871106005|f1d3.why: 3.Bd3 blocks White's own d-pawn, so White gives up the d4 break and Black develops at leisure, as in 3...Nf6 4.O-O Be7 5.Re1 O-O. 3.d4 is the main line, played in 88.8% of master games: it attacks e5 again and threatens to crack the centre open, and since the d6-pawn is pinned to the queen, Black can't comfortably recapture after dxe5 and must trade or defend at once.
8465086871106005|f1d3.principle: When Black defends e5 with a pawn, attack it again with your d-pawn before developing pieces that would block it.

8471347538789945|c2c3.headline: 3.c3 doesn't defend e4: develop the bishop to d3
8471347538789945|c2c3.why: 2...Bb7 attacks e4, and 3.c3 is a pawn move that neither develops nor defends it: 3...Bxe4 wins the pawn, and after 4.c4 e6 5.Nc3 Bb7 you have spent two moves on the c-pawn and Black is better. 3.Bd3, the main move (68.7% of masters games), defends e4 and develops a piece at the same time, keeping your edge. 3.Nc3 and 3.Nd2 also defend the pawn.
8471347538789945|c2c3.principle: In the opening, make the pawn moves that free your pieces or hold the centre; a support move like c3 is pointless when a developing move can defend the pawn under attack.

8471347538789945|g1f3.headline: 2...Bb7 attacks e4: defend it with 3.Bd3 before anything else
8471347538789945|g1f3.why: The bishop on b7 hits e4 and nothing defends that pawn, so 3.Nf3 simply drops it to 3...Bxe4 and your clear edge turns into a worse position. 3.Bd3 is the main move (68.7% of masters games): it develops a piece and defends e4 at the same time, so you keep the two-pawn centre and your edge. 3.Nc3 and 3.Nd2 also defend the pawn.
8471347538789945|g1f3.principle: When the opponent's last move creates a threat, stop it first, ideally with a developing move, and only then continue your own plan.

848566465308848|c8e6.headline: After 5.Nxe5, 5...Qd4 forks the knight and the e4 pawn.
848566465308848|c8e6.why: 5...Be6 leaves White simply a pawn up: after 6.d3 the e4 pawn is defended and the chance is gone. 5...Qd4 attacks the knight on e5 and the pawn on e4 at once, and after 6.Nf3 Qxe4+ 7.Qe2 Black has the pawn back. This ...Qd4 fork is the standard answer when White takes on c6 and grabs e5 without first defending e4.
848566465308848|c8e6.principle: After White trades on c6 and takes on e5, check what is undefended: the knight and the e4 pawn can both be hit by one queen move.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Nf6

8493377761529667|g8f6.headline: Challenge the g4 pawn with 2...h5 before putting a knight on f6
8493377761529667|g8f6.why: 2...Nf6 walks into White's plan: the theory notes that 2.Bg2 keeps the g-pawn ready to kick a knight on f6, and after 3.g5 Nh5 the knight sits on the rim and is later taken by 6.Bxh5. 2...h5 attacks the g4 pawn at once. After 3.gxh5 d5 Black takes the centre and White's kingside is left without its g-pawn.
8493377761529667|g8f6.principle: Don't develop a knight where an advancing pawn can kick it; first deal with the pawn that would chase it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. g4/1...e5

853185718049302|d4e5.headline: Keep the tension and develop: 5.Be3, not 5.dxe5
853185718049302|d4e5.why: 5.dxe5 dxe5 releases the tension on Black's terms: the e5 pawn is solid again, Black's bishop gets d6 (6...Bd6), and most of your advantage is gone. Black has made only pawn moves and a queen move, so keep adding pieces with 5.Be3. In the main line 5...Nc6 6.Nc3 Bg4 7.d5 drives the knight back with 7...Nb8, and 8.Nb5 followed by 9.Nxa7 wins a pawn.
853185718049302|d4e5.principle: When the opponent has spent the opening on pawn moves and an early queen, keep developing and let the central tension work for you instead of trading it off.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4

8545457925751746|d2d3.headline: Develop with 4.Nc3; Black's pawn moves have given you time
8545457925751746|d2d3.why: 4.d3 is too slow: 4...d5 hits the bishop on c4, and after 5.exd5 cxd5 6.Bb3 Black has a full pawn centre and the time lost on ...f6 and ...c6 no longer matters. 4.Nc3 develops a piece and adds a guard to d5, so the same break costs Black more: in the line Black needs 5...b5 and 6...b4 to dislodge the knight, more pawn moves, while White strikes in the centre with 8.d4.
8545457925751746|d2d3.principle: Black's ...f6 and ...c6 cost time, so answer with pieces and central breaks while you lead in development, not with quiet pawn moves.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f6

8567362508613525|d2d4.headline: Push 6.a4 at the b6 bishop; 6.d4 drops a pawn
8567362508613525|d2d4.why: 6.d4 exd4 just loses a pawn: taking back with the c-pawn leaves d4 under fire from Black's b6 bishop and c6 knight. In the card's line 7.Qb3 Qe7 8.O-O Nf6 9.a4 a6 10.a5 Ba7 you play on a pawn down with too little for it. 6.a4 threatens a5 against the b6 bishop, so Black spends 6...a6 and later 8...Ba7. Meanwhile you castle, play 8.d3 and 9.Nbd2, and keep a small edge without giving a pawn.
8567362508613525|d2d4.principle: Your b4 and c3 pawns give you queenside space, so play there with a4 instead of opening the centre before your pieces are out.
